[cite:ihra_text] [cite:jda_text] Whatever one concludes about the policy, a platform that adopted one side of a live dispute among credentialed scholars was not simply following expert consensus, because no consensus existed. The full record of the Meta decision, including who pressed for it and who objected, is in [scene:s00a2|the section on the platforms].

A label works by raising the price of a question, and the price has been documented. In 2025 Columbia University lost $400 million in federal funding within four days of a notice from a federal task force, and about 60 more universities received warning letters. Five days after that notice Mahmoud Khalil, a recent Columbia graduate who had negotiated on behalf of the campus protesters, was detained for deportation. Each case has its own record, and that record includes real failures at Columbia: federal investigators found that the university had no reporting system until the summer of 2024, and that swastika vandalism had gone uninvestigated. Taken together, the cases show why many people choose not to ask.

This is the chilling effect that the ACLU and the definition's own drafter warned about. [cite:politifact_aaa_2024] [cite:stern_guardian_2019] Being called antisemitic is a serious charge because antisemitism is a serious hatred, and that seriousness is exactly what gives the label its force when it is aimed at a question about a government. The person asking risks a job, a place at a university, a visa or an online account. Many stop asking, and the version of events they learned in school goes unexamined. The effect is documented as an institutional one, working through rules and penalties. The record does not measure what happens in any individual's mind, and this book makes no claim about that.

What is also true is that antisemitism is real and rising. The Anti-Defamation League counted 9,354 antisemitic incidents in the United States in 2024, the most since it began counting in 1979, with incidents on campuses up 84 percent. [cite:algemeiner_adl_2024] Some speech that calls itself anti-Zionist does cross into hatred of Jews, and even the Jerusalem Declaration, written to defend criticism of Israel, lists examples of it. [cite:jwa_jda] The long history of that hatred, older than the word itself, is told in [scene:ch01_hatred|the section on the hatred]. At the same time, many of the strongest critics of Israeli policy are themselves Jewish. Misusing the charge and ignoring real antisemitism both do damage, to Jews and to everyone asking honest questions.

A common test case is the slogan "Free Palestine," which is often described in public comment as simply code for antisemitism. That claim is an opinion, not a fact about the phrase, and the record of who uses the slogan contradicts it. Jewish organizations such as Jewish Voice for Peace campaign for Palestinian rights; [cite:w_jvp] Orthodox anti-Zionist traditions predate the state; and Israeli human-rights groups such as B'Tselem document the occupation. Some people who use the slogan do express antisemitism, and that is documented too; many do not. The record supports judging speech by its content, not by its slogan.

That leads to the test. Two questions sort almost every case. The first: is the speech aimed at Jewish people, or at what a government does? The second is the definition's own standard: would the criticism be fair if it were aimed at any other country? [cite:ihra_text_safeguard] If it concerns a government's actions, and the same would be said of Canada or Mexico, it is a political question, and asking it is not hatred. If it concerns Jews as a people, holds them responsible for a state, or recycles old tropes, it is antisemitism, whatever it calls itself.

Several things remain unsettled. The record does not decide which of the three definitions is correct; that is a live dispute among credentialed scholars, and the answer to "is anti-Zionism antisemitic?" depends on which one is adopted. It does not measure how many people have stayed silent, or why. Whether the Antisemitism Awareness Act, or a successor, will become law is open as of October 2026. And the sources used here do not record how Mahmoud Khalil's case was resolved.

chapters.label: Chapter 4
chapters.title: Peoples and Traditions
chapters.intro:
The two peoples at the center of this history are not uniform blocs, and the land has never held only two. This chapter describes the communities themselves before the political story begins: their lineages, a long shared history in the Muslim world, the minorities who fit neither side of the usual shorthand, the difference between a religion and a political movement, and the arguments each tradition has had with itself. It comes here because the history that follows is full of statements about "the Jews," "the Arabs" or "the Christians," and the record speaks instead of named institutions, movements and individuals.

It begins with the Jewish lineages, Mizrahi, Sephardi and Ashkenazi, and the genetic record: a 2010 study that compared 14 Jewish communities with 69 other populations, the 2013 test of the Khazar claim, and the recognition of Ethiopia's Beta Israel in 1973 and 1975.[cite:behar_2010_nature] [cite:behar_2013_khazar] [cite:w_ethiopian_jews_israel] A section on coexistence runs from the Babylonian exile of 586 BCE through al-Andalus and the expulsion from Spain in 1492 to the Ottoman millet, weighing the "golden age" and "persecution" readings against each other.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands] The land's other communities follow: the Druze, the Negev Bedouin, the Circassians, the Samaritans and Palestinian Christians. Then comes the distinction between Judaism and Zionism, a movement founded at Basel in August 1897, with the Jewish positions set against it, from Reform's Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 to Satmar's VaYoel Moshe of 1958.[cite:basel_program] [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] [cite:wiki_satmar] A section on dissent shows that opposition to Zionism, and critique of the state, came from every Jewish lineage, and sets a 2025 poll of American Jews beside it.[cite:wapo_jews_poll] The chapter ends with Christians and one verse, Genesis 12:3, read in opposite ways, and with the Vatican, which withheld recognition of Israel until 1993.[cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement]

The strongest case for each position is given in its own terms. What the chapter shows throughout is how much variety the collective words conceal.

sections.h: The Jewish Lineages: Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi
sections.html:
No one seriously disputes that Ashkenazi Jews are Jewish. What is disputed, often loudly and usually online, is where they come from. Two opposite errors circulate. The first holds that Ashkenazi Jews descend from Central Asian Khazar converts and carry no real Middle Eastern ancestry, and therefore no ancestral connection to the land. The second, less often stated but just as often assumed, treats all Jewish communities as genetically and historically identical, as if two thousand years spent in different countries had left no trace. The genetic record supports neither. What it shows is a set of distinct communities, each with its own documented history, sharing a detectable common origin and each carrying the marks of the places where it lived.

The word "Semitic" already names a family larger than any one people. The genealogy of Genesis 10, 11 and 25 runs from Shem through many generations to Abraham, and then divides: Ishmael, traditionally associated with Arab peoples, and, through Isaac, both Esau, traditionally associated with Edom, and Jacob, later renamed Israel.[cite:genesis_10_11_bible] [cite:genesis_25_esau_ishmael] By the text's own family tree, Jacob's line is one branch of Shem's descendants, not the whole of it, a point taken up with the history of the word itself in [scene:s00b|the section on "Semitic"]. The text establishes scope, not rank: it presents all three lines as branches of the same root. The same structure, a shared category holding real internal variety, applies to the Jewish communities themselves.

Three broad lineages make up most of world Jewry. Mizrahi Jews, the Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Egypt, Iran, Syria and elsewhere, never left the Middle East. Their presence there goes back millennia; in Iraq it is traced to the Babylonian Exile of 586 BCE, and as late as 1945 Baghdad alone held roughly 140,000 Jews, about a third of the city.[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday] The Jews of Iran, one of the oldest of these communities, are treated in their own chapter of this library, [scene:ira_src_s16|the Jews of Iran]. Sephardi Jews trace to Iberia, Spain and Portugal, where their roots predate the Muslim conquest. Ferdinand and Isabella expelled them in 1492, and most resettled across the Ottoman Empire and North Africa, regions that already held related Middle Eastern Jewish populations; Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries under Ottoman rule. Ashkenazi communities formed in the Rhineland, in Central Europe, in the early medieval period, and later moved east into Poland, Lithuania, Russia and Ukraine. By the nineteenth century Ashkenazi Jews were the demographic majority of world Jewry, and they produced most of the Jewish immigration to the United States.

These are histories, documented in the ordinary way. The question of what each community carries in its genes is a separate one, and it was answered most thoroughly by a study published in Nature in 2010. Behar, Yunusbayev, Metspalu and eighteen co-authors compared genome-wide data from 14 Jewish communities spanning Europe, the Middle East, North Africa and Central Asia against 69 non-Jewish populations.[cite:behar_2010_nature] This was a large genome-wide analysis, not a study of a single marker or a handful of anecdotes. Its core finding was that most of the Jewish populations examined, Ashkenazi, Sephardi and North African among them, cluster together genetically and share their closest non-Jewish relationships with Middle Eastern populations, more so than with the European or other populations among whom they lived. The authors' own framing was that the data support common origins in the Middle East, followed by migrations into the diaspora.[cite:behar_2010_nature]

The same study found real structure inside that shared origin. The Jewish samples divided into three groups: an Ashkenazi, North African and Sephardi cluster; a Caucasus and Middle Eastern cluster; and a distinct Yemenite cluster.[cite:behar_2010_nature] The result is therefore not that every Jewish community is genetically identical. It is that every community examined carries a detectable shared ancestral signal, with real regional differences layered on top. The study does not by itself settle the size or the timing of particular episodes of admixture, and genetic work of this kind is continually refined by newer data. It is cited here because it remains the most comprehensive genome-wide study of its kind and because its core finding has held up under later attempts to replicate it, not because any single study is beyond revision.

The Khazar hypothesis is a different claim, and it deserves to be stated precisely before it is tested. The Khazars were a Turkic people of the Caucasus and southern Russia whose ruling elite, according to the historical record, converted to Judaism around the eighth or ninth century CE. As a fact about one medieval kingdom's ruling class, that conversion is a real and separately documented event. The hypothesis takes it much further: it proposes that the Ashkenazi population as a whole descends substantially from the Khazars rather than from the ancient Levant. In its modern scientific form the claim was argued in a 2012 paper by the geneticist Eran Elhaik in Genome Biology and Evolution, which proposed a Khazar component in European Jewish ancestry.[cite:adl_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Critics faulted the paper for its method: there are no Khazars to sample, and Elhaik used modern Armenians and Georgians as their stand-ins.[cite:aap_khazar_factcheck]

The test came in 2013. Behar and colleagues, more than twenty co-authors in all, published a study in Human Biology that analyzed 1,774 samples from 106 Jewish and non-Jewish populations, including populations native to the region of the former Khazar Khaganate.[cite:nli_behar_khazar] [cite:behar_2013_khazar] They found no particular similarity between Ashkenazi Jews and the populations of the Caucasus, and in their own words "no indication" of a Khazar genetic contribution. Ashkenazi ancestry, they concluded, derives primarily from the Middle East and Europe.[cite:behar_2013_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Genome-wide and ancient-DNA studies since then have modeled Ashkenazi Jews as a mixture of Levantine and European ancestry. How large each share is remains open; one researcher, cited in a published fact-check, puts the Middle Eastern share at between 15 and 50 per cent.[cite:nli_behar_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck]

What is European in Ashkenazi ancestry is real, documented and partial. The European contribution is substantial, and it shows most clearly on the maternal line, reflecting some two thousand years of intermarriage and conversion within European societies. The same studies document a shared ancient Levantine origin on the paternal line, and the two findings sit side by side: the European layer is part of the history, not a replacement for the older one. There is no contradiction between them, only a contradiction between the data and either of the two errors with which this section began.

The Khazar theory is addressed directly here because of what it has been used to do. Since the nineteenth century it has served antisemitic arguments that portray Jews as alien impostors with no genuine connection to the Land of Israel, and so as not "really" Jewish or Semitic at all.[cite:jewishpress_khazar] [cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] Viral claims built on it continue to appear and continue to fail. One widely shared post asserted that a study had proved 97.5 per cent of Israeli Jews have no ties to the land; fact-checkers rated it false, noting that the study in question included no Israeli Jews.[cite:aap_khazar_factcheck] The finding that the Ashkenazi population as a whole is not primarily of Khazar descent does not deny that the Khazar elite converted, and it does not settle every question about European admixture. What it settles is the specific claim, which does not hold when tested.

That claim returned to a large audience in February 2026. On 19 and 20 February, Tucker Carlson interviewed the United States Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, and asked: "Why don't we do genetic testing on everybody in the land and find out who Abram's descendants are? It's really simple. We've cracked the human genome. We can do that." He went on to single out Netanyahu, citing his family's Polish origin.[cite:jta_carlson_khazar_2026] [cite:toi_carlson_khazar_2026] Huckabee, a committed Christian Zionist rather than a reflexive critic of Carlson, pushed back in the room, calling the idea a "dangerous conspiracy theory" from "some of the darkest realms of the internet." Reporters at JTA, the Times of Israel, the Jerusalem Post and the Forward identified the underlying claim as the Khazar theory: the premise that Eastern European ancestry among some Israeli Jews would undo their connection to the land.[cite:jta_carlson_khazar_2026] [cite:toi_carlson_khazar_2026] That identification was the reporters' own, made independently across outlets.

The exchange also raised a separate and more general question, which should be kept apart from the discredited one. What share of ancestry would make any identity claim, or any claim to land, "legitimate"? No geneticist, historian, court or international convention has ever defined such a threshold, for this question or for any other claim based on ancestry anywhere in the world. That is not a gap in the research. Ancestry percentages have never been the legal or historical basis on which such claims rest: treaties, borders and citizenship laws do not run on DNA, for Israel or for any other state. Collapsing the open philosophical question into the tested genetic claim is one of the ways the discredited version gets carried back into argument.

An analogy, offered as an analogy and not as a genetic argument, may help with the teaching gap underneath all this. Many people are taught that "Jewish" and "Semitic" are simple synonyms, and few are taught that Jewish identity itself contains several lineages with different histories. A Salvadoran, a Mexican and a Peruvian are all Latino, while each carries a different mix of Indigenous American, Spanish colonial and other ancestry, varying by country and family. No one is less Latino for having a different mix. In the same structural sense, Mizrahi Jews carry concentrated, continuous Levantine ancestry, and Ashkenazi Jews carry that same documented root together with substantial European admixture. The comparison borrows one idea, that a shared category can hold real internal variety, and nothing more; Jewish and Latino identities have entirely different histories, religious and genetic.

The Beta Israel of Ethiopia show that the question of who counts as a Jew has also been settled, in practice, by institutions rather than by genes. The Beta Israel, the "House of Israel," lived for centuries in the Gondar and Tigray regions of northern Ethiopia and practiced a Judaism distinct from rabbinic tradition.[cite:w_beta_israel] The familiar account holds that Israel always welcomed them as Jews. The record is slower and more conditional. Their status was disputed by Israel's religious authorities until 1973, when the Sephardi Chief Rabbi, Ovadia Yosef, ruled that they were Jews. The government applied the Law of Return to them in 1975, which made them eligible to immigrate.[cite:w_ethiopian_jews_israel] Even then, in 1985, the chief rabbinate required a symbolic conversion ritual before it accepted them fully.[cite:moment_failing] By the end of 2019 about 155,300 Ethiopian Jews lived in Israel.[cite:w_beta_israel]

The sequence shows where the power to decide lay. A religious ruling by one chief rabbi opened the door; a government decision under the Law of Return turned that ruling into a right to immigrate; and the chief rabbinate still imposed a further condition of its own twelve years after the ruling. The terms of the Law of Return itself are set out in [scene:ch01_citizenship|the section on citizenship]. The record available here does not explain why recognition took until 1973, or how the 1985 requirement was received within the community and how long it lasted; those questions remain open in this account.

Two points of discipline follow from all of this, and they apply in every direction. Genetics does not determine anyone's political rights, Jewish, Palestinian or any other. And the case against any state policy examined in this library never depends on the ancestry of the people who carry it out. A documented argument about policy stands on documents. Claims about the ancestry of Jews or of Palestinians add nothing to it, and in the Khazar case they are also false.

What the record leaves unsettled is real but narrow. The size and timing of particular admixture events in Ashkenazi ancestry are still being refined, and estimates of the Middle Eastern share vary widely. The genetic studies measure ancestry; they do not decide identity, which in the case of the Beta Israel was decided by a rabbinic ruling and a government decision. What is settled is that the Jewish lineages share a detectable Middle Eastern origin, that each also carries its own regional history, and that the claim of wholesale Khazar descent was tested and did not hold.

sections.h: Jews in the Muslim World: Coexistence Without Utopia
sections.html:
For more than a thousand years, Jewish communities lived across the Muslim-majority Middle East and North Africa: in Baghdad, Cairo, Damascus, Aleppo, Sana'a, Fez, Tunis and Casablanca. In some of these cities they formed a plurality or even a majority. A common claim holds that Jews and Arabs never lived together in peace, and that an ancient, irreconcilable hatred is the natural and permanent state between them. The documented record does not fit that frame. Neither does the opposite picture of an unbroken harmony. What the record shows is a long, uneven coexistence: real violence, and real legal inequality, alongside intellectual, commercial and civic collaboration on a scale that, in the judgment of the historians cited below, Christian Europe of the same period did not match. How that coexistence ended, between 1941 and 1972, is a separate and grave story, told in [scene:s00e2|the section on the exodus from the Arab world].

The oldest of these communities is older than Islam, older than Arab rule in the region and older than either modern state that now claims part of its story. In 586 BCE Babylon destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem, conquered Judah and deported its population to Mesopotamia, the land that is now Iraq.[cite:huc_farhud] The exiles took root and stayed. Over the following centuries the community became one of the great centers of Jewish religious and intellectual life, and between roughly the third and sixth centuries CE its scholars compiled the Babylonian Talmud, a foundational work of Jewish law that is still the primary text of rabbinic study, nearly 1,500 years after it was compiled in what is now Iraq.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:ushmm_farhud] One of the two foundational texts of rabbinic Judaism was produced there, not in the land of Israel. Popular accounts often begin this relationship in 1948, as if it started with modern statehood. Historical and religious sources agree, without dispute, on continuous Jewish presence in Mesopotamia from the sixth century BCE, more than a thousand years before the Muslim conquest of the region, and long before the Iraqi state of 1932 or the Israeli state of 1948.[cite:huc_farhud] [cite:ushmm_farhud]

That community was still large in the twentieth century. Sasson Somekh, born a Jew in Baghdad and later a professor of Arabic literature at Tel Aviv University, documents its scale in his memoir Baghdad, Yesterday (2007).[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday] The figures vary by year and by source. One account gives 140,000 Jews in 1917, about 40 per cent of Baghdad's civilian population; another gives roughly 140,000 in 1945, about a third of the city; a more cautious reckoning puts the mid-century community at 90,000 to 140,000, depending on the year and the source, but in every version close to a third of the city. Jews formed much of the commercial, banking and professional life of modern Iraq. Trading families such as the Sassoons, the Kadoories and the Basris built networks that reached across the region, into British India and across the British Empire. Iraq's first finance minister, Sassoon Heskel, was Jewish, and the community's chief rabbis served as advisers to the government. In 1917 the community welcomed the arriving British forces.[cite:somekh_baghdad_yesterday] This was not a marginal sect. It was a city community as old as Jewish life in Europe, integrated into the economy and the state. Its place in the new kingdom under Faisal is told in [scene:irq_e02|Faisal's Iraq].

The best-known chapter of this history is al-Andalus, Muslim Iberia, home to what is called the Jewish Golden Age of the tenth to twelfth centuries. Its figures include Maimonides (born in Córdoba, 1135–1204), Judah Halevi (of Toledo and Córdoba), Solomon ibn Gabirol and Samuel HaNagid. Jewish scholars wrote philosophy in Arabic, held the office of vizier and produced foundational works of rabbinic literature.[cite:menocal_ornament] The term usually attached to this period, convivencia, "living together," is contested precisely because the period was not utopian. In 1066 a pogrom struck the Jews of Granada. The historians on whom this account relies, María Rosa Menocal, David Nirenberg and Mark Cohen, do not deny such violence. Their work nonetheless documents a substantial period of Jewish and Muslim intellectual and civic collaboration that, they argue, had no parallel in Christian Europe of the same period.[cite:menocal_ornament]

The Iberian story ended in Christian hands. In 1492 the Catholic monarchs, Ferdinand and Isabella, ordered Spain's Jews to convert or leave; historians estimate that at least 200,000 people were affected. The Ottoman sultan, Bayezid II, opened his territories to receive the exiles, and Salonika became a majority-Sephardic city for centuries.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands] The expulsion's long afterlife reached into the present. Spain established diplomatic relations with Israel only on 17 January 1986, the last Western European state to do so, as a condition of joining the European Community, while pledging continued "friendship and solidarity" with the Arab world; in 1948, according to reports, Franco had sought relations and Ben-Gurion had refused because of Franco's ties to Nazi Germany.[cite:israeled_spain_1986] Spain hosted the Madrid peace conference of 1991. In 2015 the Spanish parliament passed a law offering citizenship to descendants of the expelled Sephardim, to repair what it called a "historical mistake." By the 2019 deadline 132,226 people had applied, most of them from Latin America: about 20,000 from Mexico, the largest single group, followed by applicants from Venezuela and Colombia.[cite:euronews_sephardic] [cite:yahoo_sephardic_close] Less than a decade later, on 28 May 2024, Spain, with Ireland and Norway, recognized the State of Palestine on the pre-1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital. Israel recalled its ambassador, and its foreign minister said the three states were rewarding Hamas.[cite:catalannews_spain_recognition] [cite:wiki_palestine_spain] Pro-Israel commentators read Spain's position as hostility with historical echoes; the Spanish government presents it as support for a two-state solution and for international law. Both acts, the atonement of 2015 and the recognition of 2024, are documented, and reading either as cancelling the other misses the record.

The Ottoman Empire, which lasted from 1299 to 1922, a span of 623 years, gave this coexistence its most durable legal form. It organized its non-Muslim subjects through the millet system, under which each religious community governed itself under its own leaders in matters of law, education and religion. The Chief Rabbi of Istanbul was responsible for all Ottoman Jews. Jewish communities lived under this arrangement in Istanbul, İzmir, Salonika, Damascus, Aleppo, Baghdad, Cairo and Jerusalem. The system was not one of equality: Jews held the status of dhimmi, protected non-Muslims, paid the jizya tax and lived under legal restrictions that did not apply to Muslims. It was also not the persecution of the Nazi regime or of imperial Russia. For four centuries after 1492 it framed daily civic life, and it produced Sephardi and Mizrahi literature and the mystical school of Safed, the Kabbalah associated with Isaac Luria and Joseph Caro. Norman Stillman's The Jews of Arab Lands is the standard documentary sourcebook for this history.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands]

The mechanism matters for reading this history fairly. Under the millet, a Jewish community could run its own courts, schools and religious life; it could not stand as an equal of Muslims before the state, and it paid for its protection through a special tax. That is why the same arrangement can be described, accurately, as both tolerant and unequal.

Historians divide over how to weigh this record, and both readings rest on evidence. The first, sometimes called the "golden age" reading, stresses the length and depth of the collaboration: Jewish philosophers writing in Arabic, Jewish viziers in Muslim courts, the Talmud compiled in Mesopotamia, the Ottoman welcome of 1492, and Baghdad's community still a third of the city in the twentieth century. In its strongest form it argues, with Menocal, Nirenberg and Cohen, that nothing comparable existed in Christian Europe at the same time, and that a hatred described as ancient and permanent cannot explain a millennium of shared life. The second reading stresses the limits and the ruptures: dhimmi status as a permanent legal subordination, the jizya, the restrictions, and violence such as the Granada pogrom of 1066. In its strongest form it warns that the golden-age image can idealize what was, in law, a hierarchy. The record supports both sets of facts. It does not support either extreme: not "harmonious coexistence, full stop," and not a story of unbroken persecution.

The twentieth century shows both forces at work in a single community. In Baghdad in June 1941, seven years before Israel's founding, a pogrom known as the Farhud killed an estimated 180 or more Jewish residents. Nazi-inspired, it came during the political turmoil of a short-lived pro-Axis coup, during the Anglo-Iraqi War, and was encouraged by pro-Axis Iraqi elements.[cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:huc_farhud] After 1948 came further legal restrictions, confiscations of property and violence; at the same time, the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency actively encouraged and organized emigration. Both forces are documented, and neither explains the exodus without the other. The same holds across the region. The departure of some 850,000 Jews from Arab lands between 1948 and the 1970s had several documented causes, not one: rising tension after 1948 with the Arab-Israeli conflict; the criminalization of Zionism in many Arab states, a political rather than a religious prohibition; active expropriation and expulsion in some places, Iraq in 1950–51, Egypt after 1956 and Libya after 1969; and active Zionist encouragement of emigration in others, as in the airlifts from Yemen in 1949–50 and from Iraq in 1951. The Israeli historian Tom Segev and the Palestinian historian Rashid Khalidi both document that complexity.[cite:segev_seventh_million] [cite:khalidi_hundred_years] Neither "all expelled at once" nor "all left of their own accord" survives it. The mass departure of 1950–51 followed. The community had numbered about 140,000; in the end it numbered none, and a presence of some twenty-five centuries had ended within a single decade. The full account, including its disputed episodes, belongs to the section on the exodus. Its sequel in Israel belongs there too, though one point should be recorded here: the scholar Ella Shohat has documented the second-class treatment of Iraqi Jews after their arrival, a displacement upon a displacement.[cite:shohat_sephardim_israel]

Several things remain unsettled. The figures for Baghdad's Jewish population differ by source and by year, and the record here cannot reconcile 40 per cent of the city in 1917 with a third in 1945 beyond noting that the counts and their bases differ. The toll of the Granada pogrom of 1066 is not given in the sources used here. The comparison with Christian Europe is a judgment by named historians, well supported, but a judgment all the same. And the balance between persecution and recruitment in the Iraqi exodus remains a matter of genuine dispute. What the record does establish is narrower and firmer: Jewish life in the Muslim world was long, large and productive; it was never free of inequality or violence; and the frame of an ancient, irreconcilable hatred does not describe it. The hostility of the twentieth century had dates and causes, and it is in those dates and causes, not in a supposed permanent enmity, that the history of the break has to be sought.

sections.h: The Land's Other Communities
sections.html:
A common shorthand presents the conflict as Jews against Muslims, and Palestinians as uniformly Muslim. The land's population has never fitted that frame. Alongside its Jewish and Muslim Arab majorities it holds Druze, whose faith is neither Jewish nor mainstream Muslim; Bedouin, Muslim Arabs whose relationship with the state turns on land; Circassians, Muslims from the Caucasus who serve in Israel's army; Samaritans, a community of a few hundred who trace their descent to ancient Israel; and Palestinian Christians, members of some of the oldest Christian communities on earth. Each stands in a different relationship to the State of Israel, and those differences are documented in law, in census figures and in the record of demolitions and conscription. The legal situations of Palestinians in general, and the numbers of Arab citizens of Israel as a whole, are set out earlier in this volume [scene:pr_s02|who the Palestinians are in law].

The Druze. The Druze faith took shape in the Middle Ages and has accepted no converts since the eleventh century [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze]. According to Minority Rights Group, about 150,000 Druze live in Israel proper, in eighteen villages, and about 24,000 to 25,000 more in the Golan Heights [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze]. Central Bureau of Statistics figures reported in April 2024 give a slightly higher total for Israel, about 152,000, against 14,500 in 1949; the largest Druze localities at the end of 2022 were Daliyat al-Karmel and Yarka, each with more than 17,000 people [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze].

The Druze relationship with the state was set early. Druze in Galilee and on Mount Carmel fought alongside the Jewish forces in 1948. In 1956 Druze men were included in military conscription, and in 1961 separate Druze religious courts were established [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_druze] [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze]. Those two instruments, conscription and a separate court system, gave the Druze a legal relationship with the state distinct from that of other Arabic-speaking communities. The Golan Druze followed a different course. After Israel captured the Golan Heights in 1967 it offered citizenship to the Druze living there, and, according to the same April 2024 report, most refused [cite:rs_ch01_tps_druze]. The sources used here do not say how many have since accepted, or whether Golan Druze who did not take citizenship are subject to the draft.

The Circassians. Israel's Circassians are Muslims whose origins lie in the Caucasus. They live mainly in two Galilee villages: Kfar Kama, with about 2,000 people of the Shapsug group, and Rehaniya, with about 1,000 of the Abadzakh group. According to a community-sourced account, they were settled there at the Ottoman Sultan's request in the late nineteenth century, and Circassian men serve in the army and the police [cite:rs_ch01_mjl_circassians]. That account rests on a single source drawn from a Circassian foundation, and it does not settle when and why the families left the Caucasus; this book does not go beyond what it states.

The Negev Bedouin. The largest of these communities, and the one whose position is most contested, is the Bedouin of the Negev. About 92,000 Bedouin lived in the Negev before 1948. After the war about 11,000 remained inside Israel, from 19 of the original 95 tribes, according to Minority Rights Group and the Israeli-Arab legal center Adalah [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin]. Those who stayed were concentrated in an area known as the siyag, Arabic for "fence," of about 1.5 million dunams, against some 13 million dunams they had used before [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

The legal mechanism that followed ran through two statutes. The Land Acquisition Law of 1953 and the Planning and Building Law of 1965 registered much of the Bedouin's land as state land [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. The effect was to place the power to decide where Bedouin could lawfully live with the state's planning authorities. From the 1960s the state built seven planned townships, beginning with Tel Sheva, Rahat and Kseifa [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Villages outside the townships and outside the state's plans were left "unrecognized": without legal standing as settlements, and with their buildings treated in official policy as illegal construction on state land. Israel does not recognize the Bedouin as an indigenous people [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Just over 300,000 Bedouin live in Israel today, about 3% of the population [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

Recognition has moved slowly. The Association for Civil Rights in Israel counted 46 unrecognized Bedouin villages in the Negev, of which the state had recognized 11 by about 2011, leaving 35. The same organization recorded 275 buildings demolished in 2010 and 1,000 in 2011 [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin]. The demolitions have continued. In May 2024 Israeli authorities demolished about 47 to 50 homes in the unrecognized village of Wadi al-Khalil; National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called the buildings illegal constructions and the demolition "an important step" [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin].

Even the number of people affected is disputed. Minority Rights Group puts the population of the unrecognized villages at about 100,000 people in roughly 35 villages [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. Adalah, as reported by Al-Monitor in May 2024, puts it at about half of some 300,000 Negev Bedouin, which is about 150,000 [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin]. An ACRI fact sheet from about 2011 gave about 70,000 [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin]. The figures come from different years and partly from advocacy organizations, and the sources do not explain the gap between them. Note also that Adalah's base of some 300,000 refers to the Negev Bedouin, while Minority Rights Group's figure of just over 300,000 refers to the Bedouin of Israel as a whole.

Behind the numbers lies a deeper disagreement over what the villages are. The state and its ministers treat construction in unrecognized villages as illegal building on state land, which is the basis on which demolition orders are issued and on which Ben-Gvir defended Wadi al-Khalil [cite:rs_ch01_almonitor_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. On that view, the law is the 1953 and 1965 statutes, the land is registered to the state, and the townships are the lawful alternative the state has provided. Bedouin and rights groups answer that the villages either predate the state or were placed where they stand by the state itself, and that 35 of them meet every Central Bureau of Statistics test for a settlement except the minister's declaration [cite:rs_ch01_acri_bedouin] [cite:rs_ch01_mrg_bedouin]. On that view, the illegality is a product of the land registration rather than of anything the residents did, and the Bedouin are a dispossessed indigenous people rather than squatters. The two positions do not disagree about what the statutes say. They disagree about whether the statutes' allocation of the land was just.

The Samaritans. The smallest of these communities has the longest claimed history. The Samaritans hold that they descend from Israelites who escaped the Assyrian deportation after 722/721 BCE. They keep their own version of the Pentateuch and hold Mount Gerizim sacred; their temple there was destroyed by John Hyrcanus in 128 BCE [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans]. By 1917 the community had fallen to a low of 146 people. In January 2003 it numbered 654: 349 in Holon, inside Israel, and 305 at Kiryat Luza on Mount Gerizim near Nablus [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans]. The Oslo arrangements placed the Nablus community under Palestinian administration, so that a single community of a few hundred people now lives on both sides of the lines described at the start of this volume [cite:rs_ch01_ency_samaritans].

Palestinian Christians. Palestinians include one of the world's oldest Christian communities. In the early twentieth century Christians were about 12% of Palestine's population. According to the 2017 census, fewer than 50,000 live in the West Bank and East Jerusalem today, between 47,000 and 50,000, or about 1% of the population; most are concentrated in Bethlehem, Ramallah and East Jerusalem [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025] [cite:noonpost_christians]. Gaza's Christians fell from about 3,000 in the early 2000s to about 1,000 before October 2023, and to a few hundred since [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025] [cite:noonpost_christians]. The decline is attributed to war, displacement and economic hardship [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025].

The war since October 2023 reached them directly. On 17 July 2025 an Israeli tank shell struck the compound of the Holy Family Church, Gaza's only Catholic parish, where about 600 Christians and Muslims had taken shelter. Three people were killed and the parish priest was wounded [cite:persecution_holyfamily]. Pope Leo XIV said he was deeply saddened and called for a ceasefire. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that Israel "deeply regrets" that "stray ammunition" had hit the church, and that the incident was being investigated [cite:persecution_holyfamily] [cite:lorient_pope_holyfamily]. The same month, in the West Bank, arsonists targeted the area of the ancient church of St George in Taybeh, the last all-Christian town there, in what the reporting describes as settler arson [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025]. Munther Isaac, the Lutheran pastor in Bethlehem, has warned that Palestinian Christians risk disappearing from the Holy Land [cite:aljazeera_christians_2025]. Palestinian Christians live under the same occupation and the same war as their Muslim neighbors, and their presence alone is enough to show that "Jews against Muslims" does not describe the conflict. Their fuller story belongs to a later volume [scene:pc_s03|Palestinian Christians, 1900s–2025].

What the record does not settle. Several questions remain open on the sources used here. How many people live in the Negev's unrecognized villages is disputed, with estimates from about 70,000 to about 150,000, and no source explains the gap. Whether those villages are illegal construction on state land or the homes of a dispossessed indigenous people is a question of how the land was allocated after 1948, on which the state and the Bedouin and their advocates disagree. The Druze figures differ slightly between Minority Rights Group's 150,000 and the Central Bureau of Statistics' 152,000. The Circassian account rests on one community-derived source and does not establish when or why the families left the Caucasus. The fate of the Golan Druze offer of citizenship after the first refusals is not covered here. And the figures for Palestinian Christians are drawn from news reporting that cites the 2017 census rather than from the census itself.

sections.h: Zionism and Judaism: A Movement and a Religion
sections.html:
Judaism is a religion and a set of ethnic and cultural lineages thousands of years old. Zionism is a political movement with a place and a date of birth: Basel, Switzerland, in August 1897, convened by Theodor Herzl, a secular journalist from Vienna [cite:basel_program]. The two are often spoken of as one thing, so that opposing the movement is taken to mean opposing a people. The documents of the period do not support that equation. The line between the religion and the movement was drawn by Jews themselves: by the movement's founder in his own diary, by the largest American Jewish denomination twelve years before the movement existed, by a mass Jewish labor party founded the same year, by a cultural Zionist who warned against the political version, and by the largest Hasidic dynasty in the world, which still teaches its position today.

That the line exists does not settle every argument built on top of it. Many Jews, religious and secular, have understood and still understand their support for Zionism as part of their Jewish identity, and nothing in this record shows them wrong to do so. What the record settles is narrower: the distinction between the religion and the political project was not invented by outside critics. It was argued inside Jewish life from the start.

Herzl's founding. Herzl was not a rabbi or a religious scholar. He was an assimilated Viennese Jew, secular in outlook, a correspondent for the Neue Freie Presse, whose turn to politics was a response to the antisemitism he witnessed while covering the Dreyfus Affair. He set out his program in Der Judenstaat in 1896 and convened the First Zionist Congress in Basel from 29 to 31 August 1897 [cite:herzl_judenstaat] [cite:wiki_zionist_congress]. Afterward he wrote in his diary: "At Basel I founded the Jewish State." The verb was his, written privately rather than for public consumption, and it describes a beginning: a political project that, in his own account, had not existed as such before Basel [cite:herzl_diaries].

The same diary shows that the territory was not fixed in advance. Herzl gave serious consideration to Argentina and to Uganda as candidate territories before Palestine was settled on [cite:herzl_diaries]. At its founding, political Zionism treated location as an open, practical question rather than a foregone theological conclusion. Two limits apply to this evidence. It documents the founder's own outlook and process, not the outlook of everyone who joined him; the movement drew religious and secular support alike from very early on. And it does not mean that Palestine was arbitrary to the movement's members, only that its founder weighed alternatives in writing. The rabbinic argument over whether Jews may return to the land by political means at all is a separate and older debate, told elsewhere in this library [scene:oaths_s01|the Three Oaths debate], and the Congress itself has its own section [scene:s04|the Basel Congress of 1897].

Reform Judaism, 1885. Twelve years before Basel, in November 1885, American Reform Judaism adopted the Pittsburgh Platform. Its words are explicit:

We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron, nor the restoration of any of the laws concerning the Jewish state.

This was not a reply to Zionism, which did not yet exist as an organized movement. It was an independent religious position, adopted publicly as the founding statement of what was then the largest Jewish denomination in America, that already disagreed with what would be proposed more than a decade later [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. It is difficult to reconcile with the simpler story in which Judaism naturally wanted a return to Zion and Zionism merely organized that existing desire. The platform remained mainstream American Reform's position for over half a century, until the Columbus Platform of 1937 softened it, and substantial Reform opposition to political Zionism continued after that. On this evidence, American Jewish institutional support for the political Zionist state is a development of the period after the Holocaust, not an ancient religious commitment [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. The platform documents the position of 1885. Reform Judaism's institutional stance shifted considerably over the twentieth century, and the 1885 text is no guide to its views today.

The platform's wording also carries a concession worth noticing. To declare that "we consider ourselves no longer a nation" is to acknowledge that the idea of Jewish nationhood had been there to set aside. The question that divided the 1880s and 1890s was less whether Jews were a people than what that peoplehood required.

Ahad Ha'am, 1891. That question was argued most sharply from inside the Zionist camp. Asher Zvi Hirsch Ginsberg (1856–1927), who wrote as Ahad Ha'am, "One of the People," was a committed Zionist in the cultural sense: he wanted a Jewish spiritual and cultural center in Palestine [cite:wiki_ahad_haam]. In 1891, six years before Basel, he published "Truth from Eretz Israel," a firsthand report on the country. "We are used to believing abroad that Palestine is nowadays almost totally desolate," he wrote, "but in fact this is not the case. It is difficult to find in the land any tillable land which is not already tilled" [cite:wiki_ahad_haam]. He recorded the existing Arab population and warned that a political approach that did not account for it would produce conflict. His opposition was to the political, state-building version of Zionism that Herzl went on to champion, and to its handling of the people already there, not to Jewish attachment to the land. His essay establishes that the population, and the risk, were documented from within the movement's own intellectual circle before the political project took shape. It does not establish that his alternative, a cultural center rather than a state, would have been more workable in practice.

The Bund, October 1897. Two months after Basel, in Vilna, Jewish workers founded the Algemeyner Yidisher Arbeter Bund, the General Jewish Labor Bund in Lithuania, Poland and Russia [cite:wiki_bund]. It organized across the Russian Pale of Settlement on socialist and Yiddishist lines and rejected the Zionist proposal of national return to Palestine. Its watchword was doikayt, "hereness": Jewish cultural and political life was to be built where Jews already lived, with Yiddish as its vernacular and national-cultural autonomy inside the existing states as its goal. The Bund, in other words, also spoke of Jews as a nation. It disagreed with the Zionists about where that nation's future lay.

The Bund was not a debating society. The historian Henry Tobias, in The Jewish Bund in Russia: From Its Origins to 1905, documents it as a genuine mass movement with real weight in the wider Russian and Polish socialist and labor movements; for a significant stretch of the early twentieth century, more organized Jewish political energy in Eastern Europe ran through the Bund than through the Zionist movement [cite:wiki_bund]. The sources differ on its size. One account gives a membership of more than 400,000 across the Russian Empire by 1917, larger than the Zionist movement in Eastern Europe and the largest Jewish political organization in the Empire in the decade before the Balfour Declaration; another describes it in the early twentieth century as having tens of thousands of members [cite:wiki_bund]. Either figure makes it a major current, not a fringe.

Its eclipse came from outside, not from losing an open argument with Zionism. Its membership and infrastructure were devastated by the Holocaust, and its remaining structures in the Soviet sphere were suppressed as Stalin moved against independent Jewish political organizations [cite:wiki_bund]. Most of its members, or their children, died in the Holocaust before the State of Israel was declared; their opposition to Zionism did not save them. The earlier fate of the Bund in Soviet Russia, dissolved by its Bolshevik allies, is told in the next section [scene:s00b3|Jewish dissent across every lineage]. What the Bund's existence settles is specific. It does not show that the Bund's position was the authentic Jewish position any more than Zionism's was; both were real, competing currents in Jewish political life. It does show that equating "Jewish" with "Zionist" was contested by Jews, at scale, from the movement's first year, and it means the record cannot support the statement that "the Jewish people wanted Israel" as a description of that era.

Satmar, 1958. The religious case against political Zionism received its most substantial modern statement ten years after the state was founded. In 1958 Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, published VaYoel Moshe, the central Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) theological argument against political Zionism [cite:wiki_satmar]. It rests on the Three Oaths of the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Ketubot 111a, a rabbinic tradition holding that the Jewish people swore not to reclaim the land by force or rebel against the nations before the messianic era. In this reading, a state established by human political and military effort is not the fulfillment of Jewish religious hope but a violation of a specific religious commitment. The argument does not deny the land's sanctity; it denies that the movement had the right to take it by political means before its time.

Satmar numbers roughly 130,000 people in the United States alone, concentrated in Williamsburg, Kiryas Joel and Monsey, with further communities in Israel, London, Antwerp and Montreal. It is the largest single Hasidic dynasty in the world, and it still teaches this position [cite:wiki_satmar]. That is the documented position of a specific, identifiable tradition. It is not the majority position of Orthodox or Haredi Judaism in general, and it should not be generalized into one.

Set side by side, the five positions show how many different answers Jews gave in these decades to the same questions: whether the Jewish future lay in Palestine, and by what means.

The strongest case for the other side. Read fairly, these documents also contain the materials of the Zionist argument. Jewish peoplehood was not a Zionist invention: the Bund organized Jews as a nation seeking cultural autonomy, the Reform rabbis of 1885 had to declare that they were "no longer a nation," and Ahad Ha'am, whose quarrel was with Herzl's methods, still placed the Jewish cultural center in Palestine. Satmar's objection is to the timing and the means of a return, not to the land's place in Jewish religious life. And Herzl's turn to politics was a response to antisemitism he witnessed at first hand. On this reading, Zionism was one answer among several to a question that Jews widely shared, and one that drew religious and secular support from its early years; in America, the institutional support it later won came after the Holocaust. Nothing in the record contradicts that reading. What the record contradicts is the stronger claim that Zionism and Judaism are the same thing, so that the one cannot be opposed without opposing the other.

Why the distinction carries weight. The line between a political movement founded in 1897 and a religion and set of lineages far older is one that the founders themselves recognized, that Reform recorded in 1885, that the Bund built a mass movement on in 1897, and that Satmar still teaches in 2026 [cite:basel_program] [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] [cite:wiki_bund] [cite:wiki_satmar]. It continues in contemporary Jewish life in Judith Butler's Parting Ways, in Peter Beinart's The Crisis of Zionism and in the organization Jewish Voice for Peace [cite:butler_parting_ways] [cite:beinart_crisis_zionism] [cite:jvp_org]. When the two are collapsed into one, criticism of a documented political project and the state it produced comes to read as an attack on a people and a religion. That conversion is the slide this book calls the swizzle, which the section on the word "Semitic" first names. The Jewish critique of Zionism is not an attack from outside; it is a Jewish tradition older than the state.

A test of the accusation. One argument made in this book's research takes Herzl's alternatives as a thought experiment. Had the state been built in Uganda or Argentina, could criticism of it plausibly have been called "antisemitic"? The historically dominant local languages of Uganda are Bantu languages, Luganda among them; Argentina's are Spanish and Indigenous American languages such as Quechua, Guaraní and Mapudungun. Neither population speaks a Semitic language. Palestine's population spoke Arabic, which is one [cite:wiki_bantu_languages] [cite:wiki_languages_argentina] [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology]. Since "Semitic" was coined in 1781 as a term for a language family that includes Hebrew, Arabic and Amharic together, and was never a synonym for "Jewish," the argument holds that the conflation is no more valid in Palestine than it would have been anywhere else; it simply found a surface hook there, through a coincidence of geography. The argument has firm limits. It explains a pattern in how a rhetorical move spread; it is not a claim that the move is correct anywhere. Nor does it address whether some criticism of Israeli policy is antisemitic in the settled sense of the word, which is hostility to Jews and which the following sections treat on its own terms.

The same research names an inconsistency in how the word's root is used. The correct point that Palestinians speak a Semitic language, and share substantial ancestral overlap with Levantine Jewish populations according to the genetic studies of Nebel (2000) and Behar (2010), is often deployed to argue that criticism of Israeli policy cannot coherently be called antisemitic [cite:wiki_semitic_etymology] [cite:nebel_pop_genetics_2000]. On the word's linguistic terms, that argument is accurate. But the same breadth of the word rarely appears when the subject is the displacement of some 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians in 1948, or the conditions in Gaza documented later in this library, including a formally confirmed famine. The research does not propose that "antisemitism" be applied to harm done to Palestinians. Its position is that the word has always meant hatred of Jews specifically and never fit that harm in either direction. Its point is that Palestinian displacement and casualties are documented on their own terms and deserve the same seriousness, whichever way the "Semitic" argument is being pointed.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish a distinction and a debate; they do not decide the debate. They do not show that any one of these positions was the authentic Jewish one, or how Jews outside these organizations and platforms would have answered the national question. The sources differ on the Bund's size, and the record does not show how the Bund and the Zionist movement would have fared against each other had the Holocaust and Soviet repression not destroyed one of them. Reform's 1885 position shows where a major denomination stood in that year, not where it stands now. And the existence of a Jewish tradition of dissent does not show that Zionism's supporters are wrong to experience their support as Jewish. It shows that the distinction itself is real, documented, and older than the state.

sections.h: Dissent from Every Lineage
sections.html:
A common account of Jewish opinion about Zionism runs in one of two directions. In the first, Jewish opposition to the Zionist project is a small and marginal position, held by a handful of eccentrics. In the second, it belongs to one particular community, usually imagined as the Jews of the Middle East set against the Jews of Europe. The documented record supports neither version. Organized opposition to political Zionism, and organized critique of the state it produced, appears on the record in Ashkenazi religious tradition, in Ashkenazi secular socialism, in Ashkenazi-founded Reform theology, among the cultural Zionists who rejected partition, and in the scholarship of Mizrahi Jews living inside Israel itself. The earlier section on [scene:s00c|Zionism and Judaism] set out the distinction between a political movement founded at Basel in 1897 and a religion far older than it. This section follows the people who held that distinction, what each of them actually argued, and what became of them.

The sequence matters, because the traditions differ in kind as well as in origin. Some rejected the Zionist project outright. Some accepted a Jewish national life in Palestine but rejected a Jewish sovereign state and partition. One critiques the state's treatment of its own Jewish citizens. Folding all of these into a single category called "Jewish opposition to Zionism" would flatten a real spectrum, and the record is clearer when they are kept apart.

The General Jewish Labour Bund was founded in Vilna in 1897, the same year as the First Zionist Congress. It organized Jewish workers across the Russian Empire's Pale of Settlement, the region of the 1880s pogroms and the mass emigration that followed them. It was an overwhelmingly Ashkenazi, Eastern European, socialist movement, and it explicitly rejected emigration to Palestine. Its alternative was Jewish cultural and political autonomy where Jewish communities already lived [cite:wiki_bund]. Its position was not indifference to antisemitism: its members lived through the same pogroms that gave the Zionist movement its urgency. Its argument was strategic. The two movements were born in the same year, from the same communities, in response to the same crisis, and one said leave and build elsewhere while the other said stay and fight for the right to be who you are, where you are. The Bund was a serious, organized mass movement, not a fringe dissent.

Most accounts stop at the founding. What happened next is part of the record too. When the Bolsheviks took power in October 1917, the Bund split. A majority faction, believing it was joining a genuine ally on workers' rights, merged into the Communist Party. A minority led by Vladimir Medem rejected Bolshevik rule as undemocratic and hostile to Jewish national rights. Bundists disagreed among themselves over whether the Bolsheviks could be trusted, and decided the question differently. In 1921 the Bolsheviks formally dissolved the Bund, merger or no merger. Its remaining members were imprisoned or fled abroad, under a government now hostile to independent Jewish political organizing of any kind, socialist or not. Mark Liber, one of the Bund's leading figures and its representative on the Executive Committee of the Petrograd Soviet during the revolution itself, was executed during the Stalinist purges in 1937. He was killed by the state his movement had helped bring to power two decades earlier [cite:jewishcurrents_bund_rise_fall] [cite:britannica_bund].

The Polish Bund took a different path. It survived independently through the interwar years and into the Holocaust, and its members fought alongside Zionists and Communists in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Survivors tried to regroup in Poland after the war and were suppressed again, this time by Poland's new Communist government. Within a single generation, the organization was dissolved twice, by two different governments, one of which its own members had helped install [cite:jewishcurrents_bund_rise_fall] [cite:britannica_bund]. That history shows what happened to the organization. It does not show that the Bund's argument against Zionism was refuted by it. A movement crushed by force has not thereby been proved wrong, and the record of its suppression is not a verdict on its ideas, in either direction.

American Reform Judaism's Pittsburgh Platform of 1885 defined Jewish identity as a religious community rather than a nation awaiting territorial restoration. The movement that adopted it was founded and led by Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants and their American-born successors [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885]. The timing is the point. Political Zionism as an organized movement dates from the Basel Congress of 1897, twelve years later. The Pittsburgh Platform was not a reaction against Zionism, since there was not yet an organized Zionism to react against. It was a Jewish religious position that existed first, on its own terms, and that did not adopt Zionism's framework when it later appeared. Retellings sometimes reverse the order and treat Zionism as the original position that the 1885 document set itself against, and the dates do not allow that. The record also limits the claim. American Reform Judaism's institutional position shifted considerably over the twentieth century, and what is documented here is the founding position of 1885 and its date, not a permanent stance.

Neturei Karta is today the most publicly visible Haredi Jewish community that opposes Zionism, and it is Ashkenazi in origin and practice. Its ground is theological. Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the Satmar Rebbe, set out the argument in VaYoel Moshe in 1958. In this reading, Jewish tradition holds that the ingathering of the exiles and the restoration of sovereignty are to come through divine action in the Messianic era, not through human political and military effort beforehand. To establish a state ahead of that time is itself the transgression, and the central one rather than a side issue [cite:wiki_satmar]. The rabbinic sources behind it, the Three Oaths of the Talmud, have their own history in [scene:oaths_s01|the debate over the Three Oaths].

This is not a lukewarm position. It takes the scriptural promises of restoration seriously enough to conclude that a state built by human political action violates them, the opposite of what many outsiders assume religious Jews believe. Neturei Karta continues to hold it as a current practice and appears at public demonstrations [cite:wiki_satmar]. The record is equally clear about its scale: Neturei Karta is a specific and relatively small community, and most Haredi and Orthodox institutions today hold other positions. What is documented is that a serious, theologically grounded opposition from within Orthodox tradition exists and is active, not that it speaks for Orthodox Judaism as a whole.

The binationalists are the hardest case to classify, which is why they matter. Martin Buber and Judah Magnes, with colleagues including Gershom Scholem and Henrietta Szold, founded Brit Shalom in 1925. It advocated a binational state with full civic equality between Jews and Arabs, rather than a Jewish-majority sovereign state [cite:myjewishlearning_brit_shalom] [cite:wiki_brit_shalom]. Brit Shalom was never a mass movement. It worked more as a small study circle of elite academics and intellectuals. It drew fierce, documented hostility from the dominant Labor and Revisionist Zionist currents, some of whose members called its members traitors. It also had notable public support: Albert Einstein backed it publicly, a fact seldom mentioned alongside his name. Brit Shalom dissolved around 1933, roughly eight years after its founding [cite:wiki_brit_shalom] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Historians trace its failure to a specific sequence, not simply to unpopularity. The violence at Hebron in 1929 and the Arab Revolt of 1936–39 undermined Brit Shalom's founding premise, that the Arab political leadership would accept binational equality. And the movement never grew beyond its intellectual core into a mass constituency on either side [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

The idea outlived the organization. In 1942 Buber and Magnes founded Ihud as a direct response to the Biltmore Conference's demand for a Jewish Commonwealth, again advocating a binational state with full civic equality [cite:wiki_ihud]. In 1947 the two men testified in person against partition before the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine (UNSCOP), to David Ben-Gurion's documented fury. Buber told the commission that it was "ethically and politically incumbent" on a regenerated Jewish people to live not merely alongside the Arabs but genuinely with them, developing the country for equal benefit. He called the treatment of the Arab population "the moral acid test of Zionism" [cite:britainpalestine_buber_magnes] [cite:wiki_ihud].

Hannah Arendt reached a related conclusion separately, from outside the Brit Shalom circle. Her 1944 essay "Zionism Reconsidered" warned that pursuing an exclusively Jewish sovereign state, rather than a binational arrangement, risked permanent regional conflict and long-term dependence on a great-power patron for security. She wrote it years before the state was founded [cite:researchgate_arendt_zionism_reconsidered].

The founding of Israel in May 1948 made binationalism moot, and Magnes's position changed with events. He began advocating a confederation between the new Jewish state and a future Palestinian Arab state, a documented development in his thinking cut short by his death that October. Ihud outlived the founding. The following year Buber wrote that "our cause has lost its footing, its face has been sullied, but it has not been overcome." Its publication, Ner, continued until 1964, sixteen years after the state it had argued against creating in that form already existed [cite:wiki_ihud] [cite:fathom_mandate100_binationalism].

Precision about this group is a matter of accuracy. Buber and Magnes are best described as cultural and binational Zionists who rejected the model of sovereignty and partition, not as anti-Zionists in the sense of the Bund or Neturei Karta. Their dissent came from inside the movement's own intellectual core. It shows that the argument was never only between Zionists and their opponents, but also among Zionists over what form Jewish national life in Palestine should take.

The last kind of dissent is different again. The Bund, Reform Judaism and Neturei Karta argued, in their different ways, against the Zionist project itself, before the state existed or regardless of it. The Mizrahi critique comes from people who did move to Israel, live there and are its citizens. Scholars including Ella Shohat, Sami Shalom Chetrit and Yehouda Shenhav documented specific patterns in how the Ashkenazi-dominated Israeli establishment treated Mizrahi Jewish immigrants after 1948: placement in peripheral development towns, discrimination in employment, and the cultural marginalization of Middle Eastern Jewish identity in favor of an Ashkenazi-coded national culture [cite:chetrit_mizrahi_struggle]. The arrival itself, in the transit camps and the affairs that followed, is told in [scene:s00e2|the exodus from the Arab world].

This is a Middle Eastern-lineage critique of the state's conduct, running alongside the Ashkenazi traditions rather than standing in for them. Its limits are also documented. It is a scholarly tradition with named authors and named mechanisms of discrimination. It does not show that all Mizrahi Israelis share it, or that Mizrahi communities are anti-Zionist as a whole. Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state.

Placed on one line, the traditions span more than 140 years. Reform's platform of 1885 and Teitelbaum's book of 1958 stand 73 years apart, and none of these currents waited for the others to reach the same conclusion.

The historical traditions say nothing about how many Jews hold any view today. For that, the evidence is polling, and the most detailed recent survey is of American Jews only. The Washington Post surveyed 815 American Jews between 2 and 9 September 2025, with a margin of error of 4.7 points. Sixty-one per cent said Israel had committed war crimes against Palestinians [cite:wapo_jews_poll]. Thirty-nine per cent said Israel had committed genocide and 51% said it had not; among respondents aged 18 to 34, half said genocide [cite:toi_jews_poll]. Forty-six per cent approved of Israel's military conduct and 48% disapproved, and 68% disapproved of Benjamin Netanyahu. The same respondents held other views at the same time. Seventy-six per cent said Israel's existence is vital to the Jewish future, 94% said Hamas had committed war crimes, and 91% blamed Hamas for prolonging the war [cite:jta_jews_poll]. For comparison, in February 2024 Pew had found that 62% of American Jews said Israel's conduct was acceptable.

A second set of figures separates attachment from the label. Jewish Federations data show that about 90% of American Jews support Israel's existence as a Jewish and democratic state, while only 37% call themselves "Zionist" [cite:forward_zionist]. Organized opinion spans a wide range: J Street, pro-Israel and pro-two-state; Jewish Voice for Peace, which is anti-Zionist; and Haredi groups such as Neturei Karta, which oppose a Jewish state on religious grounds [cite:forward_zionist]. The pattern in these numbers is a community and not a bloc. Most American Jews are attached to Israel and critical of the war at the same time.

Two fair readings can be drawn from this record. The first holds that dissent has mostly been held by minorities. Neturei Karta is a small community. Brit Shalom was a study circle that lasted about eight years, and Ihud never grew into a mass constituency. Reform Judaism moved away from its 1885 position over the following century. Many Mizrahi Israelis identify strongly with the state. In the 2025 poll, three in four American Jews called Israel vital to the Jewish future, and about nine in ten support its existence as a Jewish and democratic state. On this reading the dissenters were real, but the main current of Jewish life moved the other way.

The second reading holds that dissent has been a real and continuous current. The Bund was a mass movement, not a fringe, and it ended because two governments crushed it, not because its members changed their minds. The binationalists came from the intellectual center of Zionism itself and testified against partition before the United Nations in 1947. The theological case against a state is still taught and still practised. And the gap between the roughly 90% who support Israel's existence and the 37% who call themselves Zionist suggests that the word and the attachment are not the same thing for many American Jews. Both readings rest on documented facts. They differ over weight, not over the record.

What the record shows plainly is that the dividing line in these debates has not been lineage. Some of the earliest, most organized and most theologically serious Jewish opposition to Zionism was Ashkenazi, and one of the most developed critiques of the Israeli state's conduct was Mizrahi. To frame opposition as something only Middle Eastern Jews do, while European Jews uniformly support Zionism, would invert the evidence. The line runs through every lineage, between those who hold the specific political position of Zionism and those who contest or reject it.

Several things the record here does not settle. It contains no current polling on what share of Ashkenazi, Sephardi or Mizrahi Jews support or oppose Zionism, and it cannot say how any lineage divides today. It documents no distinctly Sephardi tradition of dissent alongside the Ashkenazi and Mizrahi ones. The detailed polling is of American Jews alone, and it measures views of Israel's conduct in a war, which is not the same question as support for Zionism. And none of these traditions shows by itself which side of the argument was right. The record establishes something narrower and firmer: that support and opposition have both had serious, long-standing representation within Jewish life, across every lineage it documents.

sections.h: One Verse, Two Readings: Christians and the Promise to Abraham
sections.html:
Two opposite claims are often made about the Bible and the modern State of Israel. One holds that scripture requires Christians to support the state. The other holds that scripture has nothing to do with the question. Neither describes the actual situation, which is a long-running argument among Christians themselves over what one set of verses means and to whom they now apply. The verse at the center of it is Genesis 12:3, the text Christian Zionists cite most. It was spoken to Abram, later Abraham: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse; and all peoples on earth will be blessed through you." The promise of land follows in the same narrative, at Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8.

The words themselves are not in dispute. The question is who the "you" of the promise is today. One answer identifies it with the Jewish people and, since 1948, with the State of Israel, a secular state. Another holds that the promise was fulfilled in Christ and the church and does not pass to any modern government. The two answers lead to opposite political conclusions from the same text.

The Christian Zionist reading treats the verse as a standing instruction. Groups such as the International Christian Embassy Jerusalem describe it as the biblical mandate for standing with Israel [cite:icej_cz] [cite:rmc_cz]. On this reading the blessing and the curse attach to how nations and individuals treat the Jewish people and their state now, and the land promise of Genesis 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8 remains in force. Many believers in dispensationalism, a system of reading biblical prophecy, go further and regard Israel's restoration as a precondition of Christ's return. That framework was popularized by the notes of the Scofield Reference Bible, whose history is told in [scene:s05|the Scofield Bible]. The older British and American Protestant campaign for a Jewish restoration to Palestine is told in [scene:bc_s05|the Protestant restoration lobby]. The strongest form of this reading rests on the text's plain wording: the blessing and the curse as spoken, and the land promised again at 12:7, 15:18 and 17:8.

The other reading belongs to covenant theology and to what theologians call "amillennial" theology. It holds that the promise to Abraham is fulfilled in Christ and in the church, citing Paul's letter to the Galatians (3:16 and 3:29), and that it does not transfer to a modern government [cite:studylight_gen12] [cite:pctii_gen12]. Some scholars add a point about emphasis: the passage stresses blessing to all the nations of the earth more than it stresses land [cite:pctii_gen12]. The strongest form of this reading is that it takes its key from within the Christian scriptures themselves, in Paul's own reading of the promise, and gives full weight to the verse's last clause: "all peoples on earth will be blessed through you."

The argument is old, but in June 2025 it became public in a way that reached far beyond seminaries. Senator Ted Cruz cited Genesis 12:3 in an exchange with Tucker Carlson, and Carlson asked whether the political state led by Benjamin Netanyahu is the same "Israel" as the one in scripture [cite:think_gen12]. The question he put is the hinge of the whole dispute. Cruz's position rests on the identification of the biblical Israel with the modern state. Carlson's question rests on the distinction between them. Neither man settled it, and no verse can settle it on its own, because the disagreement is about how to read the verse, not about what it says.

The first reading is the theology behind the largest pro-Israel constituency in the United States. How an annotated Bible became a political force, from the dispensationalist pulpit to organized lobbying in Washington, is drawn in the map below. Its organizations, members and money are documented in later volumes of this library, where the figures carry their own sources.

A frequent question about the dispensationalist reading is why the Roman Catholic Church never campaigned against it. The premise is half right. Rome never ran a public campaign. But it did rule on the theology. In the 1940s the Holy Office, the Vatican's doctrinal authority and the predecessor of today's Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, judged that premillennialism, the prophetic framework at the core of Scofield's system, "cannot safely be taught" [cite:catholic_answers_rapture_tract]. The rejection is still in force. Paragraph 676 of the Catechism of the Catholic Church rejects millenarianism as "the intrinsic perversity" of a falsely secularized understanding of the Kingdom of God [cite:catholicculture_five_myths_rapture]. The position is public and available to anyone. It is simply not widely known.

It stayed quiet for structural reasons. Catholic doctrinal statements are addressed to Catholics, through the Church's own teaching, not issued as public rebuttals of particular Protestant authors or their reference Bibles. Rulings against specific Protestant theological systems routinely remain inside Church documents and catechetical teaching rather than becoming public campaigns, and the Church generally does not campaign against the doctrines of Protestant denominations with which it is not in active dialogue.
