This was a general pattern, not a special case invented for dispensationalism [cite:worldfinance_vatican_bank_history]. Rome also had no authority over Protestant publishing in the first place. Its doctrinal jurisdiction runs over Catholic teaching, and the Reformation had ended any mechanism by which it could approve or block a Protestant publisher's Bible centuries before Scofield. What the ruling records is the Church's own position on the theology, not an attempt or an ability to control what Protestant publishers printed. Nor does the silence show indifference: the ruling, and its place in the current Catechism, record a sustained position, only not a public one. Whether individual Catholics or parishes ever hear of paragraph 676 is a different matter, and the record here does not measure it.

Rome's diplomatic record shows what a church that did not read the promise in dispensationalist terms actually did when Zionism came to it. In January 1904 Theodor Herzl sought an audience with Pope Pius X to ask for Vatican support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The Pope refused. His documented answer was that the Church could not support Jewish restoration to a land central to its own theology while denying Christ [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]. That refusal held as Vatican policy for 89 years. In 1949, a year after Israel's founding, the Vatican worked behind the scenes at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: allowing the return of Palestinian refugees, and formal guarantees for Christian and Muslim holy sites, particularly in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion said that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning." The campaign failed. Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Holy See had sought.

What changed the Church's course was a change in its doctrine. The Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate of 1965 revised Catholic teaching on Judaism, stating that God "holds the Jews most dear for the sake of their Fathers." That shift was the precondition for what followed. On 30 December 1993 the Holy See and Israel signed the Fundamental Agreement in Jerusalem, establishing diplomatic relations, 45 years after Israel's founding, and ambassadors were exchanged in 1994. Even then, property rights, tax exemptions and the status of Jerusalem were left for continuing negotiation under the agreement's own terms [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement]. The documented reasons for the long delay were three: the Church's theology of the Jewish people's role in salvation history, the unresolved status of Jerusalem's holy sites, and concern for the Palestinian Christian and Muslim communities under the new state [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition]. After the UN General Assembly's vote of November 2012, the Vatican formally recognized the State of Palestine, and in 2015 it signed an accord governing the Church's activity in Palestinian-controlled territory, which drew a formal Israeli protest [cite:gulfnews_vatican_palestine_accord]. The full story is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's 45 years].

Two further points complicate any picture of a simple religious alignment. Within Judaism, too, views of the state's religious meaning differ: early Zionism was largely secular, and some Haredi Jews oppose a Jewish state before the coming of the Messiah. And Palestinian Christians, about 1% of the population today, are part of this story too, as a community with its own history in the land and not only as a subject of other Christians' theology.

The record settles what the verse says, which traditions read it which way, what Rome ruled and when, and how long it took the Holy See to recognize Israel. It does not settle the theological question, which is not a historical one: whether a promise made to Abraham applies to a state founded in 1948 depends on a reader's prior commitments about how scripture is to be read. Nor does the material here say how many Christians hold each reading. What it does show is that "the Bible requires it" and "the Bible is irrelevant" are both wrong as descriptions. The verse matters a great deal to many Christians, and they draw opposite conclusions from it.

chapters.label: Chapter 5
chapters.title: Two Displacements
chapters.intro:
In the middle of the twentieth century two large movements of people reshaped the region. In the war of 1947–1949 roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, the event Palestinians call the Nakba.[cite:wiki_nakba] Between 1948 and 1972 roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries. The two are often told as one story, in which each cancels the other. This chapter tells them separately, each on its own record, and then tests the comparison.

It sits in the Baseline, ahead of the history of 1948, because the comparison is made constantly and usually without its evidence, and because the Jewish exodus belongs to many countries and runs through decades that the history of the Mandate does not reach. The Palestinian displacement is told in full in the next volume; here it appears as one side of the comparison.

The first section follows the exodus from Iraq, where the turning point came in Baghdad on 1–2 June 1941, seven years before Israel existed, with the pogrom known as the Farhud.[cite:ushmm_farhud] It traces Iraq's criminalization of "Zionism" in 1948, the law of March 1950 that made departure conditional on surrendering citizenship, the airlift called Operation Ezra and Nehemiah, the disputed Baghdad bombings and Israel's sabotage operation in Egypt in 1954, and then the arrival in Israel: the transit camps, the Yemenite Children Affair and the Ringworm Affair.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The second section goes country by country, through Libya, Egypt, Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain, Yemen, Morocco and Algeria, and sets out the arguments over the total and over the word "refugees."[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] [cite:rs_ch01_ahram_amayreh] The third compares the two displacements on mechanism, duration, the number of governments involved and citizenship afterwards, and shows why the claim of an even exchange is rejected from both directions.

Throughout, two readings of the Jewish departures are kept side by side: rescue from persecution, and active recruitment by the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency. The record documents both, in proportions that differed from country to country.

sections.h: The Exodus of 1941–1972 and Its Aftermath
sections.html:
Between 1948 and 1972, roughly 850,000 Jews left Arab and Muslim countries, from about two dozen states over some 24 years. The usual way of telling it is short: Jews were persecuted throughout Arab lands until Israel gave them refuge. That sentence contains real history, and it leaves out most of it. The documents show several causes working at once, each recorded on its own: violence and legal persecution by Arab governments, organized and named recruitment operations run by Israel and the Jewish Agency, and, in one specific and well-documented Egyptian case, sabotage carried out by Israeli military intelligence. They also show that arrival in Israel was not the end of the story. What happened to many of the newcomers in their first years is a second, separate story, in places a grave one, and Israel's own state commissions and independent researchers have investigated it without reaching full agreement.

This section follows that record in order: Iraq first, because its documentation is richest and its turning point came earliest; then the other airlifts and the Egyptian operation, briefly; then the transit camps, the disappearance of children from Yemenite and other Mizrahi families, and the mass irradiation of immigrant children for ringworm. The country-by-country figures, and the argument over the total, are set out in [scene:ch01_exodus_map|the next section].

Baghdad, June 1941. The turning point in Iraqi Jewish memory came seven years before Israel existed. Rashid Ali al-Gailani led a pro-Axis coup in Iraq. The British defeated it, and his government collapsed days before the violence began. Its fall left a vacuum in the capital and inflamed the nationalist and pro-Axis feeling it had stirred.[cite:wiki_farhud] On 1–2 June 1941, during the Jewish festival of Shavuot, crowds in Baghdad turned on the city's Jews. Iraqi soldiers and police who had backed the coup, together with the pro-Axis youth militias known as the Futuwwa, incited and led two days of killing, rape and looting. Civilian mobs and Bedouin from the city's outskirts joined them. British forces, victorious just outside the city, did not intervene.[cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:wiki_farhud] The event is known as the Farhud. The vague word "riots" is sometimes still used for it. The record describes a targeted pogrom with members of the state's own security forces among the perpetrators.

The death toll is given differently in different sources, and the differences should be stated rather than smoothed over. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, the most authoritative single source on the event, gives 150 to 180 Jews killed, 600 injured, an undetermined number of women raped, and roughly 1,500 stores and homes looted.[cite:ushmm_farhud] An official commission of inquiry appointed by the Iraqi government recorded 128 killed by its own count, with independent estimates running as high as 180; the same account gives more than 1,000 injured and roughly 900 Jewish homes and more than 1,500 businesses looted or destroyed.[cite:ushmm_farhud] Some other sources put the dead at 500 or more.[cite:wiki_farhud] On any of these counts, the event marked the point after which Iraq's ancient Jewish community began its decline toward near-total emigration within a decade.[cite:ushmm_farhud]

The date matters for the argument as much as the toll. The Farhud took place in June 1941. Israel was declared in May 1948. Whatever role the pogrom later played in hastening departures, it cannot have been a reaction to the 1948 war or to the Nakba, the Palestinian displacement of that war. It does not show, on the other hand, that every later departure from Iraq was driven by the same forces. The departures of 1950 and 1951 had their own, additional causes.

Iraq at war, 1947–1949. After the United Nations voted for partition in November 1947, anti-Jewish measures in Iraq escalated. Pogroms gave way to systematic confiscation of property and to prosecutions on what one account calls trumped-up charges.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared its independence, Iraq joined the Arab invasion. When the fighting ended, Iraq was the only Arab combatant that refused to sign an armistice with Israel, so that a formal state of war between the two has, technically, never ended.[cite:govil_aliyah] This is easy to lose inside the phrase "the 1948 war." For Iraq's Jews it meant that their state remained formally at war with the state that most of them would soon enter.

On 19 July 1948, Iraq made "Zionism" a crime punishable by up to seven years in prison. Because every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist, the law worked as a blanket criminalization of the whole community. The testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, and there was little avenue for appeal.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] On 23 September 1948, Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party. His body was left hanging for hours as a public spectacle. The case is widely cited as the one that broke what remained of the community's sense of security: if a man of his standing was not safe, no one was.[cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah]

The law of March 1950 and the airlift. On 2 March 1950, Iraq's parliament passed a law permitting Jews to leave on condition that they surrender their Iraqi citizenship.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] It was framed as permission. It worked, once people registered, as a mechanism for stripping them of nationality and then of property: a subsequent law required departing Jews to sell their property and liquidate their businesses before leaving, and the state denaturalized those who registered and stripped them of their assets.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] Economic loss was written into the exit itself.

Israel and the Jewish Agency organized the airlift that followed, Operation Ezra and Nehemiah. It was named for the biblical leaders of the return from the Babylonian exile, a deliberate echo of the community's own origins.[cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] Shlomo Hillel, an Iraqi-born agent of Mossad LeAliyah Bet, negotiated personally with the Iraqi authorities and helped organize the operation; he later described it from the inside in a memoir, Operation Babylon.[cite:wiki_shlomo_hillel] The aircraft were provided by the Near East Transport Company and El Al. One account gives the route as through Cyprus and Iran; another gives it as through Cyprus at first and later by direct flights from Baghdad to Lod.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] The cost was largely met by the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee, at about $4 million.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] [cite:govil_aliyah]

The pace overwhelmed the planning. Israeli immigration authorities had prepared to receive about 300 people a day; at the peak, 1,400 arrived daily. By the end of 1951 more than 107,000 Iraqi Jews had been airlifted, and about 16,000 more had left by other routes.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] By early 1952, a community of some 2,800 years' standing had been reduced to about 6,000 people. Israeli government sources put its size before the airlift at about 135,000; another account gives roughly 130,000.[cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah] Summary accounts give the number airlifted as about 120,000 to 130,000.[cite:encyclopedia_ezra_nehemiah]

These facts establish a real, organized, named Israeli operation and a real Iraqi legal mechanism that made departure conditional on giving up citizenship and property. They do not, by themselves, say why so many Iraqi Jews chose to go. The Farhud, the criminal law of 1948, the hanging in Basra, the conditions of the 1950 law and the airlift's own active recruitment are all documented as contributing causes. None of them is the single cause.

The Baghdad bombings, 1950–1951. One part of this story is disputed, and the dispute is real. Between April 1950 and June 1951, at least five bombing incidents struck Jewish institutions and gathering places in Baghdad, among them the Masuda Shemtov synagogue. At least four Jews were killed and others injured.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] The attacks fell in exactly the months when the March 1950 law was driving mass registration for emigration. Iraq tried men for the bombings, and two of them, Basri and Shalom, were hanged in January 1952.[cite:meforum_exodus]

Two accounts of who was responsible have stood against each other ever since. The Iraqi government of the time, and later some historians, attributed the bombings to Zionist underground agents seeking to panic the community into leaving faster. Israeli officials have consistently and firmly denied any involvement, and have called the accusation an antisemitic fabrication meant to shift blame for a persecution the Iraqi state had itself created through years of pogroms, denaturalization and criminalization.[cite:wiki_ezra_nehemiah] A review of newly released Israeli, British and American archives, published by the Middle East Forum, found insufficient evidence to confirm Israeli involvement, while not closing the question entirely. The executions do not settle it either: the fairness and evidentiary basis of the trials, held amid intense anti-Zionist feeling, are themselves disputed.[cite:meforum_exodus]

What the record shows is real bombings, real deaths, and a real Iraqi prosecution that ended in executions. What it does not show is proof of who was responsible. Both the contemporary Iraqi accusation and the Israeli denial are documented positions. The evidence now available does not decide between them, and this book does not pretend that it does in either direction.

Yemen, Morocco and Egypt. Iraq's was one of three major named operations, each in a different country on a different timetable. Operation Magic Carpet airlifted approximately 48,000 to 49,000 Yemenite Jews to Israel in 1949–50. Operation Yachin, conducted in secret from 1961 to 1964, brought Moroccan Jews, later than the other two because Morocco's political timeline was different. Both, like Ezra and Nehemiah, were organized operations of the Israeli state and the Jewish Agency, not spontaneous flight, though the hardships in the countries of origin were also real and documented.[cite:wiki_idf_operations_list] Conditions and causes were not the same in all three countries, and they are not treated here as one undifferentiated movement; Yemen's and Morocco's own circumstances, including the payments made for Moroccan departures, are set out country by country in the next section.

Egypt supplies the one documented case of sabotage, and it touches this story because of whom it used. In July 1954, Israeli military intelligence, known as Aman, activated Unit 131, a cell of Egyptian Jews it had recruited and trained for the purpose. The cell placed incendiary devices at a post office, at American information-agency libraries in Cairo and Alexandria, and at British-owned cinemas. The intention was that the attacks would be blamed on Egyptian nationalists or communists and would persuade Britain to keep its troops in the Suez Canal Zone.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] Another summary of the same operation gives the intended scapegoats as Egyptian nationalists or the Muslim Brotherhood, and the aim as damaging Western confidence in Nasser's government.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The plan unravelled when a device ignited prematurely in an operative's pocket in Alexandria, and the cell was arrested.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair]

The people who paid were the local operatives, not the planners. At the Egyptian trial Moshe Marzouk and Shmuel Azar were sentenced to death and executed in January 1955. Max Bennett, an Israeli officer, took his own life in prison. Others received long sentences. Israel did not acknowledge the operatives for decades, and publicly honored the survivors in 2005.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The operation, later called Operation Susannah, is the earliest documented case of the Israeli state attacking a close ally's facilities under a false attribution.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] That it took place is not in dispute. Who ordered it is. Defense Minister Pinhas Lavon denied giving the order; the head of military intelligence, Binyamin Gibli, claimed that he had. Lavon resigned in 1955; one account describes him as forced out. The question was reopened in 1960 amid evidence that documents had been forged, split the ruling Mapai party, and contributed to Ben-Gurion's resignation in 1963. Who gave the order was never formally resolved.[cite:wiki_lavon_affair] The full affair is told in [scene:lv_s01|the Lavon Affair]. The record documents this pattern for Egypt only; it does not establish it for any other country in this account.

Two readings. The rescue reading holds that these were communities in danger, and that Israel brought them out. Its evidence is strong and specific: a pogrom in 1941 with soldiers and police among the killers, a 1948 law that made every Jew in Iraq a presumed criminal, a public hanging meant to be seen, an exit law that took citizenship and property together. The recruitment-and-sabotage reading holds that the Israeli state did not only receive these communities but actively worked to bring them, and in one place used local Jews in an operation that endangered them. Its evidence is also specific: named operations, a named agent negotiating with the Iraqi government, organized airlifts at a pace the reception system could not absorb, and the documented operation in Egypt. The disputed Baghdad bombings sit between the two readings, and the record cannot assign them to either. Neither reading cancels the other. Persecution, recruitment and, in one documented case, sabotage all operated, in proportions that differed from country to country.

Arrival: the ma'abarot. Being airlifted out of danger and being welcomed into equal opportunity were two different things. New arrivals, disproportionately Mizrahi, were housed in crowded transit camps called ma'abarot, at first in tents and later in basic shacks. These were spartan, temporary conditions, not immediate settlement in established communities or housing.[cite:honestreporting_forgotten_refugees] Ashkenazi immigrants arriving in the same period tended to be better educated on arrival and more likely to assimilate into the existing, largely Ashkenazi-run secular establishment. They also qualified for German war-reparations payments, which Mizrahi immigrants, who had never lived under Nazi occupation, could not receive.[cite:honestreporting_forgotten_refugees] The difference in starting conditions was structural, tied to reparations eligibility and to who already ran the institutions, not to prejudice alone. Individual lives varied widely. The pattern itself is documented.

The Yemenite Children Affair. Between 1948 and 1954, hundreds of infants and small children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi immigrant families disappeared from Israeli state hospitals and transit camps. Families were frequently told that their children had died, often without receiving a body, a death certificate or any information about burial.[cite:nytimes_disappeared_children] That basic pattern, of disappearance and inadequate explanation, is not in dispute.

What lay behind it is. A state inquiry, the Cohen-Kedmi Commission, investigated for nearly seven years, from 1995 to 2001. Its official finding was unequivocal: claims that the children had been deliberately kidnapped in a government-organized plot were not substantiated. It also acknowledged that the fates of 42 children remained unaccounted for even after its work.[cite:wiki_kedmi_commission] Against that finding stands serious, evidence-based dissent, not a fringe theory. The researcher Shoshana Madmoni-Gerber and hundreds of collected family testimonies support the argument that the disappearances reflect a real, coordinated pattern rather than isolated administrative failures.[cite:nytimes_disappeared_children] The activist Uzi Meshulam campaigned prominently for a fuller inquiry and was imprisoned in connection with his campaign, which is itself a disputed chapter in how the authorities handled the issue.[cite:wiki_uzi_meshulam]

Both positions are documented, and the people who have studied the primary evidence most closely still disagree. This book does not hold the commission's finding to be definitively right, nor the dissenting researchers and families. What is not in dispute is that children disappeared, that their families were given inadequate answers, and that what happened, and why, remains contested. The state's later decisions on the affair belong to a later period; they are taken up in [scene:mz_s02|a later chapter].

The Ringworm Affair. A separate scandal touched the same communities, and the two should not be confused. Through the 1950s, Israeli medical authorities treated scalp ringworm, a common condition at the time, by irradiating immigrant children with X-rays. The children treated were disproportionately Mizrahi and North African. One frequently cited figure puts the total in this campaign at roughly 27,000 children; estimates of the affected population run from about 20,000 to more than 100,000, the higher figures including comparable campaigns elsewhere.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair]

Part of the motive was practical and is documented. Ringworm was grounds for exclusion under the immigration rules of the United States and other countries, which put direct institutional pressure on the authorities to treat and clear affected children so that their resettlement could proceed.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair] Irradiation was a recognized treatment for ringworm elsewhere in the world in the same period, including among children who were not Mizrahi, and the record does not show that each individual decision was taken in bad faith. What it does show is the scale, the disproportionate effect on Mizrahi and North African children, and the immigration-driven pressure behind it. A 2003 Israeli documentary, The Ringworm Children, presented the episode as a serious, state-linked medical scandal, and used language as strong as "holocaust" to describe it. That choice of word is itself a measure of how gravely the episode is remembered in the communities it affected.[cite:wiki_ringworm_affair]

What left, and what remained. The headline figure of 850,000 is large and real. It is not the same claim as the end of Jewish life in the Middle East. It was a minority of the total Jewish population that had lived across the Muslim-majority world for more than a thousand years, in cities where Jewish communities were sometimes a third of the population or more. The presence thinned, in some cities dramatically: one account describes Baghdad's community of 140,000 as functionally gone today. But it did not vanish everywhere, and it did not go all at once or for one reason. The flattened version, "they all left because they were persecuted," survives because it is a simpler sentence than "a partial departure with several causes took place over 24 years, with real differences from country to country." It undersells how long the shared life lasted, and it oversells how complete the departure was.

The record leaves three questions open. It does not establish who planted the bombs in Baghdad in 1950 and 1951. It does not establish who gave the order for the Egyptian operation of 1954. And it does not establish what became of the children of Yemenite and other Mizrahi families whose fates even the state's own commission could not account for. Nor can it weigh, family by family, how much each departure owed to fear and how much to recruitment. The exact total of those who left, and whether they should be called refugees, are themselves argued over, as the next section shows.

sections.h: Country by Country: How the Jews of the Arab World Left
sections.html:
The departure of the Jews of the Arab world is usually told as one event with one number attached. It was a series of departures, country by country, each with its own dates, its own laws and its own violence, and each recorded by different sources with different degrees of certainty. The previous section followed Iraq, the largest single case, and the arrival camps in Israel [scene:s00e2|the exodus and its aftermath]. This section takes the other communities in turn: what happened in each place, who decided it, and where the people went. It ends with the two arguments that still surround the whole movement: how many left, and whether they should be called refugees.

Two common shortcuts fail on the record. One says that Israel's ties to Yemen began with the Houthis and that its ties to Morocco began with the agreements of 2020. In both countries the first connection was a community of people who left decades earlier. The other shortcut makes every departure an expulsion, or every departure a voluntary emigration organized from Israel. The country record shows both, often in the same place.

Libya. Libya had about 21,000 Jews in 1911, about 4% of a population of 550,000, and 30,387 on the eve of the Second World War. Italy's racial laws of 1938 were enforced in Libya from 1940. By June 1942 some 2,584 Jews had been deported to the camp at Giado, where 562 of them died.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] The worst violence came after the war, under British military administration. In November 1945 a three-day attack on the Jews of Tripoli killed 120 Jews and destroyed at least five synagogues. Riots in 1948 killed 12 more and destroyed 280 homes.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] According to Yad Vashem, 30,972 Libyan Jews emigrated to Israel in the wake of the violence around 1948. Those who stayed were pushed to the margins by law: a 1961 law denied nearly all Jews proof of citizenship. After riots in 1967 about 6,000 were airlifted to Rome, and by 2004 no Jews remained in Libya.[cite:rs_ch01_yv_libya] In Libya, then, the sequence ran from a fascist camp to a postwar pogrom under a European administration, then a mass departure to Israel, and finally legal exclusion. The Tripoli killings of 1945 came before the partition vote and before Israel existed.

Egypt. Egypt's community numbered an estimated 75,000–80,000 at its height in 1948. That figure is an Israeli Foreign Ministry estimate, cited by the University of Washington's Stroum Center. Bombs in Cairo's Jewish quarter between June and November 1948 killed more than 70 Jews, according to the same essay.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] The decisive break came with the Suez war. From 29 October 1956 the Egyptian government treated Jews as enemies of the state. About 1,000 were arrested in Cairo and 450 Jewish-owned businesses were confiscated. From 15 November, Jews leaving the country had to sign forms renouncing their property and their Egyptian citizenship. These details rest on the historian Joel Beinin and on an American Jewish Committee factsheet of March 1957.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] According to figures cited by the Stroum Center, about 25,000 Jews left Egypt in 1956, leaving roughly 15,000 in the country in 1957.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] Egypt's departures therefore came in at least two waves, eight years apart, with different triggers: the violence of 1948, and state measures taken during the Suez war. A third episode belongs to Egypt's story, the 1954 Israeli sabotage operation in which Egyptian Jews were recruited; it is told in the previous section.

Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain: the partition vote. The United Nations voted to partition Palestine on 29 November 1947. Within a week, Jewish communities far from Palestine were attacked. According to the Center for Israel Education, rioters in Aleppo on 30 November damaged the Great Synagogue and the Aleppo Codex, a manuscript of the tenth century. They destroyed some 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues.[cite:rs_ch01_cie_nov1947] In Aden, then under British rule, rioting from 2 December 1947 killed 82 Jews and wounded 76. In Manama, Bahrain, on 5 December, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed, according to the same source.[cite:rs_ch01_cie_nov1947] These three accounts rest on one outlet, and the figures are given here as it reports them. The sources available for this book do not record how many Jews left each of these places afterwards, or where they went.

Yemen. Yemen's Jews were among the oldest Jewish communities in the world and had lived there for well over a thousand years. Between June 1949 and September 1950 Operation Magic Carpet, also called "On Wings of Eagles", airlifted about 49,000 of them to Israel. It was organized with the American Jewish Joint Distribution Committee and flown by Alaska Airlines and other carriers. Many of the emigrants first walked for weeks to reach the British colony of Aden, where the flights began.[cite:w_magic_carpet] Some accounts round the total to nearly 50,000. In Israel many were placed in transit camps, where hundreds of children were reported dead or missing. This became the Yemenite Children Affair, for which Israel expressed "regret" and paid compensation in 2021 [scene:mz_s02|the Yemenite Children Affair]. So Israel's first tie to Yemen was a people moved by airlift, some seventy years before the missiles.

Morocco. Morocco's Jewish community had been rooted there for two millennia and was among the largest in the Arab world, numbering in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s. Most emigrated after 1948, the majority to Israel. Between 1961 and 1964 a secret operation, Operation Yachin, brought about 97,000 Moroccan Jews to Israel with the Moroccan government's quiet consent. Historians record that Israel, together with American Jewish organizations, made payments to the Moroccan government to allow the departures.[cite:w_yachin] The money chain here ran in the opposite direction from Egypt's confiscations. A foreign state and diaspora organizations paid a sovereign government, and that government allowed its citizens to leave. The records available here do not give the amount. Israelis of Moroccan descent became one of Israel's largest communities. The two states' official ties came much later and did not last at first: Morocco and Israel opened low-level liaison offices in 1994, after the Oslo agreements, and closed them in 2000 during the second intifada.[cite:w_isr_morocco] The relationship formalized in 2020 rested on people and quiet arrangements that were decades older.

Algeria. Algeria shows how much the map depended on which empire held a country. The Crémieux Decree of 24 October 1870 made Algeria's Jews French citizens. The Vichy regime withdrew that citizenship on 7 October 1940, and it was restored on 20 October 1943. Rioting in Constantine in 1934 killed 25 Jews.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_algeria] According to the Jewish Virtual Library, Algeria had about 140,000 Jews in the mid-1950s, and almost 130,000 of them moved to France when Algeria became independent in 1962. Over the whole period from 1948, 25,681 Algerian Jews immigrated to Israel.[cite:rs_ch01_jvl_algeria] Most of Algeria's Jews, in other words, went to the country whose citizens they already were, at the end of a colonial war, more than a decade after 1948.

Read together, the cases show three separate mechanisms, often working at once. The first was violence by crowds, sometimes in places under British rule, as in Tripoli in 1945 and Aden in 1947. The second was the action of states: Egypt's renunciation forms in 1956, Libya's citizenship law of 1961 and, in Iraq, the denaturalization law told in the previous section. The third was organized emigration arranged from outside: airlifts by Israel and Jewish organizations in Yemen, and a paid, secret agreement in Morocco. Who could act also differed from place to place. In Morocco and Iraq governments negotiated the terms of exit. In Egypt in 1956 the government set them alone. In Algeria the decisive fact was a French citizenship that dated from 1870.

How many? The total is disputed, and the figures come from sources with different purposes. The account of the exodus in this book uses roughly 850,000 Jews leaving Arab and Muslim countries between 1948 and 1972. A survey of the regional aftermath gives estimates "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000" for Arab countries and Iran from 1948 to the 1970s.[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] Avi Beker, writing in the Jewish Political Studies Review, gives about 900,000 Jews "forced out" of Arab countries, of whom about 650,000 went to Israel.[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] Beker writes as an advocate of one side of the argument that follows, and his figure is a position in that argument, not a settled count. The spread depends on whether Iran is included, which end year is used, and whether everyone who left counts as forced out.

Refugees? The sharper dispute is over the word itself. One position holds that these Jews were refugees in the same sense as the Palestinians of 1948. Beker sets out this "dual refugee problem" case, which the United States House of Representatives took up in H. Con. Res. 311 in October 2003. In this view about 900,000 Jews were forced out of Arab countries, and their case has been forgotten through international indifference and Israel's own reluctance to call it expulsion.[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] The strongest form of the case rests on records like those above: the Giado camp, Tripoli, the partition-vote riots, the Egyptian renunciation forms, and laws that stripped people of citizenship and property.

The opposing position holds that the comparison does not fit. The Israeli sociologist Yehouda Shenhav argued in Haaretz in 2006 that Palestinians did not leave of their own volition, while Arab Jews moved to Israel under initiatives by the state and Jewish organizations, some willingly and some not. The Palestinian writer Khalid Amayreh, in an opinion piece in Ahram Online in 2012 that quotes Shenhav, called the equation propaganda meant to offset the Nakba.[cite:rs_ch01_ahram_amayreh] The strongest form of this case also rests on the record: the organized airlift from Yemen, the payments to Morocco, and the recruitment operations described in the previous section.

A middle line accepts parts of both. The Stroum Center essay treats the Egyptian departures of 1956 as an expulsion. It also warns, citing the historian Eyal Bizawe, against using Mizrahi history to cast Arab societies as permanent enemies, and asks that the history of coexistence be taught alongside the history of the expulsions.[cite:rs_ch01_uw_egypt1956] The record supports something close to this. Some communities were expelled or driven out by violence and law, some left through organized operations, many left under both pressures at once, and the balance differed by country and by year. Whether the Jewish departures and the Palestinian displacement of 1948 can be set side by side as an "exchange" is a separate question, taken up in [scene:s00e3|the next section].

Much remains unsettled. The overall total is a range, and different authors set its ends for their own reasons. For Aleppo, Aden and Bahrain this book has the violence but not the departures that followed. For Egypt it has neither the destinations nor a full count of the 1948 wave. The amount paid to Morocco under Operation Yachin is not given. The sources also leave open the question each family faced: how far a given departure was flight, how far it was choice, and how far it was the result of someone else's negotiation. The record shows only that all three happened.

sections.h: "An Even Population Exchange"? Two Displacements Compared
sections.html:
Two great displacements followed the end of British rule in Palestine. In the war of 1947–1949 roughly 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced, the event Palestinians call the Nakba. Over the next quarter-century most of the Jewish communities of the Arab world left the countries where they lived. A familiar way of settling the account sets one against the other. In this telling the two were a clean and roughly equal population exchange: Jews out of Arab countries, Arabs out of Palestine, the one cancelling the other. Both displacements are real and documented, and both were grievous for the people who lived through them. What does not hold up is the claim that they were one matched exchange. Set side by side, they differ in mechanism, in duration, in the number of governments involved and in what happened to the displaced afterwards.

Start with the Palestinian displacement. Its scale and timing are documented as concentrated: roughly 700,000 to 750,000 people displaced within a single war of about eighteen months, from 1947 to 1949. Direct military and paramilitary action substantially drove it, including massacres at named places, Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and al-Dawayima. It was carried out by an identifiable set of forces: the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi, and after independence the Israel Defense Forces.[cite:wiki_nakba] [cite:tandfonline_nakba_education] The displaced were not allowed to return. The causes, the individual episodes and the historians' arguments over them are told in their own place [scene:s10|the Nakba] and [scene:np_s01|the historiography of 1948]. For the comparison here, the shape is what matters: one war, one set of forces, a compressed timeline.

The dashboard panel above gives the round number most often used, about 700,000 Palestinians displaced in 1948, beside a United Nations estimate of about 711,000. Both fall at the low end of the 700,000–750,000 range used in this section. Precision matters less here than order of magnitude and speed: a population of that size left or was driven from its towns and villages within roughly eighteen months.

The Jewish departures had a different shape. They unfolded from roughly 1948 to 1972, nearly a quarter of a century, across many countries under separate governments, each with its own triggers. Iraq's community left largely in an airlift of 1950–51. Egypt's Jews left in two waves, in 1948 and again after the Suez Crisis of 1956. Algeria's exodus came during that country's war of independence in the early 1960s, more than a decade after 1948.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] [cite:hxstem_long_shadow_nakba] The causes ranged from persecution and violence, including the Farhud in Baghdad in 1941 and the riots that followed the partition vote, to organized emigration operations run by Israel and Jewish organizations. Even the total is disputed. Estimates run from roughly 650,000 to 900,000, depending on method and on the end year chosen.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] [cite:hxstem_long_shadow_nakba] A survey of the regional aftermath puts the figure for Arab countries and Iran, from 1948 into the 1970s, "commonly in the range of 800,000–900,000".[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] The country-by-country record, with each figure's source, is set out in [scene:ch01_exodus_map|the previous section]. None of this lessens what individual communities suffered. It describes a process of a different kind.

The two processes also sat inside the same regional upheaval. The 1947–49 war ended with about 700,000 Palestinians displaced. In the following years the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank sharply through emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution, in proportions that varied by country.[cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] The defeat discredited the Arab governments that had fought the war. Armies and publics blamed their rulers. Syria's government fell to a military coup in March 1949,[cite:w_1949_syria_coup] Egypt's monarchy in 1952[cite:w_1952_egypt] and Iraq's in 1958.[cite:w_1958_iraq] Three governments fell within a decade. Neither of the easy readings survives this record. 1948 changed a great deal, so "nothing changed after 1948" is wrong. But the revolts of the 1920s and 1930s show that the region's instability was already there, so "every problem comes from 1948" is wrong too. What 1948 added was a permanent refugee question, a state of war, and a powerful political cause. The departure of Arab Jews belongs to that upheaval, but it was spread across years and governments that the war of 1948 did not itself control.

A second difference lies in what came after. Israel's government granted citizenship to the Jewish arrivals and absorbed roughly 600,000 immigrants over four years, doubling the country's Jewish population.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] Most Arab host states did not extend citizenship to Palestinian refugees or their descendants, even after more than seven decades. The continuing work of UNRWA, a refugee agency dedicated to Palestinians alone, reflects that difference.[cite:wiki_jewish_exodus_muslim_world] Different sides cite this asymmetry for opposite arguments, but the fact itself is documented either way. It does not explain each host state's reasons, which differed by country and period.

The common question "why don't Arab countries just take the refugees?" has a different answer in each country. Jordan is the main exception. Under its nationality law of 1954 it gave citizenship to most of the Palestinians who arrived after 1948. It hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens, although Human Rights Watch has documented arbitrary revocations of that citizenship.[cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees] Lebanon hosts about 400,000 registered refugees, roughly 10% of its population. Palestinians there were barred from dozens of professions outside the camps and, under a property law of 2001, from owning real estate. Lebanon justified these measures as preventing tawteen, permanent settlement, and they are linked to the country's sectarian balance.[cite:fmr_lebanon] [cite:aj_lebanon_property] Egypt and the Gulf states offered residency without a path to citizenship.

The two sides explain the policy differently. The Arab states' stated reason is that the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return". The League's Casablanca Protocol of 1965 promised refugees rights to work and travel, but it was applied unevenly.[cite:fmr_lebanon] Critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue that the policy kept refugees in limbo as a political tool. Both readings describe the same outcome: Jordan absorbed refugees, while other states restricted them in order to keep a claim of return alive. The question returned, outside this volume's period, after 7 October. Egypt's President el-Sisi and Jordan's King Abdullah refused to take in people from Gaza. Analysts noted that Palestinians forced to leave had historically not been allowed to return, and Egypt warned of militants in Sinai. The position was summed up in reporting as "no refugees in Jordan, no refugees in Egypt": a fear that any exit would be a one-way door.[cite:pbs_egypt_refugees] Later chapters take this up in its own period.

The "even exchange" framing is rejected from both directions, which is unusual in this debate. Sources sympathetic to the Palestinian narrative call the comparison "profoundly unfounded", given the different mechanisms involved.[cite:palestineremembered_arab_jews_expelled] Some sources sympathetic to the Israeli narrative reject it for the opposite reason. They argue that the Jewish displacement, sometimes cited as the larger in raw numbers, has been ignored in international discourse.[cite:israelfactcheck_jewish_refugees] The two camps agree on nothing beyond this point, and their own preferred framings differ sharply. They do agree, for opposite reasons, that treating the two processes as one symmetrical event flattens real differences. The strongest version of the Palestinian objection is that a war-driven displacement by one set of forces, with return then barred, cannot be offset by departures from other countries that unfolded over decades, often through organized emigration. The strongest version of the opposing objection is that hundreds of thousands of Jews lost homes, property and citizenship and have received little recognition, while Palestinian refugees have a dedicated international agency of their own.

The record leaves several things open. The Jewish total remains a range, and the Palestinian figure is itself a range of estimates. This section does not rank the two displacements or judge which caused greater suffering. Its point is narrower. Two real events had different shapes, and the word "exchange" fits neither of them. The sources here also do not give each Arab host state's full reasons for withholding citizenship, beyond the Arab League's stated rationale and Lebanon's stated fear of permanent settlement. Recognizing that the two histories differ does not make either group's loss count for less. It means each has to be told on its own record.

chapters.label: Chapter 6
chapters.title: How the Story Is Told
chapters.intro:
The Baseline ends with the channels through which most people meet this history: the classroom, the historians, organized state messaging, and the platforms on which the argument is now conducted. The chapter comes last because the reader can now set those channels against the record laid out in the chapters before it, and because the contest over how the story is told is itself part of the documented history.

The first section follows the story as American students meet it: the textbooks of four publishers, a federal law that bars the Department of Education from directing curriculum, publishers who certify their own accuracy, and the day schools and Birthright trips that reinforce the story for some Jewish students.[cite:usc_20_1232a] [cite:wiki_birthright_israel] It holds the Palestinian Authority's textbooks to the same test, through a study commissioned by the European Union and published in 2021.[cite:gei_faq] The second section maps how historians argue about 1948: the older Israeli account, the "new historians" who worked in archives opened in the 1980s, their critics, and the dispute between the settler-colonial and national-liberation frames.[cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:massad_settler_colonial] The third sets out coordination on the record: a pollster's language guide of 2009, a covert campaign that Israeli officials tied to a ministry which denies it, and paid influencer contracts disclosed under American foreign-agent law, alongside an Iran-linked network aimed at Israelis.[cite:luntz_pdf] [cite:toi_stoic] [cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:calcalist_iran_social_media_network] The last examines content moderation: a Human Rights Watch report of 1,050 cases, Meta's own commissioned review, the takedown requests of Israel's Cyber Unit, and antisemitic content that evaded moderation in the same years.[cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:adl_tiktok_antisemitism_loopholes]

The record in this chapter runs in more than one direction, and the sections say so. What it supports is narrower than either familiar story: not purely organic opinion and not a single directing hand, but named institutions, documented sums and stated limits.

sections.h: How the Story Is Taught
sections.html:
Most Americans meet this history long before they meet its documents. It reaches them in a sequence: a textbook, then a teacher, then a museum, a film and the evening news. Each pass reinforces the one before it. The version that results is usually remembered as the story itself, the true account of an ancient people returning home. What it actually is, on inspection, is one framing of a documented modern political project, and the framing and the project are not the same thing. This section is an inventory rather than an accusation. It sets out where the story is taught, who pays for which parts of the teaching, what the teaching leaves out, and how the same test applies to the textbooks on the other side.

The first stage is the classroom. Four publishers, Houghton Mifflin Harcourt, Pearson, McGraw-Hill and Holt McDougal, reach the great majority of American world-history students in grades 6 through 12. How their books cover Israel and Palestine has been studied in the peer-reviewed literature: Sean Yom examined the framing of American world-history textbooks in 2013, and Nurit Peled-Elhanan published a mirror study of Israeli school textbooks in 2012. [cite:peled_elhanan_textbooks] The pattern these studies describe is not falsehood. It is emphasis. Some events are named: the Holocaust, the 1948 declaration, the 1967 war. Others are compressed: the Nakba, the 1953 CIA coup in Iran that reshaped the region, the Sabra and Shatila massacre of 1982. Some words are used, such as "conflict," "war" and "unrest." Others tend to be avoided. One is "occupation," a status that, in the research behind this book, international law has applied for 59 years. Another is "apartheid," the subject of published reports since 2021 by B'Tselem, [cite:btselem_apartheid_2021] Human Rights Watch [cite:hrw_israel_apartheid] and Amnesty International. [cite:amnesty_israel_apartheid] The effect, on this account, is that a student can reach adulthood with a vocabulary and a set of reflexes but without the record itself.

"Emphasis, not lies" can sound like a small distinction. A concrete case shows how large it can be. A textbook can say, accurately and in one clean sentence, that Jewish settlers purchased land in Palestine. A fuller account would add what this library's own research on the land-purchase mechanism had to assemble from scratch, because the survey textbooks did not supply it. The Ottoman government passed a Palestine-specific law in 1881–82 barring land purchase by foreign Jews. In 1892 it required imperial approval even for purchases by Ottoman Jewish citizens. Buyers worked around these rules through Ottoman-citizen intermediaries and through the consular protections known as the "capitulations," and in the 1890s the United States State Department found itself in a dispute over Russian Jewish emigrants who had naturalized as Americans in order to claim consular protection for land purchases in Palestine. Entire villages of tenant farmers were evicted as a result of such sales. None of this is obscure. It appears in Wikipedia's article on Jewish land purchase in Palestine and in the United States government's own published diplomatic archive. It does not appear in the four publishers' coverage. Both versions "cover the topic." Only the second describes the laws, the loopholes and the institutions through which the process actually ran, and a reader who knows only the first has no way to ask the next question, because nothing signals that there is one.

That example has limits, and they should be stated. It shows one significant mechanism missing from mainstream coverage. It does not show that every omission is this consequential, and it does not show that the omission was deliberate rather than the ordinary product of space limits in a survey course. What it does show is that emphasis alone, without one false sentence, can remove a documented mechanism from what a reader is able to know.

Compression works on people as well as events. Jews are not one lineage. The documented traditions include the Ashkenazi of Central and Eastern Europe, the Sephardi of Iberia and the diaspora after 1492, the Mizrahi of the Middle East and North Africa (including Iraq, Yemen, Morocco, Iran, Syria and Egypt), the Beta Israel of Ethiopia, the Bene Israel of India, the Jews of Kaifeng in China, the Bukharan Jews of Central Asia, and Georgian, Yemenite and Karaite communities. No one disputes that any of these are Jewish. The point is that they exist, and that American K-12 material typically folds the whole tradition into a single narrative centered on Ashkenazi experience, with Mizrahi and Sephardi Jews appearing briefly or not at all. Ella Shohat's 1988 essay documented the same asymmetry inside Israel. [cite:shohat_sephardim_israel] The compression has a consequence. Political Zionism, organized in 1897, emerged in specifically European Jewish settings, and an education that leaves out the non-European traditions makes it easier to treat "Zionism" and "all Jews" as one thing, a conflation the record does not support. The lineages themselves are treated at length elsewhere in this volume.

Why the textbook chain carries no correction is a question of structure, and each link in it is a matter of law or record. Federal law, at 20 U.S.C. § 1232a, bars the Department of Education from exercising any "direction, supervision, or control" over school curriculum. [cite:usc_20_1232a] That is a legal prohibition, not an oversight gap. Approval of textbooks falls to the states, and even there the review process places responsibility for accuracy on the publishers, who certify their own books. Virginia's textbook review documentation says so directly. [cite:va_textbook_review] In 2015, after a widely publicized error, Texas considered adding independent university historians to check textbooks for factual accuracy, and the state board voted the proposal down. [cite:tx_board_rejects_factcheck] The third link is ownership. A major textbook publisher is a private company in a market with no ownership screening related to accuracy, so anyone may acquire one, for any reason and with any history.

Once an unchecked claim enters a textbook, it can also compound. Students and later writers meet it in good faith and cite it; others cite them; and each new citation looks like independent confirmation when it is the same uncorrected origin repeated. The cartoonist Randall Munroe coined a name for this sequence, "citogenesis." [cite:xkcd_978_citogenesis] A tracked case shows it at work: a false claim about the history of health economics began on Wikipedia with no real source behind it, was repeated across several apparently independent articles, and was finally cited as settled fact by a newspaper columnist who had no way of knowing that the whole trail led back to one unverified starting point. [cite:cornell_citogenesis_blog] No one in that chain acted in bad faith. Each assumed that someone earlier had done the checking.

The mechanism is general. Any well-funded owner of a major textbook or reference publisher inherits the same structural gap, on any subject, not because of a conspiracy but because no layer of the system performs an accuracy check. Each link is legal and, taken alone, unremarkable. Chained together, they describe a system in which the absence of a check is a matter of design rather than neglect.

The ownership link has a documented example. The story travels through the press, and the ownership of the press is a matter of record. Robert Maxwell was born Jan Ludvik Hoch in Czechoslovakia in 1923. He survived the Holocaust, which killed most of his family, served in the British Army and anglicized his name after the war. Between 1984 and 1991 he assembled Mirror Group Newspapers, publisher of the Daily Mirror, one of Britain's highest-circulation tabloids, which reached millions of readers a day; the academic publisher Pergamon Press; the language-education company Berlitz; and Macmillan Publishing, one of the largest textbook and reference publishers used in American schools, which he acquired in 1988 for $2.6 billion. His relationship with Israeli intelligence is described in Seymour Hersh's The Samson Option, [cite:hersh_samson] in the work of Tom Bower, whose biography Maxwell: The Outsider appeared in 1988, [cite:bower_maxwell] and in Gordon Thomas and Martin Dillon's Robert Maxwell, Israel's Superspy of 2002; the name Bergman also appears among the sources on the point. The biographies, working from different sources, describe a relationship with Mossad that reportedly included helping to sell software from Israeli technology firms to intelligence services around the world. The exact mechanism is contested in its specifics. The broader pattern, a well-connected publisher with intelligence relationships on several sides, including British ties and alleged Soviet-era contacts through Pergamon's dealings with Eastern Bloc academic publishing, appears in more than one of these books rather than resting on any single one.

Maxwell died on 5 November 1991, found floating near his yacht, the Lady Ghislaine, off the Canary Islands. The official Spanish autopsy and a later Israeli examination both concluded that he fell overboard, with drowning the probable cause. Whether that was an accident, a suicide amid mounting financial exposure or something else was never settled to the satisfaction of every investigator, and this book leaves the uncertainty as uncertainty. He received an Israeli state funeral on the Mount of Olives, with six intelligence chiefs in attendance. Days after his death it emerged that he had taken hundreds of millions of pounds from his companies' pension funds to cover debt. His daughter Ghislaine was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking with Jeffrey Epstein, a later turn the record captures but does not explain. His full story is told in [scene:s16|Robert Maxwell and the press empire].

What the Maxwell case shows must be stated as carefully as what it does not. It shows that a man who owned major British media and a major American textbook publisher is described, in independently researched biographies, as having ties to Israeli intelligence. It does not show that any Daily Mirror story about Israel or Zionism was ordered by an intelligence service, and it does not show that Maxwell altered any Macmillan textbook. No primary source located for this book makes either claim, and this book does not make them. The point is structural. Ownership is a documented fact; editorial influence is a separate and much harder claim that would need its own evidence, case by case. What the case establishes is that the opportunity existed in a chain designed with no one checking the checker.

Beyond the drift of editorial emphasis there is a second, different thing: a formal, state-funded operation built to shape this same narrative. Its name is hasbara, Hebrew for "explanation." It was formalized as Zionist institutional policy before the Second World War, a step credited to Nahum Sokolow, and it has served continuously since as Israel's own name for its public diplomacy and propaganda. It is not a term invented by critics; it is the word the apparatus uses for itself. According to reporting on the 2026 budget, Israel quadrupled its public-diplomacy budget to $730 million, and the foreign minister described the matter as an "existential issue." [cite:nuclearnews_730m_budget] Israel's Institute for National Security Studies mapped, in a single research pass after October 2023, more than 120 civilian "war rooms," 40 organizations building hasbara technology and 100 databases, which is the apparatus documenting its own scale rather than an outside estimate. A documented influencer scheme has reportedly offered roughly $7,000 per pro-Israel social-media post. Many still-circulating talking points have been traced to a named source, Frank Luntz's 2009 "Global Language Dictionary," commissioned by The Israel Project. [cite:medium_luntz_kryptonite_hasbara] The contracts, filings and budgets of this operation are examined in [scene:s00a3|coordination on the record].

The difference between the two mechanisms matters. Textbook emphasis is closer to organic drift: many editors, trained alike, reaching for the same framing without coordination. Hasbara has a name, a budget and a stated goal. Neither explains all pro-Israel opinion. Many people hold pro-Israel views independent of any funded campaign, just as many hold critical views independent of any funded campaign. What is documented is the existence and the scale of the organized effort, not a claim that it accounts for every view.

For a subset of Jewish students, the story is reinforced twice more, through two separate programs at two different ages. The two should not be merged into one organization, which would overstate what is documented. The first is the day school. Jewish day schools set their own curricula, and disclosed philanthropic funding, from the Jim Joseph Foundation among others, specifically supports Israel-centered educational content, including elementary-level pilot programs. Comparable day-school systems exist in other countries. The schools are expensive. According to SAPIR journal's 2025 reporting, average annual tuition nationally is about $24,000, and runs from $25,000 to $50,000 a year in cities such as New York; according to reporting in JNS and the Cleveland Jewish News, a full K-12 day-school education for one child can cost about half a million dollars before college. In 2026 the Israeli government approved a NIS 100 million ($33.4 million) budget, matched by philanthropic donations through the Jewish Federations of North America, to raise day-school enrollment in the United States and Canada, a combined $66.7 million. A further NIS 200 million plan, about $67 million, was approved unanimously by the Israeli cabinet in 2026 with a focus on enrolling more American Jewish children in day schools, a direct government line for Diaspora education. The sources describe these as separate plans; whether they overlap is not established in the material behind this book. Behind both stands the broader base of the Jewish Federations of North America, whose combined endowments are described as holding "tens of billions" in assets and whose annual campaigns raise "hundreds of millions."

The second program is Birthright Israel, also known as Taglit. Founded in 1999, it offers a free ten-day trip to Israel to young adults aged 18 to 26. Benjamin Netanyahu made the first Israeli government funding guarantee in 1998, during his first term. More than 800,000 young adults have taken the trip. [cite:wiki_birthright_israel] Roughly 27 percent of the funding comes directly from the Israeli government; about 67 percent comes from individual donors, among them Sheldon Adelson, who gave more than $400 million before his death in 2021; the remainder comes from the Claims Conference and other sources, including Jewish Federations. More than $2 billion has been spent over the program's history. The Birthright Israel Foundation's own figures put current annual worldwide programming at $172 million to $175 million, up from a reported $92.9 million budget in 2023. Security has historically been its single most expensive line, at $72 million. An Ernst & Young study found that in its first 13 years the program brought more than $825 million into the Israeli economy through tourism, hotels and meals, separate from its own budget.

The program is international. Participants come from roughly 68 to 70 countries, and the foundation itself presents the trip as "part of a global movement," naming Argentina, Brazil, Mexico, France, the United Kingdom, South Africa and India among them. About 80 percent of participants come from the United States and Canada; the remaining fifth is spread across dozens of countries. [cite:birthright_global_movement] Birthright has also served as a model that heritage-trip programs in Hungary, Greece and Macedonia were built to copy.

Its effect has been measured by its own commissioned research. A 2025 Brandeis University study, funded by Birthright, found that the year's participants came back "much more connected to Israel, and much more likely to identify with the political right," and more likely to "provide a counterargument to claims that Israel is committing genocide." [cite:intercept_birthright_2025] This is the program's own research describing its own effect, not an outside accusation. It measured an average across a cohort, not a uniform outcome for every participant, and it describes only the subset of students who attend day school and later take the trip, not Jewish education as a whole.

The cumulative product of textbook, press, museum, film, news and, for some, school and trip is described here as a reflex rather than a conclusion. A person who has passed through the sequence reaches adulthood with associations already in place: Israel with democracy, Palestinians with terrorism, criticism with antisemitism, the conflict with antiquity. These are associations, not findings the record supports. The research behind this section points to Daniel Kahneman's work on fast, intuitive "System 1" thinking, in which emotional associations bypass analytical review. The practical test is simple. When the reflex fires against something the documents show, the sequence is doing its work, and noticing that is where examination begins. How the same associations were first put before the American public, through the themes of refuge, the Bible and democracy, is the subject of [scene:sell_s01|how Israel was sold to Americans in 1948].

A standard applied to one side's schoolbooks must be applied to the other's. The familiar claim runs in two forms: that Palestinian children are taught to hate, or that their textbooks are fine. A study commissioned by the European Union tested the question. The Georg Eckert Institute for International Textbook Research analyzed about 200 Palestinian Authority textbooks and teachers' guides released in 2020, and published its findings in 2021. It concluded that the books "adhere to UNESCO standards" on human-rights education while expressing "a narrative of resistance" and "antagonism towards Israel." It found some content with "escalatory potential," including in science, technology and mathematics subjects, and some antisemitic depictions. It found no direct calls for violence against Israelis. [cite:gei_faq] The Institute's director later told the European Parliament that books containing antisemitism or incitement do not comply with UNESCO standards. [cite:hansard_textbooks]

Each side reads the same study as proof of its case. IMPACT-se, a monitoring group whose reports the European Parliament has cited, says the study confirms systemic incitement. [cite:impactse_gei] That reading draws its strength from the study's documented findings of antagonism, escalatory content and antisemitic depictions, and from the director's statement that such material falls short of UNESCO standards. Others, including European analysts, say the study largely disproved exaggerated claims, and they note that it did not examine Israeli textbooks, which other researchers have also criticized. [cite:eumep_textbooks] That reading draws its strength from the study's finding of UNESCO-standard human-rights content and its finding of no direct calls for violence. Peled-Elhanan's work on Israeli schoolbooks, mentioned above, is one such criticism. Read as a whole, the study supports neither headline. Problem content exists and is documented; a curriculum of incitement to violence is not what the study found.

Several things remain unsettled. The research behind this section establishes what the four American publishers emphasize and omit, but not why: whether through deliberate choice or the ordinary compression of a survey course. It establishes Maxwell's ownership and the biographies' account of his intelligence ties, but not that he used either to shape a single story or textbook, and it does not resolve how he died. It measures Birthright's effect on one cohort through a study the program paid for, and has no independent study to set beside it. It reports the hasbara budget and the influencer payments through secondary reporting, not the budget documents themselves. And the European study covered one side's textbooks only. The method that follows from all of this is the one this book uses throughout: name the source, say who made it and who paid for it, separate what a document shows from what it is said to show, and apply the same test to both sides.

sections.h: How Historians Argue About 1948
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that historians agree on what happened in 1948, and that only politicians and activists dispute it. They do not agree. The scholars whose work is cited throughout this library divide in two separate ways. The first division is over events and intent: what happened to the Palestinian Arabs who left or were driven from their homes, and how far it was planned. The second is over framing: what kind of movement Zionism was in the first place. Knowing where each scholar stands does not settle either question, but it allows a reader to see, when a later chapter cites a historian, whose interpretation is being offered and what the other camp would say in reply. This section maps the camps. It is a guide to the interpreters, not a verdict on them.

The first debate has a history of its own, and it turns on access to documents. Until the 1980s the dominant Israeli account held that the Palestinians had largely left on their own, or at the urging of Arab leaders. In the 1980s Israel began to declassify its state and military archives, and a group of scholars who came to be called the "new historians," Benny Morris and Ilan Pappé among them, went into those files. What they documented was expulsions, massacres and the deliberate prevention of Palestinian return. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The older account had denied these things; the archives recorded them.

The new historians did not reach one conclusion. Morris and Pappé, working with the same newly opened material, came to sharply different judgments about how far the expulsions were planned. That disagreement matters because the documents of the period can be read in more than one way: an order or a pattern of operations can be taken as evidence of a design, or as the outcome of local decisions in a war. The arguments over one such document are traced in [scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet and the argument about what it was]. The historian Walid Khalidi, writing on Deir Yassin, argued that the Haganah, a Jewish armed force of the period, was involved there at every stage. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] These are claims about intent and responsibility, and they are the claims on which the archive itself is least conclusive.

The new historians have their own critics. Historians such as Efraim Karsh reject the expulsion-centered account altogether. In their reading, the decisive facts of 1948 are the choices of Arab leaders and the Arab rejection of partition; the departure of the Palestinian population follows from those choices rather than from a design on the Jewish side. [cite:dailyalert_194_karsh] The strongest form of this case is that a war launched against partition carries responsibility for its consequences, and that an account which begins with expulsions has already chosen where the story starts. The strongest form of the new historians' case is that the expulsions, massacres and the barring of return are recorded in Israel's own state and military files, and that no account of the war's causes removes what those files show was done. The two camps are not arguing about whether the archives exist. They are arguing about what the archives show regarding intent, and where responsibility lies.

A second debate concerns framing rather than events, and it runs alongside the first. Scholars such as Joseph Massad describe Zionism as a settler-colonial project. Their evidence is, in part, the movement's own vocabulary: Zionist leaders used the word "colonization" of their own work, including Vladimir Jabotinsky in his 1923 essay "The Iron Wall." [cite:massad_settler_colonial] On this reading, the events of 1948 are one phase of a longer process of settlement and displacement. Others describe Zionism as a national liberation movement, and as a refugee movement: the effort of a people with ancient roots in the land to find safety after centuries of persecution. On that reading, the same events belong to the founding of a refuge and to a war over partition. Each frame can point to documents. Neither is settled by them, because the dispute is over which category best describes a set of facts that both sides can read.

How the older account came to be told, and how it changed as the files opened, is the subject of [scene:np_s01|how the Nakba was told]. For further reading across these positions, the works this library draws on include Shlaim's The Iron Wall, [cite:shlaim_iron_wall] Masalha's Palestine: A Four Thousand Year History [cite:masalha_four_thousand] and Said's work on the question of Palestine. [cite:said_question_palestine]

Part of the record is still closed. Material in Israeli military archives on some events, including Deir Yassin, remains classified. That means some of the questions above cannot be answered by any historian on the documents now available: claims about planning and about responsibility for particular events rest, in part, on files that no one outside the archive has read. The framing dispute will not be resolved by new files at all, because it is a disagreement over interpretation rather than over evidence.

The working rule that follows is to read the document first and the interpreter second. Facts drawn from the archives, such as an order, a report or a dated record of what was done in a given village, are shared ground, and historians on every side work from them. Judgments about intent, and the choice of frame, are where scholars divide. The chapters that follow cite the documents and say whose interpretation is whose, so that a reader can keep the two apart and reach a judgment of their own.

sections.h: Who Coordinates What Gets Posted
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that pro-Israel content on social media is organic grassroots enthusiasm, and that any suggestion of coordination is conspiracy thinking. The opposite assumption, that every pro-Israel post is centrally directed, is just as common in other circles. The record for the years from 2009 to 2025 supports neither. It names a pollster and the organization that hired him, government ministries and the sums they spent, consulting firms and the contracts they registered with the United States Justice Department, the instructions sent to paid influencers, and a meeting attended by a head of government. It also documents an Israel-aligned campus organization caught running fake pages, and influence networks aimed against Israel. What follows sets out each piece in turn, with the weight each piece of evidence can bear.

A point of method comes first. Knowing where a talking point came from is one step; checking it against the record is another. A talking point that was written, tested and paid for is not false for that reason. Many are sincerely held by people who were never paid to repeat them, and some are accurate. The origin of a claim is not a verdict on it. That is why the coordination documented here sits beside, rather than replaces, the graded catalog of claims elsewhere in this library. The contracts tell the reader who chose a message and paid to spread it. They do not tell the reader whether the message is true.

Where the talking points come from. In 2009 The Israel Project commissioned the pollster Frank Luntz to test which language would win Americans' support.[cite:wiki_tip] The result, the Global Language Dictionary, was an internal document marked not for distribution. It was leaked to Newsweek.[cite:archive_luntz] Its rules read as a manual of persuasion rather than a statement of belief. Advocates were told not to pretend that Israel was without fault, and to concede a point before making their own. They were told to repeat the phrase "Iran-backed Hamas." They were told that "no matter what you're asked," they should "bridge to a productive pro-Israel message," and that Israel should be framed in "the language of America: democracy, freedom, security, and peace."[cite:luntz_pdf] The guide's own polling found that settlements were unpopular with the American public, even among Israel's supporters, and so it advised advocates to turn conversations toward peace.[cite:luntz_pdf]

The guide matters for two reasons. First, it shows that phrases a reader may meet as spontaneous opinion were, in at least this documented case, selected by survey for their effect on an American audience. Second, its own findings undercut the idea that support for Israel in the United States meant support for every Israeli policy: the polling located a weak point, settlements, and the advice was to steer around it rather than defend it. An earlier section traces how some of the guide's phrases still circulate [scene:s00a|how the story is taught]. The guide itself does not show that any given statement online came from it.

STOIC: a ministry, a firm, and fake accounts. The most concrete case of covert activity concerns STOIC, a political consulting and marketing firm based in Tel Aviv.
