According to the New York Times, which cited four Israeli officials and documents, Israel's Ministry of Diaspora Affairs allocated about $2 million in October 2023 and hired STOIC to run the campaign.[cite:toi_stoic] The Times reported that the operation ran fake accounts and three fake news sites aimed at members of the United States Congress, especially Black Democrats such as Hakeem Jeffries and Raphael Warnock, urging them to keep funding Israel's military.[cite:toi_stoic] [cite:opb_stoic] Hundreds of the accounts posed as Americans.[cite:opb_stoic] NPR's account of the same operation describes AI-generated content aimed at younger, progressive Americans, carrying pro-Israel messaging on the Gaza war.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence]

The operation was first identified by FakeReporter, an Israeli watchdog group that tracks misinformation. It was an Israeli organization, not a foreign critic, that found it, and it tied five websites to the operation.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] The New York Times confirmed the reporting independently. The platforms then acted. Meta removed 510 Facebook accounts and 32 Instagram accounts that had posed as Jewish students, Black Americans and "concerned citizens."[cite:cyberscoop_stoic] OpenAI called STOIC a "for-hire Israeli threat actor."[cite:cyberscoop_stoic] Meta stated that it had deleted the accounts before they gained traction with real users, and both companies said the campaign won little engagement.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] [cite:cyberscoop_stoic]

The reports do not agree in every detail, and the differences are worth setting out rather than smoothing over.

The central fact is disputed by the party named in it. The Ministry of Diaspora Affairs denied involvement.[cite:toi_stoic] Against that denial stands the Times's sourcing to four Israeli officials and documents, the watchdog's findings, and the two platforms' own enforcement actions. Criticism also came from an Israeli former diplomat: Michael Oren, a former ambassador, called the campaign damaging interference.[cite:toi_stoic] STOIC did not respond to interview requests.[cite:npr_stoic_ai_influence] The record therefore shows a covert operation with a named firm, a specific sum and a ministry identified by officials as its funder, caught by a watchdog and removed by the platforms. It does not show that the operation was the only one of its kind, or the largest, and the companies' own statements indicate it failed to reach many real people.

The budget behind the open campaign. STOIC was covert. The larger effort that followed was conducted largely in the open, under American disclosure law. In December 2024, during coalition negotiations, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar secured an allocation of $150 million for global public diplomacy, hasbara in Hebrew. According to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, that was about twenty times previous hasbara budgets, and the ministry received the funds from May 2025.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] An earlier section records a separate figure for 2026, a public-diplomacy budget of $730 million, and the history of the word hasbara.[cite:nuclearnews_730m_budget] The two figures belong to different years and come from different sources; this book does not have a basis for breaking either down line by line.

The paper trail: the foreign-agent filings. The details of how that money was spent in the United States became public through filings with the Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act, known as FARA. Every figure in the paragraphs that follow exists because that law compelled its disclosure.

The first track was run by Bridges Partners LLC, a Washington-based firm. It worked for Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs through an intermediary, Havas Media Group Germany.[cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara] Its filings show it was hired to manage an influencer network code-named the "Esther Project," from June to November 2025, under a contract of up to $900,000.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] The contract was itemized: $60,000 upfront for recruitment; $140,000 as five or six influencers began posting; up to $250,000 a month for influencer fees and production; and $50,000 for wrap-up.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] HonestReporting's reading of the same filings found roughly $900,000 invoiced for an "Influencer Campaign," of which roughly $552,946 remained for payments to the influencers themselves once administrative and production costs were taken out.[cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara] The campaign expected 75 to 90 posts. Dividing the money by the posts, analysts arrived at roughly $6,100 to $7,400 per post.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] That calculation is the source of the figure of about $7,000 per post that circulates widely.[cite:globeistan_7000_per_post] [cite:honestreporting_bridges_partners_fara]

The second track was larger. Brad Parscale, formerly Donald Trump's campaign manager, registered his firm, Clock Tower X LLC, as a foreign agent for Israel under a reported $6 million contract for "strategic communications." It promised 100 ads or pieces of content a month, plus 5,000 variations, an output the Jewish Telegraphic Agency notes would likely require automated tools.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara] [cite:globeistan_7000_per_post] A related trip in 2025 was partly funded by a foreign-ministry contract worth $86,000.[cite:jta_esther_project_fara]

The money can be followed from its source to its effects, as far as the filings and the complaint they prompted allow.

What coordination looked like from the inside. A payment shows that someone was hired. It does not show what they were told to say. That second layer was documented by an investigation in Time magazine, which found private group chats in which influencers taking part in a pro-Israel campaign were guided on the specific language to use in posts on X, Instagram and TikTok, and were paid up to $4,250 per post.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] A separate case shows the mechanism from the side of someone who said no. A Jewish influencer reported receiving a confidential brief from a different campaign, offering $1,500 to promote specific talking points under a non-disclosure agreement. He declined to sign it.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] Refusal is part of the record too: the offer was made, and it was not universally accepted.

The effort reached the top of the Israeli government. In September 2025, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met several American social media influencers in New York, specifically to enlist them in amplifying pro-Israel messaging in the United States.[cite:meo_israel_influencer_backfire] This was not a campaign run by a communications office several steps removed from political leadership; the head of government took part himself. The meeting's occurrence is documented. What was said in it, and whether every influencer present agreed to take part, is not in the public record these sources draw on.

The several payment figures in these reports, $1,500, up to $4,250, and roughly $6,100 to $7,400 per post, come from different campaigns and different documents. They should not be read as one price list, and the sources do not say whether the chats Time examined belonged to the Bridges Partners campaign.

The complaint and the open question. The firms registered. The influencers, as far as the filings show, did not. Public Citizen filed a formal complaint with the Justice Department's FARA Unit. It alleged that approximately 14 to 18 US-based influencers paid through the Bridges Partners contract were acting as unregistered agents of Israel's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and it asked the department to require disclosure of their names and contracts.[cite:citizen_fara_complaint] The sources available to this book do not record a ruling on the complaint. Whether individual influencers paid through a registered firm must register themselves is the legal question it raises, and it remains open. There is also a naming question. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency noted that it is unclear whether the "Esther Project" has any link to the Heritage Foundation's similarly named Project Esther, which a later volume of this library examines.[cite:wiki_esther_project_israel] [cite:citizen_fara_complaint]

The disclosure itself says something about how the law works. The same statute that a later volume of this library shows going unapplied to AIPAC did apply to these contracts, which is the only reason the campaign is documented in such detail. Openly registered persuasion and covert fake accounts are different things, and the record contains both.

A campus organization and a takedown. The record also contains a case where a platform acted against an Israel-aligned group on its own authority. The Israel on Campus Coalition (ICC) is the main convening organization of pro-Israel campus groups. Two claims about it carry different weight and should be kept apart. The first is reported, and less independently verified: that ICC gathered information on pro-Palestinian students through informants inside Jewish and pro-Israel student organizations, and passed it to Israel's Ministry of Strategic Affairs.[cite:wiki_israel_campus_coalition] The second is more concretely documented. ICC secretly ran misleading Facebook pages and advertisements aimed at the Palestinian-American poet Remi Kanazi, and in 2018 Facebook itself removed the pages, citing its own policies against misrepresentation.[cite:wiki_israel_campus_coalition] That is a platform's enforcement action, not only an outside accusation. Neither claim shows that such tactics are unique to ICC among advocacy organizations, or that every campus group affiliated with it engaged in them; what is documented is attributed to its national organization.

The other direction. An account that documented only one side's influence operations would not be a fair account. Operations aimed against Israel are documented in the same record. An Iran-linked network ran fake profiles, bots and groups across WhatsApp, X, Telegram, Facebook, TikTok and Instagram. It spread disinformation, impersonated journalists and rabbis, and worked specifically to stoke tensions among Israelis themselves, including content aimed at Israel's LGBTQ+ community and at ultra-Orthodox Jews.[cite:calcalist_iran_social_media_network] A 2025 report by an independent research organization, titled "Conflict Amplified: Disinformation and Hate in the Israel-Hamas War," documented disinformation and coordinated hate campaigns from several sides of the conflict, not from one alone.[cite:isd_conflict_amplified_2025] These sources establish that both kinds of operation exist. They give no basis for saying that the Iran-linked operations and the Israeli-funded ones were of comparable size or reach, in either direction. How the platforms themselves policed this content is the subject of the next section [scene:s00a2|the platforms].

What the record shows, and what it leaves open. Taken together, the documents establish a funded and coordinated messaging apparatus. Its parts can be named: a pollster's tested vocabulary; a ministry's covert contract, which the ministry denies; a foreign ministry's budget and the registered firms it paid; private instructions to paid influencers; and a prime minister's personal recruitment. That is the familiar claim of pure organic enthusiasm answered by the record. The same record does not support the opposite claim, that every pro-Israel or pro-Palestinian post is centrally directed. Unpaid supporters exist alongside the paid campaigns, one influencer turned the offer down, and influence operations run against Israel as well.

Several questions remain unsettled. The Ministry of Diaspora Affairs' denial of the STOIC campaign stands against the New York Times's sources, and the published accounts differ on its target and its number of websites. The breakdown of the $150 million beyond the single Bridges Partners contract is not public in these sources, nor is the outcome of Public Citizen's complaint. What was said in the September 2025 meeting is unknown. The informant claim against ICC is reported but less independently verified. No source here measures the relative scale of the Israeli-funded and Iran-linked operations, or how many people any of them persuaded. The firms' names, the sums and the dates are documented. How much effect the money had is not.

sections.h: The Platforms: Moderation as Contested Ground
sections.html:
The [scene:s00a|classroom and the textbook] are older arenas. A newer one is entirely contemporary: what happens to Palestinian and pro-Palestinian content on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and X, and what those platforms remove, suppress or leave up. Two simple stories dominate that argument. One holds that moderation is neutral, a matter of each company applying its own rules. The other holds that it is a secret, coordinated campaign to silence one side, and which side depends on who is telling it. The record for 2021 to 2026 is made up of formal human rights investigations, reviews the platforms commissioned themselves, a government office's own request figures, leaked internal data, the platforms' written policies and their denials, and watchdog findings that cut the other way. Read in full, it supports neither story.

The heaviest finding rests on two inquiries, begun by different parties two years apart. The first was Meta's own. In 2021 the company commissioned an independent investigation from Business for Social Responsibility (BSR) into its handling of content during the escalation of May 2021. The review, published in September 2022, concluded that Meta's moderation "appear[s] to have had an adverse human rights impact on the rights of Palestinian users." [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] The same review did not identify intentional bias. [cite:ibt_echoicide] The second inquiry came from outside. In December 2023 Human Rights Watch published a 51-page report, Meta's Broken Promises: Systemic Censorship of Palestine Content on Instagram and Facebook, which documented 1,050 cases of content being removed or suppressed, from more than 60 countries. [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] After its publication, Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote to Meta's chief executive, Mark Zuckerberg, demanding accountability. [cite:hrw_meta_broken_promises] An outside critic's conclusion is one kind of evidence. A conclusion reached by reviewers the company itself hired and paid is a stronger kind, and here the two point the same way on harm, while differing in emphasis on intent.

The number most often repeated from the Human Rights Watch report is "1,049 to 1." The cases were gathered from October and November 2023. Of the 1,050 the organization reviewed, 1,049 involved peaceful pro-Palestinian content and one involved content supporting Israel. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:bhrrc_hrw_meta] The report named the causes it found: flawed Meta policies, opaque enforcement, heavy reliance on automated systems, and deference to government requests, among them those of Israel's Cyber Unit. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] What the number can and cannot show matters as much as the number. Human Rights Watch described its cases as a collected dataset, not a representative global sample and not a comparison of censorship across platforms. The cases were reported by users who chose to send them in. [cite:ibt_echoicide] A set built that way can establish that a pattern of suppression occurred and what it looked like. It cannot, by its construction, measure the ratio of all pro-Palestinian to all pro-Israel content removed on Meta's services. Meta, for its part, disputes that it deliberately or systemically suppresses any voice. [cite:ibt_echoicide]

A methodological critique of the report also exists, and it belongs beside the report rather than after it. Calcalist, an Israeli technology publication, examined the Human Rights Watch study and identified potential biases in its sampling and in its choice of platforms, which could have affected its findings. [cite:calcalist_hrw_methodology_critique] The critique and the organization's own statement of its limits overlap: both turn on how the cases were collected.

The most precise reading of these sources together is narrower than either popular story. The record documents lopsided harm to pro-Palestinian speech on Meta's platforms. It does not document a deliberate plan. What it does document, in the BSR review and in the causes Human Rights Watch listed, is a design: policies, automated enforcement at scale, and a channel through which a government's requests reach the moderators. That finding is harder to dismiss than an accusation of intent, because it does not depend on proving what anyone wanted.

That channel has a name and its own published figures. Israel's Cyber Unit sits inside the State Attorney's Office. It sends what it calls "voluntary" requests to platforms asking them to remove content it considers incitement or support for terrorism. The requests carry no public legal process. [cite:eff_cyber_unit] The platform decides whether to act, and it almost always has. Since the office began reporting, the compliance rate has never fallen below 77 percent. In 2018 the Unit sent more than 14,000 requests to Google and Facebook, with compliance of about 90 to 92 percent. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] [cite:cjr_cyber_unit] In 2021 it sent 5,990 requests with 82 percent compliance, about 90 percent of them to Facebook and Instagram during the May escalation, the same weeks the BSR review examined. [cite:cjr_cyber_unit]

After 7 October 2023 the volume rose sharply. Between 7 October and 14 November 2023, a little under six weeks, the Unit sent 9,500 takedown requests, 60 percent of them to Meta. According to an Israeli official, the compliance rate was 94 percent. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] Leaked internal data reported by Drop Site News in 2025 indicates that Meta removed more than 90,000 posts at Israel's request, often within seconds and without human review. [cite:dropsite_meta_leak] Drop Site also reported that Meta expanded its automated removals after 7 October, affecting an estimated 38.8 million additional posts. These are reported figures from leaked material and are attributed here as such. [cite:dropsite_meta_leak]

The gap in this part of the record is one of accountability. Meta's Oversight Board recommended that the company formalize and publish how it handles government requests. Human Rights Watch asked the Cyber Unit which policies the removed posts had violated, and received no response. [cite:hrw_meta_promises] Israel describes the Unit's work as countering incitement and terrorism, which is a legitimate aim, and no source here disputes that some of what it flags is exactly that. The dispute is over scope, over transparency, and over who ends up silenced when a state office routinely asks platforms to remove speech and nearly always gets its way, with little public accounting of what was removed or why.

Human Rights Watch concentrated on Meta and noted that it received fewer reports about TikTok. [cite:sada_social_digital_rights_index_2024] A more granular, platform-by-platform count comes from Sada Social, a tracking organization, whose Digital Rights Index 2024 documented more than 25,000 violations against Palestinian digital content across the major platforms. It broke them down as Instagram 31 percent, TikTok 27 percent, Facebook 24 percent and X 12 percent. [cite:sada_social_digital_rights_index_2024] The breakdown is real and should be read precisely. A larger share for one platform can reflect more suppression on that platform. It can equally reflect a larger user base, easier complaint mechanisms, or the reach of Sada Social's own monitoring. The difference in reporting volume between Meta and TikTok is documented. What it says about each platform's actual moderation rate is not settled by these figures.

TikTok's ownership changed in the period. After the Oracle-led acquisition of TikTok's US operations in 2025–26, a Palestinian journalist and influencer known as Owda was banned from the platform. The new ownership has not publicly addressed the case. [cite:meo_us_tiktok_ownership_bans] Larry Ellison, central to the Oracle side of that deal, has an extensively documented history of major personal donations to Israeli military-support causes, traced elsewhere in this library. Those two facts, the ownership history and the ban, stand side by side in the record. The causal link between them has been discussed by observers. It has not been documented, and one named, dated case after a change of owner is not, on its own, proof of a new policy.

The rules themselves are another layer, and here the companies' own texts are the best evidence. Meta's Transparency Center states that the term "Zionist" "often refers to supporters of a political movement, which is not itself a protected characteristic under our policies, but in some cases may be used as a proxy to refer to Jewish or Israeli people, which are protected characteristics." [cite:meta_transparency_zionist_update] The distinction between a political movement and a people, which [scene:s00c|an earlier section of this volume] draws at length, is therefore written into the platform's own policy. Under its longstanding approach, Meta treated "Zionist" as a proxy for a protected group in two narrow circumstances: comparisons to rats, a documented antisemitic trope, and clear contextual substitution for "Jew" or "Israeli." Following a Policy Forum in March 2024, it expanded that proxy treatment further. [cite:meta_transparency_zionist_update] The policy text sets out the framework. It does not record the individual enforcement decisions made under it.

Meta's own press materials say it consulted roughly 145 stakeholders on the 2024 expansion, among them more than 10 pro-Palestinian, Muslim and Arab organizations, and Jewish Voice for Peace, an anti-Zionist Jewish organization. Jewish Voice for Peace was, in other words, inside the consultation, and it remained among the policy's critics. An academic co-signer of the Jerusalem Declaration on Antisemitism publicly criticized the resulting policy as ambiguous. Existing frameworks, including that declaration, already give clearer guidance on separating anti-Zionism from antisemitism, the critic argued, and under the new wording a call for equality within a single state could be misread as an antisemitic "denial of existence." [cite:novara_meta_zionist_ban] How much weight any one participant's input carried in the final text is not on the public record.

The case for the policy also rests on documented evidence. The American Jewish Committee, which advocated for it, cited its own 2023 survey, which found that 80 percent of American Jews say caring about Israel is an important part of being Jewish. On that basis it argued that "Zionist" is a meaningful proxy for Jewish identity in moderation decisions. [cite:ajc_meta_policy_welcome] The figure is real, and it carries weight: for a large majority of American Jews surveyed, caring about Israel is, by their own account, part of Jewish identity. By the same survey's arithmetic, roughly one in five American Jews do not say this. The survey figures do not describe what that fifth believe, only that a rule built on the proxy does not straightforwardly fit them.

TikTok moved separately to treat "Zionist" as hate speech in circumstances comparable to Meta's. [cite:chrisbennett_tiktok_zionist_label] As of July 2025, its Public Policy Manager for Hate Speech, who joined in 2025, was Erica Mindel, an American-Israeli former soldier in the Israel Defense Forces, described in press coverage including the Jerusalem Post and Jewish Insider as a "proud Zionist." [cite:wiki_erica_mindel] That is a fact about who holds the role that shapes the platform's rules on this exact question. It is stated here as such. No source here documents any specific biased decision by her, and none is implied.

Meta's rules then moved again. In January 2025, after a reported six-week internal review led by Zuckerberg and a small group of confidants, the company rolled back broader hate-speech enforcement and permitted content it had previously banned. The Anti-Defamation League's chief executive, Jonathan Greenblatt, publicly criticized the reversal. Meta did not immediately clarify whether the "Zionist" proxy rule survived it. [cite:jta_meta_reversal] Separately, a formal letter from Senator Warren's office set out that Meta had applied uneven moderation standards to Palestinian-related content compared with other comparable material. [cite:warren_senate_meta_letter]

The record also runs in the other direction, and it is just as documented. In November 2023 the Anti-Defamation League published a study finding specific loopholes in TikTok's own moderation that were being used to spread antisemitic content. It named two: slideshows made in TikTok's Photo Mode, and hashtag manipulation, both of which slipped past automated detection. [cite:adl_tiktok_antisemitism_loopholes] In January 2025 CyberWell, a watchdog organization, praised TikTok for improved removal of Holocaust-denial content relative to other platforms. And TikTok has formally denied the bias accusations made against it: Reuters reported the company calling claims from Malaysia that it suppressed pro-Palestinian content "unfounded." These findings do not cancel the earlier ones. Moderation failures that harm Palestinian users and moderation failures that let antisemitic content through are not mutually exclusive, and on this record both occurred, on the same platforms, in the same years.

Users, for their part, adapted. Palestinian and pro-Palestinian users developed documented ways around automated filters, the most visible being the watermelon. Its red, green, black and white match the colors of the Palestinian flag, and users turned to it because keyword- and image-based filters that flagged the flag did not flag the fruit. It is now recognized worldwide as shorthand for solidarity with Palestine, and it became that because of its origin as a way around moderation. [cite:wagingnonviolence_watermelon_algorithms] The workaround is evidence that the moderation of flag-related content was experienced widely enough to prompt one. It does not, by itself, measure how widespread or systematic the underlying pattern was. That measurement is what the other sources in this section attempt, each with its own limits.

Held together, the record looks like this. A formal human rights investigation and a review Meta commissioned and paid for both found an adverse pattern affecting Palestinian users, and the review found no intentional bias. A government office's own figures show it asking platforms to remove speech at scale, through a channel without public legal process, with compliance above 90 percent in its busiest period. A platform's written policy distinguishes a political movement from a protected people and then defines when it treats one as the other, a rule opposed by an anti-Zionist Jewish organization it consulted and defended with survey evidence by a Jewish organization that advocated it. A separate watchdog found antisemitic content evading moderation on TikTok, and another credited TikTok with improvement. TikTok denies systemic bias, and a named methodological critique of the most prominent report exists. The "neutral platforms" story does not survive the Cyber Unit's own numbers or Meta's own review. The "coordinated conspiracy" story does not survive the absence of documented intent, the antisemitic content that got through, or the limits the investigators stated themselves.

What the record does not settle should be stated plainly. No source here measures the overall rate at which pro-Palestinian and pro-Israel content was removed across any platform, and the best-known dataset was not built to. No source documents intent behind Meta's pattern, and Meta's own reviewers found none. Whether the "Zionist" proxy rule survived Meta's January 2025 overhaul was left unclear. Whether the ban that followed TikTok's change of ownership reflects a new policy is unknown. And the Cyber Unit did not tell Human Rights Watch which rules the posts it asked to remove had broken. How the same years were covered by the major newspapers, where the record shows a different kind of asymmetry, is examined in [scene:gx_s07|the study of how press coverage differed].

chapters.label: Chapter 7
chapters.title: The Lines You've Heard
chapters.span: A field guide to the claims repeated most online
chapters.intro: You now have the ground under the story. This chapter is a field guide to the lines you will meet in comment sections, posts and arguments. Each one is checked briefly against the record, with a verdict and a pointer to the volume that holds the full account. The same standard applies to every line, including the ones aimed at Jews.
chapters.outro:
A reader who has come this far holds three kinds of knowledge: what the record settles, what it leaves in dispute, and the questions the history ahead has to answer.

The present is settled in its outline, though not in any final agreement. Israel is the state within the 1949 armistice lines. The West Bank was divided by the Oslo II agreement into Areas A, B and C, about 18, 22 and 61 percent of the territory, in an arrangement written as temporary that has lasted three decades. Israel annexed East Jerusalem under a law that the Security Council, by 14 votes to none, declared null and void.[cite:anera_areas_abc] [cite:unsc478_text] About 14.8 million Palestinians live in four legal situations, and at the end of 2023 Arabs made up 21.3 percent of Israel's population.[cite:alquds_pcbs_refugees] [cite:rs_ch01_jiis_pop] The Law of Return extends a right of immigration to every Jew, while the residence route of 1952 decided, by dates and registers, which Arabs who stayed in 1948 became citizens.[cite:rs_ch01_lor_text] [cite:rs_ch01_nationality_1952] On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice advised that Israel's continued presence in the occupied territory is unlawful; no court has decided whether genocide has been committed in Gaza.[cite:icj_press_19jul24] [cite:jta_un_coi_genocide]

The deep past is settled as two documented histories, not one. A people called Israel is named on an Egyptian stele of about 1207 BCE, and a Jewish presence survived Rome. An Arabic-speaking majority lived on the land for centuries and was counted by the Ottoman state: 381,954 people in 1871–72, excluding the Bedouin, about 85 percent Muslim, 11 percent Christian and 4 percent Jewish.[cite:rs_ch01_cojs_merneptah] [cite:cjpme_historical_demography] A Jewish community lived in the four holy cities before Zionism. Modern national identity took formal shape late on both sides, at Basel in 1897 and, in Rashid Khalidi's account, in the late Ottoman years and sharpening in 1917–1923.[cite:rs_ch01_nli_oldyishuv] [cite:cup_khalidi_palestinian_identity]

Several words are settled too. "Semitic" names a family of languages that includes Hebrew and Arabic, and "antisemitism" has meant hostility to Jews since the 1880s, a hatred documented long before the word.[cite:wiki_antisemitism_etym] [cite:rs_ch01_ushmm_bloodlibel] The claim of wholesale Khazar descent was tested and failed, and genetics decides no one's rights.[cite:behar_2013_khazar] Zionism and Judaism are distinct, and Jews from every lineage have argued over the difference. Jewish life in the Muslim world was long, unequal and productive, and the frame of a permanent, ancient hatred does not describe it.[cite:stillman_jews_arab_lands]

Much remains disputed, and the Baseline has set out each dispute with the strongest case on both sides. No ancient source says why Rome renamed Judaea.[cite:rs_ch01_totf_hadrian] Whether Jews formed Jerusalem's majority depends on whether the city or the sub-district is counted, and the two 1922 totals for the city, 62,578 and 52,081, do not agree.[cite:rs_ch01_un_s10138] [cite:rs_ch01_jvl_jerpop] The family-unification ban is defended as security and attacked as demography, and its 2022 text names the Jewish majority among its aims.[cite:rs_ch01_idi_citizenship] The IHRA definition and the Jerusalem Declaration give different answers to whether anti-Zionism is antisemitic.[cite:peacenow_ihra_faq] [cite:jda_text] Who planted the bombs in Baghdad in 1950–51 is unproven, and the fates of 42 Yemenite children remained unaccounted for after the state's own inquiry.[cite:meforum_exodus] [cite:wiki_kedmi_commission] Whether some 850,000 or about 900,000 Jews left Arab lands, and whether they should be called refugees, is argued by named authors with stated positions.[cite:rs_ch01_beker_jpsr] [cite:rs_ch01_ahram_amayreh] Historians divide over how far the expulsions of 1948 were planned, and over whether Zionism is best described as settler colonialism or as national liberation.[cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:massad_settler_colonial]

The volumes ahead test what the Baseline has cleared. The next volume follows the road to 1948 in order. It asks how a land of which Jews were about 11 percent at the British census of 1922 came, by the United Nations committee's estimate for late 1946, to be about a third Jewish, and through which laws, purchases and institutions; the change in land title begins with [scene:ot_s01|the Ottoman Land Code]. It asks whether the expulsions of 1948 followed a design, the argument that turns on [scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet], and what became of the property the refugees left, governed by [scene:ap_s01|the Absentees' Property Law]. It tests the claims the Baseline met in miniature, about consent, about promises and about who decided, against the documents of each stage.

The rule for that reading is the one this volume has used throughout. Read the document first and the interpreter second, keep what is shown apart from what it is said to show, and hold both peoples' claims to the same standard. Neither history erases the other, and the story that follows is about what was done with both.

sections.h: The land and who lived there
sections.html:
Lines about whether Palestine was a real, populated place before 1948, and whose history it holds.

Palestine never existed. There was never a country called Palestine.

False

Palestine was a real, named, populated and governed place long before 1948, even though it was not an independent state. The line leans on one true technicality: the Ottomans named provinces after their capital cities, so no Ottoman unit was officially called "Palestine." [cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] But the region was administered as three districts that map closely onto the later Mandate boundary, and from 1872 the district of Jerusalem reported directly to Constantinople because of its importance. [cite:wiki_mutasarrifate_jerusalem] Roughly 600,000 people lived there by the late 19th century, in cities such as Jerusalem, Gaza, Jaffa, Hebron and Nablus. [cite:ips_ottoman_palestine]

The name itself goes back to 135 CE, when Rome renamed the province Syria Palaestina after crushing the Bar Kokhba revolt. [cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] From 1922 to 1948, "Palestine" was a polity in international law, with its own citizenship order (1925), about 70,000 passports, the Palestine pound (1927) and its own stamps. [cite:banko_palestinian_citizenship]

Read more [scene:s00h|Volume I, The Baseline: Ottoman Palestine] · [scene:s07|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Mandate]

The Palestinian people were invented in the 1960s.

False

Palestinian national identity is documented decades before the 1960s; historians date its emergence to the late Ottoman and British Mandate periods, the same era in which Jordanian, Syrian and Israeli identities formed. On 15 January 1911, two Arab Christian cousins in Jaffa, Issa and Yousef El-Issa, founded a newspaper called Filastin, "Palestine." [cite:wiki_falastin] By 1914 it was openly opposing Zionist land purchases, and it published until 7 April 1948. Israel's own National Library holds 6,692 issues. [cite:nli_filastin_archive]

From 1919, Muslims and Christians organized together in seven Palestine Arab Congresses. Their central demand was a national government answerable to an assembly elected by the country's inhabitants. [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress] Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people in Palestine. [cite:jvl_census_1931] The PLO was founded in 1964, but the people it claimed to represent were already on the record.

Read more [scene:cmt_s06|Volume I, The Baseline: "The Palestinian People Were Invented in the 1960s"] · [scene:fil_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Filastin]

It was a land without a people for a people without a land.

False

Every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country. Britain's 1922 census counted 757,182 people, 83,794 of them Jews, about 11%. [cite:jvl_census_1931] At the end of 1946, the UN's investigating committee estimated about 1,846,000 people: some 1,203,000 Arabs (65%) and 608,000 Jews (33%). [cite:rebelion_unscop_figures]

The slogan was not Zionist in origin. It first appeared in print in 1843, in a book by Alexander Keith, a Scottish clergyman who had visited Palestine in 1839 and knew it was inhabited. The first Zionist use came in 1901, from Israel Zangwill. [cite:meq_land_without_people] Historians debate whether it meant "empty" or "without a nation." The census figures also refute a slogan from the other side: the claim that Palestinian Arabs privately owned 94% of the land counts large areas of state land as Arab-owned. The 1945 Village Statistics survey separates private ownership from state land. [cite:wiki_village_statistics]

Read more [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War'] · [scene:cen_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Counting the Country]

Jews are the indigenous people of the land, and Arabs are the colonizers.

Half true

The first half of the line rests on real history; the second half does not. Jewish kingdoms existed in the land in the first millennium BCE, and after Rome crushed the Bar Kokhba revolt (132–135 CE), barred Jews from Jerusalem and renamed the province Syria Palaestina, a smaller Jewish presence continued, centered in Galilee. [cite:wiki_syria_palaestina] [cite:encyclo_israel_history] That ancient connection is not in dispute among mainstream historians.

But the Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians who became the majority over the following centuries were a resident population, not a colonial one. The Ottoman census of 1871–72 counted 381,954 residents, roughly 85% Muslim, 11% Christian and 4% Jewish, and genetic and archaeological studies find strong continuity with long-term local ancestry. [cite:cjpme_historical_demography] [cite:factually_archaeological_evidence] Formal national identity is modern on both sides: Rashid Khalidi dates Palestinian national consciousness to the late Ottoman period and 1917–1923, just as political Zionism was founded at Basel in 1897. [cite:cup_khalidi_palestinian_identity] Both histories are documented; neither erases the other.

Read more [scene:s00i|Volume I, The Baseline: Indigenous, Colonizer, National Identity] · [scene:ah_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 3,000 Years in One Scene]

Jordan is already the Palestinian state.

False

Jordan is a separate state whose own government rejects the idea that it is the Palestinian state. The line starts from a real event: in 1921–23 Britain separated Transjordan from the rest of the Palestine Mandate under Article 25, exempting it from the Jewish national home provisions. [cite:w_transjordan] [cite:wiki_transjordan_memorandum] But the 1947 UN partition plan divided only the land west of the Jordan River. Many Jordanians are of Palestinian origin because they became refugees in 1948 and 1967, not because Jordan was a partition. [cite:w_black_september]

There is a twist: Jordan's own rulers once made a version of the claim. In 1948 King Abdullah I said Palestine and Jordan were one country, backing Jordan's annexation of the West Bank. [cite:meforum_jordan_west_bank] On July 31, 1988, King Hussein formally dissolved Jordan's legal and administrative ties to the West Bank. [cite:springer_jordan_palestine_history] Asked whether Jordan should be the de facto Palestinian state, King Abdullah II answered: "Jordan is Jordan." [cite:davidsinger_jordan_palestinian_state]

Read more [scene:cmt_s04|Volume LXII, The Comment Section: "Jordan Is the Palestinian State Set Aside in the Partition"] · [scene:s06a2|Volume II, The Road to 1948: "Jordan Is Already Palestine"] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Jews and Muslims have been fighting over that land for thousands of years.

False

The conflict over the land is about a century old, not thousands of years. It began with modern political Zionism in 1897 and the British Mandate, and the first Palestinian national movement was organized jointly by Muslims and Christians. Before that, Jews, Muslims and Christians lived together under Ottoman rule, where the millet system gave Jewish communities their own legal, educational and religious self-governance, though not equality with Muslims.

Across the Muslim-majority world, Jewish communities lived for more than a thousand years, from the Golden Age of Muslim Iberia [cite:menocal_ornament] to Baghdad, where some 140,000 Jews made up about one-third of the city in 1945. Coexistence was never utopian; there was real violence, such as the Granada pogrom of 1066. And the region was not peaceful before 1948: revolts in Iraq, Syria and Palestine followed the European carve-up of 1916–22. But the documented record does not fit a story of ancient, permanent hatred.

Read more [scene:s00e|Volume I, The Baseline: Semitic Jews Coexisted with Semitic Arabs] · [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War']

sections.h: 1948 and the refugees
sections.html:
Lines about how Israel was founded, how the war went, and why some 700,000 Palestinians became refugees.

Israel was created because of the Holocaust.

Misleading

The Holocaust changed the urgency, the politics and the world's willingness to act, but the plan for a Jewish state, and much of the machinery to build it, existed decades before Hitler took power in 1933. Theodor Herzl published The Jewish State in 1896, weighing Palestine against Argentina. [cite:herzl_judenstaat] The Zionist movement formally rejected a British offer in East Africa in 1905 and kept Palestine as its goal. [cite:wiki_seventh_zionist_congress] Britain pledged support for "a national home for the Jewish people" in Palestine in 1917, [cite:balfour_letter] the Allied powers ratified that at San Remo in 1920, [cite:san_remo_wiki] and the League of Nations Mandate approved in 1922 bound Britain to facilitate Jewish immigration. [cite:mandate_palestine_wiki]

By then the movement also had a bank (1899), a land fund (1901) and an organized American lobbying and fundraising base. What the war years did change is real: the Biltmore Program of May 1942 was the movement's first explicit, public demand for a "Jewish Commonwealth." [cite:biltmore_wiki] The Holocaust accelerated statehood; it did not originate it.

Read more [scene:s07a|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Five Dates That Predate the Holocaust] · [scene:us_s08|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Whole Play, Step by Step]

Israel accepted the UN partition plan; the Arabs rejected it and started the war.

Half true

The first half of the line is accurate; the second half compresses the sequence. When the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181 on November 29, 1947, by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstentions, the Jewish Agency accepted it, with real reservations about its borders. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected it entirely and vowed armed resistance. [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] [cite:palquest_un_partition_1947] The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine, about 70% of the population, had no vote on the plan, which gave the Jewish state about 55% of the territory. [cite:britannica_res181]

The war did not begin with a single Arab attack. Violence escalated from December 1, 1947, as a civil war inside Mandate Palestine, with documented attacks from both sides: a car bomb in Jaffa killed 26 people in early January 1948, and Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya on February 15, 1948. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] Neighboring Arab armies invaded on May 15, 1948, five and a half months later, the day after Israel declared independence.

Read more [scene:s09b|Volume II, The Road to 1948: "Israel Accepted, the Arabs Rejected and Started the War"] · [scene:s09|Volume II, The Road to 1948: UN Resolution 181]

Palestinians left in 1948 because Arab leaders told them to.

False

No general Arab order to leave has ever been found, and mainstream scholarship no longer defends this account. In 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers reported in The Spectator that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of 1948 Arab broadcasts and found no evacuation orders, but repeated appeals to civilians to stay. [cite:spectator_childers_1961] In 1988 the Israeli historian Benny Morris, working from Israel's own military and state archives, concluded that military attack, expulsion and fear were the main causes of flight. [cite:w_morris_birth]

There is a small kernel: Morris found that some local Arab commanders ordered evacuations of women and children in particular places. But expulsions are documented at Deir Yassin, Lydda, Ramla and elsewhere, and about 500 villages were depopulated as 700,000 to 750,000 Palestinians were displaced. [cite:morris_1948] Historians still disagree about whether the Haganah's Plan Dalet of 10 March 1948 was a blueprint for removal or a military plan that gave local commanders discretion. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

Read more [scene:np_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: How the Nakba Was Told] · [scene:s10|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Independence, Nakba, and the Czech Guns]

The Nakba is exaggerated; there were no massacres in 1948.

False

Massacres in 1948 are documented, much of the evidence coming from Israeli archives, historians and veterans themselves. On 9 April 1948, Irgun and Lehi forces, supported by the Haganah and Palmach, attacked Deir Yassin, west of Jerusalem, and killed about 110 villagers, many of them women, children and elderly people; a Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies in a cave. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] At Tantura in May 1948, Israeli veterans in their nineties described killings and a mass grave in a 2022 documentary; others deny it, and the number killed cannot be established. [cite:npr_tantura]

One number in this story was inflated: the Deir Yassin toll was long given as 254, and current scholarship puts it at 107–120. Atrocities ran both ways; four days later, a reprisal attack on a convoy to Hadassah Hospital killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The displacement itself is not in doubt: between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians were displaced and about 500 villages depopulated. [cite:morris_1948]

Read more [scene:ma_s01|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy, and Tantura] · [scene:hd_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: How Historians Argue About 1948]

Tiny Israel won the 1948 war against impossible odds.

Misleading

The underdog picture fits only the opening weeks of the 1948 war; after that, the balance reversed. From the Arab armies' invasion on May 15 until the first truce in June 1948, Israeli forces are described as initially inferior in numbers and armament. A contemporaneous US government assessment dated July 1, 1948 put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000, about 35,000 of them used for active operations, and found the Arab armies stronger in artillery and tanks at that point. [cite:frus1948_military_situation]

After the truce, new enlistments and arms, including Czech shipments, let Israel seize the initiative; one historical anthology concludes that for most of the war "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization." [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] By the later stages, Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly 2 to 1. Many of the popular "outnumbered" figures trace back to John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion, who historians note had reason to exaggerate Israeli numbers. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

Read more [scene:s10b|Volume II, The Road to 1948: The Actual Military Balance]

Why don't Arab countries just take the Palestinian refugees?

Half true

One Arab state did take most of its Palestinian refugees in, and others chose not to, for stated reasons. Under its 1954 nationality law, Jordan gave citizenship to most Palestinians who arrived after 1948; it hosts more than 2 million registered Palestinian refugees, most of them citizens. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:adl_refugees] Lebanon, with about 400,000 registered refugees, has never naturalized them, barring them from dozens of professions and, since a 2001 law, from owning property, a policy widely tied to its sectarian power-sharing balance. [cite:fmr_lebanon] [cite:aj_lebanon_property] Egypt and the Gulf offer residency without a path to citizenship.

The Arab League told members not to grant citizenship, to protect refugees' identity and their right of return; critics, including Israeli and pro-Israel analysts, argue this kept refugees in limbo as a political tool. [cite:fmr_lebanon] After October 7, Egypt and Jordan refused to take Gazans, citing the fear that Palestinians who leave would never be allowed back. [cite:pbs_egypt_refugees]

Read more [scene:sq_s20|Volume I, The Baseline: 'Why Don't Arab Countries Just Take the Refugees?'] · [scene:ilb_s03|Volume II, The Road to 1948: Lebanon's Refugee Policy: A Documented Choice]

sections.h: October 7 and the Gaza war
sections.html:
Lines about the attack itself, Israel's response, and how the dead and the hungry are counted.

October 7 came out of nowhere; there was no context at all.

Misleading

The October 7 attack was an atrocity, and it also had a documented context; the record holds both. Hamas fighters killed 1,195 people in Israel, 828 of them civilians and 36 children, and took 251 hostages, the largest single-day loss of Jewish life since the Holocaust. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] It came after 16 years of an Israeli-Egyptian blockade of Gaza, which by 2022 had left 97% of its water contaminated by UN standards and unemployment at 46.6%. [cite:blockade_unrwa] In the West Bank, the UN documented more than 2,150 settler violence incidents in 2023 alone. [cite:gzr_btselem_settlers] That context explains grievances; it does not justify the attack.

Nor was the attack unforeseen inside Israel. Israeli intelligence obtained Hamas's attack plan more than a year earlier and judged it aspirational, and Unit 8200 observers who reported unusual Hamas training were told it was routine. [cite:nyt_jericho_wall_2023] That warnings were dismissed is documented; claims that the attack was deliberately allowed to happen are not established.

Read more [scene:iaa_s12|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: October 7] · [scene:gzr_s06|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: Ten Years of Stories Americans Largely Missed] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas beheaded 40 babies on October 7.

Unsupported

The specific claim that Hamas beheaded 40 babies has not been supported by the record, and it was walked back after spreading. In the first days after the attack, the "beheaded babies" line was amplified by US media and repeated by President Biden before it was retracted. It became part of what reached American audiences while much of the documented context, reported mainly by Israeli outlets, did not.

Debunking that number does not shrink the attack. Hamas killed 1,195 people on October 7, 828 of them civilians and 36 of them children, took 251 hostages, and committed sexual violence documented by UN rapporteur reports and Israeli forensic teams. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] It was the largest single-day loss of Jewish life since the Holocaust. The record supports the atrocity in full; it does not support this particular, widely repeated figure.

Read more [scene:o7_s06|Volume LII, October 7 Architecture: The American Narrative] · [scene:o7_s08|Volume LII, October 7 Architecture: The Record vs. The Narrative] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas are terrorists and Israel has the right to defend itself.

True, with limits

Both parts of the line have a real basis, and the law attaches conditions to the second. The October 7 attack, in which Hamas killed 1,195 people, 828 of them civilians, and took 251 hostages, was a crime. [cite:wiki_october7_attacks] Article 51 of the UN Charter recognizes every member state's "inherent right" of self-defense. In 2004, however, the International Court of Justice advised that Article 51 did not justify Israel's separation wall, because the threat came from territory Israel itself occupies. That opinion was non-binding and not unanimous. [cite:icj_wall_op] Israel's defenders argue that Gaza has not been occupied since 2005 and that the right applies against non-state groups like Hamas. [cite:justia_selfdef]

Both sides agree on one thing: the laws of war, including distinction, proportionality and precaution, bind every party, Hamas included. Whether specific Israeli operations met that standard is disputed. Israeli military lawyers say they did; B'Tselem and international law scholars have documented operations they assess as violations. [cite:btselem_casualties]

Read more [scene:sk_s03|Volume LXVI, Street Questions: 'Israel Has the Right to Defend Itself'] · [scene:s20|Volume XIII, October 7 and the Reckoning: Oct 7 · Gaza · Foreknowledge] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

The IDF is the most moral army in the world.

Unsupported

"Most moral army in the world" is a self-description, not a finding any independent body has made, and the documented record of the Gaza war cuts against it. In September 2025 a UN Commission of Inquiry found that Israeli authorities "deliberately deprived Palestinians in Gaza of resources indispensable for their survival" and found underlying acts of genocide, findings the Israeli government disputes. [cite:un_coi_sept2025]

Israeli intelligence officers' own testimony adds detail. According to a +972 Magazine and Local Call investigation based on six officers who used it, an AI system called Lavender flagged about 37,000 Palestinians as potential targets at its peak. The officers acknowledged roughly a 10 percent error rate and described reviewing each target for only seconds before authorizing a strike, and said 15 to 20 civilian deaths were accepted per junior operative in the war's early weeks. [cite:972mag_lavender_ai_machine] [cite:aljazeera_ai_assisted_genocide_lavender] Nor is there an outside check that could confirm the superlative: no Knesset oversight committee has access to operational detail.

Read more [scene:s19h|Volume VI, The Machine, Named: IDF and Mossad] · [scene:u82_s05|Volume XXXII, Unit 8200 Architecture: 37,000 Names, Seconds of Review, and a System Built to Find Them at Home] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Hamas uses human shields, so the civilian deaths in Gaza are on Hamas.

Half true

There is documented evidence that Hamas used civilian sites for military purposes, but under the laws of war that does not move responsibility for civilian deaths entirely onto Hamas. In November 2023 the White House said US intelligence, separate from Israel's, indicated that Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad used some Gaza hospitals, including Al-Shifa, and tunnels beneath them to conceal military operations; it called this a war crime. Gaza doctors denied it. [cite:jns_us_intel_hospitals] The record also runs the other way: Israeli soldiers, former detainees and the veterans' group Breaking the Silence described Israeli units sending Palestinians, including a 16-year-old, into buildings and tunnels ahead of troops, a practice nicknamed the "mosquito protocol." The IDF says its directives prohibit this. [cite:cnn_mosquito_protocol] [cite:cbs_human_shields]

Using civilians as shields is prohibited for every party, and a shield's presence does not lift the attacker's duties of distinction and proportionality. Whether specific Israeli operations met those duties is contested. [cite:btselem_casualties]

Read more [scene:hs_s01|Volume LXVI, Street Questions: 'Human Shields'] · [scene:hma_src_s15|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: What the Architecture Has Produced for Civilians] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Gaza's death toll is made up by Hamas.

False

Independent research points to the Gaza Health Ministry undercounting deaths, not inventing them. The ministry is under Hamas's authority, which is why Israel disputes its figures, but the UN has generally treated them as reliable. [cite:gulfnews_lancet_toll] A study in The Lancet in January 2025, cross-checking ministry hospital lists, a ministry online survey and social-media obituaries, estimated 64,260 traumatic-injury deaths by 30 June 2024, against 37,877 reported, an undercount of about 41%. [cite:transcend_lancet_toll] A 2026 household survey in The Lancet Global Health, not relying on ministry records, estimated more than 75,000 violent deaths in the first 15 months, versus about 49,000 reported at the time. [cite:cyprusmail_lancetgh_2026]

As of August 2026, the ministry's count, as reported by UN OCHA, stood at about 73,400 killed. [cite:un_ocha_opt] The real open question is different: the totals do not separate combatants from civilians. Israel says it killed about 20,000 fighters, a figure not independently verified. [cite:yahoo_record_dems_fighters]

Read more [scene:tl_s01|Volume LXVII, Products of the Machine: Is the Gaza Death Toll Reliable? What Peer-Reviewed Studies Found] · [scene:gzr_s03|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: The Numbers Americans Missed: Gaza Death Tolls Across the Last Decade] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

There is no famine in Gaza; the starvation stories are propaganda.

False

Famine in Gaza was formally declared by the body that exists to make that call. On August 22, 2025, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) declared famine in Gaza Governorate, the first ever declared in the Middle East and only the fifth since the system was created in 2008. A declaration requires three thresholds to be breached at once: extreme food deprivation, acute malnutrition and starvation deaths. [cite:ipc_famine_aug2025] The IPC called it "entirely man-made." [cite:gzr_ipc_famine_wiki] WHO had recorded 206 starvation deaths in 2025 by July, and 12,000 children were identified as acutely malnourished in July alone. [cite:gzr_who_famine]

The famine followed more than 60 days in spring 2025 when all humanitarian and commercial supplies were blocked from entering. [cite:ipc_may2025_blockade] Some data points have been challenged: the Times of Israel disputed parts of the IPC's data, though not the existence of severe food insecurity, and an earlier famine claim was revised down. January 2026 brought a brief period when aid met basic food needs.

Read more [scene:gzr_s01|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: Confirmed Famine: The First in the Middle East's Recorded History] · [scene:s19k|Volume XVI, Gaza, Documented: The Starvation Question] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

The world court has already ruled that Israel committed genocide.

False

The International Court of Justice has not ruled on whether Israel committed genocide; South Africa's case, filed on December 29, 2023, is still pending. [cite:icj_report_un] What the court did, on January 26, 2024, was issue provisional measures: it found that Palestinians' rights under the Genocide Convention were plausibly at risk of irreparable harm and ordered Israel to prevent genocidal acts and allow aid. That is an emergency order, not a verdict, and it did not order a ceasefire. [cite:mee_icj_explainer] Separately, the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants of November 21, 2024 for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant charge war crimes and crimes against humanity, not genocide. [cite:justiceinfo_gaza]

The line blurs courts with other bodies. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch (December 2024), the Israeli groups B'Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights–Israel (July 2025) and a UN Commission of Inquiry (September 2025) have concluded genocide or acts of genocide. Israel rejects all of these findings. [cite:jta_un_coi_genocide] [cite:ips_amnesty_hrw_genocide]

Read more [scene:arm_s05|Volume XXXIX, The Arms Supply Architecture: The International Legal and Political Context] · [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide'] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

sections.h: Wars, occupation and peace
sections.html:
Lines about who starts the wars, what the occupation is in law, and who walked away from peace.

Israel never starts wars; it only responds.

False

The record shows Israel has opened at least two of its major wars. On June 5, 1967, Israel struck first, destroying most of the Egyptian air force on the ground within hours; its initial claim that Egypt had attacked first was false, and US intelligence knew it at the time. [cite:war1967_adl] The threat was real: Egypt had expelled UN peacekeepers, blockaded the Strait of Tiran and massed 100,000 troops on the border. Whether that justified striking first is still argued by lawyers and historians. Israeli historians such as Tom Segev also document planning that predated the crisis. [cite:segev_1967]

In 1982, Israel invaded Lebanon after its ambassador in London was shot by the Abu Nidal Organization, a rival and enemy of the PLO. Told this by the Shin Bet, General Rafael Eitan replied, "Abu Nidal, Abu Shmidal. We have to strike at the PLO!" [cite:war1982_eitan] Real grievances existed, including 270 PLO attacks despite a ceasefire, but "only responds" does not fit the record.

Read more [scene:iaa_s04|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: 1967] · [scene:iaa_s06|Volume XXVI, Israel Aid Architecture: 1982] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel gave Gaza back in 2005 and got rockets in return.

Half true

The withdrawal was real, but "gave Gaza back" overstates it. Between 15 and 23 August 2005, Israel evacuated all 21 Gaza settlements and about 8,000 settlers, mobilizing up to 55,000 soldiers and police. [cite:crs_disengagement_2005] But Israel kept control of Gaza's airspace, coastline and most crossings, which is why the UN and the International Court of Justice continued to treat Gaza as occupied, while Israel argued its occupation had ended. [cite:wiki_disengagement]

The purpose matters too. Sharon's top aide described the plan as a way of isolating Gaza and avoiding international pressure for a political settlement. Nothing was handed to a Palestinian government by agreement. Hamas won the January 2006 legislative elections, took control of Gaza in June 2007 after fighting Fatah, and Israel and Egypt then imposed a blockade. Leaving the inside while holding the edges, with no negotiated settlement, produced the arrangement every Gaza war since 2008 has been fought inside.

Read more [scene:dis_s01|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Disengagement] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

There is no occupation; the West Bank is disputed territory.

False

Under international law, the West Bank is occupied territory, and the world's highest court has said so directly. On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice advised that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful, that it must end "as rapidly as possible," and that Israel must stop all new settlement, evacuate settlers and make reparation. Several of those findings passed 14 to 1. [cite:icj_press_19jul24] The court noted that occupation law sets no time limit; it was annexation-like policies and the denial of self-determination that made the presence unlawful. [cite:transcend_icj_ao]

The UN Security Council reached the same view of settlements in December 2016, voting 14 to 0 in Resolution 2334 that they have "no legal validity." [cite:deccan_unsc_2334] Israel rejects these findings, and the 2024 opinion is advisory, not an enforceable judgment. But "disputed" is Israel's position, not the finding of any court or UN body.

Read more [scene:icj_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: The ICJ's 2024 Opinion] · [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide']

The Palestinians rejected every peace offer they were given.

Half true

The record includes real Palestinian and Arab rejections, but "every offer" leaves out the other half. Arab leaders did reject the 1937 Peel plan and the 1947 partition plan. At Lausanne in 1949, Israel offered to take back 100,000 refugees, but "only as an integral part of a general and final peace settlement"; the Arab states demanded return first, and Israel later withdrew the offer. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report]

Camp David in July 2000 is the case most people mean, and its participants disagree. Clinton blamed Arafat for rejecting reported proposals of a state on roughly 91–92% of the West Bank and all of Gaza. Robert Malley, Clinton's own Middle East director at the talks, wrote with Hussein Agha that errors were shared and no offer was ever put in writing. [cite:independent_malley_barak] Palestinian negotiators said the real territory was smaller. The Clinton Parameters followed, and both sides answered with reservations; Taba in January 2001 ended without agreement. [cite:jvl_camp_david_overview]

Read more [scene:sq_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'A Land Without a People,' 'They Rejected Every Offer,' and 'A 2,000-Year Religious War'] · [scene:cd_s01|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Camp David 2000] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel wants coexistence; peace is up to the Palestinians.

Misleading

The record of Israel's own governments does not support the idea that the only obstacle is on the Palestinian side. On 21 February 2024 the Knesset voted 99 to 9 to back Netanyahu's opposition to "unilateral" recognition of a Palestinian state, and on 11 September 2025, at the Maale Adumim settlement, Netanyahu said "there will be no Palestinian state." [cite:toi_knesset_99] [cite:globalsecurity_two_state] From the signing of Oslo in 1993, the West Bank settler population grew from about 110,000 to about 500,000 by 2025, plus about 250,000 in East Jerusalem. [cite:peacenow_settlement_population]

Former minister Haim Ramon has said Netanyahu told Likud lawmakers in 2019 that letting Qatari money reach Hamas would help "foil the establishment of a Palestinian state"; Netanyahu calls that "a big lie." [cite:alandowty_strong_hamas_netanyahu] [cite:ynetnews_netanyahu_ridiculous_denial] Rabin, who signed Oslo, was killed in 1995 by an Israeli opponent of the deal. Support for two states has also fallen among Palestinians, to 33% by December 2022, so neither side's public is the whole story.

Read more [scene:ts_s02|Volume V, Oslo and the Interregnum: Is a Two-State Solution Still Possible? Recognition at 157 Nations, a 99–9 Knesset Vote, and Falling Support on Both Sides] · [scene:hma_s01|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: Netanyahu's Own Reported Words] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Israel's real plan is a Greater Israel from the Nile to the Euphrates.

Depends on what's said

"From the Nile to the Euphrates" is not official Israeli policy, but the idea of a larger Israel is held by people in the governing coalition. The phrase comes from Genesis 15:18 and is the most extreme of three versions of "Greater Israel"; it is rejected as literal policy even by most religious Zionists. [cite:genesis_1518_text] The more mainstream version is the Likud platform, which says "between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty." [cite:likud_charter_platform]

Some statements go further. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich spoke in Paris in March 2023 beside a map that included Jordan, and has said Jerusalem's future is to "extend all the way to Damascus." [cite:smotrich_map_paris_2023] In August 2025, asked if he connects to a pendant map reaching into Egypt, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq, Netanyahu replied "very much so," and 31 Arab and Islamic states condemned it. [cite:netanyahu_jewelry_2025] On the ground, Israel annexed the Golan in 1981 but returned Sinai in 1982. "A secret master plan" overstates it; "no one in power wants more land" understates it.

Read more [scene:gia_src_s02|Volume II, The Road to 1948: What Greater Israel Actually Is: Ideology, History, and the Three Versions] · [scene:gia_s01|Volume XXVII, Greater Israel Architecture: The Map He Held Up at the UN] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

sections.h: Democracy, rights and Palestinian politics
sections.html:
Lines about Israel's democracy, the rights of the people it governs, and the record of Palestinian leaderships.

Israel is the only democracy in the Middle East.

Half true

For its own citizens, the line holds up on the main international measures, but it leaves out millions of people Israel governs. In its 2024 report, the V-Dem Institute still ranked Israel as the only electoral democracy in the Middle East and North Africa, a region where 98% of people live under autocracies. [cite:globes_vdem] Israel holds competitive elections, has a free press, and Arab citizens vote and sit in the Knesset.

The same report demoted Israel from "liberal democracy" for the first time in about 50 years, citing attacks on the judiciary and a decline in freedom from torture; Freedom House's score fell from 80 in 2017 to 73. [cite:toi_vdem] The Israel Democracy Institute called this "troubling, but not catastrophic." [cite:idi_vdem] Both indices assess Israel without the occupied territories. Palestinians in the West Bank live under Israeli military control but cannot vote in Israel's elections; by one count, about 5.5 million of roughly 15.5 million people under Israel's control lack citizenship. [cite:prio_democracy]

Read more [scene:sk_s02|Volume I, The Baseline: 'The Only Democracy in the Middle East'] · [scene:s19d|Volume VI, The Machine, Named: The Coalition Hostage Architecture] (one volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Arab citizens of Israel have exactly the same rights as Jewish citizens.

Half true

Arab citizens of Israel vote, stand for the Knesset and hold citizenship, but the law has not treated them identically. From 1949 to 1966 most lived under a military administration requiring permits to travel, with curfews and closed zones. Under that regime, on 29 October 1956, a Border Police unit killed 49 villagers at Kafr Qasim returning home after a curfew they had not been told of; the brigade commander was fined one-hundredth of a lira. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre]

The 1950 Absentees' Property Law took the property even of Arabs who never left Israel and became citizens; by 2001 these "present absentees" were estimated at about 200,000 people. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] The law remains in force. In 2018 the Knesset passed, 62 to 55, a Basic Law stating that national self-determination is "unique to the Jewish people," with no equality clause. [cite:jta_nsl_upheld] The Supreme Court upheld it 10 to 1 in 2021, saying individual rights are protected by other laws; supporters say it only states what Israel already is.

Read more [scene:mg_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: Eighteen Years of Military Rule Over Citizens] · [scene:nsl_s01|Volume I, The Baseline: The Nation-State Law]

Israel is an apartheid state.

Depends on what's said

"Apartheid" has a legal meaning, and several serious bodies have applied it to Israel, though no court has convicted anyone of the crime. Under the 1973 Apartheid Convention and the Rome Statute, apartheid is an institutionalized regime of systematic domination by one racial group over another. Human Rights Watch and the Israeli group B'Tselem concluded in 2021 that Israel commits apartheid, and Amnesty International reached the same conclusion in February 2022. [cite:fara_amnesty_explainer]

In July 2024 the International Court of Justice, in an advisory opinion on the occupied territory, found that Israeli policies breach the prohibition on racial segregation and apartheid. [cite:11kbw_icj_ao] Israel rejects the label. So the honest answer depends on the wording: "human-rights groups and the ICJ have found apartheid-related violations" is accurate; "a court has ruled Israel guilty of the crime of apartheid" goes further than the record, and "it is a slur with no legal basis" ignores it.

Read more [scene:pr_s03|Volume I, The Baseline: Start Here: 'Occupation,' 'Apartheid,' 'Genocide']

Palestinian schoolbooks teach children to hate Jews.

Half true

The most detailed independent study found real problems in Palestinian textbooks, but not a curriculum of incitement to violence. In 2021 the Georg Eckert Institute, commissioned by the EU, published its analysis of Palestinian Authority textbooks and teachers' guides released in 2020. It found they "adhere to UNESCO standards" on human-rights education while expressing "a narrative of resistance" and "antagonism towards Israel." [cite:gei_faq] It also found some content with "escalatory potential," including in STEM subjects, and some antisemitic depictions. It found no direct calls for violence against Israelis.

The Institute's director later told the European Parliament that books containing antisemitism or incitement do not meet UNESCO standards. [cite:hansard_textbooks] IMPACT-se, a monitoring group, says the study confirms systemic incitement; [cite:impactse_gei] some European analysts say it disproved exaggerated claims. [cite:eumep_textbooks] The study did not examine Israeli textbooks, which other researchers have also criticized.

Read more [scene:sk_s05|Volume I, The Baseline: 'Palestinian Schools Teach Hate']

Israel created Hamas.

Half true

Israel did not found Hamas, but it did register and tolerate the network Hamas grew out of. In 1979 Israeli authorities officially registered Mujama al-Islamiya, the Islamist charity led by Sheikh Ahmed Yassin, as an association. Avner Cohen, who handled religious affairs in Gaza, later said "Hamas, to my great regret, is Israel's creation," and David Hacham, an adviser to seven defense ministers, called the 1979 recognition Israel's "original sin." [cite:portside_higgins_hamas]

Hamas itself was founded by Yassin and six co-founders in December 1987, at the start of the first intifada, twenty years into the occupation of Gaza. [cite:npr_hamashistory] Its ideology draws on the Muslim Brotherhood, founded in Egypt in 1928, before Israel existed. Its 1988 charter called for Israel's destruction and included antisemitic content, and its later choices, from suicide bombings during the Oslo years to October 7, were its own. [cite:hamas_charter1988] Israel helped make room for Hamas; it did not write its program or make its decisions.

Read more [scene:sq_s02|Volume LXVI, Street Questions: 'The IDF Exists Because of Hamas'] · [scene:hma_src_s13|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: Hamas as an Independent Actor] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Netanyahu kept Hamas afloat with Qatari money to block a Palestinian state.

True, with limits

The core of this line is on the record: from 2018 Netanyahu's governments approved Qatari cash reaching Hamas-run Gaza, carried in suitcases through Israeli-controlled crossings under Israeli escort. Reported monthly totals ranged from roughly $15 million to $35 million. [cite:cnn_qatar_hamas_funds] In December 2023 Netanyahu said the goal had been to keep the Palestinians divided between Gaza and the West Bank, adding that the security cabinet approved it unanimously on the security services' advice. [cite:ara_netanyahu_admission] A Shin Bet investigation made public in March 2025 found the money helped Hamas build military strength, including $4 million diverted to its military wing from March 2022. [cite:haaretz_qatar_funding_report]

The limit is motive. That the policy was meant to block a Palestinian state rests mainly on former minister Haim Ramon's secondhand account of a 2019 Likud meeting. [cite:alandowty_strong_hamas_netanyahu] Netanyahu calls the idea that he wanted to build up Hamas "a big lie." [cite:ynetnews_netanyahu_ridiculous_denial]

Read more [scene:o7_s03|Volume LII, October 7 Architecture: Netanyahu Funded Hamas] · [scene:hma_s01|Volume XX, The Hamas Architecture: Netanyahu's Own Reported Words] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

sections.h: Iran and the neighbors
sections.html:
Lines about Iran, the armed groups it backs, and Israel's ties with Arab states.

Israel isn't the enemy of the Arab countries; Iran is.

Half true

For several Arab governments, the record does show Iran replacing Israel as the main strategic concern, but that is a statement about governments, not about the countries as a whole. Through the 2010s Saudi Arabia and Israel came to share a threat assessment centred on Iran's nuclear program, missiles and allied armed groups, producing largely unofficial security contacts well before any public opening. Saudi Arabia's own war with the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen, ongoing since 2015, hardened that view.

The peace that exists is narrow. Egypt signed the first Arab peace treaty with Israel in 1979, and embassies have operated since 1980, but scholars call it a "cold peace": trade, tourism and cultural ties have stayed limited for over four decades. [cite:wikipedia_egypt_israel_treaty] The 2020 normalization deals were decided by monarchs or military rulers, with no referendum or ratification by an elected legislature in Bahrain, Morocco or Sudan, and protests followed in Morocco and Bahrain during the Gaza war. [cite:mwn_morocco_upgrade] [cite:w_isr_bahrain]

Read more [scene:isa_src_s07|Volume XXIX, Israel-Saudi Architecture: Quiet Convergence Against a Shared Threat] · [scene:oa_s08|Volume LIX, The Other Accords: The Ledger] (volume in preparation; opens in the simulation for now)

Iran has always been a hostile theocracy.

False

Iran became a theocracy in 1979; before that it was a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, the Majlis. On March 15, 1951, the Majlis voted to nationalize the British-controlled oil industry, and Mohammad Mosaddegh became prime minister. [cite:w_iran_oil_nationalization] Britain answered with a worldwide embargo on Iranian oil; production fell from 242 million barrels in 1950 to 10.6 million in 1952. Mosaddegh's own record was not spotless: in August 1953 he dissolved parliament by a plebiscite his opponents called rigged. [cite:loc_mossadeq]

Days later, on August 19, 1953, a coup organized by the CIA and Britain's MI6 removed him and restored the Shah's power. [cite:w_1953_coup] The CIA formally acknowledged its role only in 2013.
