Two opposite misconceptions frame most popular talk about Palestine before the twentieth century. One holds that the Middle East has always been a set of hostile nations locked in permanent war. The other comes in two forms that contradict each other: that the Ottomans "occupied" Palestine the way later settlers did, or that Palestine was an empty Ottoman backwater. The record supports none of these. For four centuries the land that this book follows was neither a nation among nations nor an empty space. It was a group of districts inside one large, multi-religious empire.

From 1516 to 1917 the Ottoman Empire governed most of the Arab Middle East as provinces of a single state, without international borders between them. Damascus, Baghdad, Jerusalem and Beirut were provincial cities of the same state, and people and goods moved among them without passports. The states that define the region's later conflicts, Syria, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan and Israel, did not exist. Iran stood apart: it was never Ottoman, and it had its own dynasty, its own language and a Shia majority. Almost every border that matters in today's conflicts was drawn later, in a six-year window between 1916 and 1922, by two European powers, Britain and France.

Inside the empire, religion rather than territory organized much of law. Under the millet system, recognized religious communities (Muslims, Christians of several churches, and Jews) administered their own religious law, courts and schooling, and governed marriage, inheritance and education under their own leaders. [cite:w_ottoman_millet] The arrangement was not a golden age, and nothing in the record presents it as one. Its costs were real: heavy taxation, conscription, periodic violence, and a second-class status for non-Muslims, who paid special taxes and held lesser standing. Revolts were suppressed. The point the record makes is narrower than nostalgia. The order was imperfect, but it was not the patchwork of rival states the twentieth century created.

Palestine sat inside this order as a set of administrative units rather than as a country with its own frontier. Apart from a period of Egyptian rule from 1831 to 1840, it was administered as Ottoman provinces, chiefly the district of Jerusalem and parts of the provinces of Beirut and Damascus, with no border separating it from what are now Syria, Lebanon or Jordan. The precise word for that rule is imperial. Governors, garrisons and tax collectors ruled over a population that remained largely Arabic-speaking Muslims and Christians, with long-established Jewish communities in Jerusalem, Hebron, Safed and Tiberias. Rule came through administration and taxation, not through replacing the population. It ended when British forces captured Jerusalem in December 1917, and the Republic of Turkey, founded in 1923, formally renounced all rights over the former Arab provinces in the Treaty of Lausanne that year. [cite:w_lausanne] Modern Turkey is the empire's successor state, not a claimant to the land. Lausanne belongs to a later volume. It is mentioned here only to mark where the Ottoman story ends.

Two maps drawn for this library begin at this point. In the first, the Ottoman order of 1516 to 1917, with no internal borders, is the root from which the later layers of the region grow, beginning with the Anglo-French carve-up of 1916 to 1922. In the second, Ottoman rule is the first station in the long relationship between Turkey and Israel, and the next is the 1923 renunciation at Lausanne. Only their first box belongs to this chapter. Every later station is told in later volumes.

The period from 1799 to 1840 shows how this imperial order behaved under pressure from outside. Within a single generation, a French army, an Egyptian army, a peasant revolt and a coalition of European fleets all fought over the coast and hills of Palestine. Each time, the decisive choices were made in Paris, Cairo, Istanbul or London, and each time the people of the land bore the cost.

The first pressure came from France. During his Egyptian and Syrian campaign, Napoleon Bonaparte besieged Acre in 1799, and the campaign was defeated by combined British and Ottoman forces. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] He never reached Jerusalem. The Jewish Virtual Library's account dates his retreat from Acre to 22 May 1799. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] That is also the date given for a French newspaper report about him. A reference summary of the scholarship records that the Gazette nationale of 3 Prairial, Year VII (22 May 1799) printed a short report that Bonaparte had invited the Jews of Asia and Africa to gather under his flag. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] Whether one source has run the two events onto one date has not been settled in this book's research.

That newspaper item is the root of one of the most contested documents in the prehistory of Zionism. A much fuller text, a "Letter to the Jewish Nation," headed "General Headquarters, Jerusalem, 1st Floréal [Year VII], April 20th, 1799" and addressed to the "rightful heirs of Palestine," was first published only in 1940, when Franz Kobler announced a German translation in The New Judaea. No original has ever been found. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_akadem] The letter is dated and placed in Jerusalem, a city its supposed author never reached.

Historians have divided sharply over what, if anything, Napoleon proclaimed. The case for forgery is made by four of the scholars the sources name. Simon Schwarzfuchs (1979), Henry Laurens, Ronald Schechter and Jeremy Popkin regard the German text as forged. Schechter goes further and reads even the 1799 newspaper report as a rumour. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] A French Jewish educational site calls the forgery "almost certainly established" and attributes it to Frankist circles. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_akadem] The strongest form of this case rests on the document's history: it surfaces only in 1940, in translation, with no original, and its heading places Napoleon where he never was.

The other side does not defend every word of the 1940 text, but it does not dismiss the episode either. Mordechai Gichon argues that Napoleon did conceive of a Jewish national home in the Land of Israel. Nathan Schur reads the 1799 report as genuine but as wartime propaganda aimed at local Jews. [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_wiki] The Jewish Virtual Library prints the letter and says only that its authenticity "has been debated ever since." [cite:rs_rd0_napoleon_jvl] The strongest form of this side's case is that a contemporary French newspaper did print a report of an appeal to Jews in May 1799, so that something was said or rumoured at the time, whatever became of the text. What the record does not settle is whether Bonaparte himself issued any appeal, what it said, and who composed the letter that appeared in 1940.

The second pressure came from Egypt, whose ruler, Muhammad Ali, fielded his own army against the Sultan. Ibrahim Pasha, son of Egypt's ruler Muhammad Ali, invaded Ottoman Syria on 31 October 1831 and made Haifa his main base from December 1831. According to a reference summary, Palestine remained under Egyptian rule until 1840. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Ibrahim's conscription order of 25 April 1834 required one Muslim man in five, beginning with 200 from Jerusalem, and conscripts were to serve for life. He also disarmed Nablus and the Hebron district and imposed new taxes, including one on the Muslim administrative class. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

The result was a revolt. Judith Mendelsohn Rood reconstructed it from the records of Jerusalem's Islamic court. In her account, the revolt was led from Nablus by Qasim al-Ahmad, with 'Isa Amar leading the Hebron district, while the mufti of Jerusalem, Tahir Afandi al-Husayni, acted as mediator and was later exiled. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] He should not be confused with Muhammad Tahir al-Husayni, who appears later in the [scene:rd0_limits|campaign against land sales in the 1890s]. The sources name them as separate men.

On 19 and 20 May 1834, about 36 rebels entered Jerusalem through an abandoned sewer near the Dung Gate and opened the gate to the rest. The first day's fighting killed 50 peasants, 16 townspeople and five soldiers. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Rood reports that Ibrahim lost 1,500 of his 9,000 soldiers in rebel ambushes. The violence did not run along a single line: 33 Christian men and women of Bayt Jala were killed on suspicion of looting. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834]

The sources differ on Hebron, the revolt's last stronghold, and both versions are given here. In Rood's account, Hebron was besieged on 24 July, and 630 young men were afterwards sent to Egypt for the army. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834] A reference summary instead dates Hebron's defeat to 4 August and gives about 500 killed and 750 men conscripted. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] Rood's study rests on the Jerusalem court records, but neither figure can be confirmed against the other with the material in hand. Qasim al-Ahmad was captured in Transjordan in August 1834 and beheaded in Damascus. His sons were beheaded in Acre. [cite:rs_rd0_rood_1834]

The wider cost is known only from the reference summary, and it is reported here as that source's figure. It states that some 10,000 peasants were deported to Egypt, and that deportation, conscription and flight together reduced Palestine's male population by about one-fifth. The same source records the rebels' stated aim: to expel the Egyptians and restore Ottoman rule. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

That stated aim lies at the centre of a real argument among historians. The question is whether 1834 was an early moment of Palestinian national identity. Baruch Kimmerling and Joel Migdal, in The Palestinian People (2003), treat the revolt as formative, because it joined disparate groups against a common enemy, and those groups later re-emerged as the Palestinian people. Their strongest evidence is the shape of the revolt itself: peasants and townspeople from Nablus, Jerusalem and the Hebron hills, with the city's religious leadership as intermediary, acting together against one ruler. Benny Morris argues the opposite. The rebels demanded no independence, they likely saw themselves as Ottoman subjects, Arabs or Syrians, and they left no lasting national tradition. The reference summary that reports his view adds that the revolt is largely absent from Palestinian collective memory, and that its declared purpose was to restore the Ottomans, not to replace them. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki]

Two further readings complicate both positions. Shimon Shamir sees the Egyptian period as the first application of the territorial state in Palestine, since a centralizing government reached its villages with conscription, disarmament and direct taxation. Adel Manna argues that the way twentieth-century writers felt about the Ottomans and about Muhammad Ali shaped how the revolt was later written about, on every side. [cite:rs_rd0_revolt1834_wiki] On Manna's point, the debate over 1834 is partly a debate about the twentieth century carried back into the nineteenth. What the sources do not settle is what the rebels thought they were: the court records preserve their acts and their stated demand, but not a statement of identity in their own words.

The third pressure came from Europe, and it ended the Egyptian interlude. On 15 July 1840, in the Convention of London, Britain, Austria, Prussia and Russia backed Sultan Abdülmecid I against Muhammad Ali. They offered him hereditary rule of Egypt if he withdrew from Syria. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_ellison] British and allied ships then shelled Beirut and Sidon on 11 September 1840 and bombarded Acre on 3 November 1840. On 27 November 1840 Muhammad Ali accepted terms. He withdrew from Syria and the Holy Land in return for hereditary rule of Egypt and Sudan. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_wiki] Acre, which had held against a French army in 1799, fell to European naval guns in 1840.

Britain's reason for acting was stated plainly, and it was not about Palestine as such. In William Erich Ellison's 2024 analysis of the crisis, Britain sought to "preserve Turkey" as a route to India and as a bulwark against Russian expansion. [cite:rs_rd0_oriental1840_ellison] The same years saw a separate, religious current in British policy towards Jerusalem, which is told in [scene:bc_s05|the section on Protestant restorationism]. The two converged in 1840 without being the same thing. The interest that moved the fleets was imperial and strategic. In the same years, Istanbul began its own programme of reform, the subject of [scene:rd0_tanzimat|the next part of the Ottoman story].

Seen as a mechanism, the four decades follow a single pattern. The power to decide who ruled Palestine lay with the Sultan in Istanbul, with the ruler of Egypt in Cairo, who could raise his own army, and, by 1840, with a concert of European powers that could settle the question by treaty and enforce it with ships. The people of the land had one instrument of their own, revolt, and in 1834 they used it against conscription, disarmament and new taxes. They could make Egyptian rule costly, at the price of deportations, executions and a lost fifth of the male population, if the reference figure is right. They could not decide the outcome. That was settled in London in July 1840 and enforced off Acre in November, and the settlement returned the land to the empire that the rebels of 1834 had said they wanted back.

Several things remain open. No original of Napoleon's supposed letter has been found, and the scholars who have studied it disagree about whether even the 1799 report reflects anything he said. The Hebron figures differ between the court-record study and the reference summary. The deportation total and the one-fifth estimate rest on a reference summary rather than on a study of the records. And whether the revolt of 1834 was the first stirring of a Palestinian national identity, a provincial rising for the old order, or both at once remains a matter of interpretation on which the historians named here continue to disagree.

sections.h: N M Rothschild & Sons: The London House and Its Legend
sections.html:
The best-known story about the Rothschilds in London is a single episode. Nathan Rothschild, it says, watched the Battle of Waterloo, raced the news to London, and made the family fortune by buying up British bonds before anyone else knew the result. The story is still repeated. The documented record of the London house is a different kind of history, slower and more ordinary: a merchant bank that lent to a foreign state on new terms, supplied the Bank of England in a panic, sent the first Jewish member to the House of Commons, and found the money for Britain's Suez Canal shares while Parliament was not sitting. The legend can be traced to a pamphlet published in 1846, ten years after Nathan's death, and written to stir hostility toward Jews.

The house began as one part of a family design. Mayer Amschel Rothschild of Frankfurt placed five sons in five European financial centres: Frankfurt, London, Paris, Vienna and Naples. The result was a cross-border house that could move capital and information between capitals faster than most governments could. That structure, rather than any single trade, is the documented source of the family's position in the nineteenth century. [cite:wiki_nathan_mayer_rothschild] The father's rise, and the dispersal of the five brothers, are told in [scene:s01|the chapter's opening section].

The London house was founded by Nathan Mayer Rothschild, who lived from 1777 to 1836. Its founding date is given two ways in this book's sources. One account dates N M Rothschild & Sons to 1809, and places Nathan in London from that year. [cite:wiki_nathan_mayer_rothschild] Another gives 1811. [cite:schama_two_rothschilds] The sources do not explain the difference, and both dates are recorded here. This Nathan, the founder, should not be confused with a later namesake, Nathan Mayer Rothschild, 1st Baron, the father of the Walter Rothschild to whom the Balfour Declaration was addressed in 1917.

The house's first great contribution to state finance came in 1818. It arranged a £5 million loan for Prussia, denominated in sterling, with interest payable in London. Until then, British investors who bought a foreign government's bonds carried the risk that the foreign currency would fall. A loan written in sterling and paid in London removed that risk. The Rothschild Archive describes the Prussian loan as "the true precursor of the public borrowing which transformed the international capital market in the nineteenth century." [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] That description is quoted from the family's own institutional record, and it should be read as such: the archive's judgment of the loan's importance, not an independent one. In this book's sources it reaches the reader through a personal website that reproduces the archive's words, since the archive's own page could not be checked directly.

In 1825, during a banking panic, the house supplied the Bank of England with specie, that is, hard coin. The institution that had been chartered in 1694 to lend to the Crown [scene:rd0_bank1694|as the chapter has shown] now drew on a private house in a crisis. The two were not rivals. They were parts of the same London system of state credit.

The London house's political ties to the state came through Nathan's son, Lionel de Rothschild. Lionel was elected to the House of Commons repeatedly from 1847, but he could not take his seat, because members were required to swear an oath as Christians. When the Jews Relief Act ended that requirement, he took his seat in 1858 as the first Jewish member of the House of Commons. [cite:wiki_lionel_de_rothschild]

Lionel was also head of the house when it carried out its most famous transaction with the British state. The Suez Canal had opened in 1869. It was owned by French financiers and by the Khedive of Egypt, but by 1874 four-fifths of its trade was British. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] On 15 November 1875, Benjamin Disraeli learned that the Khedive meant to sell his shares. Ten days later, on 25 November 1875, the purchase was concluded: Britain acquired 44% of the company's shares for £4,000,000. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023]

The speed is what made the house necessary. Parliament was not sitting, so the government could not vote the money. N M Rothschild & Sons, under Lionel de Rothschild, advanced it. The Rothschild Archive calls it a "technically unsecured loan" and says it was repaid within five months. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023] The mechanism matters more than the drama of the story. An executive that wanted to act before the legislature could meet borrowed from a private house in the City, and asked Parliament to approve the act after it was done.

The purchase did not pass without objection. William Gladstone attacked it for its "lack of reference or consent from Parliament." The purchase also left France as the majority shareholder. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] Disraeli answered his critics in the House of Commons on 14 and 21 February 1876, and his own words, preserved in Hansard, state the government's reason without ambiguity. He defended the purchase "as a political transaction, and one which I believe is calculated to strengthen the Empire," and said it "secures to us a highway to our Indian Empire." He did not recommend it, he said, "as a financial investment." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] He also explained why only a house like the Rothschilds' would serve. After the first £1,000,000, he told the House, a further £2,000,000 "might be demanded in gold the next day." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] Parliament approved the purchase on 21 February 1876. [cite:rs_rd0_hefler_2023]

What the house earned is the one point in the Suez story that the sources leave open. Critics in Parliament said the Rothschild commission amounted to 15 per cent interest. Disraeli rejected that reading, and denied that the commission had "anything to do with the interest on the advance." [cite:rs_rd0_disraeli_1876] The critics' case is that a short loan to a government in a hurry was priced at a rate no ordinary borrower would have paid. Disraeli's case rested on the terms: he denied that the commission was interest at all, and set it beside the house's undertaking to produce millions in gold at a day's notice. None of the sources consulted for this book states the actual commission rate. [cite:rs_rd0_rotharchive_suez] Who was right cannot be settled from them. Disraeli's stated aim, the route to India, belongs to the story of why Britain wanted the region at all, which is taken up in [scene:or_s01|a later volume].

Set against that record, the Waterloo story belongs to a different category. It first appears in 1846, in a pamphlet by Georges Dairnvaell, published under the name "Satan." Dairnvaell wrote it after a railway accident on a line the Rothschilds had financed, and he wrote it explicitly to inflame hostility toward Jews. [cite:wiki_dairnvaell_satan_pamphlet] Nathan had died in 1836. He could not answer it. The story's origin is antisemitic. The sources describe that aim as explicit, not as something read into the pamphlet afterwards.

The family's archive rejects the story on the evidence. According to the Rothschild Archive, nothing in the record suggests that Nathan was the first in London to know of the victory. Niall Ferguson, author of the family's authorized history, estimates that any quick profit Nathan could have made on British bonds after the battle could not have exceeded about £7,000. The archive's verdict, as quoted in this book's sources, is short: "The legend of Nathan Rothschild and Waterloo is just that: a legend." [cite:jwatte_rothschild_myths_record] [cite:leonardo_english_rothschild_waterloo] These words reach this book through the same personal website noted above, and are given here as the archive's position as reported there.

Not every account in this book's research tells the story the same way. The chapter's opening section draws on a summary that credits Ferguson with a different verdict: that Nathan's information advantage was real, that the market timing was more complex than the mythology, and that the version in which Nathan "cornered the market" was a nineteenth-century antisemitic caricature by Édouard Drumont, later amplified. That version and the one given here agree that the legend's popular form is an antisemitic invention. They differ on its origin, Dairnvaell in 1846 or Drumont, and on whether Nathan had any advantage in news at all. The record reached for this section, the archive's statement and the £7,000 ceiling, points toward the narrower reading: at most a small and ordinary trade, and no evidence that Nathan knew first.

The story outlived its author because it served a purpose. The claim that the family secretly directed governments rests on the line that runs from the 1846 pamphlet and on later elaborations. The family's own archive, Ferguson's authorized history and the journalist Mike Rothschild's 2023 study each take those claims apart. [cite:publishersweekly_jewish_space_lasers] The Waterloo legend is antisemitic in origin, and naming it as such is part of the record.

The documented house, in short, was a creditor and contractor to states, not a puppeteer of them. Its relationships with the British government were contracts: sovereign loans, a central bank supplied in a panic, the Suez advance, and a seat in Parliament won by election and delayed by an oath. All of them operated inside the City of London that the chapter began with. The documents also show who held the power to decide. The Suez purchase was Disraeli's to make, Parliament's to approve and Gladstone's to attack. Disraeli's own justification for it was the empire, not the bank.

Some things remain open. The founding year of the London house is recorded two ways. The size of the Suez commission, and so the real cost of the advance to the Treasury, is not stated in any source consulted. The Rothschild Archive's verdict on Waterloo reaches this book secondhand, and the summaries of Ferguson that this book draws on describe his findings differently. None of these gaps changes the central finding. The record of the London house is a record of public, contractual business with states, and the legend that replaced it in popular memory was made, from its first printing, as an attack on Jews.

sections.h: The Pope's Bankers: Torlonia, the Rothschilds and the Papal Loans, 1794–1870
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that the papacy has always managed its money through its own institutions, apart from any private banking family. For the nineteenth century the record points the other way. Before 1870 the Pope was also the ruler of a territorial state, the Papal States, and like other rulers of his time he borrowed. The first lender was a Roman banker who was paid partly in titles. The next was the Rothschild houses. The arrangement between them, and the hostility it drew, are a small but revealing part of the European board on which Palestine's future would later be decided.

This section rests on a narrower base of evidence than most in the chapter, and the reader should know that from the start. Almost every detail of the papal loans below reaches this book through a single reference article on the Rothschild loans to the Holy See, which in turn relies on Niall Ferguson's history of the house of Rothschild. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The specific terms of the 1831 arrangement, its reported exclusivity clause, the 1834 episode and the 1906 encyclopedia phrase have not been independently checked for this book. The accounts also contradict one another at several points. Those contradictions are set out below rather than resolved.

The story begins with Giovanni Torlonia, who lived from 1754 to 1829. According to the account summarized here, he was born to modest circumstances in the Auvergne region of France and built one of the largest banking fortunes in Rome through cloth trading, money-lending and papal patronage. He opened his banking house in Rome in 1780. By the 1790s he had become the Holy See's principal banker, providing loans, managing financial transactions and handling the papacy's increasingly complex needs during the Napoleonic period. Pope Pius VI made him a noble in 1794, on 9 March according to the date the account gives from the Archivio di Stato, as Don Giovanni Torlonia, 1st Prince of Civitella Cesi. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see]

The mechanism here is plain. The banker supplied the papacy with financial services, and the papacy supplied the banker with aristocratic standing. The account describes the exchange as mutually reinforcing: the Torlonia house became the papacy's main financial institution and gained the social legitimacy of papal nobility at the same time. The French Revolutionary period enlarged its role. When French forces occupied Rome in 1798 and 1799 and papal finances were thrown into disorder, the account says, Torlonia's house managed the transfer of papal funds and lent the money that kept the papacy's operations going through the occupation and the restoration that followed. By Napoleon's final defeat in 1814, the family was established as the papacy's principal financial manager. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see]

The papacy also stood at the centre of an older Roman aristocracy. The Orsini and the Colonna, two of its oldest families, had held the ceremonial office of Prince Assistant to the Papal Throne in alternation since 1735. The Orsini had produced three popes: Celestine III in 1191, Nicholas III in 1277 and Benedict XIII in 1724. None came in the modern era. [cite:wiki_black_nobility] [cite:wiki_orsini_family]

In 1823 the new banking family married into this old one, when Giovanni's son Alessandro Torlonia married an Orsini. The bride's name is itself recorded two ways in the same account: once as Maria Luisa Orsini, and once as Teresa Orsini. The account cites the evidence of the marriage as Rome diocesan records, the Orsini family genealogies held in the Archivio Segreto Vaticano and in private family archives, and Pompeo Litta's Famiglie celebri d'Italia (1819–83), a record of the great Italian noble lineages. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] It goes on to interpret the match: Alessandro needed the legitimacy that only centuries-old noble blood could provide, while the Orsini needed to keep their finances afloat after the disruptions of the Napoleonic years, and the marriage was arranged, as such marriages were, with both families' positions in mind. In this telling, the timing of the Rothschild connection eight years later was "not accidental." That is the account's own interpretation. No document quoted in it shows the marriage being made with the later banking arrangement in view.

The Rothschilds entered Roman finance in 1831. The reference account explains why. After the Napoleonic wars and the Restoration, the Papal States were in fiscal distress. The Torlonia house lacked the capital to meet the papacy's needs at the scale now required. And the Rothschild houses were, by 1830, the dominant private banking operation in Europe. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] On 30 November 1831, according to the account, Alessandro Torlonia co-signed a contract in Rome with James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house. The account's short summary describes the contract as giving the Rothschilds an exclusive right of first refusal on all papal sovereign debt, by a clause kept secret. Its more detailed description, drawn from Ferguson, describes the terms differently, as exclusive management of papal loan issues and key papal financial operations through the London house of Nathan Mayer Rothschild and the Paris house of James Mayer de Rothschild, with the Torlonia house as local intermediary. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] A right of first refusal and the exclusive management of loans are not the same thing. The record available here does not settle which description fits the contract, because the contract itself is not quoted.

The loan that followed is better documented. In 1832 the Rothschilds lent £400,000 to Pope Gregory XVI. The loan was negotiated through Carl Mayer von Rothschild, with James acting as the official papal banker. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] According to the account, a letter from Gregory XVI dated 15 January 1832 acknowledges the Rothschilds' help in terms that confirm the relationship. Who repaid the loan, over what term and at what rate are not stated in the sources available for this section. Nor do they say from what revenues of the Papal States it was serviced.

The episode of 1834 is where the sources diverge most sharply, and the two versions cannot both be true as told. In one, the 1834 affair was the enforcement of the secret clause. A cardinal named Tosti tried to refinance the papal debt with six other banks, and Carl Mayer de Rothschild travelled to Rome, produced the original contract and blocked him. In the other, Antonio Tosti was not a cardinal refinancing the debt but the papal treasurer (elsewhere, the papal envoy), and he had embezzled papal funds. The Rothschild houses' records of their dealings with the papacy could be compared against the papacy's own accounts, the discrepancies revealed the embezzlement, and the Rothschild correspondence, as Ferguson describes it, refers to the affair and to the banking relationship's role in uncovering it. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The second version comes with an interpretation: that the papacy's own financial management could not detect fraud by its own treasurer, that the external auditor, however informal, was the Rothschild house, and that the papacy's finances before any internal institution existed, before the Vatican bank, the IOR, was founded in 1942, depended on this outside relationship. That reading depends on which version of 1834 is right, and the record available here does not decide it.

The question of which Rothschild house was the counterparty is itself unsettled. The account's summary names James Mayer de Rothschild of the Paris house as the signatory in 1831. Its detailed description names the London and Paris houses together. A separate explanatory treatment in this book's research names the Paris house and the Naples house of the Rothschilds as the lenders, and in another version names the London house, N M Rothschild & Sons. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] What the sources agree on is that the papacy borrowed from more than one Rothschild brother, through the family's network of houses, and that Carl Mayer and James both appear in the record of the 1832 loan.

The same explanatory treatment offers an analogy for the relationship, and it is worth giving in its own terms as an analogy, not a finding. Imagine a family that takes out one loan from one lender in a crisis. From then on, whenever money is needed, everyone simply calls the same number. Nobody decides it each time. It was decided once, long ago, and the number stays taped to the wall. The analogy's authors insist that this is not a conspiracy but the way long-lived institutions prefer to work: a relationship that is expensive to set up and hard to replace, so that the first lender becomes the default for every later need. As a description of institutional habit it is useful. As history it claims more than the sources show, because it assumes a continuity of lending that the record of this period does not document beyond the loans of the 1830s.

The relationship was public knowledge by the early twentieth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia, published by Funk & Wagnalls between 1901 and 1906, and compiled, according to the account, by about 400 Jewish and non-Jewish scholars, describes the Rothschilds in its "Rothschild" entry as "guardians of the papal treasure." [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] The account reads the phrase in strong terms: as proof that the connection was publicly known by 1906, was not treated as secret by the parties, and was understood as a custodial relationship in which the Rothschilds managed papal assets rather than simply lending. The phrase itself has not been checked against the encyclopedia for this book. Even if it is exact, a single phrase in a reference work describes a reputation. It does not show what assets, if any, were held, or on what terms.

The loans drew hostility from Catholic critics, and the record is clear about its character. Catholic criticism at the time, as a remark by Alfred de Vigny shows, centred on the Rothschilds' Jewishness. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] Objection to the terms of a loan, or to a sovereign's debts, is a political argument. Objection to a lender because he is a Jew is antisemitism, and this book names it as such. The documented business was a set of loans to an indebted state. The trope built on top of it is a different thing.

The territorial state that did the borrowing ended in 1870, with the fall of the Papal States. The Roman families who stayed loyal to the Pope afterwards, the Black Nobility, including the Orsini and the Colonna, distanced themselves from the new Italian monarchy in a specific act of protest: they kept the doors of their palaces closed in mourning. [cite:wiki_black_nobility] From this point the papacy was a church without a state, and it remained so until 1929. The settlement that later compensated it for the lost territory, and what it did to the Black Nobility's court positions, belong to 1929 and are told in [scene:vat_s00d|a later volume].

Some writers draw a line from these loans to the present. One version runs from the 1831 arrangement through the Torlonia family's rental of their Roman villa to Mussolini (from 1923 in one account and from 1925 in another, until 1943) to the appointment in 2026 of François Pauly, a former chief executive of the Edmond de Rothschild group, as president of the supervisory board of the Vatican bank, dated 25 March 2026 in one account and 28 April 2026 in another. [cite:wiki_rothschild_loans_holy_see] Those events lie far outside this chapter and are told in [scene:bc_s08|a later volume]. The discipline that applies to them applies here too: each is separately documented, nothing in the record shows that they form one continuous project, and the 2026 appointment is an institutional adjacency, a former executive of a bank that bears the Rothschild name, not a family tie.

What this section's record establishes is modest and real. A Roman banker rose by serving the papacy and was ennobled for it. His son married into the old papal aristocracy. When the Papal States needed more than a Roman house could provide, they borrowed from the Rothschilds, and the 1832 loan of £400,000 to Gregory XVI is documented. Catholic critics attacked the arrangement in terms of the lenders' religion, and that attack is part of the record. What the record available here does not establish is the exact text of the 1831 contract, whether it contained an exclusive clause and of what kind, which house signed it, what happened in 1834, and whether "guardians of the papal treasure" meant more than a reputation. Each of those rests, for now, on a single reference account and its reading of one historian, and each awaits a check against the documents themselves.

sections.h: Restoration Before Zionism: The Protestant Lobby, 1839–1891
sections.html:
A common assumption holds that Christian political support for a Jewish state was a product of the twentieth century: a response to the Holocaust and to the founding of Israel in 1948. The documents place its political beginnings more than a century earlier, and in a different place. Before any Jewish political movement for a state existed, a Protestant current in Britain and the United States had already put the idea of a Jewish "restoration" to Palestine before a Foreign Secretary and a President. Restorationism, the belief that a Jewish return to Palestine would fulfil biblical prophecy, was an organized political current decades before Theodor Herzl. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism]

The British story begins inside a family. Anthony Ashley-Cooper, Lord Shaftesbury, was an evangelical peer and reformer. He was also Palmerston's stepson-in-law: the Foreign Secretary, Lord Palmerston, was his wife's stepfather. In 1839 Shaftesbury pressed Palmerston to sponsor Jewish settlement in Palestine under British protection. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] The access mattered. Shaftesbury's request needed a government to carry it, and the Ottoman sultan, who ruled it, answered to no British minister. What Shaftesbury had was the ear of the one man in London whose instructions reached Constantinople.

Palmerston acted. In 1840 he instructed his ambassador at Constantinople to urge the Ottoman sultan to encourage Jewish settlement, and Britain's new consulate in Jerusalem was given a brief to protect Jews. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] Those were the two instruments available to a European power in the Ottoman lands of the time: diplomatic pressure on the sultan's government, and a consul on the ground who could take named people under his protection. Neither could settle anyone. The decision to admit or encourage settlers lay with the Porte, and the instruction asked the sultan to use a power that only he held.

The sources are frank that the motive was double. Restorationism was theological and imperial at once. Shaftesbury and Palmerston saw a protected Jewish presence as a British foothold in Ottoman Syria; American evangelicals read the same prospect as prophecy. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] A minister could pursue it as policy and an evangelical as faith, and the two readings did not have to agree for the request to be made. What neither reading drew on was Jewish opinion. Most Jewish communal bodies of the period opposed restorationism or ignored it. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The idea was advanced on behalf of Jews, by Christians, for reasons of prophecy and empire.

The restorationist current also produced the most quoted slogan in the later conflict, and its history is not the one usually told. The earliest published version of "a land without a people for a people without a land" appeared in an 1843 book by Alexander Keith, a Church of Scotland clergyman and an advocate of Jewish "restoration" who had travelled to Palestine in 1839. Shaftesbury used similar wording in 1853. [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] His own phrase for Palestine was a country without a nation for a nation without a country. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] [cite:wiki_shaftesbury] The first use by a Zionist came only in 1901, when Israel Zangwill wrote that Palestine was "a country without a people." [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] The phrase, in other words, was coined by a Christian restorationist more than half a century before any Zionist adopted it.

What it meant is debated. One reading takes it literally: the land was described as empty. The other holds that it meant a land "without a nation," a country whose inhabitants were not organized as a people with a state, and that its authors were making a political claim rather than a demographic one. Shaftesbury's own wording, "without a nation," is consistent with the second reading. Against the first, the counts are plain: every Ottoman and British census shows a populated country. Keith, the man who first published the phrase, had visited Palestine and knew it was populated. [cite:meq_land_without_people] [cite:aijac_slogan_origin] Whichever reading is preferred, the phrase described a country that had people in it. The same set of checks examines two other claims that are often paired with this one, that Arab leaders "rejected every offer" and that the conflict is a religious war two thousand years old; both concern later periods and are taken up in [scene:sq_s05|three slogans checked against the record].

The American counterpart came half a century after Shaftesbury. In March 1891 the Chicago evangelist William E. Blackstone presented President Benjamin Harrison with a petition urging American support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine. The Blackstone Memorial, as it became known, was signed by more than four hundred prominent Americans, among them John D. Rockefeller, J. P. Morgan and the Chief Justice. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] It preceded Herzl's Der Judenstaat by five years and the first Zionist Congress at Basel by six. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The instrument was different from Palmerston's. Shaftesbury had worked through a minister who could instruct an ambassador; Blackstone worked through public petition, using the names of men of finance and law to press a head of state. The President, like the Foreign Secretary before him, could only ask; the land was still the sultan's.

Set side by side, the two currents show the sequence that most accounts reverse. The familiar order runs from a Jewish political movement to Christian sympathy for it. The documents run the other way: Christian political support for a Jewish return came first, and Jewish political Zionism came second. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] By the time the Zionist movement had an organization, a Christian political base for a Jewish state already existed in Britain and the United States, at a time when most Jewish communal bodies still opposed or ignored the idea. That ordering helps explain why the Balfour Declaration of 1917 found a ready constituency in Britain's governing class. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism]

The constituency did not stand still after 1891. In 1909 the Scofield Reference Bible gave it a theology: its dispensationalist reading made support for a Jewish state a mass Protestant doctrine. Balfour, whose name the 1917 declaration bears, was himself a Christian restorationist. Later still, Christians United for Israel in the Hagee era stands at the twentieth-century end of a lineage that begins in 1839, not in 1948. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] The Scofield Bible and its public belong to the next part of this book, in [scene:s05|the Scofield Reference Bible, 1909].

The finding should be kept at its proper size. Before the Zionist Congress, and before Rothschild money built colonies in Palestine, Protestant restorationism had already made a Jewish return a live question in British and American politics, for reasons of prophecy and empire that had little to do with Jewish opinion. That constituency, not any single family, was the pre-existing structure into which the Zionist project would later connect. It does not follow that restorationists created Zionism, which had its own Jewish sources in prayer, persecution and nationalism, nor that they could deliver Palestine: in 1840 and in 1891 the land was the sultan's, and neither a Foreign Secretary nor a President could do more than ask.

Much is left open by the record as it stands here. The text of Palmerston's 1840 instruction is not quoted in these sources, and neither the sultan's response nor any settlement it produced is recorded. The consulate's brief to protect Jews is documented; what the consuls did with it in these decades is not described here. The record does not say how Harrison answered Blackstone, or whether the memorial changed anything in American policy. And the statement that most Jewish communal bodies opposed or ignored restorationism is made in general terms, without naming the bodies or their statements. Those are the limits of what can be said about this current before 1896.

sections.h: Reform from Istanbul: Edicts, a Constitution and Jerusalem's Deputy, 1839–1878
sections.html:
A claim met earlier in this chapter, in the sketch of the Ottoman Empire on the board of 1789–1815, holds that the Ottoman parliamentary reforms of 1876 gave Palestine representation and that "Palestinian delegates sat in the Ottoman parliament." [cite:wiki_ottoman_palestine] The claim is right in substance and loose in its detail. The record supports one named deputy for the district of Jerusalem in the parliament of 1877, a man who used his seat to oppose the sultan and lost it within a year. To see what that seat was, and what it was not, the story has to begin almost four decades earlier, with a series of promises issued from Istanbul to all the sultan's subjects.

The reform era the Ottomans called the Tanzimat opened on 3 November 1839. On that day Sultan Abdülmecid I proclaimed the Edict of Gülhane, at the urging of his Grand Vizier, Mustafa Reşid Pasha. According to the standard reference account, which draws on Cleveland and Bunton and on Liebesny, the edict promised three things: security of life, honour and property; a regular system of taxation in place of tax farming; and regular conscription. [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] Its concessions were said to extend "to all our subjects, whatever religion or sect they may belong to." [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] The same account is careful about its force. The edict changed no laws by itself and was never fully implemented. [cite:rs_rd0_gulhane_wiki] It was a declaration of the state's intentions, and its force depended on the legislation and enforcement that followed.

The mechanism matters for Palestine. The two practical promises of Gülhane, regular taxation and regular conscription, required the state to know who its subjects were and what they held. That need is the thread that runs from this edict to the registration of land under the Land Code of 1858, the subject of the next section, where many cultivators avoided the register precisely because it brought taxes and conscription with it. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] The promise of security of property and the demand for a regular revenue were, from the start, the same reform seen from two sides.

The second great instrument came at the end of a war. The Reform Edict of 18 February 1856 was issued as the Crimean War ended. According to the reference account, it promised equality in education, government appointments and justice regardless of creed, freedom of worship, and mixed tribunals for cases between Muslims and non-Muslims. Among its provisions was military service for non-Muslims, which proved unpopular. [cite:rs_rd0_reform1856_wiki] Where Gülhane had extended its concessions to all subjects in general words, the 1856 edict spelled out equality in particular fields of public life. Both remained edicts: promises made from the centre, whose effect in a given province depended on how far they were enforced there.

The third step went further than any edict. On 23 December 1876 an Ottoman constitution was promulgated, and on 19 March 1877 the first Ottoman parliament opened at Dolmabahçe Palace. Its deputies were not elected directly by the population. They were chosen indirectly, through the provincial councils. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] That detail shapes what "representation" meant. A deputy was the choice of a provincial council, not of a popular vote.

The sources disagree on the size of the chamber. The Institute for Palestine Studies' PalQuest counts 120 deputies, fourteen of them Arab. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] The reference account of the First Constitutional Era gives 115 members, and for the second elections a split of 69 Muslim and 46 non-Muslim deputies. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] The sources do not reconcile the two figures, and neither is adopted here as settled.

Jerusalem's deputy in that chamber was Yusuf Diya al-Khalidi. Born in Jerusalem in 1842, he was educated well beyond the city's own schools. He studied at the al-Fakhriyya school, at the British Diocesan Boys' School in Jerusalem, at a Protestant college in Malta, and in Istanbul. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] In 1875, two years before he took his seat, The Jewish Chronicle published two of his letters on the Jews of Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] He had also served as head of Jerusalem's municipality, though the sources date that service differently. PalQuest gives his mayoralty as 1870–1874, with two later terms. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] Jerusalem Story says he was appointed in September 1865, at the age of 23, and headed the municipality for nine years. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] Both agree that he governed the city before he represented it.

In 1877 al-Khalidi was elected as the sole deputy for the Jerusalem mutasarrifate, and by PalQuest's count he was one of fourteen Arab deputies among 120. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] He did not sit quietly. Both biographical sources describe him as a prominent opponent of Sultan Abdul Hamid II in the chamber. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] How that district was constituted, and how many people lived in it, is set out in [scene:s00h|the Baseline account of Ottoman Palestine].

The parliament was short-lived. Abdul Hamid II suspended both the parliament and the constitution in February 1878, on 14 February in one account and on 13 February in another. [cite:rs_rd0_firstconst_wiki] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] When the chamber was dissolved, al-Khalidi was one of ten opposition deputies ordered out of Istanbul. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] The chain of power is visible in that sequence. The constitution had created a chamber, but it had not created a body the sultan could not dismiss. The man who had promulgated it could suspend it, and the deputies who had opposed him could be sent away from the capital. Jerusalem's representation in the imperial parliament had lasted less than a year.

Measured against this record, the earlier claim can now be stated exactly. It is documented that the 1876 constitution produced a parliament in which the Jerusalem district had an elected deputy, and that this deputy, al-Khalidi, was a Jerusalem notable, a former head of the city's municipality and an outspoken member of the opposition. That is a real fact of formal political representation, and it answers any account in which the people of the country had no part in the empire's politics. What the record assembled here does not support is the plural. It names one deputy for Jerusalem. Fourteen Arab deputies sat by PalQuest's count, but the sources used here do not say which, if any, of the others sat for districts that lay in what would later be Palestine. "Palestinian delegates" should therefore read, on present evidence, "Jerusalem's deputy."

In the same year the parliament closed, religious equality in the Ottoman lands was written into an international treaty. Article 62 of the Treaty of Berlin of 1878 declared that "in no part of the Ottoman Empire shall difference of religion be alleged against any person." [cite:rs_rd0_fo1893_berlin62] Where the edicts had been the sultan's own promises to his subjects, Article 62 stood in a treaty, and foreign diplomats could invoke it. British diplomats later did exactly that, citing the article against Ottoman restrictions on Jews. [cite:rs_rd0_fo1893_berlin62] How those restrictions arose, and how Britain and the United States contested them, is told in [scene:rd0_limits|the Ottoman limits of 1882–1896].

These decades also saw the first departures in the other direction. From the 1870s Palestinian emigration to the Americas began, mostly of Christian families from Bethlehem, Beit Jala and Beit Sahour who travelled on Ottoman papers and were therefore long called "Turcos." [cite:palquest_sv] Where they settled and what became of their communities is told in [scene:dsp_s01|the account of the Palestinian diaspora].

Al-Khalidi's part in this book does not end in 1878. On 1 March 1899, through Zadok Kahn, Chief Rabbi of France, he wrote to Theodor Herzl urging that Palestine be left in peace, and on 19 March Herzl replied that Jewish immigration would benefit the country. [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_palquest] [cite:rs_rd0_khalidi_jstory] That exchange belongs to the next part of this book.

Several questions remain open on this record. The reference accounts of the two edicts say what was promised and that Gülhane was never fully implemented, but they do not measure how far either edict was carried out in the district of Jerusalem, or how the people of Palestine received them. The size of the 1877 chamber stands at 115 or 120, depending on the source. Al-Khalidi's years as head of the municipality are dated from 1865 in one biography and from 1870 in the other. The day of the suspension is given as 13 or 14 February 1878. And the sources consulted here are silent on what the people who chose al-Khalidi through the provincial councils expected of him, beyond the fact that he went to Istanbul and opposed the sultan.

sections.h: The Land Code of 1858: How the Deeds Became Sellable
sections.html:
A familiar account of the early Zionist land purchases holds that Jewish buyers acquired empty or unused land in Palestine from willing local owners. That account begins at the moment of sale. The legal history begins earlier, in a set of Ottoman laws of 1856 to 1867 that decided who could hold a deed, whose name went on it, and who could buy it. Those laws did not concern Zionism, which did not yet exist. They concerned revenue, conscription and the control of foreign purchasers. But they produced the documents through which land in Palestine would later change hands, and they explain how a sale could be perfectly lawful between owner and buyer and still pass over the heads of the people who farmed the land.

The starting point is a prohibition. According to a reference summary drawing on work by Ruth Kark published in 1984, foreigners were officially barred from buying land in Palestine from 1856, and the ban held in practice until 1867. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] For a decade, then, the question of who could own land was settled against outsiders, whatever the paper said about who owned it inside the country.

Inside the country the paper itself was about to change. In 1858, as part of the reforms known as the Tanzimat, the Ottoman state issued a Land Code, the Arazi Kanunnamesi. It classified land into categories and required titles to be registered individually. The purpose was fiscal and military: registration would secure tax revenue and the conscription rolls. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] The same year brought the Tabu law, the law of title deeds. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The two were the practical side of the promises made in the Edict of Gülhane of 1839, which had pledged security of property, a regular tax system and regular conscription, as the [scene:rd0_tanzimat|previous section] describes. A state that wished to tax and conscript its subjects needed a register of what they held.

In Palestine the register opened a gap between who owned land on paper and who worked it. Many cultivators did not register the land they farmed. A reference summary, citing Nasser Abufarha, gives the reason: registration brought taxes and conscription, and cultivators resisted it for that reason. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Title was recorded instead in other names: village heads, urban merchants or notables, and absentee families living in Beirut and Damascus. The fellahin, the peasant cultivators, went on working the same fields, in practice as tenants. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Nothing on the ground had to change for this to happen. The village continued to plough and harvest. What changed was the document, and the document now named someone else.

Historians have described the result in strong terms. The same reference summary quotes Yehoshua Porath, writing in 1977, that the 1858 code "brought about the appropriation by the influential and rich families of Beirut, Damascus" and other cities of vast tracts. [cite:rs_rd0_landpurchase_wiki] Kark, in a study published in 2017, finds that land came to be concentrated in "families of urban effendis (absentee landlords)" who lived in cities in Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The two readings agree on the shape of what happened: title flowed to urban families, often living outside the district, while cultivation stayed in the villages.

The third law opened the door to outside buyers. In 1867 the Ottoman state issued a law allowing foreigners to acquire real property. Its Article II, as quoted by the United States minister at Constantinople in a dispatch of 5 January 1898, placed foreign landowners "upon terms of equality with Ottoman subjects in all things that concern their landed property." The United States accepted the law by protocol in 1874. [cite:rs_rd0_frus1898_law1867] The barrier of 1856 was gone, and a foreign buyer stood, on paper, where an Ottoman subject stood.

Kark treats the three measures, the 1858 Land Code, the 1858 Tabu law and the 1867 law on foreigners, as one process of privatization, the process that began land survey, registration and mapping in nineteenth-century Palestine. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] In her account, effendi ownership made it easier for Jewish immigrants to buy part of this land. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] She also counts what the purchases built on. According to Kark, more than 52 estate buildings became the first core of Jewish agricultural settlements, and at least 15 became the core of German Christian settlements or religious institutions. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] Those numbers matter for the claim at the head of this section. The estates were not empty ground. They were properties with buildings on them, held by owners who could sell, and they were bought by more than one kind of newcomer: German Christians as well as Jews.

That finding also adjusts the timing in the familiar account. The deeds did not wait for the British Mandate to become saleable. By Kark's count, estates bought under Ottoman rule were already the cores of the first Jewish agricultural settlements. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The settlements of the First Aliyah, described in [scene:rd0_aliyah|the section on the First Aliyah], were built on land that this legal sequence had made purchasable.

Historians characterize the 1867 law differently, and the difference is real. A thesis written at Marmara University in Turkey on land ownership by foreigners and Jews in late Ottoman Palestine calls the 1867 law, the "Safer Kanunu," an attempt to bring foreigners' purchases under legal control. On that reading the law was meant to regulate, and Jews used gaps in it to buy fertile, strategic land on which the first settlements were later built. [cite:rs_rd0_marmara_thesis] The strongest form of this case is that the Ottoman state did try to keep control of land sales to outsiders, and that the purchases succeeded where the law fell short. Kark's reading is structural. The 1858–1867 laws together concentrated land in effendi hands, and that concentration made both Jewish and German Christian purchases easier. [cite:rs_rd0_kark_2017] The strongest form of her case is that no loophole was needed: the law worked as written, and the sales followed from who held the deeds. The first reading places the weight on the buyers' use of the law; the second on the structure of ownership the law produced. The sources do not settle which is right, and the two are not entirely exclusive.

The consequence reached its largest scale after this chapter's period. Under the British Mandate the registered titles were the instruments that could be sold. The largest single transfer to Zionist purchasing companies was the sale of the Beirut-based Sursock family's holdings in the Jezreel Valley in the early 1920s. The land was populated and cultivated, and after the sale its tenant cultivators were evicted, with compensation on terms set by the purchaser. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Who bought, from whom and at what cost is told in [scene:s04j|the account of the Mandate-era land purchases].

The finding should be stated at its proper size. The 1858 code did not cause the Zionist project. It created a documentary form: a registered deed held in the name of someone who did not farm the land. Through that form, populated land could be lawfully transferred over the heads of the people living on it. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] That is why the phrase "willing local owners" is both accurate and incomplete. The owner on the register might be willing. The family in the field was often not on the register at all, having stayed off it to avoid taxation and conscription.

The record leaves important questions open. The sources here give no figure for how much land in Palestine went unregistered or was recorded in absentee names, and none for how many cultivators stood in the gap between title and tillage. Kark's counts of more than 52 and at least 15 estate buildings are not broken down here by date or place. The Marmara thesis is known only through its abstract, and the 1856 ban and the Porath and Abufarha passages only through a reference summary. Nor do these sources say how often, before 1896, a sale under these laws displaced the people who worked the land; for that period the documented consequence is the settlements themselves, and the evictions on record belong to the 1920s.

sections.h: Does Scripture Forbid a Jewish State? Jeremiah, the Three Oaths, and a Debate Older Than Zionism
sections.html:
Two confident answers circulate about what Jewish tradition says on a Jewish state. One holds that Judaism commands it. The other holds that Judaism forbids it. Each speaks as if the tradition had one voice. The texts tell a different story: the question was argued inside Judaism long before anyone founded a political movement, and it is still argued now. This section sets out the argument as the sources give it. It does not rule between the sides, because the tradition itself holds both readings.

The oldest text in the debate comes from the book of Jeremiah. The prophet instructed the exiles carried off to Babylon to build lives where they had been taken, and to "seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it" (Jeremiah 29:7). [cite:sefaria_jer29] The verse does not speak of a state at all. Its weight in the later argument lies in what it asks of exiles: to build lives where they are, and to seek the welfare of the place that holds them.

The second text is legal and far more specific. The Babylonian Talmud, in tractate Ketubot (110b–111a), derives from the Song of Songs three oaths. Israel was not to go up to the land "as a wall", meaning en masse and by force. Israel was not to rebel against the nations. And the nations, in turn, were not to oppress Israel excessively. [cite:w_three_oaths] Two of the three oaths bind Israel; the third binds the nations. That structure matters, because each side of the later debate reads the three clauses together and draws a different conclusion from them.

For many Orthodox authorities, the oaths settle the matter. On this reading, a sovereign Jewish state established before the coming of the Messiah violates them: a return to the land could come only through divine redemption, not human political action, and to force it is a transgression. [cite:w_vayoel][cite:neturei_karta] The fullest statement of this view came well after the period of this chapter. Rabbi Joel Teitelbaum, the rebbe of Satmar, built his work Vayoel Moshe, published in 1959, on the three oaths, and Neturei Karta holds the same view today. [cite:w_vayoel] Earlier, in 1912, Orthodox opposition to secular Zionism took organized form with the founding of Agudat Israel, whose story belongs to a later part of this library [scene:dh_s01|the first political assassination].

The opposite case rests on a different set of authorities. Religious Zionists cite Nachmanides, who counted settling the land among the commandments. On that view, living in and building up the land is not a forbidden forcing of the end but a religious duty in its own right. They cite as well Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, who would become the first Ashkenazi chief rabbi of Mandate Palestine and who saw even secular Zionism as part of the process of redemption. [cite:w_religious_zionism][cite:w_kook] Rav Kook's office, like Agudat Israel, lies beyond 1896; he enters this account as the clearest named voice of the reading that would answer the oaths. Against the oaths themselves, religious Zionists have made two further arguments. Some argue that the oaths lapsed after centuries of persecution. Others argue that the Balfour Declaration and the League of Nations supplied the nations' consent. Both arguments are recorded as positions some religious Zionists hold, not as the view of every authority on that side.

The strongest form of each case deserves to be stated plainly. The anti-Zionist reading can point to a Talmudic text that speaks directly to a mass return by force, and to the many Orthodox authorities who read it as barring a state before the Messiah. The religious-Zionist reading can point to Nachmanides, a classical authority who treated settlement of the land as a commandment, and to the argument that the conditions the oaths assumed no longer held. Neither side invented its texts. Both are arguing from inside the same tradition, over the same pages.

A third position stood outside both religious readings and falls squarely inside this chapter's period. In 1885 American Reform Judaism, in its Pittsburgh Platform, rejected a return to Palestine altogether, on the ground that its members were "no longer a nation, but a religious community". [cite:pittsburgh_platform_1885] Reform did not argue from the oaths; it set the whole expectation of national restoration aside. It later reversed that position. The platform and its place among the responses of the 1880s are told in full in [scene:s02|the idea appears, 1862–1885].

Why did the argument become so sharp at the end of the nineteenth century? Part of the answer lies in who led the new movement. Early Zionism was mostly secular, and the record gives that as one reason so many rabbis opposed it at first. For readers of the oaths, a movement of this kind raised the objection the oaths name: a return pursued by human political action rather than awaited. The shift from a return awaited in prayer to a return pursued by human action, and the rabbis who first argued for that shift, are traced in [scene:ideo_s01|from prayer to program].

Where does the debate stand today? Most Orthodox Jews in Israel accept or support the state. Anti-Zionist Haredi groups, Neturei Karta among them, remain a minority. The minority's existence is the point. A religious tradition that still contains, in organized and named form, both a reading that commands settlement and a reading that forbids a state before the Messiah cannot be summed up as saying either thing alone. Zionism is a political movement; Judaism is a religion whose authorities have argued over that movement from its beginning.

Several things the record available here does not settle. It does not give the text of Nachmanides' ruling or its date, so the strength of his statement can be reported only as religious Zionists cite it. It does not measure how many rabbis or communities held each reading between the late eighteenth century and 1896; "many Orthodox authorities" is as precise as the sources allow.

sections.h: From Prayer to Program: The Thinkers and Groups Before Herzl, 1840–1890
sections.html:
A common account has Zionism springing fully formed from the mind of Theodor Herzl in 1896. The record shows something slower and more interesting. The idea passed through stages over half a century: a hope held in prayer, then an argument by two rabbis that people might begin the return themselves, then a political program written by a secular socialist and a frightened doctor, then small societies, a conference and a handful of pioneers, and finally a name. Herzl came last. What he added was not the idea but the organization.

For centuries before any movement, the return to Zion lived in the liturgy. It was prayed for daily and awaited as a messianic event, an act of God rather than a matter for politics. It was a hope, not a plan. That distinction matters for everything that follows, because the religious argument over the Three Oaths, set out in the previous section, turns on exactly this question: whether the return is something people may bring about, or something they must wait for.

The first break came from inside that religious world. Yehuda Alkalai, a Sephardi rabbi in Semlin, urged practical settlement in the land as a step toward redemption. He did so after the Damascus affair of 1840, a blood-libel case. [cite:w_alkalai] Zvi Hirsch Kalischer, a rabbi in Thorn, made a parallel case in a book of 1862: redemption, he argued, could begin by natural means, through settling and farming the land. [cite:w_kalischer] These two were the first to argue that human settlement could begin redemption. [cite:w_alkalai][cite:w_kalischer] In the terms of the older debate, they stood on the side that treated action in the land as part of a religious process rather than a forcing of the end. The earliest step from prayer toward program, in other words, was taken by rabbis and argued in religious terms.

The step into secular politics came from two very different men, whose work is told in full in the next section [scene:s02|the idea appears, 1862–1885]. In the same year as Kalischer's book, 1862, the secular socialist Moses Hess published Rome and Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Twenty years later, after the pogroms of 1881, the Odessa physician Leon Pinsker published Auto-Emancipation (1882), which argued that Jews needed a territory of their own, not necessarily Palestine. [cite:wiki_auto_emancipation] Between them, a socialist and a doctor turned a religious hope into a national program.

Ideas became groups in the 1880s. Local societies calling themselves Hovevei Zion, "Lovers of Zion", spread across the Russian Empire. In 1884 they met in conference at Kattowitz, under Pinsker's leadership. [cite:w_hovevei] The record holds a small irony here. Pinsker's own pamphlet had not insisted on Palestine; he and other early organizers of Hovevei Zion discussed several possible territories, including Argentina, before the movement's centre of gravity settled on Palestine. [cite:wiki_leon_pinsker] Yet the man whose argument was territorially open chaired the conference of societies named for Zion. Two years earlier, in 1882, a student group called BILU had sent its first pioneers to the land. [cite:w_bilu] A few hundred pioneers went in these years; the settlements they and others founded, and the numbers who stayed and left, are counted in [scene:rd0_aliyah|the Old Yishuv and the First Aliyah]. Finally, in 1890, the Viennese writer Nathan Birnbaum coined the word "Zionism". [cite:w_birnbaum] By then there were societies, a conference and colonists. There was still no single organization.

Why did people move from prayer to program in these decades? The motives recorded across these writers are four: persecution and pogroms; the failure of emancipation to end antisemitism; the age of European nationalism; and religious longing. A fifth current pushed from outside the Jewish world altogether: Christian restorationism in Britain and America. That story is told in [scene:bc_s05|restoration before Zionism]. The motives did not all point the same way. Alkalai and Kalischer argued from redemption; Hess from nationalism and socialism; Pinsker from physical safety. What they shared was the conclusion that waiting was no longer enough.

The familiar account deserves its strongest form. Herzl's role was real and decisive in one respect: he did not invent the idea, but he gave a scattered movement an organization, a diplomacy and a bank, beginning in 1897. Before him there were groups without a single organization; after him there was a movement with its own organization, its own diplomacy and its own bank. That is a large contribution. It is a different claim from saying that the idea began with him, and the record of the half-century before 1896 does not support that second claim.

What the record available here does not settle is also worth stating. It names Kalischer's 1862 book but does not give its title or its argument beyond its central claim. It dates Alkalai's call after the Damascus affair of 1840, but does not establish how directly the one produced the other beyond that sequence in time. It gives no membership figures for the Hovevei Zion societies and no account of what the Kattowitz conference decided. And it does not show whether Hess, Pinsker or Herzl read the two rabbis; the four stages followed one another in time, but the record does not trace a single line of influence running through them.

sections.h: The Idea Appears, 1862–1885
sections.html:
The familiar account holds that Zionism is millennia old and that Jews always yearned for the land of Israel. Part of that is true: the hope of return lived for centuries in prayer, as the previous section showed. But a prayer is not a program. Zionism as a written political idea appears in the documents between the 1860s and the 1880s, in scattered proposals that answered a modern problem, modern European antisemitism. The record of those decades also shows two things the familiar account leaves out. When persecuted Jews in the Russian Empire could choose where to go, the great majority chose America. And the largest Jewish religious movement in the United States formally rejected a return to Palestine in 1885.

The first of the proposals came from an unlikely author. Moses Hess (1812–1875) was a German-Jewish philosopher and an early, influential figure in socialist thought. In the 1840s he collaborated and corresponded with Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, and some historians credit him with introducing Marx to communist ideas before Marx had fully formulated his own. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] In 1862 Hess published Rome and Jerusalem: The Last National Question. Its argument was that Jewish assimilation into European society had failed to end antisemitism, and that Jews therefore needed national self-determination. It proposed, explicitly, a socialist Jewish commonwealth in Palestine, joining Hess's two commitments, socialism and Jewish nationalism, in a single dated text. [cite:wiki_moses_hess]

Almost no one listened. The book sold poorly and drew little serious engagement from socialist or Jewish intellectual circles. Mainstream European Jewish thought in the 1860s and 1870s was moving toward emancipation and integration, not national separation, and Hess's socialist nationalism belonged to neither camp. He died in 1875 a minor and largely unread figure. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Only after the Zionist Congress of 1897 was he rediscovered and placed in the movement's own origin story as a founding intellectual, a common pattern in political movements, which canonize an ignored forerunner once a later effort succeeds. His actual influence on the events of 1897 was close to nil. There is no strong documented evidence that Herzl, who reached his own position chiefly through the Dreyfus Affair, was significantly influenced by Hess's book before writing his own. [cite:wiki_moses_hess] Hess is best read as an early, isolated voice making a real proto-Zionist argument thirty-five years before the movement organized, not as the hidden origin of a plan that then unfolded on schedule.

The pressure that turned scattered ideas into a wider response came from Russia. The Romanov Empire was home to roughly five million Jews, the largest Jewish population in the world, confined by law to the Pale of Settlement. In March 1881 Tsar Alexander II was assassinated. Waves of pogroms followed across the Pale: organized mob violence against Jewish communities, in many cases with the complicity of local officials. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] Under his son Alexander III, who reigned from 1881 to 1894, the state then wrote the hostility into law. The May Laws of 1882 formally restricted where Jews could live, what they could study and how they could earn a living. Further decrees imposed quotas on Jewish admission to universities and barred Jews from rural areas. [cite:wiki_may_laws] This was antisemitism as state policy: specific, named legal restrictions with a date, not a vague climate of prejudice. The pogroms and the May Laws were separate pressures, and the record keeps them apart. The law was the legislated escalation; the pogroms that came before it were often the more immediately violent cause of flight, and not every emigrant's decision can be traced to the law itself. [cite:wiki_may_laws][cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire]

The wave of 1881–1884 was only the first. A second, from 1903 to 1906, included the Kishinev pogrom of April 1903, which killed 49 people, wounded hundreds and became an international scandal. [cite:wiki_kishinev_pogrom] The third, during the Russian Civil War of 1917–1921, was by far the deadliest, with an estimated 100,000 to 250,000 Jews killed in Ukraine and the surrounding regions. [cite:wiki_pogroms_russian_empire] Those later waves belong to later parts of this library. They are named here because the three should not be flattened into one: the death tolls differ by orders of magnitude, and the founding texts of the 1880s answered the first wave, not the later ones.
