The buyers were three institutions with distinct roles. The Jewish National Fund held purchased land as the inalienable property of the Jewish people. The Palestine Land Development Company did the actual purchasing, led by Yehoshua Hankin, who had worked with the Sursock family since 1891, personally negotiated the Sursock deal and most of the major Jezreel Valley acquisitions, and became head of the company in 1932. The Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, PICA, founded in 1924 by Edmond de Rothschild, became through parallel acquisitions the largest single Jewish landowner in Palestine [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. By the early Mandate years land sold by absentee owners to Jewish buyers went for roughly six Palestine pounds a dunam. Purchasing agents such as Hankin sometimes bought first, at their own financial risk, and were reimbursed by the Jewish Agency or the Fund afterward [cite:emory_zionist_land_acquisition] [cite:palquest_wzo_funding]. The banks and campaigns that supplied the capital are described in the section on the Mandate economy.

What a purchase cost the people living on the land is documented for one group of sales. In the largest single group of Sursock-related purchases, 1,746 Arab farming families, 8,730 people, were evicted. Under the tenure system they were owed no compensation, but they were paid about $17 a person as a goodwill settlement. Across all the Sursock-linked purchases, an estimated 20 to 25 villages were depopulated [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin]. The sources do not date this group of evictions within the sale period, and the figure of $17 describes that group only, not every transaction. Selling land to Jewish buyers was seen by some Arabs as a serious betrayal. In at least one documented case, negotiations stalled for years because the selling landowners did not want to be seen as responsible for the evacuation [cite:wiki_sursock_purchases] [cite:wiki_yehoshua_hankin].

The Jewish National Fund turned each purchase into a permanent holding. Its land was leased long-term rather than sold, so that no later transaction could reverse an acquisition; its founding resolution called the land "the eternal possession of the Jewish people" [cite:jnf_wiki]. The Fund's own history, from its founding in 1901, is told in [scene:s04d|the Jewish National Fund]. Its holdings in these years show the scale. It held 22,363 dunams in 1920. By 1935 it held about 89,500 acres, some 362 square kilometres, across 108 communities [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg].

The chart of the Fund's holdings shows how the 1920s and early 1930s changed its course. From a first gift of 200 dunams in 1903, it took seventeen years to reach 22,363 dunams in 1920. In the fifteen years that followed it grew to about 362,000 dunams by 1935, more than sixteen times the 1920 figure, and the curve kept rising, to 516,000 dunams in 1940 and about 936,000 by 1947–48 [cite:jnf_wiki] [cite:wiki_isaac_leib_goldberg]. Because Fund land was never resold, the line could only climb. The 1935 point is the 89,500 acres of the sources expressed in dunams, and should be read as an approximation.

The Mandate's role was that of regulator, not seller, and as regulator it failed. Between 1920 and 1940 Britain enacted five separate laws meant to protect tenant cultivators from eviction after a sale. A documented analysis of the period concludes that they "failed to provide the protection that Palestinian Arabs demanded, often due to loopholes, which allowed individuals and agencies to circumvent the legislation" [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. The Shaw Commission said the same in 1930 about the laws then in force: the Land Transfer Ordinances of 1920 and 1921 had failed, the Protection of Cultivators Ordinance of 1929 did not stop evictions, and the evictions were creating a landless class, "a potential danger to the country" [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. Later in the decade British policy moved the other way: in 1938 the Mandate authorities allowed Zionist officials to copy land-registration and tax records of Arab ownership in order to facilitate further purchases [cite:israeled_jnf_cultivators_ordinance] [cite:badil_land_ownership_palestine]. Britain's record on land was inconsistent rather than a single policy, and its restrictions on immigration in 1939 cut in the opposite direction.

The case that tested the system came at the end of the 1920s. In 1929 the Jewish National Fund bought 30,800 dunams at Wadi al-Hawarith at auction from absentee landlords; the historian Weldon Matthews counts it as the third-largest single acquisition the Fund made in the whole Mandate period. The Bedouin Palestinian tenants who lived there refused to leave, and the Fund began legal proceedings to evict them. Awni Abd al-Hadi, a leading Palestinian national figure, represented the residents through a court battle that lasted several years. The final eviction order was issued on 15 June 1933. The response was organized and crossed party lines: the Istiqlal Party, the Palestine Communist Party and the Congress of Youth called strikes and issued public declarations of protest [cite:wiki_wadi_al_hawarith]. The case was decided in the Mandate's own courts, under its own law. It shows that resistance reached formal legal representation and cross-party protest when the stakes were high enough. It does not show that every sale met such opposition; many went through with less.

The fullest measurement of all this came from Sir John Hope Simpson. His report, Palestine: Report on Immigration, Land Settlement and Development (Cmd. 3686), carries a covering letter dated 22 August 1930 and was published in October 1930 [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. It is the most detailed British land study of the Mandate period [cite:w_hopesimpson]. He adopted the Director of Surveys' estimate of 8,044,000 metric dunams of cultivable land, including 1,500,000 in the Beersheba region, and found that only 40 per cent of the hill country was cultivable, not the 66.6 per cent that had been assumed. He put Jewish-held land in June 1930 at about 1,250,000 Turkish dunams. Deducting about 900,000 metric dunams of Jewish holdings, he left 5,644,000 metric dunams for non-Jewish cultivators [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The two Jewish figures are in different units, Turkish and metric dunams, and the report as summarized here does not reconcile them further.

His village figures carried the human finding. In 104 surveyed villages, 6,940 of 23,573 families, 29.4 per cent, held no land at all. His own enquiry into 688 Arab families displaced by land sales found that only 379 were cultivating land again; the other 309 had joined the landless. He estimated the land available for new settlement at "100,000 dunams at the outside" [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. Without development, he concluded, there was no margin for further Jewish agricultural settlement [cite:w_hopesimpson].

Hope Simpson also examined labour, and here he quoted the movement's own documents. The Jewish National Fund's draft lease required the lessee to cultivate "only with Jewish labour", on penalty of ten Palestinian pounds for each breach and repossession of the land after three breaches. The Jewish Agency's constitution of 1920 committed it to colonization "based on Jewish labour". And fewer than one in three of the immigrants who had arrived since 1921 had settled on the land [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The clause had a plain consequence for the purchase chain: a tenant evicted from land the Fund bought could not be hired back to work it, because the lease forbade the lessee to employ him. Shaw had added two further findings: the allocation of labour-schedule immigration certificates by political creed was indefensible, and Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits [cite:rs_rd3_shaw_palquest_e]. The labour movement's own doctrine of "Hebrew labour" is described in the section on the Histadrut.

The Jewish Agency contested Hope Simpson's numbers. In 1931 it published a memorandum, The Statistical Bases of Sir John Hope Simpson's Report, to challenge the report's figures [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The two positions stand side by side. Hope Simpson held that without development there was no margin for settlement, that at most 100,000 dunams were available, and that a landless class was forming [cite:rs_rd3_hope_simpson_unispal]. The Agency held that his statistical foundation was unsound [cite:rs_rd3_cojs_ja_1931]. The research for this book has not verified the memorandum's specific arguments, so they are not summarized here. On the Agency's side, the strongest evidence in the record used here comes from a British inquiry: Shaw's finding that Jewish immigration within the country's absorptive capacity had brought material benefits. What London did with these findings is told in [scene:pf_s01|the Passfield White Paper and its reversal].

Several things the record does not settle. The total number of Arab families displaced by land sales in these years is not established; Hope Simpson's 688 families were those his own enquiry traced, and the 1,746 Sursock-linked families are one group of sales. Whether there was room for more settlement in 1930 is a question on which Hope Simpson and the Jewish Agency disagreed, and the Agency's arguments have not been examined here. The full Jewish holding in 1930 is given in two units that the summarized report does not reconcile. What is documented is the mechanism: a private sale by an absentee owner, a purchase by a Zionist company, a permanent holding by the Fund, a lease that barred non-Jewish labour, and protective ordinances that the Mandate's own inquiry found had failed to protect.

sections.h: The Armed Line: The Haganah, the Irgun and the Jaffa Barrels, 1920–1935
sections.html:
A familiar picture of the Mandate years shows one Jewish defence force, the Haganah, acting under a single political direction until it became the army of the new state in 1948. The record for these years shows something less tidy. By the end of 1931 there were already two Jewish armed organizations in Palestine, the Haganah and the Irgun, and by 1940 there would be three. They were divided by documented disputes over strategy and politics, they went through periods of open hostility toward one another, and even at the declaration of statehood they had reached only a partial, negotiated coordination. This section follows the line from its small beginnings in the 1920s to the arms shipment found in the port of Jaffa in 1935, and then points forward to where it led.

The starting point was modest. When the Histadrut, the Jewish labour federation, was founded in December 1920, it took responsibility for defence, and the Haganah was placed under its direct control. Through the 1920s the Haganah had only "a few hundred" volunteer members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was a volunteer body of the labour movement, not an army. In 1924 its senior commanders drew up a "Constitution of the Haganah," a first attempt to give the organization written rules. The labour camp was not of one mind about it. In 1926 former members of Ha-Shomer formed a separate underground of their own inside the Gedud ha-Avodah [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. Even before the Revisionist split that is the usual subject of this story, the Yishuv's armed structure was divided.

The violence of August 1929 changed the Haganah's position. In that month its volunteers helped defend the Jewish communities of Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa. The massacres of that August happened where the Haganah was absent or weak: in Hebron, in Safed and at Motza [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The lesson the movement drew was organizational. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's account describes the result as a shift toward wider organization and toward public control of the force [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

That shift took formal shape in 1931. A national command of six members was set up, with parity between the labour movement and everyone else: three members came from the Histadrut, Eliyahu Golomb, Dov Hos and Meir Rutberg, and three were non-labour members [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The mechanism matters. A defence force that had answered to one party's federation now answered to a body in which labour held half the seats and the non-labour parties held the other half. The commander who opposed public control was removed [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah].

Not everyone accepted the arrangement. A group led by Avraham Tehomi, who had been the Haganah's Jerusalem district commander from 1929 to 1931, seceded. Together with Revisionist groups it formed the Irgun Zvai Leumi, also known as Etzel [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi]. Tehomi is the same man whose 1985 account of the 1924 killing of Jacob de Haan is weighed in [scene:dh_s01|the de Haan section]. He did not stay with the organization he founded: he returned to the Haganah in 1937 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_tehomi].

The Irgun's founders were officers aligned with Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist movement, and the point of principle on which they broke was havlagah, the Haganah's policy of restraint in the face of Arab attacks, which they rejected [cite:wiki_irgun]. Through the 1930s and 1940s the Irgun conducted an armed campaign against British rule and against Arab civilian targets. From 1943 it was commanded by Menachem Begin, who later became Israel's sixth Prime Minister [cite:wiki_irgun]. That is a direct, documented personal line from the command of this organization to the country's highest office. The source establishes the founding rationale and the line of command; it does not, on its own, give a full operational history of the Irgun, and this section does not attempt one.

The two positions can be stated in their own terms, as far as the sources record them. The Haganah's leadership held to restraint and, after 1931, to a command shared equally between labour and non-labour members, removing the commander who opposed that public control. The Irgun's founders rejected restraint in the face of Arab attacks and left rather than serve under that command. Both answers came out of the same experience of 1929, which had shown how few defenders there were and what happened where there were none.

Between 1931 and 1935 the Haganah built itself into something more permanent. It had urban branches in Jerusalem, Tel Aviv and Haifa, each with memberships "in the hundreds," it ran annual officers' courses, and it had workshops producing hand grenades [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. It was still small. It was also now an organization that trained its own officers and made some of its own weapons.

The clearest single episode of these years came at the port of Jaffa in 1935. Rifles and ammunition had been shipped from Belgium hidden in barrels of cement. British authorities seized 537 barrels at Jaffa, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. One account, drawing on the Palestine Post and the Peel report among other sources, gives the contents as 25 Lewis machine guns, 800 rifles and 400,000 rounds, found in 359 of the drums, and says they were consigned to a merchant in Tel Aviv who was never identified. The same account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. Those details rest on that one account and are given here as its report.

The sources do not agree on when the shipment was found. The account just cited, relying on Palestine Post reports and the Peel report, dates the discovery to 16 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. The Encyclopaedia Judaica's entry on the Haganah dates it to 18 November 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. This book has not resolved the difference. The earlier date sits before the reported strike of 26 October; the later one would fall after it. Neither source, as gathered here, names who in the Yishuv ordered the shipment.

One claim about these years does not hold up as stated. A compiled account of Zionist intelligence before 1948, drawn on elsewhere in this library, says that the first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine was established under the Haganah in 1929. The same account also dates the founding of the Shai, the Sherut Yediot or Information Service, the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm, to 1940 [cite:shai_wiki]. The two statements may describe different bodies, an informal service in 1929 and a formal one in 1940, but the account does not say so, and this book has not been able to confirm a founding date for any Haganah intelligence body in 1929. The claim is reported here as unconfirmed. The Shai's wartime and American story belongs to a later period and is not told here.

Where the line led is told in later chapters, but its shape follows from what was built in these years. In 1940 the Irgun split in turn. Avraham Stern led a faction out to form Lehi, Lohamei Herut Israel, "Fighters for the Freedom of Israel," often called the Stern Gang, rejecting the Irgun's decision to suspend operations against the British during the Second World War [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. Stern's group is documented as having explored contact with Fascist Italy and, most controversially, Nazi Germany, in search of any power willing to oppose British rule in Palestine. The episode was widely condemned at the time, including within the broader Zionist movement. The record shows exploratory contact, not a completed cooperation or alliance [cite:wiki_lehi_stern_gang]. That story is told in [scene:lh_s01|Lehi].

In 1944 and 1945, in what became known as the "Hunting Season," the Haganah, under Jewish Agency direction, moved against members of the Irgun and Lehi through surveillance, exposure to the British authorities and detentions, in an attempt to suppress their independent operations and keep political control unified [cite:wiki_hunting_season]. The source documents the pattern rather than every operation. And at independence, when the Haganah became the core of the Israel Defense Forces and the Irgun and Lehi were formally absorbed, the merger was contested. In June 1948 the Altalena affair, an armed confrontation between the new army and Irgun forces over a weapons shipment, left sixteen Irgun members and three soldiers dead; the ship was shelled and burned off Tel Aviv on Ben-Gurion's direct order. Begin's refusal to let the clash become a civil war, in his words "there will be no civil war with the enemy at our gates," is documented as decisive in preventing a wider fight [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. Most of the roughly 940 passengers aboard were inducted into the army without incident, so the flashpoint was not the whole of the integration [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]. The wreck was found intact on the Mediterranean seafloor in 2026, 78 years later [cite:jpost_altalena_wreck_2026]. That ending is told in [scene:mil_s01|1948].

The reason to tell this line in a chapter about building institutions is a matter of consistency. This library gives full weight to the internal divisions on the political side: the Bund, Reform Judaism's early ambivalence, Neturei Karta. A history that tracked those divisions carefully but treated the armed side as a single force would be holding the two to different standards [cite:jvl_altalena_affair]. The record of 1920 to 1935 shows the armed side divided almost from the start: between the labour federation and the old Ha-Shomer men in 1926, between labour and non-labour in the command of 1931, and between restraint and its rejection in the secession of the same year.

Some things the record gathered here does not settle. It gives no membership figures for the Irgun in its first years and no count of the Haganah beyond "a few hundred" and "in the hundreds." It does not name the three non-labour members of the 1931 command or the commander who was removed. It does not establish who arranged the Belgian shipment, or the date it was found. And it does not support the claim of a Haganah intelligence service founded in 1929.

sections.h: The American Palestine Committee, 1932
sections.html:
In 1932, while the Zionist movement in Palestine was building its labour federation, its banks and its defence force, one of its executives in the United States began building something of a different kind: a committee of prominent Americans who were mostly not Jewish. Emanuel Neumann, a member of the Zionist Executive, founded the American Palestine Committee that year to organize prominent, mainly non-Jewish Americans in support of a Jewish homeland [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. The committee's existence and its founder are documented in the records of the American Jewish Archives [cite:aja_neumann_bio].

The committee matters for what it shows about method. A common account of the 1940s holds that the wave of Christian and elite American support for a Jewish state arose on its own. The record shows that the most visible bodies expressing that support were founded and later revived by one Zionist official, working from inside the movement's political office. The support was real; so was the organization behind it. The two facts are not in tension, and this section keeps both.

The sources gathered here say little about the committee's first decade. They record its founding in 1932 and its purpose, and they do not record its membership, its activities or its funding in the 1930s. What they do record is what happened when Neumann returned to it. In January 1941 he joined the Emergency Committee for Zionist Affairs as head of public relations and political action, and from that post he revived the American Palestine Committee, with Senator Robert Wagner as its chairman [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. The mechanism is plain in the titles. The person charged with the Zionist emergency body's public relations and political action was the same person who rebuilt the committee through which prominent non-Jewish Americans would speak.

In December 1942 Neumann organized a second, parallel body for clergy, the Christian Council on Palestine [cite:aja_neumann_bio]. Its founding minutes describe it as an "autonomous committee working in cooperation with the American Palestine Committee" [cite:aja_ccp_minutes_1942]. By the end of the war the American Palestine Committee claimed some 6,500 members, among them senators, congressmen, cabinet members and governors, and by one description mayors; the Christian Council claimed about 3,000 clergy [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee] [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. These are the committees' own membership claims, not independent counts. In 1946 the two merged into the American Christian Palestine Committee, which disbanded after 1948 [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee]. How these committees fitted into the wider American campaign of the 1940s is told in [scene:s07f|the American Zionist Emergency Council].

The dispute is over a single word. The Christian Council's founding minutes call it "autonomous" [cite:aja_ccp_minutes_1942]. The historian Peter Grose described the committees' operations as "hardly autonomous" [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. Reporting that draws on Grose's work states that Zionist funds, reaching up to $150,000 by 1946, sustained them [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby]. That figure is reported, not drawn from a primary financial record, and it should be read that way: this book has not seen the accounts it describes.

The strongest case for "autonomous" is that the committees' members were real people who lent their own names. Nothing in the record gathered here suggests that any of them signed on against their convictions. The strongest case for "hardly autonomous" is structural: both committees were founded by the same Zionist official, the larger one was revived from the Emergency Committee's political office, and, according to reporting on Grose's work, the money that kept them running came from Zionist funds. A body can be sincere in its membership and organized from outside in its operations. The distinction this book draws is between real names lent and organized direction, and the record shows both.

The same arrangement, organized support presented as independent, appears again in later decades, and this library documents it for the predecessors of AIPAC in its own place. The scale should be kept in proportion. The reported $150,000 appears as a bar, labelled $0.15 million, on the chart of documented dollar flows embedded in [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement section], where it sits beside sums hundreds of times larger. Its significance is not its size but what it bought: a public voice that appeared to come from outside the movement.

Several questions remain open on the evidence gathered here. The record does not say what the committee did between 1932 and 1941, whether it was active or dormant, or who paid for it in those years. It does not give a year-by-year account of the reported $150,000 or name its paying body. And it does not show how much direction Neumann's office gave the committees day to day, which is the real substance of Grose's phrase.

sections.h: The Jews of the Arab World, 1929–1936: Baghdad and Constantine
sections.html:
The story of these years in Palestine was not the only story of Jews in the Arab world. Two places show how differently the early 1930s could run for Jewish communities outside Palestine, and how much turned on the decisions of states and of named individuals. In Iraq, a Jewish community that had taken part in building the new state's institutions found itself, after independence, under a series of restrictions. In French Algeria, a city's Jews were killed in a riot whose causes a recent historian has traced to the politics of the colonial state. Neither case is evidence about Arabs or Muslims as a whole, and neither should be read that way. Each has its own dates, its own actors and its own documentation, and the documentation for the two is not of equal strength.

Iraq first. Under the British Mandate there, according to Sephardi Voices UK, Jews held government posts, Hebrew could be taught, and several Zionist organizations were permitted to operate until 1929 [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. Iraq became independent in 1932. In the years that followed, the same source reports, prominent Jews helped build the Iraqi civil service, and several sat in the first independent parliament [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. The Mandate-era history of Iraq, and how its independence came about, is told in [scene:irq_e02|Iraq under the Mandate].

From 1934 the picture changed. According to Sephardi Voices UK, Iraqi Jews from that year had to pay a deposit of £50 to travel abroad. In 1935 the teaching of Hebrew was barred, and state secondary schools set quotas on the number of Jewish pupils. In 1936 Jews were dismissed from the civil service [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. These measures, if accurately reported, amounted to discrimination by the state against its Jewish citizens in movement, education and employment, within four years of a period in which Jews had helped staff that same state. They rest, however, on a single source, and this book has not found a second, independent account of them. The 1936 dismissals in particular are stated in that source in sweeping terms, and the source does not say how many people were affected or whether every Jewish official was removed. They are given here as that source reports them.

The same source records an episode from 1933 that connects Iraq to the events in Germany described in [scene:hol_s01|Weimar's collapse]. During the first premiership of Rashid Ali al-Gaylani, in 1933, the German chargé d'affaires in Baghdad, Fritz Grobba, was allowed to publish Mein Kampf in Iraqi newspapers [cite:rs_rd3_sephardivoices_iraq]. That was antisemitic propaganda, placed in the Iraqi press by a German diplomat with the permission of an Iraqi government. It is again attested here by one source. What these years led to in Baghdad, the Farhud of 1941, belongs to a later chapter.

Algeria second. In Constantine, in French Algeria, in August 1934, over a few days of violence, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims were killed [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. Those figures come from the historian Joshua Cole, whose book Lethal Provocation: The Constantine Murders and the Politics of French Algeria (Cornell University Press, 2019) is the fullest study used here.

Cole's argument is about the state, not about the crowd alone. He argues that the French colonial state had an interest in "provoking and nurturing" tension between Jews and Muslims, because that tension helped it resist demands to extend citizenship rights to Algerian Muslims [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. Cole also identifies Mohamed El Maadi, a veteran with ties to the extreme right, as a key participant in the violence [cite:rs_rd3_cole_constantine]. His account therefore names both a structure, the colonial state's interest, and a specific person with extreme-right ties, rather than attributing the killings to Muslims in general.

That is a historian's argument and should be weighed as one. The source gathered here presents Cole's case through an interview about his book, and it does not set out a rival interpretation; this book has not gathered one. What can be said is that Cole's reading rests on the colonial context of citizenship and on a named participant, and that the killings themselves, 25 Jews and 3 Muslims, are not in question in the sources used here.

Set side by side, the two cases make one point plainly. Antisemitism in these years reached Jewish communities in the Arab world through more than one channel: in Iraq, through state measures and through Nazi propaganda placed by a German diplomat; in Algeria, according to Cole, through violence that a European colonial state had reasons to tolerate or encourage, with a veteran tied to the extreme right among its key participants. Neither source used here ties these events to Palestine.

The gaps are considerable. The Iraqi measures of 1934 to 1936 rest on a single source, and their scale is not recorded: how many travellers paid the deposit, how many pupils the quotas excluded, how many officials lost their posts. The record gathered here says nothing about the Jews of Syria, Lebanon, Egypt, Yemen or Morocco in these years. For Constantine it gives the toll and Cole's argument, but not the course of the riot day by day, or what the French authorities did afterwards.

sections.h: The Transfer Agreement, 1933–1939
sections.html:
On 25 August 1933 Zionist bodies signed an agreement with the government of Nazi Germany. It let German Jews who were emigrating to Palestine take part of their assets with them, not as money but as German goods. Over the following six years it helped roughly 60,000 people reach Palestine. It also undercut the worldwide boycott of Nazi Germany that had begun in 1933, and it divided the Jewish world more sharply than any other financial arrangement of the pre-state period. It was called the Haavara, Hebrew for "transfer."

A common assumption holds that the Zionist movement and Nazi Germany were simply adversaries from 1933 onward. The documents show something harder to summarize. The two were adversaries, and they also made a commercial agreement, each for its own reasons. Two popular versions of the story each keep only half of that record. One calls Haavara a straightforward rescue; the other calls it collaboration. The documents support both halves at once: a mechanism that moved some 60,000 people out of Nazi reach, and a commercial accommodation that the Nazi state wanted for reasons of its own, chosen by the Zionist movement's own Congress over the objections of some of its own leaders [cite:jvl_haavara].

The agreement had three parties: the Zionist Federation of Germany; the Anglo-Palestine Bank, acting for the Jewish Agency; and the Reich Economics Ministry [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. Its mechanism was straightforward in outline. An emigrating German Jew deposited assets in an account in Germany. Those funds were used to buy German export goods, which were shipped to Palestine. When the goods were sold there, the emigrant was repaid in Palestine from the proceeds [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara].

The design explains why each party signed. For the emigrant, it was a way to move part of a lifetime's assets out of Germany. For the Zionist bodies, it brought immigrants and goods to Palestine. For the Nazi state, according to the record, it served two aims. The regime wanted Germany Judenrein, emptied of Jews, and it wanted to break the anti-Nazi boycott of 1933, which had mass Jewish support and which German officials regarded as an economic threat [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. Haavara did both. Jews left, and German goods found a market abroad at the very moment a boycott was trying to close markets to them. The rise of that regime and the destruction of the Weimar Republic are told in [scene:hol_s01|Weimar's collapse].

The scale was large for its time. The agreement was a major factor in the emigration of approximately 60,000 German Jews to Palestine between 1933 and 1939 [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. By the end of 1937, goods worth 77.8 million Reichsmarks had moved; by the outbreak of war, about 105 million [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. The Jewish Virtual Library records the total transfer as £8.1 million in Palestine pounds, roughly $40.4 million at the time, and states that this included £2.6 million provided by the Reichsbank [cite:jvl_haavara]. The war ended the program. How these German arrivals fit into the immigration of the 1930s as a whole, including the peak year of 1935, is set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section].

One figure in the sources does not agree with the others. The Center for Israel Education's account of the period gives the total moved through Haavara as $100 million [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]. The Jewish Virtual Library's figure, built up from the £8.1 million total, is about $40.4 million [cite:jvl_haavara]. The sources gathered here do not explain the difference, and this book uses the lower, itemized figure while noting the higher one. The same account ties the German trip that Chaim Arlosoroff, head of the Jewish Agency's political department, made shortly before his murder in June 1933 to the Haavara agreement; that claim is weighed in [scene:rd3_arlosoroff|the Arlosoroff section].

Two charts compiled for this library set Haavara beside the other documented money of the pre-state years. The first, of US-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949, shows Haavara at about $40 million for 1933–39, one of the largest bars on the chart. The chart's own note warns that its figures are nominal dollars of the year reported, not adjusted for inflation, and that Haavara has been converted at the period estimate [cite:jvl_haavara]. The smallest bars matter too: the reported $0.15 million that sustained the American Christian committees founded by Emanuel Neumann, discussed in the section on the American Palestine Committee, appears near the foot of the same chart [cite:counterpunch_origins_lobby].

The second chart, of documented fundraising and transfers in US dollars before independence, again places Haavara at about $40 million, converted from the 105 million Reichsmarks. Its note is a necessary caution: the bars record separate events, in different years and different currencies, and should not be added together as one budget [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. The other bars on both charts belong to the 1920s and to 1948–49 and are discussed in their own chapters.

The opposition was real and came from inside the movement as well as outside it. The Revisionist leader Ze'ev Jabotinsky, Rabbi Stephen Wise of the American Jewish Congress, and Abba Hillel Silver all opposed the agreement, on the ground that it sabotaged the boycott [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. Their case at its strongest was that the boycott had mass Jewish support and was regarded by German officials themselves as an economic threat, so that a Zionist agreement moving German goods abroad weakened pressure the regime actually felt. The defenders' case at its strongest was the one the numbers make: people were leaving Germany, they could take something with them only by this route, and tens of thousands reached Palestine through it.

The question went to the movement's highest body. The Nineteenth Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in August 1935, voted by a large majority to continue the agreement and placed Haavara under the supervision of the Jewish Agency [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] [cite:jvl_haavara]. The opponents failed to persuade it. The decision was taken knowingly, two years into the agreement's operation and a month before Germany enacted the Nuremberg Laws. The historian Edwin Black wrote that the agreement "tore the Jewish world apart" [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. Haavara also served as the model for a smaller arrangement with Czechoslovakia on the eve of the war [cite:jvl_haavara].

The Haavara transfer appears as one stream among many on the map of how the pre-state build was financed, between the American donors of the 1920s and the fundraising and arms purchases of 1948.

What the record gathered here does not settle is considerable. It does not say how much of each emigrant's assets were lost in the transfer, or on what terms the goods were priced, so the cost to the emigrants themselves cannot be stated. It does not measure how much damage Haavara did to the boycott, only that it undercut it. It does not resolve the gap between the $40.4 million and $100 million totals. And it cannot answer the counterfactual on which the moral argument turns: how many of the 60,000 would have reached safety without it.

sections.h: A Murder on the Beach and a Peace That Failed, 1933–1935
sections.html:
On the night of 16 June 1933, Chaim Arlosoroff was walking on the beach at Tel Aviv with his wife, Sima, when he was shot. He died early the next morning, 17 June [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. Arlosoroff was the head of the Jewish Agency's political department. His killing opened two years of open conflict between that leadership and the Revisionist movement led by Ze'ev Jabotinsky, a conflict that ran through a murder trial, a Zionist Congress, an attempt at reconciliation and a vote of the labour federation's members, and ended with the Revisionists leaving the Zionist Organization altogether.

Arlosoroff had come back from Germany about two days before he was shot. The Center for Israel Education links that trip to the Haavara transfer agreement with Nazi Germany, which was formally signed on 25 August 1933, some ten weeks after his death [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]. That link is reported by one source and is given here as its account; the agreement itself is examined in [scene:hv_s01|the Transfer Agreement section]. The same source gives a figure of $100 million for the total Haavara moved, far higher than the roughly $40 million recorded elsewhere [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff].

Three Revisionists were charged. Abba Ahimeir was accused of plotting the killing, and Avraham Stavsky and Zvi Rosenblatt of carrying it out as the gunmen. Sima Arlosoroff identified Stavsky and Rosenblatt [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff]. The case did not hold. Only Stavsky was convicted, and in 1934 he was cleared on appeal for lack of corroborating evidence. No one else was ever charged with the murder [cite:rs_rd3_cie_arlosoroff] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst].

The trial was fought in politics as much as in court. Jabotinsky, who believed the accused innocent, campaigned on their behalf for more than a year [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. The labour movement's leaders accused Revisionist extremists of the killing. At the Eighteenth Zionist Congress, which met in Prague from 21 August to 3 September 1933, the Revisionists were accused of the murder in the movement's own parliament [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. The Revisionists, for their part, charged that the accusation against them was a "blood libel" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1985_panel].

The two camps' accounts can be set side by side, as far as the sources record them. Labour's account was that Revisionist extremists, the three accused, had killed Arlosoroff, and it rested above all on his widow's identification of two of the men. The Revisionists' account was that the accused were innocent and that the accusation was a defamation of their movement; the acquittal on appeal, for want of corroborating evidence, was their strongest support. The sources gathered here record the accusation, the identification, the acquittal and Jabotinsky's campaign. They do not record the speeches or articles on either side.

Half a century later the state took the question up again. In March 1982 the government of Menachem Begin appointed a three-member commission chaired by David Bechor, a former Supreme Court justice. It reported in June 1985. It cleared Ahimeir, Stavsky and Rosenblatt. It could not determine who had killed Arlosoroff, or whether the killing was a political act at all. And it cleared the labour movement of the Revisionist charge that the accusation had been a "blood libel" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1985_panel]. Each side was thus partly vindicated: the Revisionists in the innocence of the accused, labour in being cleared of the charge of a "blood libel." The murder itself remains unsolved.

The conflict did not wait for the courts. In 1934 Ben-Gurion and Jabotinsky, the leaders of the two camps, signed three agreements in London [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists_j] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst]. One of them was a labour agreement. The sources gathered here do not give the exact dates on which the agreements were signed or set out their full terms. The labour agreement was put to the members of the Histadrut, the labour federation, who rejected it in a referendum [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists_j] [cite:rs_rd3_jabotinsky_inst].

The referendum was held on 25 March 1935. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency's report the next day gave early returns: about 12,000 votes against the agreement and about 9,000 for it. In Tel Aviv the count was 3,983 against and 3,296 for; in Haifa, 3,785 against and 1,555 for [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_referendum]. The newspaper Haaretz called the result "a grave mishap for the entire Zionist movement" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_referendum]. The final totals were not in that report, and this book has not found them; the figures above are partial tallies only. Even so, they show where the opposition was strongest. In Tel Aviv the vote was close; in Haifa it was more than two to one against.

With the agreement dead, the break followed. Later in 1935 the Zionist General Council adopted a "discipline clause" barring independent political action, the Revisionists voted to secede, and in September 1935 Jabotinsky's New Zionist Organization held its constituent assembly in Vienna [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]. That story, and the growth of the Revisionist movement that preceded it, is told in [scene:s07a3|the Revisionist line].

The episode mattered beyond the fate of one man. The murder, and the accusation that followed it, hardened a division between the labour leadership and the Revisionists that the London agreements tried and failed to close. The secession that followed left the Zionist movement, by the end of 1935, with two rival organizations and two rival armed lines.

The record leaves the central question open. No court and no commission has established who killed Arlosoroff or why. The Bechor commission, half a century later, could not say whether the killing was political. The link between his German trip and Haavara rests on one source. The exact dates and full terms of the London agreements, and the final count of the 1935 referendum, are not in the sources gathered here.

sections.h: The Nuremberg Laws, 1935: Persecution Written into Statute
sections.html:
On 15 September 1935 the Reichstag met in special session at Nuremberg, where the Nazi Party was holding its annual rally. It passed two laws, and it passed them unanimously [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws]. The parliament that voted had already surrendered its own authority two and a half years earlier, when the Enabling Act of March 1933 allowed Hitler to make law without the approval of the Reichstag or the President, a measure carried after Communist deputies had been forcibly kept from voting [cite:history_weimar_republic]. What met at Nuremberg was a chamber with no opposition left in it. The two statutes it approved that day did not burn a synagogue or open a camp. They did something that came first and made the rest administrable: they wrote antisemitism into the law of the German state, defining Jews as a separate category of person by descent and removing them from the body of citizens.

A familiar way of telling this history begins with violence: the mob, the broken windows, the deportations, with laws following later to tidy up what force had already done. The order in the documents runs the other way. By the autumn of 1935 Germany had a complete legal framework that defined who was a Jew, stripped Jews of citizenship and made marriage between Jews and other Germans a crime. That framework stood three years before the mass violence of Kristallnacht, told in [scene:hol_s03|the next stage]. Exclusion was legislated first and then enforced through escalating violence. Law came before the pogrom, not after it.

The first of the two statutes, the Reich Citizenship Law, turned on a single definition. A citizen of the Reich was a person "of German or related blood" who proved through conduct a willingness to serve the German people and Reich [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws] [cite:yadvashem_nuremberg_blood_law]. German Jews were reduced from citizens to "subjects" of the state, without full political rights [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws]. One sentence of law, defining citizenship by blood rather than by birthplace, residence or belief, removed an entire population from political membership in the state. No shot was fired to do it.

The second statute, the Law for the Protection of German Blood and Honor, passed the same day, reached into private life. It banned marriage between Jews and "subjects of the state of German or related blood," and it declared such marriages void even when they had been concluded abroad for the specific purpose of evading the law. It made "extramarital intercourse" between Jews and non-Jewish Germans a crime. It barred Jews from employing non-Jewish German women under the age of 45 in their households. Violations were punishable by imprisonment [cite:yadvashem_nuremberg_blood_law]. The regime had its own name for the new offence: Rassenschande, "race defilement" [cite:wiki_rassenschande]. The word carried the ideology of the statute in a single term. It presented ordinary love, marriage and domestic employment between Jews and other Germans as a contamination that the state was entitled to punish.

Both laws depended on knowing who was a Jew, and here the regime made its most consequential choice. It did not define a Jew by religion. Under the Nuremberg Race Laws a person with three or four Jewish grandparents was a Jew, whatever that person believed or practised [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_race_laws]. Germans who had not practised Judaism in decades fell within the definition. So did people who had formally converted to Christianity. Belief, conversion and long non-observance offered no exit, because the test was not what a person did or believed but who that person's grandparents had been. The definition was racial in the plainest sense, and it is the clearest evidence that the target of the laws was not a faith but a people the state had decided to classify by blood.

The bureaucracy then extended the classification downward. On 14 November 1935 the First Supplementary Decree to the Reich Citizenship Law created the category of Mischling, "mixed blood," for people with one or two Jewish grandparents, and attached its own separate legal restrictions to it [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_race_laws]. The decree distinguished degrees of Jewish ancestry, each carrying its own legal consequences. Charts were produced so that officials, and ordinary citizens, could work out a person's racial status under the law [cite:facinghistory_nuremberg_laws]. A person's legal standing became the answer to a genealogical sum. The arithmetic was the mechanism: once ancestry could be counted, a clerk could place any German in a category, and the category decided whom that person could marry, whom he or she could employ, and whether he or she was a citizen at all.

The structure of power behind this is simple to state. The decision was made inside the Nazi state and ratified by a parliament that could no longer refuse it. The instrument was statute, followed by decree. The people classified had no means of acting against it: they had lost the standing of citizens by the very law that classified them. The burden fell on German Jews, including converts and the non-observant whom the ancestry test caught, and, through the Mischling decree, on people with one or two Jewish grandparents.

What the 1935 laws meant for Palestine can be stated only as far as the sources go, and they do not go far. Jewish immigration to Palestine reached its highest recorded level of the Mandate years in 1935. The figures compiled by the US State Department from British returns give 61,854 Jewish immigrants that year, against 42,359 in 1934 and 29,727 in 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]; a second series, printed by the Jewish Virtual Library after Yehoshua Porath, gives 66,472 for 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table]. The difference between the two series, and the composition of the 1935 arrivals, are set out in [scene:rd3_aliyot|the immigration section]. The research does not break the year's arrivals down by country of origin or by month, so it cannot show how many German Jews came, or whether any of the rise followed September rather than preceding it. The surge had begun in 1933, two years before Nuremberg, when the same series records 30,327 arrivals [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828]; and the British labour schedule, which governed one channel of entry, was cut from 8,000 places for April–September 1935 to 3,250 for October 1935–March 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. The most that can be said is that the laws were passed in the year of the peak, and that the transfer agreement through which German Jews had been moving to Palestine since 1933 [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement] was upheld by the Zionist Congress at Lucerne in August 1935, a month before the Nuremberg session, as told in [scene:hv_s01|the Haavara Agreement]. The sources here do not measure the effect of the laws themselves on emigration.

The text of the two statutes and of the November decree is documented, and it is unambiguous; on what the laws said, the sources present no dispute. What they leave unsettled is the record of enforcement. The documentation here establishes the provisions and the penalties, not a count of prosecutions for Rassenschande, which varied in intensity across regions and years; it establishes that the Mischling system existed and how it worked, not the full detail of the distinctions it drew between its categories. Nor do the sources say how many people the classification touched in 1935. What they do establish is the sequence, and the sequence is the finding: by the end of 1935 a modern state had defined a part of its own population by ancestry, removed it from citizenship and criminalized its private life, all by unanimous statute and orderly decree, years before the violence that the next stage records.

sections.h: Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam: From Jabla to Ya'bad, 1882–1935
sections.html:
On 20 November 1935, in the hills near Ya'bad, close to Jenin, a British police force fought a small armed band for six hours. When it was over the band's leader, a preacher from Haifa in his fifties, was dead [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. Shaykh 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam had spent fifteen years in Palestine as a teacher, imam and official of the Muslim religious courts, and the last several of them, by the accounts that survive, organizing in secret for armed struggle. His life in the field lasted eight days. His death drew the largest funeral Haifa had held, and the argument over what to call him has not ended.

He was not born in Palestine. Al-Qassam was born in 1882 in Jabla, on the Syrian coast south of Latakia, and studied at al-Azhar in Cairo [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. After the First World War, when France took control of the Syrian coast, he joined the revolt of 1919–20 against the French there, and the French sentenced him to death [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. He reached Haifa in late 1920, or in December 1920 in another account, taught at the Burj school, and became imam and preacher at the Istiqlal Mosque [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. (The mosque's name, "independence," is a coincidence of vocabulary; it is not the Istiqlal party founded in 1932, though the two would later cross paths through one of that party's founders.) The preacher who settled in Haifa already carried a death sentence from one European mandatory power for fighting it.

Through the 1920s his career ran through the ordinary institutions of Muslim public life under the Mandate. In July 1928 he was elected president of the Haifa branch of the Young Men's Muslim Association, and in 1930 the Haifa Shari'a court appointed him a ma'dhun, an official post conferred by the religious court [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. These were positions of standing, held in the open. They gave him a pulpit and an association of young men.

Alongside that public life, according to the accounts of his movement, he built a clandestine one. Those accounts describe cells of no more than five men, organized into units for preaching, for intelligence and for military training, and guerrilla attacks on Jewish settlements beginning in 1931 that soon paused after leaks reached the British [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. This part of the record rests on reporting rather than on documents, and it is thin. The research behind this book holds no verified list of those attacks, no verified count of their victims and no verified account of their dates and places; figures for them that circulate elsewhere rest on a single unconfirmed source and are not used here. What is reported is the structure: a small, compartmented organization that kept religious teaching, intelligence and arms in separate hands, and that chose Jewish settlements as well as the British as targets.

The decision to go to the hills came in the autumn of 1935, and the leadership did not support it. Al-Qassam wrote to Rashid al-Haj Ibrahim of his plan to take to the hills [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim_h]. Al-Haj Ibrahim was one of the eleven founders of the Istiqlal party, which had named British imperialism as the main enemy [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim]. According to Al Majalla, the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, declined to back a revolt, saying the time was not right [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. That account is reported, from one outlet; the research does not hold the Mufti's own words. If it is accurate, al-Qassam went to the hills without the backing of the Mufti, whose place among the rival leaderships and parties of these years is described in [scene:rd3_arab_politics|Palestinian politics, 1928–1935].

The autumn was tense. In October or November 1935 (the sources disagree on the date) the British seized 537 barrels at Jaffa port that had been shipped from Belgium with rifles and ammunition hidden in cement, and the discovery caused significant unrest among Palestinian Arabs; one account dates a protest general strike to 26 October 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_cement]. That shipment and the armed bodies of the Yishuv belong to [scene:s07e2|the armed line]. The sources used here do not say whether the seizure bore on al-Qassam's decision, and this book does not assume it did.

On 12 November 1935 al-Qassam declared jihad in Haifa and left for the forests of Ya'bad, near Jenin, with about eleven companions [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. Eight days later, on 20 November, he was killed in a six-hour fight with a larger British police force near Ya'bad [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. The nearest thing to a contemporary official account in the research is an American one. Leland Morris, the US Consul General, reporting to Washington in April 1936, wrote that al-Qassam's bands had caused the death of one British constable, and that four of his men died and five were captured [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_h].

How large his following was, and how many died with him, are disputed. Al Majalla, drawing on British archives, puts his fighters at between 50 and 200 and calls a claim of 800 "grossly exaggerated"; it says he died with two colleagues [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. The Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question says al-Qassam and four of his men were killed, and the US consul's despatch likewise reports four of his men killed and five captured [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_h]. The consul's figure is the only one here written at the time by an outside official; it agrees with the Palestinian encyclopedia and not with Al Majalla on the dead. None of the sources reconciles the counts.

The response to his death showed a reach that his small band had not. Haifa declared a general strike on 21 November 1935 and held the largest funeral procession the city had seen; he was buried at Balad al-Shaykh [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. It came at a moment of unusual Palestinian unity. By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the same American consul described as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. The established leaders had not followed al-Qassam into the hills; a crowd of Haifa's people followed his coffin.

What to call him is the oldest dispute about him, and both readings rest on documented ground. Palestinian accounts present al-Qassam as a leader of resistance to British occupation whose death helped ignite the revolt of 1936–39 [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam] [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. In that reading he was a man who had already fought one European mandatory power in Syria and chose arms against a second; the fight in which he died was a fight with British police. The other reading starts from the targets. His group's attacks were directed at Jewish settlers as well as at the British, and he called for confronting Jewish settlers "as enemies and not as immigrants or guests" [cite:rs_rd3_globalsecurity_qassam]. In that reading, a movement that attacked civilian settlements was not only an anti-colonial insurgency, whatever its leader's death later came to symbolize. The two descriptions are not mutually exclusive. The documented record supports both halves: an armed campaign against the Mandate power, and attacks on Jewish settlements, with civilians among the targets. This book does not choose between the labels; it sets out what each rests on.

His name outlived him. In 1991 Hamas named its military wing the 'Izz al-Din al-Qassam Brigades, according to Al Majalla [cite:rs_rd3_majalla_qassam]. That later use has shaped how he is remembered on every side, and it is one reason the disputes over his following and his targets are argued with such heat. It belongs to a different era from the one in which he lived.

Much about al-Qassam remains unsettled by the sources available here. The size of his organization rests on estimates that run from 50 fighters to a claimed 800. How many died with him on 20 November is given as two or four. The attacks of 1931 onward are reported in outline but not documented case by case, so their number and their victims cannot be stated. The Mufti's refusal rests on a single reported account. What is solid is the arc: a Syrian-born cleric condemned by the French, a respected Haifa preacher and court official for a decade, a clandestine organizer, and a man killed by British police eight days after declaring an armed revolt that the Palestinian leadership had declined to call. Within months the country would be in the general strike and revolt told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].

sections.h: The Last Offer Before the Revolt: Wauchope's Council, 1935–1936
sections.html:
On 23 December 1935 the High Commissioner for Palestine, Sir Arthur Wauchope, called in the leaders of the Jewish community and laid before them a plan for a legislative council. It would have 28 members: 14 Arabs, 7 Jews and 7 Britons. The government, he told them, was "determined to establish the assembly" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. It was not the first such offer: an earlier one, made in 1922, is told in [scene:rd2_council|the council of 1922–1923]. Thirteen years later the question behind it was still open. Who would have a voice in governing Palestine, in what proportion, and over which questions?

The demand for an elected body had come, from the beginning, from the Arab side. From 1919 the Palestine Arab congresses had asked Britain for a national government responsible to a representative assembly chosen by the country's inhabitants [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]. As recently as December 1934 Raghib al-Nashashibi's new National Defense Party had called for parliamentary government [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]. The Zionist Congress, meeting at Lucerne in 1935, had taken the opposite view, resolving against any council that would fix the Jews as a minority [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. Wauchope's offer therefore tested both sides at once, and the way each answered it is the best single view of where Palestinian and Zionist politics stood at the end of 1935.

The terms mattered as much as the numbers. As reported at the time, the basis of representation was to be fixed for five years; one of the elected Arab members was to be a Bedouin; the High Commissioner could nominate members to fill the seats of any community that boycotted the elections; and the council could not deal with the labour immigration schedule [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. That last exclusion went to the centre of the conflict. The labour schedule was allotted in half-year periods. It had stood at 5,500 for April–September 1933 and risen to 8,000 for April–September 1935, before being cut to 3,250 for October 1935–March 1936 [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. It was also only one channel of entry. Of the 61,854 Jews recorded as entering Palestine in 1935, 14,653 came under the labour schedule and 13,076 were their dependants; an American official estimated that the remaining 44,000 entered in other categories, such as capital holders, professionals and skilled artisans [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d531]. A council barred from the labour schedule would have had no hand on the immigration of workers, a question the Arab congresses had raised since 1919, when they rejected mass Jewish immigration [cite:wiki_palestine_arab_congress]; and the High Commissioner's power to fill a boycotting community's seats meant that refusing to take part would not stop the council from sitting.

The Zionist answer was given on the spot. Chaim Weizmann rejected the plan as contrary to the Mandate, citing the resolution of the Zionist Congress at Lucerne that such a council would fix the Jews as a minority. Yitzhak Ben-Zvi, speaking for the Vaad Leumi, concurred, and so did A. L. Maleh for the Sephardi community [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. The case behind the rejection is best put in its own terms. The Zionist reading of the Mandate held that Britain's obligation ran not only to the Jews already in Palestine but to the Jewish people as a whole; the British government itself had put it that way in 1931, calling the Mandate "an undertaking to the Jewish people and not only to the Jewish population of Palestine" [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]. On that reading, a legislature apportioned by the population of the moment and frozen for five years would hand a permanent majority a veto over the growth that the Mandate was meant to permit, at the very time that growth was fastest. The Jewish Agency's own figures, prepared for its case to the Peel Commission and so to be read as advocacy, put the Jewish population at 84,000, or 13 percent, in 1922 and 375,000, or 28 percent, in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]. Seven seats of 28 was a quarter.

Not every Jewish voice gave the same answer. Rabbi Moshe Blau, speaking for Agudath Israel, said only that the time was "not yet ripe" [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. Agudath Israel had been founded in 1912 as a movement of Torah-observant Jews that held itself apart from secular Jewish nationalism [cite:unpacked_neturei_karta_history]. Its answer was a postponement, not a rejection on the Zionist ground of minority status.

The Arab answer was slower and less unanimous. Arab leaders withheld their reply and objected to women voting; the Mufti of Jerusalem, Hajj Amin al-Husseini, was reported to be still opposed [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1935_council]. The arithmetic of the offer allows the Arab objection to be reconstructed in outline, though the sources here do not record it in the leaders' own words. By the Jewish Agency's figures for 1935, the non-Jewish population was 975,000 against 375,000 Jews [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937], roughly seven in ten of the inhabitants; the council would have given Arabs half its seats, with British officials holding a quarter and the High Commissioner able to fill boycotted seats, and it would have had no say over immigration under the labour schedule. To a movement that had asked since 1919 for a government responsible to a representative assembly, it offered half the seats of a body with no hand on immigration under the labour schedule. To the Zionist leadership, the same body offered the majority too much. The record held here does not give the detailed arguments of the Arab parties, and it should not be assumed that all of them shared the Mufti's position. Some, as events showed, did not.

The decision did not rest in Jerusalem. On 24 March 1936 the Prime Minister, Stanley Baldwin, announced a debate on the council in the House of Commons, and the Colonial Secretary, J. H. Thomas, said that final action would wait for it. The Jewish Telegraphic Agency reported that day that Jewish organizations were "unitedly opposed" and that some Arab groups were accepting [cite:rs_rd3_jta_1936_commons]. The chain of authority is plain in the record: the High Commissioner proposed, the Colonial Secretary held final action, and a Commons debate could hold it up. The research behind this book does not establish what the Commons debate concluded, and this account does not guess.

The offer's most lasting effect was on Palestinian unity. By late 1935 the five Arab parties had formed a united front, which the American Consul General described as a response to a "national emergency" [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512]. In April 1936 the same consul reported that the council proposals had broken that front, and that "all thought of united Arab action" on the council had been abandoned [cite:rs_rd3_frus1936_d512_m]. On 5 May 1936, according to the Center for Israel Education, the Mufti and other Arab leaders declined to attend a conference in London on the proposal [cite:rs_rd3_cie_mufti_council]. By then events in Palestine had overtaken the council entirely; what followed belongs to [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt].

A common way of telling this period holds that one side or the other simply refused every chance at shared government. The record of 1935–36 is more specific. The offer was made to Jewish leaders first and in a fixed form; the Zionist leadership rejected it at once and in principle; Agudath Israel deferred; the Arab leadership hesitated, divided, and in its most powerful figure opposed it; and the decision was in any case held in London. Several things remain unsettled by the sources available here: what the Commons debate decided, what reasons the Arab parties that accepted gave, how the women's-suffrage objection weighed against the others, and whether the council would ever have sat had the country not moved into revolt.

The council's failure is a fitting place to close this stage, because it showed the structure that fourteen years of building had produced. At the top stood the British state. The Mandate had been in force, by the League Council's own minutes, since 29 September 1923, a date that Professor John Quigley argues had no legal force, so that Britain held Palestine without title [cite:rs_rd3_unispal_mandate_force] [cite:rs_rd3_quigley_2026]. Under it the High Commissioner proposed policy, allotted the labour schedule in half-year periods, and answered to the Colonial Secretary and, through him, to Parliament.

Beside the Mandate government, the Jewish community had built the institutions of a state in all but sovereignty. The Jewish Agency, enlarged in 1929 to give half the seats on its Council to non-Zionists, with Keren Hayesod as its main financial instrument [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14], was chaired from 1935 by David Ben-Gurion [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The Histadrut, founded in 1920 and restricted to Jews, ran its own construction company, bank and health fund [cite:wiki_histadrut]. The Haganah, placed under the Histadrut's direct control in December 1920, had since 1931 been led by a six-member national command with parity between three Histadrut members and three non-labour members; its urban branches had memberships "in the hundreds," and it ran workshops producing hand grenades [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. Outside this structure, and against it, stood the Revisionists. Their New Zionist Organization had met in Vienna in September 1935, said to have been "elected by 713,000 voters," with Ze'ev Jabotinsky as president [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists], and the Irgun had existed since 1931, formed by Avraham Tehomi's group with Revisionist groups after their secession from the Haganah [cite:rs_rd3_ej_haganah]. The Jewish population, by the Agency's count, had grown from 84,000 to 375,000 in thirteen years [cite:rs_rd3_horowitz_1937]; Tel Aviv alone had about 120,000 people in 1935 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_telaviv].

The Palestinian Arab side had no comparable apparatus and no recognized representative body. The Arab Executive, never recognized by Britain, had dissolved in 1934, the year Musa Kazim al-Husseini died [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. In its place stood parties built around rival families and rival programmes: Nashashibi's National Defense Party, founded in December 1934 and close to Emir Abdullah [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_nashashibi]; the Palestine Arab Party, established on 27 March 1935 under Jamal al-Husseini, close to the Mufti [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_jamal]; and the Istiqlal, announced in August 1932, which named British imperialism as the main enemy but never built a large membership [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_hajibrahim] [cite:rs_rd3_wiki_istiqlal]. In late 1935 the five parties stood briefly together, and outside all of them a Haifa preacher had taken a band to the hills and died there, as told in [scene:rd3_qassam|the section on al-Qassam].

The year-by-year ledger below sets these years side by side, and most of its rows can be read against the sections of this stage. The Revisionist line runs through it from Betar in 1923 [cite:wiki_betar] to the Paris founding of 1925 [cite:rs_rd3_ej_revisionists]; the Hebrew University opened on 1 April 1925 [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_hebrew_univ]; the 1929 row pairs the violence of August with the enlarged Jewish Agency [cite:israeled_weizmann_vol14]; the 1930 and 1931 rows record the Shaw and Hope Simpson inquiries, the Passfield White Paper and MacDonald's letter of February 1931, which Arab leaders called the "Black Letter" and which withdrew the White Paper's restrictions within four months [cite:w_passfield] [cite:rs_rd3_macdonald_unispal]; and 1933 carries the Haavara Agreement with about 105 million Reichsmarks of goods moved by the outbreak of war [cite:wiki_haavara_agreement]. The 1934 row marks the dissolution of the Arab Executive [cite:palquest_musa_kazim]. The 1935 row gathers the stage's ending in a single line: the peak of immigration, recorded as 61,854 in the State Department series and 66,472 in the Porath series [cite:rs_rd3_frus1939_d828] [cite:rs_rd3_jvl_porath_table], the Nuremberg Laws [cite:ushmm_nuremberg_laws], and al-Qassam's death [cite:rs_rd3_palquest_qassam]. The "what it built" column is the ledger's own summary rather than a finding of this book, and one entry, for 1926, rests on a figure that the research behind this book has not sourced and that is not relied on here.

Read as a whole, the architecture at the end of 1935 was lopsided in a specific, documented way. One community had a funded agency, a labour federation with its own economy, an armed organization under shared command and a rival one outside it, and, by its own agency's count, a population that had more than quadrupled since 1922. The other had a national movement of long standing, a demand for representative government it had pressed since 1919, five parties that could unite only briefly, and no institution that Britain recognized as speaking for it. Britain held the decisions, and had just offered one that neither side would take on its terms. That was the structure that entered 1936.

chapters.label: Stage Four
chapters.title: Pivot to America
chapters.intro:
In the spring of 1936 the Mandate for Palestine was in its second decade, and the forces that would contest it were already organized. Hajj Amin al-Husseini had been Mufti of Jerusalem since 1921, and the Palestinian parties led by his family and by the Nashashibis had spent the previous ten years competing with one another. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] On the Zionist side the Haganah existed without British recognition, Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionists had claimed both banks of the Jordan since 1925, and the Irgun had formed in 1931. [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] In November 1935 British forces killed Izz al-Din al-Qassam. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] Five months later, on 15 April 1936, two Jews were killed near Tulkarm, and within ten days a general strike had been called from Nablus and local committees across the country had united as the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] In the United States there was not yet a law requiring anyone working for a foreign cause to register, and the leaders of American Zionism were citizens acting as citizens. [cite:doj_fara]

This stage asks how the centre of the Palestine question moved, in less than a decade, from a British administration putting down a rural revolt to the committee rooms of the United States Congress and the platforms of both American parties. It asks with equal weight what each party to the question did as the doors closed on Europe's Jews: what Britain decided and why it abandoned what it had proposed, what the Palestinian Arab leadership chose and what those choices cost, what the Zionist movement demanded and by what means, and what the American president said in public, in private and in writing. The answer is not a single turn but a sequence of them, each documented, and several still argued over.

The cast is wide. In London stood the royal commission known after its chairman as the Peel Commission, a technical commission under Sir John Woodhead, Malcolm MacDonald defending the enforcement of the White Paper of 1939, and its critics in the Commons, Leo Amery, Winston Churchill and Herbert Morrison; in July 1945 Clement Attlee formed a Labour government. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_jvl_debate] [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] In Palestine and in exile were al-Husseini, Raghib and Fakhri Nashashibi and the peace bands Britain paid, Jamal al-Husseini's delegation in London, and the neighbouring Arab rulers who mediated the strike's end in 1936 and sent delegations of their own to London in 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] The Zionist movement spoke through Chaim Weizmann and David Ben-Gurion, and in America through Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, while Hillel Kook, calling himself Peter Bergson, ran an insurgent campaign of his own and Lehi offered to fight on Germany's side. [cite:biltmore_medoff] [cite:azec_case] [cite:w_kook] [cite:academickids_lehi] In Washington Franklin Roosevelt, his State and War Departments, and Senators Robert Wagner and Robert Taft each held a lever; aboard the USS Quincy, King Ibn Saud held another. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] Behind all of them stood the Nazi state, which turned to open violence in November 1938 and to the coordinated murder of Europe's Jews. [cite:ushmm_kristallnacht] [cite:ushmm_wannsee_conference]

The sections follow that sequence. They open with [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt] from its first killings to its suppression and its disputed death toll, and with the Peel Commission's partition plan, its proposal to move some 225,000 Arabs, and the three answers it drew. Woodhead and the London conference show how partition was dropped. Évian, where 32 countries declined to take more refugees and Palestine was kept off the agenda, and Kristallnacht four months later frame [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of May 1939] and the fight over whether it broke the Mandate. [cite:wiki_evian] The war years follow: British training of Jewish fighters, the clandestine fleet and the ships the limit turned away, Lehi and Lord Moyne, al-Husseini's road through Iraq to Berlin, the Vatican's wartime record, and the Holocaust from Wannsee to the counting of six million. The American turn runs through the Biltmore Program, the Bergson campaigns, the watchers in Washington, the Emergency Council's letter machine and the resolutions of 1944–45. The stage closes with Roosevelt's two registers, his concealed illness and the choice of Truman, the meeting at Great Bitter Lake, and Labour's arrival in office.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1945 the Mandate's structure still stood, but the weight resting on it had moved. Britain still held the Mandate and still governed by the White Paper of 1939. The argument over what should replace it was now being made as loudly in Washington as in Jerusalem or London.

The legal layer had been altered without being resolved. Cmd 6019 of 17 May 1939 ruled out a Jewish state, promised an independent Palestine state within ten years, allowed some 75,000 Jewish immigrants over five years, and made any further immigration depend on Arab acquiescence; Parliament approved it on 23 May. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] Whether Britain had the right to adopt it is the one question of the stage that was formally put to a tribunal and never decided. The Permanent Mandates Commission held unanimously that the policy departed from the interpretation it had always placed on the Mandate, and found by four votes to three that it could not say the policy conformed; the war came before the League Council could act.
