[cite:rs_rd4_wp_jvl_league] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_wiki_pmc] The Jewish Agency's strongest case was that a duty to "facilitate Jewish immigration" could not be turned into a power to end it. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_bjpa_jacase] The strongest case for it was the Commission minority's, that existing circumstances could justify the policy provided the League Council did not object, together with Britain's own stated objective of an independent state within ten years. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_jewishlink] The record leaves the question where the war left it.

The administrative layer was coercive. To end the revolt Britain sent about 20,000 troops, demolished houses, imposed collective fines on whole neighbourhoods, detained and deported, and hanged between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs and two Jews. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The White Paper then placed the remaining levers with the High Commissioner: when 25,000 refugees could enter, general powers over land transfers, and a rule deducting every unauthorized arrival from the quota, which became the ground for suspending the whole six-month quota in July 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] At sea the same rule was enforced against particular ships, and the Patria and the Struma together cost more than 1,000 lives. [cite:wiki_patria_disaster] [cite:wiki_struma_disaster] The wartime High Commissioners and Colonial Secretaries are not named in the sources for this stage.

The institutional and financial layer belonged largely to the Yishuv. On the figures in this library's funding ledger, the Jewish Agency's 1939 budget of £720,000 carried £80,000 for defense, and the Kofer HaYishuv levy of 1938 funded the Haganah. Britain trained parts of that force when it needed it, at Ein Harod in 1938, in the Palmach in 1941 and in the Jewish Brigade Group of 1944–45, and jailed members who trained outside its control. [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:archiveshub_wingate] [cite:wiki_zvi_brenner] The Mossad LeAliyah Bet was created as a branch of the Haganah in 1938, and the Haganah founded the Shai, its intelligence arm, in 1940. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:shai_wiki] In October 1942 the Zionist General Council made the Biltmore demand for a Jewish Commonwealth binding policy. [cite:biltmore_enc] The movement's fringe stood outside this discipline: Lehi offered in 1941 to fight on Germany's side and killed Lord Moyne in 1944, and the Zionist Executive called its members "traitors." [cite:academickids_lehi] [cite:daat_moyne] In America, by the same ledger's reckoning from Marc Lee Raphael's history, the United Jewish Appeal raised more than $124 million between 1939 and 1945, split among European relief, the Palestine programme and resettlement in the United States in shares the record here does not give; the Emergency Council's own files document a method, not a budget.

The Palestinian Arab side ended the stage with the heaviest losses and the weakest institutions. The Arab Higher Committee of April 1936 had joined rival parties under one leadership; by the autumn of 1937 it was outlawed, its members arrested or deported to the Seychelles, its president in exile. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] Walid Khalidi's count of 5,032 Arab dead, against official British figures that are lower and higher estimates that reach 8,000, measures the revolt's cost, and the internal war between the Mufti's followers and the Nashashibi peace bands added hundreds of Palestinian dead at Palestinian hands. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] The leadership rejected Peel outright and rejected the White Paper, though a US consul reported "very obvious relief" among the Arab public at its terms. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d826] Its strongest case was a majority's claim to an independent government and to a halt to immigration it had never consented to. The strongest case against its choices is the record of rebel violence against other Palestinians and of al-Husseini's own road to Berlin, which remains one man's documented choice, not the record of a people. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini]

The regional layer widened in every direction. Arab rulers mediated the end of the 1936 strike; Egypt, Iraq and Saudi Arabia sat at St James's Palace; Iraq's pro-Axis coup collapsed in 1941 into the Farhud, the pogrom whose death toll the sources give as 150 to 180 or higher. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:ushmm_farhud] [cite:wiki_farhud] By 1945 the Saudi king, whose kingdom was already tied to the United States through ARAMCO, held a written presidential undertaking on Palestine. [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud]

The American layer was the stage's new construction, raised under a 1938 law that for the first time required agents of foreign principals to register. [cite:doj_fara] The Emergency Council, founded in August 1943, ran letter and telegram campaigns from 342 Madison Avenue; the Bergson committees bought pages and filled Madison Square Garden; both parties wrote Palestine into their platforms in 1944, "the first time in American history." [cite:azec_powerbase] [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] [cite:w_wwnd] [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944] Against them stood the War and State Departments, which twice asked Congress to wait, and a president who approved silence on Palestine for the war while assuring Arab leaders in writing that he would consult them. [cite:djn_1944_marshall] [cite:brandeis_center_fdr_zionism] [cite:state_dept_oct1945_release] Congress's resolution of December 1945 spoke not of a Jewish commonwealth but of equal rights "regardless of race or creed." [cite:frus1945_concres]

What was settled, then, was narrower than either side's hopes: Britain's partition plan was dead, its White Paper stood, and the Palestinian leadership that might have negotiated its terms was scattered. What was contested ran through the whole stage: whether the White Paper broke the Mandate, whether the Zionist Congress accepted Peel, what Ben-Gurion's letter to his son meant, how many died in the revolt, whether Roosevelt's two voices were statecraft or duplicity. What the record leaves open is the question the stage handed on. A Labour government pledged against the White Paper took office in July 1945, and the State Department forecast that it would modify the immigration limits and not act on its conference's call for Arabs to "move out." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] Roosevelt had died on 12 April 1945, and his promise of consultation passed to a successor who had not been told how ill he was. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] [cite:globalsecurity_fdr_veiled_decline] How those two inheritances would meet the survivors of the Holocaust is the subject of the next stage.

sections.h: The Arab Revolt, 1936–1939
sections.html:
The revolt that opened this period had a prelude. In November 1935 British forces killed Izz al-Din al-Qassam, and historians name his death as part of the background to what followed. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The broader timing is also documented. The uprising of 1936 followed the sharpest rise in Jewish immigration under the Mandate, and it came in the same decade that produced the Irgun (1931) and, later, Lehi (1940). Each of these movements, Arab and Jewish, formed in reaction to the other side and to British policy. Naming that pattern explains when the armed movements arose. It excuses none of them, and their attacks on civilians are part of the record on every side.

The immediate trigger came on 15 April 1936. Palestinian Arabs killed two Jews near Tulkarm, Jewish retaliation followed, and riots broke out in Jaffa and Tel Aviv. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The sources do not agree on the first incident. The Jewish Virtual Library describes it as an attack on a Jewish bus and gives three Jewish dead, not two. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots]

The strike that followed did not begin at the top. On 19 April a newly formed Arab National Committee in Nablus called for a general strike, the withholding of taxes and a boycott of Jewish products. Local national committees across the country then united on 25 April as the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] The new committee was led by Hajj Amin al-Husseini, Mufti of Jerusalem. It declared a general strike with three demands: an end to Jewish immigration, an end to land sales to Jews, and an independent national government. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Another account dates al-Husseini's own strike call, as the committee's president, to 16 May 1936. [cite:ushmm_arab_revolt] Read together, the dates suggest that local committees moved first and the national leadership then took up the strike, though the sources do not explain the gap between them.

The committee's membership was its most striking feature. According to the list drawn from the Peel report, it brought together the leaders of rival clans and parties that had spent the previous decade competing with each other. Amin al-Husseini was president. Raghib al-Nashashibi represented the National Defence Party, Jamal al-Husseini the Palestine Arab Party, Yaqub al-Ghusayn the Youth Congress, Abd al-Latif Salah the National Bloc and Husayn al-Khalidi the Reform Party. Awni Abd al-Hadi of the Istiqlal was general secretary and Ahmed Hilmi Pasha treasurer. The coalition did not last long: Raghib al-Nashashibi left soon after it was formed. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc]

The familiar description of the revolt as a spontaneous, leaderless outburst with no lasting result does not fit this record. The strike had a dated origin, a named committee with named officers, a written list of demands and a structure of local committees. Yet the opposite simplification fails too. A named leadership establishes an organized origin and an overall direction. It does not mean that every participant in three years of fighting took orders from al-Husseini, and the sources do not make that claim. The revolt's consequences, as this section and the next show, were large.

The general strike lasted about six months. Its end is recorded in a British document. On 12 October 1936 the General Officer Commanding issued a Special Order announcing that the strike and armed rebellion had been "called off unconditionally by the Higher Arab Committee." [cite:rs_rd4_ar_cojs_gocorder] The rulers of neighbouring Arab states had mediated its end. Different sources name them as the rulers of Transjordan, Iraq, Saudi Arabia and Yemen. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Historians weigh the causes differently. Some sources stress the rulers' appeal, together with British concessions and the threat of martial law. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Others also point to economic pressure, especially the approaching citrus harvest. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] The two explanations are compatible, and the evidence does not let us rank them.

The same Special Order gave the British army's own count of the cost of the strike period. It recorded 25 British soldiers killed and 120 wounded, 7 British police killed and 40 wounded, and 9 Palestine police killed and 64 wounded. It put the total cost of the rebellion so far at no fewer than 300 dead and 1,300 wounded. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_cojs_gocorder] This is the figure of one side, issued at the moment that side declared the rebellion over, and it should be read as such. It is also the earliest official tally there is.

London's political answer was already in motion. A royal commission had been appointed in August 1936, during the strike, to investigate the causes of the revolt. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:wiki_peel_commission] Its report of July 1937 proposed partition, and its reception is told in [scene:s07a6|the Peel Commission].

Peel's proposal was followed by the revolt's second phase. On 26 September 1937, four gunmen described as followers of al-Qassam killed Lewis Andrews, District Commissioner for Galilee, as he left a service at Christ Church in Nazareth. His police bodyguard died of his wounds. Within 24 hours police had detained about 100 Palestinian Arabs. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked]

Britain then moved against the political leadership. It outlawed the Arab Higher Committee, around 30 September 1937, stripped al-Husseini of his offices, arrested members of the committee and deported several of them to the Seychelles. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_wiki_ahc] The sequence of al-Husseini's flight is told slightly differently in different sources. One account has him taking sanctuary in the Dome of the Rock on 17 July 1937 to avoid arrest, and then losing his positions after the district commissioner's killing in September. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] The research sources place his refuge in the Haram al-Sharif and his escape in the autumn of 1937. They disagree on where he went: Lebanon, according to Unpacked, or Syria, according to the Jewish Virtual Library. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_andrews] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The account that sends him to Lebanon continues to Iraq, and historians document that he went on directing the revolt from exile. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] By Unpacked's account, he authorized attacks from abroad on Britons, on Jews, and on Palestinians considered collaborators. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The record establishes that he continued to give direction. It does not itemize every order he sent.

With the leadership gone, the revolt moved into the countryside. Rebel bands set up their own administration there and taxed the peasants. The uprising peaked in the autumn of 1938, when rebels held large parts of the country, and was suppressed by the summer of 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert]

Britain sent about 20,000 troops. Its measures included house demolitions, executions, the outlawing of the Arab Higher Committee, arrests and expulsions of activists, indefinite detention, collective fines on whole neighbourhoods, and the disarming of Palestinians. Matthew Hughes's 2019 study of the campaign groups these methods into eight categories. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The instruments mattered because of where they fell. Collective fines landed on whole neighbourhoods, not only on fighters, and indefinite detention and expulsion removed activists without a fixed term. These were powers of the Mandate administration, and from the autumn of 1937 they were used after the Arab Higher Committee itself had been outlawed and its members arrested or deported.

Executions give one measure of the campaign. Between 108 and 122 Palestinian Arabs were hanged in the 1930s. The reviewer of Hughes's study compares this with the 1,090 Kenyans hanged during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s. Two Jews were hanged. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes]

The revolt was also a civil conflict. Raghib al-Nashashibi, a former mayor of Jerusalem, favoured compromise with the British; the Mufti opposed it. Their rivalry produced hundreds of killings of Palestinians by Palestinians. The Nashashibi-aligned "peace bands" were raised with British and Jewish military and financial help to fight the rebels. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands]

Hughes's study of the peace bands supplies the detail. By March 1938 Fakhri Nashashibi was organizing them from Lebanon. Fakhri 'Abd al-Hadi, a former rebel commander, returned to Palestine on 21 September 1938 with backing from the British consul in Damascus, Gilbert MacKereth. The money is documented. Britain paid band members £P6 a month. The insurgents paid their own men between 30 shillings and £P4. Both men were later killed: Husseini-backed gunmen killed Fakhri Nashashibi in Iraq in 1941, and 'Abd al-Hadi was murdered in 1943. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] The 1941 killing belongs to al-Husseini's exile, which continued into an alliance with Nazi Germany from 1941: he met Hitler and recruited for the Waffen-SS, a record set out in [scene:rd4_mufti_war|the Mufti's war]. [cite:wiki_amin_al_husseini] It is his own documented record. The overwhelming majority of Palestinian Arabs had no part in it and no say over it.

The money ran both ways. The rebel bands taxed the villages they held. Britain paid the bands that fought them. And the general strike itself, by withdrawing Arab labour and trade, pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full]

Jewish attacks on Arab civilians are part of the same record. In November 1937 the Irgun abandoned the policy of restraint and killed ten Arab civilians on the day later called "Black Sunday." After an attack on an Arab bus in April 1938, the British hanged Shlomo Ben-Yosef in June 1938. He was one of the two Jews hanged during the revolt. By Unpacked's count, at least 250 Palestinian Arabs had died at Irgun hands by the summer of 1939. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] The Irgun was formed in 1931, and its turn to reprisal belongs to the pattern the opening of this section described. Like the rebels' attacks on Jewish civilians, it is named here for what it was.

How many people died is the most contested question about the revolt. The figures come from different sources, count different things, and should be set out side by side.

For Arab deaths, the most detailed figure comes from Walid Khalidi's analysis of British statistics. He counts 3,832 Palestinian Arabs killed by the British and 1,200 killed in internal strife, 5,032 in all, with 14,760 wounded. Official British figures are lower and divided differently. They give over 2,000 Arabs killed in combat, 108 hanged and 961 killed by "gang and terrorist activities." Reference works round the total to about 5,000. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] The Jewish Virtual Library estimates roughly 5,000 dead, 15,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] Middle East Eye gives about 5,000 killed, 15,000–20,000 wounded and 5,600 imprisoned. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] At the high end, Unpacked (Noam Weissman, 2024), drawing on Oren Kessler, gives 5,000–8,000 Palestinian Arab dead and says about 20 percent of Palestinian Arab men were jailed at some point. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] The summary published by the Palestinian church committee states that over 10 percent of Palestinian Arab men aged 20 to 60 were killed, wounded, imprisoned or exiled. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc]

For Jewish and British deaths, the scholarly and reference figures cluster closely. Ori Yehudai gives about 415 Jews and 100 British. The Jewish Virtual Library gives 415 Jewish deaths for 1936–39. Fred Strickert gives nearly 400 Jews and 200 Britons. Hughes's reviewer writes of "hundreds" of Jews. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_jvl_riots] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_ebsco_strickert] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] Much higher Jewish and British figures also circulate: 2,652 Jews and 618 British personnel killed, alongside roughly 5,000 Arabs, a breakdown attributed to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. [cite:ushmm_arab_revolt] None of the other sources consulted for this book supports the Jewish and British numbers, which run six times and three to six times higher than theirs, and the museum's own page could not be checked. They are recorded here as a claim in circulation, not as a finding.

The revolt also moved people. According to the review of Hughes's study, about 40,000 Christian Arabs and others left for Syria and Lebanon during the revolt. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes]

How to characterize the revolt is itself in dispute, and each reading rests on real evidence. In the Palestinian national reading, as Middle East Eye puts it, the revolt was "the most sustained armed resistance" against the Mandate, a national uprising crushed by brutal British repression. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_mee_strike] The demolitions, collective fines, hangings and detentions described above are its evidence. A critical reading, given by Unpacked, stresses that the rebels also turned on Palestinians, extorting and killing those they deemed disloyal, with leaders encouraging it. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_unpacked] Its evidence is the intra-Palestinian killing and al-Husseini's reported authorization of attacks on supposed collaborators.

Hughes's scholarship takes both seriously. He concludes that the peace bands "never won the war for the British." Collaboration, he finds, was driven more by survival, personal gain and feuds than by political conviction, and "Palestinian collaboration in the 1930s was too partial to damn the Arab revolt." [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hughes_peacebands_full] On that reading the internal violence was real and the uprising was still a national one. Neither fact cancels the other.

On the outcome, historians agree. The revolt failed militarily. The Palestinian leadership was left weak, divided and in exile. Military cooperation between Britain and the Zionist movement deepened, a story taken up in [scene:br_s01|Wingate's Night Squads and the Palmach]. And the general strike pushed the Yishuv toward a more self-reliant economy. [cite:rs_rd4_ar_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_shindler_hughes] [cite:rs_rd4_ar_hcc] The ledger of these years shows the sequence at a glance: the revolt in 1936, Peel's partition and transfer proposal in 1937 with the Arab Higher Committee objecting, and in 1939 the White Paper's limit on immigration, which the Zionist movement opposed.

Much remains unsettled. The death toll is the clearest gap: the Arab figures range from British official counts to 8,000, and the Jewish and British figures differ between sources, with higher figures circulating that could not be verified. The sources do not settle the exact date of al-Husseini's flight or its first destination, or how much of the second phase he actually directed from abroad. Nor do they give firm totals for detentions or demolitions. What the record does establish is narrower and firmer. A strike began in local committees and was taken up by a cross-party national committee. It became a rural insurgency. Britain put it down with collective punishment and with Palestinian allies it paid. It left a divided and exiled leadership on the eve of the decisions that would follow from London.

sections.h: The Peel Commission: Partition's First Draft
sections.html:
Britain's political answer to the revolt was a royal commission. The Palestine Royal Commission, known after its chairman as the Peel Commission, had six members. It was appointed in August 1936, while the general strike was still under way. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] Its task was to investigate the causes of the uprising. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

Its report, published in July 1937, went much further than an inquiry into causes. It proposed ending the Mandate. In its place there would be an independent Arab state, formed by joining part of Palestine to Transjordan, and an independent Jewish state in another part of the country. Jerusalem and some other places would stay under British mandate,, in a British-administered corridor that included the city. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:wiki_peel_commission] It was the first official proposal to partition the territory. The Jewish state would be small. The sources give its size differently: 17 percent of the country according to Ori Yehudai, about 20 percent according to Fred Strickert. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_ebsco_strickert] The sources consulted here do not explain the difference, and this book gives both figures.

The report did not stop at borders. Beside its partition map it recommended an "exchange of population," compulsory in the last resort. That recommendation, the first time population transfer appeared in an official British document, is the subject of the next section, [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"].

A common belief holds that partition was the United Nations' original idea in 1947, reached through a neutral international process. The record shows otherwise. A British royal commission proposed partition a decade earlier, and both sides had already responded to it, in different ways, before the United Nations took up the question. The UN committee's 1947 map bore a documented resemblance to this earlier partition thinking, which is examined in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the 1947 plan]. [cite:peel_report_1937] The resemblance is one of concept and structure. The two maps were not identical line for line, and the claim here is only that the idea came first from London.

Three responses mattered, and they were not alike.

The first came from the Twentieth Zionist Congress, which met in 1937. The movement was deeply divided over the plan, and the Congress produced a carefully balanced position. It rejected the proposed boundaries. It accepted partition in principle, or at least did not reject it, and it authorized continued negotiation with Britain. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] Historians do not settle on a single verb for this. Some write that the Congress "accepted" the principle of partition; others that it "did not reject it outright." [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] The difference matters for anyone who later summarizes 1937 in a sentence. A United Nations working paper of 1949 put it more starkly than either: it summarized the outcome as rejection of the plan by both Jews and Arabs. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] The strongest form of the "acceptance" reading is that the movement's leadership accepted the idea of a Jewish state in part of the country and wanted to bargain over its size. The strongest form of the "rejection" reading is that the Congress refused the plan actually on the table, since the boundaries were the plan. Both readings fit the resolution, which was built to allow both. This book does not choose between them.

The second response was the Arab Higher Committee's, and it was unambiguous. The committee, led by al-Husseini, rejected the plan outright, with no conditional language. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] His role in the violence of 1929 is examined in an earlier chapter. The committee's rejection was its own formal institutional position. It does not show that every person in the Arab population held identical views on partition, and the sources do not measure what others thought.

The third response came from the Revisionist movement. Ze'ev (Vladimir) Jabotinsky had founded the Union of Revisionist Zionists, Hatzohar, in 1925. Its core territorial claim was that the Jewish state must cover both banks of the Jordan River: what later became Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, and the whole of Transjordan. [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] In 1929–1930 Jabotinsky put the argument in geographical terms:

"What does the word Palestine mean? Palestine is a territory whose chief geographical feature is this: that the River Jordan does not delineate its frontier, but flows through its center."

The movement's anthem made the same claim in verse: "Two Banks has the Jordan — This is ours and, that is as well." [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] The claim was territorial and historical rather than primarily religious; Jabotinsky was not himself religious. He argued that Britain's 1922 separation of Transjordan from the Palestine Mandate had been an arbitrary partition, one that denied Jews the land needed to absorb millions of future immigrants. [cite:jabotinsky_revisionist_1925] Testifying before the Peel Commission, he argued forcefully against any partition and for Jewish rights to the whole of Mandate Palestine, Transjordan included. [cite:wiki_jabotinsky] This was a consistent position, given on the record to the commission itself. It was not the mainstream Zionist position of 1937, which, as the Congress's resolution shows, was far more ambiguous. The later history of this claim, through Herut and Likud, is traced in [scene:gia_src_s02|the versions of "Greater Israel"].

The plan's effect on the ground was immediate. According to Unpacked and the Jewish Virtual Library, Peel's partition proposal prompted rebel groups to restart the revolt in the autumn of 1937. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] The second phase of the uprising, told in the previous section, began within weeks of the report.

The 1937 rejection is often used as evidence for a later slogan: that the Arabs "rejected every offer." What the record shows is narrower. Arab leaders did reject the 1937 Peel plan, and later the 1947 partition plan. But the slogan compresses a record that runs in two directions. Israel's 1949 refugee offer at Lausanne was made only within a full peace and was later withdrawn. The 2000 Camp David offer is disputed by participants, and some on the American side say it was never written down. Offers in this history were conditional, and both sides refused at different points. Peel, in particular, was refused by both: outright by the Arab Higher Committee, and in its actual boundaries by the Zionist Congress. The slogan is short, and the history behind it is longer and less flattering to whichever side repeats it.

Some questions the record here does not settle. The precise share of the country allotted to the Jewish state differs between sources, and the boundaries of the plan are not set out in the material drawn on for this section. The documents do not say how the Congress's delegates divided, beyond the description of the movement as deeply divided. Nor do they settle whether "acceptance in principle" was a real commitment or a bargaining position. What is firm is the sequence. In 1937 Britain put partition on paper for the first time. The Arab Higher Committee rejected it, the Zionist Congress refused its borders while keeping the idea alive, and Jabotinsky demanded the whole territory on both sides of the river. Within eighteen months, as the next sections show, London abandoned the plan.

sections.h: Peel's "Exchange of Population": Transfer Enters the Record
sections.html:
The Peel report of July 1937 is remembered for its partition map. Beside the map it made a second recommendation. It proposed an "exchange of population" between the two states it would create. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

The model was explicit: the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey in 1923. Approximately 225,000 Arabs would be moved out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and about 1,250 Jews out of the Arab state. The report stated that in the last resort the exchange should be compulsory. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] It was the first official British document to put population transfer in writing. The sources round the figures differently. Ori Yehudai gives about 200,000 Arabs and about 1,000 Jews. Middle East Eye gives about 225,000 Palestinians against 1,250 Jews, matching the figures above. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_origins_yehudai] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_mee_strike] Either way, the scale was lopsided. The movement the report envisaged was overwhelmingly of Arabs out of the proposed Jewish state.

A widely held view is that the idea of removing the Arab population from a future Jewish state was invented by Israeli extremists after 1948. The documents do not support that chronology. Compulsory transfer entered the official record in a British royal commission report in 1937. It was then discussed, and not rejected, at the top of the Zionist movement more than a decade before the displacement of 1948. That leaves open what any individual leader privately intended. The concept itself was on the table well before the Nakba.

The mechanism matters. The recommendation was Britain's, made by a royal commission of the Mandatory power, and it would have been Britain's to adopt or drop. The Zionist movement and the Arab Higher Committee could only respond to it. The Arab response was a plain rejection. The Zionist response is the disputed part of the record.

The most quoted evidence is a private letter. In October 1937 David Ben-Gurion wrote to his son Amos. The letter welcomes partition as a stage toward a larger state and discusses the Arab population. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] His diary and letters of the period discuss compulsory transfer as a possibility. One sentence in the Amos letter has become the centre of a dispute over its wording. It has been quoted as support for expelling Arabs. In a different reading of the handwritten Hebrew, it says the opposite. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] Historians have not only disagreed about the sentence; some have changed their own positions on it, Benny Morris among them. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

Each side of this dispute has a serious case. Those who read the sentence as support for expulsion can point to its context: a letter welcoming partition as a stage, written in the same months in which Ben-Gurion's diary and letters weighed compulsory transfer as a possibility. Those who read it the other way rest on the handwritten original itself, arguing that the text does not say what the familiar quotation makes it say. This book does not resolve the sentence. The original wording is not reproduced in the sources available here, and without it no reader can judge between the readings. The dispute should be presented as a dispute.

What is not disputed is the movement's formal response. The Twentieth Zionist Congress met in Zurich in August 1937. It accepted partition in principle as a basis for negotiation, and it did not reject the transfer clause. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] The Congress's wider position on Peel, with its rejection of the proposed boundaries, is described in [scene:s07a6|the previous section]. Transfer was therefore a live subject at the highest level of the movement eleven years before 1948. The Arab Higher Committee rejected the Peel report outright, the transfer recommendation with the rest. [cite:wiki_peel_commission]

The word did not leave British politics either. In December 1944 the Labour Party's conference adopted a resolution on Palestine that again spoke of Arabs moving out as Jews moved in. That resolution, and what Labour did with it once in office, is told in [scene:rd4_labour|Labour and the end of the war].

The record leaves several things unsettled. The exact wording, and so the meaning, of Ben-Gurion's sentence to Amos remains disputed between historians. The sources here do not show how the Congress debated the transfer clause, only that it did not reject it. And the figures themselves differ slightly by source: about 225,000 and 1,250 in the report as cited here, about 200,000 and 1,000 in Yehudai. What is firm is that in 1937 a British royal commission proposed moving some 225,000 Arabs and about 1,250 Jews, by compulsion in the last resort, and that the Zionist Congress that met a month later did not reject the proposal.

sections.h: Partition Dropped: Woodhead and St James's Palace, 1938–1939
sections.html:
The Peel plan did not survive its first two years. Its publication in July 1937 had been followed, according to Unpacked and the Jewish Virtual Library, by the restart of the revolt in the autumn of 1937. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unpacked] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] The Arab Higher Committee had rejected the plan outright. The Twentieth Zionist Congress had rejected its boundaries while accepting partition in principle, and a United Nations paper later summed up the outcome as rejection by both sides. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_jvl_riots] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] London's next step was not to impose the plan but to test whether it could be carried out at all.

For that purpose Britain sent a technical commission under Sir John Woodhead. It had four members: Woodhead, Sir Alison Russell, Percival Waterfield and Thomas Reid. It investigated in Palestine from April to early August 1938. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead] Those were the months in which the revolt was building toward its peak, told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt]. The difference from Peel was one of mandate. Peel had been asked to investigate the causes of the revolt. Woodhead's commission, formally the Palestine Partition Commission, was asked a narrower practical question: whether partition could be made to work.

Its report, dated 9 November 1938, set out three boundary plans, labelled A, B and C. The commission preferred Plan C. It proposed that the two states remain in a customs union with the Mandatory government, and it questioned whether partition was economically and politically viable at all. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_ecf_woodhead] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead] Its conclusion was that no practical partition plan could be devised, because both Jews and Arabs refused partition. The British government accepted that conclusion. It found that partition was politically, administratively and financially impossible. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_woodhead]

The political ground is the one the commission spelled out: both communities refused partition. The economic doubt shows in the commission's own proposal, since a customs union with the Mandatory government would have kept the two states tied together after separation. The sources consulted here record these grounds, the three plans and the preference for Plan C. They do not give the population each plan would have placed in each state, and this book does not supply those figures.

Having dropped partition, Britain tried negotiation. It invited the Palestinian Arabs, the neighbouring Arab states and the Jewish Agency to a conference in London in early 1939, known as the St James's Palace conference. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] The exact dates on which it opened and closed rest on a single reference source and are not given here.

The delegations are documented by name, though from a reference source rather than the conference records. The Palestinian delegation was led by Jamal al-Husseini, a founding member of the Arab Higher Committee in 1936, and included Awni Abd al-Hadi, Musa al-Alami and others, with George Antonius as a secretary. Raghib al-Nashashibi joined two days after the opening. Egypt sent a delegation, as did Iraq, under its Prime Minister Nuri al-Said, and Saudi Arabia, under Prince Faisal. The Jewish Agency's delegation was led by Chaim Weizmann, with Ben-Gurion dominant in its decisions. It included non-Zionists and Rabbi Stephen Wise. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] Two features of these lists stand out. The Arab side came as a regional coalition, with three states represented alongside the Palestinians, a sign that Palestine had become a question for the surrounding governments as well. And the Palestinian delegation brought Husseini and Nashashibi figures together in one delegation, after the split described in the revolt section.

The conference never met as one. The Arab Higher Committee's delegation refused to sit with the Zionist delegation, so the British held separate meetings with each side. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] Britain was the only party that sat with both.

One strand of the talks went back to the First World War. An Anglo-Arab committee under the Lord Chancellor, Lord Maugham, examined the Hussein–McMahon correspondence of 1915–16. It found that the Arab case had been given too little weight. But the two sides on the committee could not agree on the central point: whether Palestine had been included in the British pledge of Arab independence. [cite:rs_rd4_pw_wiki_london1939] The finding mattered because of who chaired it. A committee under Britain's Lord Chancellor found that the Arab case had received too little weight. It did not settle the question on which that case rested.

The conference failed, and the British government said so in its own words. In the White Paper that followed, it recorded that after talks lasting several weeks, "Neither the Arab nor the Jewish delegation felt able to accept these proposals, and the conferences failed to reach an agreement." [cite:rs_rd4_pw_cojs_text] Britain then issued its own policy. That policy, the White Paper of May 1939, is the subject of [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper].

How to read this sequence is a matter of emphasis more than of fact. One reading stresses British retreat: having proposed partition, London dropped it within sixteen months, once the revolt reached its height and both communities had refused the plan. Another stresses that the refusals were real and mutual, as Woodhead's own conclusion and the 1949 United Nations paper both record. The documents support both. Britain's stated reason for abandoning partition was the refusal of both peoples, and the timing places that decision at the peak of the Arab revolt.

Some questions this record does not answer. The sources here do not name the British ministers who ran the London talks, nor give the conference's exact dates or the populations of the Woodhead plans. They do not record what the separate meetings with the Arab states' delegations discussed. They also do not show whether any version of partition was ever put to the conference. What they do show is the arc. In July 1937 Britain proposed partition. By November 1938 it had declared partition impossible. By the spring of 1939 it had failed to broker an agreement, and it set the country's course by a statement of policy of its own.

sections.h: "No One Wants Them": Évian, Bermuda and the Closing Doors
sections.html:
A common belief about the years before the Holocaust is that the world did what it could for Europe's Jewish refugees. Two conferences, five years apart, show how little that was. The first met in the summer of 1938, when the Nazi state was pushing Jews out of Germany and newly annexed Austria and the question was where they could go. The second met in the spring of 1943, when the question had become whether any of them could still be reached. Both ended the same way. And at both, the territory the Zionist movement regarded as the answer was kept off the table by the power that governed it.

President Roosevelt called the first meeting after Germany annexed Austria. Delegates of 32 countries met at Évian from 6 to 15 July 1938. [cite:wiki_evian] They spoke with sympathy, and almost all of them declined to take more refugees. Britain's delegate, Lord Winterton, said that the United Kingdom "is not a country of immigration." France said it had reached saturation. Brazil asked for certificates of Christian baptism. Canada wanted only experienced farmers. The United States offered only to fill its existing German–Austrian quota, which had gone unfilled in earlier years. [cite:wiki_evian] [cite:newhumanitarian_evian] [cite:facinghistory_evian] The American offer opened no new places. It promised to use places that the law already allowed and that had not been used.

One country made a large offer: the Dominican Republic, under the dictator Rafael Trujillo. The offer came from a regime whose soldiers had massacred thousands of Haitians the year before, in 1937. [cite:wiki_evian] The record here gives no figure for how many refugees the Dominican Republic proposed to take or how many it eventually received, and it does not set out Trujillo's reasons. It records only that the most generous answer at Évian came from a government that had just carried out a massacre.

Palestine was the one destination that a Jewish delegation could plausibly have pressed, and it was not discussed. At Britain's insistence, any mention of Palestine as a destination was excluded from the agenda. [cite:holocaust_au_evian] [cite:wiki_evian] Golda Meir attended as the Jewish observer from Palestine. She was not permitted to take part. [cite:holocaust_au_evian] The mechanism is plain in the record. Britain held the Mandate and therefore controlled entry to Palestine, and an international conference convened by the United States did not challenge that control. The sources here do not give Britain's stated reasons for the exclusion. What they show is the result: the conference was free to discuss any door except the one the Zionist movement was trying to open, and the power that held that door kept it shut.

The conference's failure was noticed in Germany. The Nazi party's newspaper summed it up in three words: "No one wants them." [cite:wiki_evian] Chaim Weizmann gave the Jewish side of the same conclusion. He told the Manchester Guardian that the world was now divided into two kinds of places for Jews: places where they could not live, and places they could not enter. [cite:wiki_evian] The two remarks came from opposite ends of the question and reached the same conclusion. Four months later the pogrom of November 1938 showed what remaining in Germany would mean ([scene:hol_s03|Kristallnacht]).

Five years later the Western powers met again, under far worse conditions. In April 1943, with the extermination of Europe's Jews under way, the United States and Britain held a conference on refugees in Bermuda. A program proposing that Britain open Palestine to refugees was put forward and was not considered. The conference produced little and was widely judged ineffective. [cite:usf_bermuda_evian] Palestine had been kept off the agenda at Évian in peacetime. At Bermuda, in the middle of the killing, it stayed off.

The two conferences matter to the story of 1948 in two ways, and both belong in the account. The first is the argument they handed the Zionist movement. When nearly every country refused, the case that Jews needed a place of their own, where no one could refuse them, gained force. It was no longer an abstract claim about national identity. A conference of 32 states had shown it in practice, and the Nazi press had said so in public. Much of what came after in this chapter rests on that demonstration: the clandestine ships ([scene:ab_s01|Aliyah Bet]), the American campaign for a Jewish commonwealth, and the argument that only a state could guarantee entry.

The second is where the decision lay. Britain, which kept Palestine off the agenda at Évian and off the table at Bermuda, held the one door the movement was pushing against. From 1938 the question of Jewish refugees could not be separated from the question of British policy in Palestine. Ten months after Évian, Britain set that policy out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of May 1939], and the clandestine ships of the following years sailed against its limits.

Some things are left open by the record gathered here. It does not list the positions of the other 26 countries at Évian. It does not give the Dominican offer in numbers or say how much of it was carried out. It does not say why Britain insisted on excluding Palestine, or who proposed opening Palestine at Bermuda and on what terms. What it does establish is narrow and firm. In July 1938, 32 countries were asked to take Jewish refugees and almost all declined. In April 1943, during the extermination, the proposal to open Palestine was not even considered.

sections.h: Britain Trained the Army That Would Fight It
sections.html:
The Jewish fighting force of 1948 is often remembered as self-made, built in defiance of Britain. Defiance is part of the record, and from 1945 it became the larger part. But the documents show something the familiar account leaves out. Between 1938 and 1945, much of that force's training, its fighting method and its future officers came through British channels. Britain opened those channels when it needed Jewish fighters, first against the Arab Revolt and then against the Axis, and closed them, sometimes with arrests, when the need passed. Three episodes show the pattern: Wingate's Special Night Squads in 1938, the Palmach in 1941 and the Jewish Brigade Group in 1944–45. Running beside them was a second story, of the money the Jewish community in Palestine raised to pay for its own defense.

The first channel opened in 1938, at the height of the Arab Revolt ([scene:s07a5|the revolt of 1936–1939]). Captain Orde Wingate was a British intelligence officer and a devout Christian restorationist who embraced the prophetic vision of a Jewish return to the land. He proposed a joint unit of British soldiers and Jewish supernumerary police drawn from the Haganah, the Jewish defense organization that Britain never officially recognized. The Jewish Agency eventually agreed. The Special Night Squads operated from Kibbutz Ein Harod from June to October 1938. About 75 Haganah volunteers served in them. Among them were Moshe Dayan and Yigal Allon, both future generals, and Pinchas Kopel, who later founded the Border Police. [cite:nli_wingate_hebrew] [cite:wiki_special_night_squads] [cite:israeled_wingate]

The arrangement shows how the Mandate's security system worked in that year. The Haganah had no legal standing. Its members could serve the government only by being enrolled in a form the government recognized, here as supernumerary police under British command. The initiative came from a British officer, the Jewish Agency's consent was needed to supply the men, and the unit existed for as long as the British authorities found it useful. It lasted five months.

What Wingate taught was a method: small units moving at night and raiding into Arab villages. Critics argue that the method outlasted him. The Israeli writer Uri Avnery traced a line of retaliation-raid doctrine from Wingate through the Palmach to the Israel Defense Forces. [cite:avnery_dayan_wingate] That is a critic's reading, not a settled finding, and the record gathered here does not test it against the army's own doctrine. It does show two things plainly. The men Wingate trained went on to command. And the squads were a British instrument against the Arab Revolt, staffed partly by Haganah volunteers, whose targets were Arab villages.

The same administration that sponsored the squads also prosecuted Haganah members caught training with arms. Dayan, one of Wingate's trainees, was imprisoned in 1939. [cite:archiveshub_wingate] [cite:avnery_dayan_wingate] The two facts fit one policy. Training under British command served British aims; training outside it led to arrest.

The second channel opened under the pressure of the world war. Facing a possible Axis breakthrough in North Africa, Britain cooperated with the Haganah in forming the Palmach in May 1941. After El Alamein, when the danger receded, so did British support. [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] The pattern was the same as in 1938: cooperation while the threat was acute, distance once it passed.

The third channel took longest to open. After long negotiation, the British Army announced a Jewish Brigade Group, formed in 1944. It fought the Germans in northern Italy in March 1945. [cite:wiki_zvi_brenner] [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] The record here says nothing more about the Brigade: not its strength, its casualties or the negotiations that produced it. Nor does it say how many Jews and Arabs from Palestine volunteered for the British forces during the war. Those numbers are not given here, and this book does not supply them from elsewhere.

British training was one input. The other was money raised inside the Jewish community. By 1939 the Jewish Agency's budget carried an £80,000 line for "security service (defense)" within a total of £720,000, about one-ninth of the whole. In 1938, the year of the Night Squads, the community created the Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund the Haganah. These are the first two steps of a funding chain that later ran through American donors and charity channels, a story told in full in [scene:gf_s02|the account of the pre-state army's budgets].

The two streams fit together. The Agency's budget and the levy paid for an organization that Britain did not recognize. Britain trained parts of it when British interests required, and it jailed members who trained outside British control. The result by 1947 was a force the Mandate had never legalized: about 10,000 mobilized men and 40,000 reservists, under officers many of whom had learned their trade in British service. [cite:wiki_haganah_mirror] From 1945 those cadres would turn against Britain itself.

How much the British contribution mattered, compared with what the Haganah built for itself, is a question of weight that the record here does not settle. It documents the channels, the dates and the men, but not a measure of how far the 1948 army's effectiveness came from Ein Harod, the Palmach or Italy rather than from its own training. The money record has a matching gap. No audited total of the Haganah's budget is publicly available. The levy and the 1939 budget line are documented individually, and no full account of the army's funding before 1948 can yet be added up from them.

sections.h: Aliyah Bet: The Clandestine Fleet
sections.html:
Postwar Jewish immigration to Palestine is often pictured as a flight of desperate refugees acting on their own. The passengers were desperate, and many of them were refugees in the strictest sense. But the ships that carried them were not spontaneous. From 1938 to 1948 they were organized, financed, crewed and routed by a network built for the purpose, run from within the institutions of the Jewish community in Palestine. Both things are true, and the history of Aliyah Bet only makes sense when they are held together.

Aliyah Bet means "immigration B." It was the name for the clandestine immigration of Jews to Palestine against the limits Britain set on legal entry. In 1938, the year of Évian, the Jewish leadership created the Mossad LeAliyah Bet as a branch of the Haganah to coordinate it. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:wiki_aliyah_bet] It did not hold a monopoly. Revisionist groups ran their own voyages separately. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] It was founded in the same year that 32 countries met at [scene:ev_s01|Évian] and almost all declined to take more Jewish refugees, while Britain kept Palestine off the agenda.

How the operation worked can be read from its parts. The Mossad LeAliyah Bet was an arm of the Haganah, the defense organization of the Jewish community, not an independent charity. It organized ships from Europe's ports, against a British limit on entry that the Royal Navy enforced at sea. The record gathered here does not break the voyages down year by year, and it does not detail the wartime sailings beyond their outcome. Two of the wartime ships, the Patria in 1940 and the Struma in 1942, ended in mass death and are told in [scene:s07b2|the ships the White Paper turned away].

After the war the operation changed in scale. With Britain's quota at about 18,000 a year, the clandestine route became the main one. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] The Brihah ("flight") network, run with Mossad emissaries, partisans and youth movements, moved nearly 200,000 survivors out of displaced-persons camps in Germany, Austria and Italy to ports in Italy, France, Yugoslavia and Greece. Zionist youth movements inside the camps supplied the passengers. [cite:hsb_aliyah_bet_exodus] [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] Ships, including a fleet bought and crewed largely by American volunteers, made about 142 voyages in all. More than 90 percent of them were intercepted by the Royal Navy. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:wiki_aliyah_bet]

Interception did not end the journey, and Britain needed somewhere to put the people it stopped. From August 1946 it interned intercepted immigrants in camps on Cyprus. By 1948 it held about 52,000 people there. The last camp closed in February 1949. [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] Cyprus was meant to deter. In July 1947 the Exodus 1947, carrying about 4,500 people, was boarded in international waters, and its passengers were sent back not to Cyprus but to camps in Germany. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum reads that decision as an admission that the Cyprus deterrent had failed. [cite:ushmm_cyprus_camps] [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] What the Exodus did to international opinion, and whether it moved the United Nations vote, belongs to the next stage and is set out, with both sides of the argument, in the account of the ships linked above.

By 1948 well over 100,000 people had come to Palestine this way, including more than 70,000 Holocaust survivors. [cite:ushmm_aliyah_bet] [cite:jvl_aliyah_bet] Set against the whole of Jewish immigration under the Mandate, that is a large share. Britain's own records count 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946. A separate estimate puts total Mandate-era immigration, legal and illegal together, at about 480,000. [cite:jvl_aliyah_bet] The two figures measure different things. The British count stops in 1946 and records the entries Britain registered. The larger estimate runs to the end of the Mandate and includes people who entered without Britain's leave. The gap between them is consistent with a clandestine movement of the size given above, but the record here does not reconcile the figures line by line, and the reader should not treat the difference as an exact count of illegal entries.

The two numbers on those panels also show how the population was changing. In Britain's 1922 census, 757,182 people were counted in Palestine. By UNSCOP's estimate in late 1946, the population was about 1.85 million. Immigration, legal and clandestine, was one of the forces behind that growth.

The question of what Aliyah Bet was has two answers, and both have evidence behind them. One is the passengers' story. They were survivors with nowhere else to go after the doors closed at Évian. The other is the organizers' story. The movement that carried them was an organized state-in-waiting, with its own intelligence service, logistics, fleet and recruitment, and every intercepted ship became a public argument against the Mandate. An account that keeps only the first misses the organization. An account that keeps only the second misses the people. The record supports both, and neither cancels the other. The youth movements that supplied the passengers in the camps and the Haganah branch that bought the ships were part of the same operation as the people on board.

Some questions remain open on this record. It does not say how the fleet was paid for, beyond noting that American volunteers bought and crewed much of it. It does not break down how many voyages or passengers fall before 1945 and how many after, or how many of the people who took the route were stopped and how many reached Palestine directly. It does not give the Revisionist voyages separately. Those are the next questions for research. What is established is the structure: a branch of the Haganah from 1938, a network from the camps to the ports after 1945, a British blockade that stopped most of the ships, and well over 100,000 people who came anyway.

sections.h: How Did They Get Here? Citizens, Ships and a Law of 1938
sections.html:
This chapter follows the Zionist movement's turn toward the United States, and a practical question comes with it. Who were the people running the American side of the movement, how did leaders from Palestine and Europe reach them, and under what law did any of it operate? A common assumption is that foreign agents entered the country in secret and worked outside the law. The record points the other way on almost every count.

The leaders of American Zionism were Americans. Louis Brandeis, Rabbi Stephen Wise and Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver were United States citizens, and their advocacy was the legal political activity of citizens. Some of the movement's figures from Palestine had American lives of their own. Golda Meir, then Golda Meyerson, grew up in Milwaukee and emigrated in 1921. She later became Israel's prime minister. [cite:w_golda] David Ben-Gurion, expelled from Ottoman Palestine, lived in New York from 1915 to 1918. There he recruited volunteers for the Jewish Legion, and there he married. [cite:w_bengurion]

Travel was by sea. Visiting leaders such as Chaim Weizmann crossed the Atlantic by ocean liner, as most travelers did. Regular transatlantic passenger flights began only in 1939, with Pan Am's flying boats. [cite:w_boeing314]

The legal frame changed in 1938. Before that year no American law required people working for foreign principals to register at all. Congress passed the Foreign Agents Registration Act in 1938. [cite:doj_fara] The gap before it is real and documented. Anyone who acted for a foreign principal before 1938 could not have been breaking a registration law, because none existed.

Whether the law applied, and to whom, became a real question only later. During the war the Bergson group was watched by the FBI, and that story is told in [scene:fa_s01|who Washington watched]. The first test of the act against the movement's main American apparatus came in 1962, with a Justice Department order to the American Zionist Council ([scene:s11a|the FARA order]). Both came after the law existed; before 1938 there was none to apply.

This short account leaves some things open. The record here does not say how often the visiting leaders crossed or who paid for their travel. It establishes three points: the movement's American leaders acted as citizens, its visiting leaders crossed by ocean liner, and a registration law existed only from 1938.

sections.h: Kristallnacht: The Turn to Open Violence
sections.html:
Four months after the Évian conference ended with almost no country willing to take Germany's Jews ([scene:ev_s01|Évian and Bermuda]), the German state showed what staying would mean. Over the night of 9–10 November 1938, synagogues burned and Jewish shops were smashed across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. More than 30,000 Jewish men were sent to concentration camps. The event marked the turn in Nazi policy from mainly legal persecution toward open, state-organized mass violence.

The familiar account holds that Kristallnacht was spontaneous popular outrage, a crowd reacting to the assassination of a diplomat. The record supports half of it. The killing that served as the pretext was real. The response was neither spontaneous nor simply popular.

The chain began with a deportation. Germany forcibly expelled Polish Jews living in the country to the Polish border town of Zbąszyń, where thousands of them were held in harsh conditions. Among them were the parents of Herschel Grynszpan, a 17-year-old German-born Polish Jew living in Paris. On 7 November 1938, after learning what had happened to his family, Grynszpan shot the German diplomat Ernst vom Rath at the German embassy in Paris. Vom Rath died of his wounds two days later, on 9 November. [cite:ushmm_kristallnacht] [cite:yadvashem_november_pogrom] Grynszpan's motive was personal and is documented: his own parents had just been deported and held at the border. Stating it does not justify or excuse the killing of a man. It records why the shots were fired, which is a different matter from what the German state then did with them.

What the state did was organize. Historians identify the propaganda minister, Josef Goebbels, as seeing in vom Rath's death the moment to unleash violence he had long advocated, and as using it to call for exactly that. [cite:wiki_kristallnacht] The pogrom that followed was coordinated across Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland within a 48-hour window. A crowd that rises on its own does not coordinate itself within hours across three countries and regions and strike more than a thousand synagogues at once. The scale and speed are themselves evidence of direction from above. That does not mean every participant was an agent of the state. Genuine popular participation in the violence is also documented. The point is about organization at the top, not a denial that ordinary people took part.

The physical scale gave the event its name. Over that night rioters destroyed more than 1,400 synagogues and prayer rooms across the three territories, burning or desecrating Torah scrolls and religious objects. About 7,500 Jewish-owned businesses were looted and destroyed. The glass that littered the streets afterward, from Berlin to Vienna, gave the night its German name, Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass. [cite:wiki_kristallnacht] [cite:jmberlin_november1938] The figures matter because they are specific. "Widespread destruction" is a phrase. More than 1,400 synagogues and about 7,500 businesses is a count that can be checked.

The human toll followed. More than 30,000 Jewish men were arrested and sent to concentration camps in Germany, Austria and the Sudetenland. The historian Nikolaus Wachsmann calls this "the first mass imprisonment of Jews in concentration camps solely because they were Jews." [cite:wiki_kristallnacht] The claim is precise. Anti-Jewish violence under the Nazi regime had come earlier, on a smaller scale. What was new in November 1938 was mass imprisonment in the camps of Jews as Jews. At least 91 Jews were murdered during the pogrom itself. Historians note that the true toll, counting deaths from mistreatment after arrest and suicides driven by the terror, reaches into the hundreds. [cite:wiki_kristallnacht] The record here gives the lower figure as a firm minimum and the higher one only as a range of "hundreds," without a count.

Then the state sent the bill to the victims. The regime held the German-Jewish community collectively responsible for the destruction and imposed a fine of $400 million at 1938 rates. [cite:history_kristallnacht] The mechanism inverted the ordinary logic of damages. Property destroyed in violence that the state had organized and tolerated was charged to the people whose property it was. The record here documents the fine and its size. It does not show how the fine was collected or what it did to individual families.

Exclusion went on alongside the violence. By the end of 1938 Jews were barred from schools and most public places in Germany. Abroad there was one documented official response of note. On 15 November 1938, President Franklin Roosevelt recalled the US ambassador to Germany in protest.

Kristallnacht belongs in a history of Palestine because of where it falls. It came four months after Évian had shown that almost no country would take Germany's Jews, and six months before Britain's White Paper of May 1939 set new limits on Jewish immigration to Palestine ([scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper]). In that half-year the danger to Jews in the Reich became open and violent, while the places they might go stayed closed or were narrowed. The pogrom also marks a stage in the Nazi record that runs from legal exclusion through open violence to the bureaucratic planning of murder, the next step of which was taken at [scene:hol_s04|Wannsee] in January 1942.

The record gathered here leaves some things unsettled. It does not give an exact death toll beyond the minimum of 91. It does not detail how the arrested men were treated or released, or how the $400 million fine was raised. And while it establishes direction from the top and documents popular participation, it does not measure the balance between the two. What it does establish is enough to set aside the familiar account. The pretext was a real shooting with a real personal cause. The pogrom was a state operation.

sections.h: What the Vatican's Authority Covered
sections.html:
The wartime record of the Catholic Church, taken up in the next section, is often argued over with a loose idea of what the Church could and could not do. A common assumption holds that the Vatican has, or claims, authority over Christian scripture and doctrine in general, Catholic and Protestant alike. It has not held such authority since the sixteenth century, and the limits of what it did hold are the frame for any fair reading of what it did between 1939 and 1945.

The Scofield Reference Bible shows the boundary plainly. Discussed elsewhere in this library as the document that did most to shape American Christian Zionism, it was never submitted to Rome for approval, and Rome was never in a position to demand its retraction. That was not an oversight on Rome's part. It follows from the structure of Church authority itself.

That authority is called the magisterium: the Church's teaching office, exercised through the Pope and the bishops. It binds Catholics, which in practice means Catholic doctrine, Catholic clergy and Catholic religious publications. It has never claimed, and has no mechanism to exercise, binding authority over people or institutions outside the Catholic Church. [cite:catholic_imprimatur_explained]

The instrument through which it governs what Catholics print is the imprimatur, Latin for "let it be printed." It is an approval process applied to Catholic religious publications specifically: catechisms, devotional works, and translations of scripture intended for Catholic use. Protestant publishers never sought it and never required it. Among them was Oxford University Press, which published the Scofield Bible.

The reason for the boundary lies in the Reformation. Its founding premise was the rejection of Rome's authority to bind the conscience of believers. The principle of sola scriptura held that scripture, not the Church hierarchy, was the final authority. Evangelical Protestants who read the Scofield Bible stood, by their own tradition's founding principle, entirely outside any claim Rome could make on their beliefs. To ask why the Vatican did not stop Scofield is a little like asking why one country's supreme court did not strike down another country's law. The jurisdiction was never there.

That answers the narrow question and sharpens a wider one. Authority to bind and the capacity to speak in public are two different things. The Vatican has routinely issued prominent public statements on subjects entirely outside its binding jurisdiction: climate policy, nuclear weapons, immigration law, and the birth-control policies of secular states. It exercises the second capacity constantly on matters where it has none of the first. [cite:wiki_pius_xii_holocaust]

So the fair question about Scofield is not why Rome failed to force a retraction; it never could have. It is why the Church, which by the account in this library's sources had already ruled against premillennial dispensationalism internally in the 1940s, did not use its considerable public voice to say so loudly, as it has on other questions equally outside its jurisdiction. The same distinction, between what the Church could command and what it could say, runs through the far graver wartime question of [scene:vat_s00b|Pius XII and the Holocaust].

This section is a frame, not a finding. It establishes the reach of the Church's formal authority and nothing more. It does not settle why the Church spoke on some subjects and kept quiet on others; the sources here state the distinction, not the motives behind any particular silence.

sections.h: Pius XII and the Holocaust: The Wartime Record
sections.html:
Eugenio Pacelli became Pope Pius XII in March 1939, six months before the war began, and he led the Catholic Church through the whole of the Holocaust. He came to the office with unusual knowledge of the regime he would face. He had served as the Vatican's Secretary of State and, before that, as nuncio to Germany, which gave him direct, personal experience of the Nazi state before the war began. [cite:wiki_pius_xii_holocaust]

His record is one of the most seriously contested questions in the history of the period, and this book does not pretend to resolve it. Two popular versions circulate. One holds that historians agree the Vatican did essentially nothing to help Jews. The other holds that Pius XII was a quiet hero whose actions saved hundreds of thousands. Neither matches the historians' actual debate. That debate rests on two sets of facts, each documented and each undisputed, which stand in real tension with each other.

The first is an absence. Pius XII never issued a public statement during the war that directly and explicitly condemned the Holocaust, or Nazi genocide, by name. [cite:vatican_1942_christmas_address] The closest he came was his Christmas radio address of 24 December 1942, which is the most cited single piece of evidence in the whole debate and deserves to be read closely rather than by reputation. In it he spoke of a vow humanity owed to bring society back to law, and to recognize the dignity of

the hundreds of thousands who, without any fault on their part, sometimes only because of their nationality or race, are marked down for death or gradual extinction.

The address did not mention Jews. It did not mention Germany or Nazism. It did not mention death camps, gas chambers or systematic genocide. [cite:vatican_1942_christmas_address]

How to read that obliqueness is itself in dispute. Historians working in the Vatican archives have documented that Vatican diplomatic staff at the time privately acknowledged that the address was intentionally indirect. It was understood inside the Vatican as a coded reference that informed listeners would recognize, while staying vague enough to avoid direct confrontation with Germany. Some historians take this as evidence of deliberate, calculated caution. Others hold that whatever the private intent, the address accomplished nothing meaningful. Pius XII never issued a more direct statement at any later point in the war, even as details of the systematic genocide were more thoroughly confirmed through Allied and other channels. That absence of escalation, as certainty grew, is a large part of why the question of motive remains open. [cite:vatican_1942_christmas_address]

The second set of facts is a presence. Substantial documented evidence shows Jews sheltered in convents, monasteries and Vatican-connected properties in Rome and elsewhere during the German occupation. Some historians, drawing on Vatican archives opened in 2020, argue that this reflected a real, if quiet, rescue effort, carried out with degrees of papal awareness and tacit approval, and some later archival researchers credit coordinated Church rescue networks with saving substantial numbers of lives. [cite:wiki_pius_xii_holocaust] What remains contested is how much of the sheltering reflected direct papal direction and how much was local clergy acting on their own.

Historians who study the question seriously offer several explanations for the public silence. They are not mutually exclusive. The first is fear: that an explicit condemnation would worsen the persecution, or provoke Nazi retaliation against Catholics and Church institutions. The second is diplomacy: a strategy of preserving the Vatican's neutrality so that it could help broker an eventual peace. The third is that the silence was a documented moral failure, whatever justification was offered for it. Each has a strong form. The case from fear rests on the possibility that a direct condemnation would have been answered by harsher persecution and by reprisals against the Church. The case from diplomacy rests on the documented private understanding that the 1942 address was meant to be read between the lines. The case for moral failure rests on the plain fact that the Pope's voice, which the Church used freely on other subjects, was never raised by name against the murder of the Jews, even as the evidence mounted. Serious historians remain divided among these readings, and this book does not choose among them.

A related claim holds that ancient noble families secretly controlled Vatican policy in this period and that hidden financial incentives drove the Church's silence. The documented financial background is narrower and more specific. Vatican finances had been close to bankruptcy before they were bolstered by the 1929 Lateran settlement with Mussolini's government, which compensated the Holy See for the loss of the Papal States in 1870. The settlement came to $92.1 million: 750 million lire in cash plus 1 billion lire in Italian government bonds. [cite:wiki_bernardino_nogara] The treaty was negotiated between Cardinal Secretary of State Pietro Gasparri and Mussolini's government, and Pope Pius XI was reportedly so pleased with it that he called Mussolini "the man sent by providence." The Pope's chosen envoy for the negotiations was Francesco Pacelli, the brother of Eugenio Pacelli, who ten years later became Pius XII. [cite:lateran_treaty_wiki] [cite:nybooks_pope_who_tried]

The money that resulted was managed by a named professional. Bernardino Nogara served as the Vatican's financial adviser from 1929 to 1954. Pius XI appointed him the first Director of the Special Administration of the Holy See, and Pius XII kept him in that post through the whole of the Holocaust period. [cite:wiki_bernardino_nogara]

These facts establish real context. The Vatican had recently received a large financial settlement from the same Italian state that later allied with Nazi Germany. The settlement was administered by an adviser kept on across the change of popes, and it had been negotiated in part by the future Pope's own brother. What they do not establish is a proven causal link between that financial history and Pius XII's public silence during the war. No primary source connects the 1929 settlement to the statements of 1939 to 1945, and historians offer the competing explanations set out above. Financial context and documented motive are different claims, and this book keeps them apart.

The question belongs in a history of the road to 1948 because it is one instance of a recurring pattern in the Vatican's dealings with this story: real, documented concern paired with limited direct public confrontation. The same shape appears later in the Holy See's long withholding of recognition of Israel, which ended in 1993, and in its response to Gaza in 2023–25. Whatever a reader concludes about Pius XII himself, the wartime record is that pattern tested at the highest possible stakes.

What the record does not settle is why Pius XII chose as he did, and how far the rescue in Rome was his own work. The absence of a public condemnation is not in dispute; neither is the sheltering. The weight to give each, and the motive behind the silence, remain open questions among historians, and the sources here do not close them.

sections.h: The White Paper of May 1939
sections.html:
Partition had been proposed in 1937 and abandoned by the end of 1938, and the London conference of early 1939 had ended without agreement (see [scene:rd4_woodhead|how partition was dropped]). Britain then set its own course. The result was a command paper, Palestine: Statement of Policy, Cmd 6019, dated 17 May 1939. Parliament approved the policy on 23 May. [cite:rs_rd4_wp_cojs_text] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_frus_d841] [cite:rs_rd4_wp_kramer]

The familiar account treats Israel's founding as the gradual fulfilment of the Balfour Declaration's promise, unfolding step by step from 1917 to 1948. The White Paper is the clearest evidence against that picture of a smooth path. In 1939 the power that had issued the Balfour Declaration and held the Mandate wrote down, in its own words, a policy that pointed in the other direction, and the men who led the Zionist movement read it as Britain reneging on Balfour entirely. [cite:whitepaper1939]

The text was direct on the central question. It declared that "it is not part of their policy that Palestine should become a Jewish State."
