The council pooled their resources for one purpose, domestic political influence, and ran them as one coordinated operation [cite:azec_powerbase]. Rabbi Abba Hillel Silver and Rabbi Stephen Wise were its first co-chairs [cite:azec_case]. Its importance outlasted its own years: through a documented line of succession, the council became the direct institutional predecessor of AIPAC [cite:azec_powerbase]. That later history belongs to other volumes of this library. What matters here is that the organization existed, and worked, during the war.

It came into being a little more than a year after the Biltmore conference of May 1942 had committed the movement to a "Jewish Commonwealth" in Palestine, and as another, rival campaign was already filling American newspapers with full-page advertisements: the Bergson group's committees, whose story is told in [scene:bg_s01|the Bergson group's campaign]. The council was the mainstream's answer, and its method was different. Where the Bergson committees bought space and staged pageants, the council built a standing national network that could be pointed at Congress on a given week.

Silver's break with quiet diplomacy. The two co-chairs did not share a view of how the work should be done. Silver argued for energetic public-opinion pressure and firm political mobilization. Earlier Zionist leaders had preferred a more cautious diplomatic approach, and Silver's course was an explicit and named departure from it, not a continuation of established practice [cite:azec_case]. Not everyone in the council or the wider movement agreed with the shift. The same period saw a comparable contest over method between Chaim Weizmann and David Ben-Gurion, told in the section on [scene:s07b|the Biltmore programme]. Inside the council the disagreement was serious enough that Silver resigned as co-chairman during a controversy in 1944–45 over how hard the organization should confront the American government; his own archived papers document the episode. He was later reinstated and led the council through 1949 [cite:azec_powerbase]. The internal conflict is part of the record, not a footnote to it.

The method, from the council's own files. The fullest account of how the council worked comes from its internal correspondence, preserved among the Abba Hillel Silver Papers at the American Jewish Archives. These are the organizers' own memos, and they describe a national method run from a New York headquarters at 342 Madison Avenue. Instructions went out to "Chairmen of Local Emergency Committees" in cities across the country [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

The first test came quickly. When Senators Robert Wagner and Robert Taft introduced their Palestine resolution in January 1944, a memo told the local chairmen that they would be sent sample letters, so that within a concentrated period letters from all over the country would "pour into Washington." The same instructions told local committees to interview their senators and representatives in person and to place letters to the editor in their local newspapers [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] [cite:aja_azec_local_1945]. The sequence below follows those instructions step by step.

Telegram campaigns were aimed at particular members by name. Among them was Representative Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]. The council also published a book, America and Palestine, and sent it to every member of Congress. It printed the pro-Zionist statements of nearly 400 members of the 78th Congress, so that each legislator could see in print the public commitments his own colleagues had already made [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation]. The book turned scattered statements into a visible majority, and it put each member on notice that his own words were on record.

The same machinery carried on after the war ended in Europe. In 1945, with Harry Truman now president, local councils mobilized thousands of telegrams to the White House. In Detroit alone, 150 Zionist and community leaders organized the appeal [cite:aja_azec_local_1945]. The council did not reserve its pressure for opponents. In 1948, after Bloom remarked that Truman was "on the right track" during the administration's retreat toward a trusteeship for Palestine, an AZEC staff memo called the remark "horrible" and urged that people in Bloom's district take it up with him [cite:aja_bloom_1948]. That episode lies beyond this chapter, but it shows the method fully formed: an ally who drifted was handled through his own constituents.

One further claim comes from a critic's history rather than from the council's papers, and it should be read as such. According to that account, mail addressed to Senator Wagner in his capacity as chairman of the American Palestine Committee was opened and kept at Zionist headquarters, and Wagner was sent a copy [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. The council's own files, as cited here, do not confirm or refute it. It remains a reported claim from a single critical source.

What the campaign achieved, and when. The results came fast. Silver's biographical record credits his lobbying in 1944 with securing a Palestine resolution in Congress, and in the same year both major parties wrote Palestine into their platforms [cite:azec_case]. The congressional record, set out in the next section, is more exact about what "passage" meant. The House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution on 30 November 1944; the full Congress deferred it that December, and a version was adopted only in December 1945 [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:frus1945_concres]. Both accounts agree on the substance: within roughly a year of its founding, the council had moved Palestine into the language of both parties and through a congressional committee, four years before there was a state. How those votes and platforms came about is told in [scene:us_s05|Palestine in Congress and the party platforms].

The money behind the movement. The council's files document a method, not a budget. They show organization: memos, sample letters, a book mailed to Congress, telegrams. They do not show money changing hands with legislators, and that is the finding the record supports. The money in the American movement during these years flowed through a different and far larger channel: philanthropic giving through the United Jewish Appeal.

The scale of that giving is set out in the library's funding ledger, drawing on Marc Lee Raphael's history of the United Jewish Appeal. In its first year, 1939, the appeal raised $14 million, about $324 million in 2025 dollars. Across the war years, 1939 to 1945, it raised more than $124 million, about $2.4 billion today. The ledger converts each sum using the federal consumer price index, and it carries one caution that matters for any reading of these figures. The campaign split its money three ways: relief for Jews in Europe, the Palestine programme, and the resettlement of refugees in the United States. Counting the whole sum as "funding Israel" would overstate what went to Palestine. The ledger's precise split is documented for 1948, when about half of the year's $150 million went to the Palestine arm, about 43% to relief in Europe and the rest to resettlement in the United States; for the war years the record here gives the three destinations but not the shares.

The second panel places the wartime giving on the longer curve. The war years averaged roughly $0.35 billion a year in today's dollars. After 1945 the totals rose steeply, to about $1.65 billion in 1946 and about $2.0 billion in 1948. The rise belongs to the next stage of the story. What the wartime figures show is a giving network that existed alongside, not inside, the political campaign the council ran. The appeal's money went to relief, the Palestine programme and resettlement; the council's work in Congress ran on letters, visits and telegrams.

Organized and sincere. The council's papers settle one question and leave another open. They settle that American political support for a Jewish commonwealth did not simply arise of its own accord. It was organized, timed and aimed, from a headquarters with a mailing list, against named members on named dates. They do not show that the sympathy behind the letters was manufactured. The letters were sincere, and the sympathy was real; the council's achievement was to organize both. That method, not money, is what the movement's own files document most fully. Both statements hold together, and neither cancels the other.

Two maps place the council within the larger structure. The first shows the two American machines of the 1940s, the Bergson committees and the council, side by side and moving toward Congress, the platforms and the White House. The second shows where the council fits in the half-century from the Basel Congress to the State of Israel: the "US political machine" between the Jewish Agency and the United Nations.

What the record does not settle. The council's files prove a sustained, organized campaign. They do not prove that the council alone set American policy toward Palestine. Truman's eventual decision to recognize Israel in 1948 had several causes, among them domestic electoral calculation and the competing objections of the State Department, and the council's five years of pressure were one factor among them, not the sole or sufficient explanation [cite:azec_powerbase]. Nor does the record here measure how many letters were drafted from the council's samples and how many were written unprompted, or how far any member's vote moved because of them. The papers show what the organizers did; they cannot show what each legislator would have done without them.

sections.h: Palestine in Congress and the Party Platforms, 1944–1945
sections.html:
It is often assumed that Congress and the two American parties took up Palestine only after the war, and then on its merits. The record of 1944 tells a different story. In that election year a resolution for a Jewish commonwealth went before both houses, the Army and the War Department asked Congress to shelve it, both parties wrote Palestine into their platforms for the first time, and the War Department dropped its objection days before the November vote. The State Department then held the resolution back again. A changed version passed only in December 1945. The story turns as much on the timing of these moves as on their content, and much of it can be read in the American Zionist Emergency Council's own records.

The longer frame. Congress had spoken on Palestine before. After President Wilson endorsed the Balfour Declaration in 1918, Congress passed the Lodge–Fish resolution unanimously in 1922, an episode told in an earlier chapter of this library. Over the following three decades its pattern held. Congress passed or pushed resolutions of support. It never voted to create a Jewish state or to recognize one: partition and recognition, when they came, were acts of the executive [cite:w_celler] [cite:w_sol_bloom]. Congress shaped the climate; the executive made the decisions. The resolutions of 1944–45 belong to that pattern.

The resolutions of January 1944. Early in 1944 two matching resolutions were introduced, each with one Democratic and one Republican sponsor. In the House they were Representatives James Wright, a Democrat of Pennsylvania, and Ranulf Compton, a Republican of Connecticut. In the Senate they were Robert Wagner, a Democrat of New York, and Robert Taft, a Republican of Ohio. Both called for unrestricted Jewish immigration to Palestine and for a "free and democratic Jewish commonwealth" [cite:djn_1944_hearings] [cite:aja_azec_dec1944]. Both demands ran against the British policy of the day, set out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of 1939]. The council's local committees began their first nationwide letter campaign the same month, as the previous section describes [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

The House Foreign Affairs Committee held hearings. Not every Jewish witness supported the resolution. Among the opponents was Rabbi Morris Lazaron, who told the committee that Zionism was an internal Jewish matter and not a question for Congress [cite:djn_1944_hearings]. His testimony is a reminder that American Jewish opinion in 1944 was not unanimous, and that some of the resistance came from inside the community the council claimed to speak for.

The generals ask for delay. In March 1944 the Army Chief of Staff, General George Marshall, and the Secretary of War, Henry Stimson, asked Congress to postpone action for military reasons. The committee deferred [cite:djn_1944_marshall]. The council's records describe the same step: Stimson opposed the Wagner–Taft resolution on military grounds, and it was put aside [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. The War Department's case was about the conduct of a war still being fought. The sources here do not set out its full reasoning. The State Department, for its part, had its own plan, approved inside the administration, to keep public discussion of Palestine quiet for the duration of the war; that plan and Roosevelt's two registers on Palestine are examined in [scene:s07c2|Roosevelt's wartime position].

"The first time in American history." Blocked in Congress, the issue moved to the parties. That summer both party conventions adopted Palestine planks. The council's own appraisal of the year called it "the first time in American history that Palestine was included in the party platforms" [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944]. For an organization founded only the previous August, this was a striking result. It meant that in a presidential election year Palestine had become a matter on which both parties had taken a public position, and on which their candidates could be held to account.

The objection withdrawn, days before the election. In October Stimson wrote to Senator Taft. According to the record of that letter, he told Taft that political considerations now outweighed military ones [cite:aja_silver_1944]. Days before the November election, the War Department had in effect withdrawn its objection [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. On 30 November, after the election, the House Foreign Affairs Committee approved the resolution [cite:aja_azec_dec1944]. Then, in December 1944, action was deferred again. The council's records attribute the deferral to the insistence of the State Department; another account describes it as a deferral at the administration's request [cite:aja_azec_dec1944] [cite:aja_silver_1944]. The setback prompted an internal crisis at the council [cite:aja_azec_1944_record]. Silver resigned as co-chairman during a 1944–45 controversy over how hard to press the government, as the previous section notes; the record here does not say whether that controversy and this crisis were one and the same.

December 1945: a different text. The resolution came back after the war, with Truman in the White House. On 17 and 19 December 1945 both houses adopted a concurrent resolution [cite:frus1945_concres]. It had the support of the American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine [cite:wiki_american_palestine_committee]. Its wording had changed, and the State Department noticed. A department memorandum observed that the resolution called not for a "Jewish commonwealth" but for a "democratic commonwealth in which all men, regardless of race or creed, shall have equal rights" [cite:frus1945_concres]. The phrase that had defined the 1944 text was gone.

Who carried it. The champions in Congress were named members of both parties. Wagner and Taft led in the Senate. In the House, Representative Emanuel Celler of Brooklyn and Sol Bloom, chairman of the Foreign Affairs Committee, were among the leading supporters [cite:w_celler] [cite:w_sol_bloom]. Bloom was also, as the council's own files show, a target of its telegram campaigns: the council pressed its allies as well as its opponents [cite:aja_azec_local_1944].

How the structure worked. The episode shows who held which lever. Members of Congress could introduce and approve resolutions, and the party conventions could adopt planks; both were open to organized constituent pressure, which is where the council concentrated its work. The War Department and the State Department could not vote, but they could ask committees to wait, and in 1944 they did so twice. The force of a resolution or a plank, as the council's own use of them shows, lay in putting members and parties on record. By 1944 Palestine had become a party-platform and election-timing issue, with the military and diplomatic bureaucracies on the other side. It is the same alignment the record shows again in Truman's decisions of 1947–48.

Reading the timing. The sequence invites two readings, and the record supports parts of each. One reads the year as the work of electoral politics: a resolution shelved on military grounds in March was cleared by the Secretary of War in a letter to a Republican senator days before a presidential election, after both parties had written the issue into their platforms. Stimson's own reported words, that political considerations now outweighed military ones, give this reading its strongest support [cite:aja_silver_1944]. The other reading takes the military objection at face value. The resolution came while the war was still being fought; Marshall and Stimson asked only for postponement, not rejection; and after the election the executive branch, through the State Department, again asked Congress to wait, which an administration acting only on electoral motives had no reason to do. The second deferral fits that reading better than the first.

What the record does not settle. The sources here do not show who asked Stimson to write to Taft, or what he weighed beyond the one sentence the record preserves. They do not give the vote counts of December 1945, or explain who changed the resolution's wording from "Jewish commonwealth" to "equal rights," and why. They do not say whether the 1945 text kept the 1944 call for unrestricted immigration. And they do not measure how far the council's letters, telegrams and visits moved any member's position, as against the views members already held. What they do show is that by the end of 1944, four years before statehood, Palestine had been placed inside American electoral politics by an organized campaign, and that the War and State Departments were already its main opponents inside the government.

sections.h: Roosevelt's Hidden Decline and the Choice of Truman, 1944
sections.html:
On 28 March 1944, seven months before the presidential election, a Navy cardiologist examined Franklin Roosevelt and found serious heart disease. The familiar account of the 1944 campaign treats the president's health as a private matter and the doubts raised about it as partisan exaggeration by his opponents. The medical record shows otherwise. The diagnosis was kept secret. Roosevelt's official physician told the public the opposite of what the cardiologist had found. A second doctor's written judgment that the president would probably not survive another term was locked in a vault for more than sixty years. And the man chosen that summer as Roosevelt's running mate, who would inherit the presidency and with it the American decisions on Palestine, was kept as uninformed as the voters.

The story belongs in a history of Palestine for one reason. The American commitments of these years, Roosevelt's private assurances to Arab leaders and the public promises of the 1944 platforms, would be carried out or broken by his successor. Who that successor would be was settled in the summer of 1944, by a party convention working without the medical facts.

The diagnosis. The examination took place at Bethesda. The cardiologist, Dr. Howard Bruenn, found acute congestive heart failure, an enlarged heart, hypertension and hypertensive heart disease. Bruenn was sworn to secrecy. He did not volunteer a prognosis even to Roosevelt himself, who, by the available account, asked no questions [cite:wiki_dying_president_ferrell]. One historian later wrote that the findings were guarded "on a level with the Manhattan Project." The comparison is striking, but it rests on a documented examination with specific findings, kept from public knowledge by design. What the record does not show is Roosevelt's own state of mind: that he asked no questions is documented; what he privately understood or suspected is not.

The public statement. Roosevelt's official physician since 1933 was Ross McIntire, an ear, nose and throat specialist with no training in cardiology. McIntire assured the press and the nation that the president was "in excellent condition for a man of his age" and that his health was "excellent in all respects" [cite:boston_globe_lahey_memo]. These were not vague reassurances or a difference of medical interpretation. They were specific, quoted public statements, and they contradicted the cardiologist's findings of the same period. The record documents the contradiction. It does not establish McIntire's motive, or exactly how much of Bruenn's findings he knew at the moment he spoke.

The Lahey memorandum. A second physician was consulted separately. Frank Lahey, a Boston surgeon, set down his conclusion in a written memo dated 10 July 1944: Roosevelt was unlikely to survive a full fourth term. The memo was placed in a Boston law firm's vault. It was not found and made public until decades after Roosevelt's death, more than sixty years after it was written [cite:boston_globe_lahey_memo]. The record establishes the memo's content, its date and its eventual disclosure. It does not establish who knew of it in the intervening decades.

Why the vice-presidency mattered. That same July the Democratic convention replaced the sitting vice-president, Henry Wallace, with Senator Harry Truman of Missouri [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] [cite:wiki_choosing_truman]. The reasons for Wallace's removal, and the question of whether Palestine had anything to do with it, are examined in [scene:s07c4|Henry Wallace and Zionism]. Set beside what Roosevelt's doctors knew, the choice of a running mate was in practice, though not in public understanding, the choice of the next president, and the voters who ratified it in November did not know that. The record draws a line here that should be kept. It does not show that every party leader involved in replacing Wallace knew the specifics of Bruenn's or Lahey's findings. Historical accounts document a general awareness among them that the president's health was declining and that this had political consequences, not knowledge of the diagnosis itself.

Why Truman. The documented reasons for choosing Truman were political. As chairman of the wartime Truman Committee, which investigated profiteering by defense contractors, he had earned real credibility and was ranked by 1944 among the most respected officials in Washington. He was acceptable to the labor unions and had supported the New Deal. But he had also opposed Roosevelt's earlier bid for a third term, which made him tolerable to the conservative Southern Democrats who distrusted Wallace's leftward tilt. Contemporary observers mocked the choice as "the Missouri Compromise," because Truman was no faction's first choice, only a candidate enough factions could accept [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:wiki_1944_dem_vp_selection] [cite:legalclarity_truman_1944_vp].

One complication in his background was real, and it was political. Truman's career had been launched by Tom Pendergast, the corrupt political boss of Kansas City, and party leaders had to work to establish that Truman was not "a Pendergast lackey" [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:legalclarity_truman_1944_vp]. The connection was discussed and had to be answered. A different theory is sometimes offered: that Truman was chosen because his personal finances or tax affairs left him open to pressure. No documented evidence connects his selection to his finances or to any tax matter [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] [cite:wiki_1944_dem_vp_selection]. On the record, Truman won the nomination by being broadly tolerable, not because anyone held something over him.

Truman kept in the dark. Several historical accounts describe the new vice-president as kept "entirely in the dark" about how ill Roosevelt was [cite:globalsecurity_fdr_veiled_decline]. The man about to inherit the presidency, and with it the American side of every decision on Palestine that this library follows through 1948, had no more medical information than the public. That claim has a limit. Public speculation about Roosevelt's appearance and vigor was itself widespread and documented, and the accounts do not say Truman had no sense at all that the president was failing. What they say is that he lacked the specific findings Bruenn and Lahey had made.

Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945, two months after his meeting with King Ibn Saud aboard the USS Quincy and a week after his written assurance to the king [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud]. That meeting and the letter that followed it are told in [scene:s07ca|the Great Bitter Lake meeting]. Their fate passed to a president who had not been told how soon he might have to keep, or break, them.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish the diagnosis, the public statements that contradicted it, the hidden memo and Truman's exclusion from the medical facts. They do not establish what Roosevelt himself believed about his prognosis, what McIntire knew when he spoke, or which party leaders, if any, knew the specific findings when they chose Truman. Nor can they say how the election, or the vice-presidential choice, would have gone had the voters known. Whether the course of American policy on Palestine would have differed under a healthier Roosevelt is a question this record cannot answer, and this book does not speculate on it.

sections.h: Henry Wallace and Zionism
sections.html:
In 1944 the Democratic Party replaced Vice President Henry Wallace on its ticket with Senator Harry Truman, the man who would become president within a year and who, in 1948, would recognize the state of Israel. Seen backwards from 1948, the swap invites a suspicion: that Wallace's views on Palestine had something to do with his removal. A version of the story circulates in which Zionist-aligned donors and organizations preferred Truman after Wallace said something unfavorable about Palestine or about Jews. The documented record answers the question directly, and at each point it runs the other way.

Start with Wallace himself. His interest in Zionism began in the 1930s, while he was serving as Roosevelt's Secretary of Agriculture, and it came through a working relationship rather than a political one. The soil scientist Walter Clay Lowdermilk had examined agricultural conditions in British Mandatory Palestine, and Wallace absorbed his enthusiasm. Wallace later recalled of Lowdermilk: "I don't think he has any Jewish blood, but he was the most complete Zionist convert anyone could ask for." Through that influence Wallace came to see the Jewish settlers in Palestine as frontiersmen on the American pattern. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] [cite:algemeiner_wallace_zionist] The point that matters for 1944 is the date. Wallace's sympathy was a personal conviction that he described in his own later recollection, and it predated the convention fight by roughly a decade. That fixes where the conviction came from. It does not prove that every later public statement he made on Palestine was free of political calculation, and the sources do not claim that it was.

Then the removal. Historical accounts state plainly that Roosevelt grew wary of Wallace's left-wing, pro-Soviet political tilt, and that this broader concern, not any statement about Palestine, Jews or Zionism, drove the push to replace him. [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] Nor was the decision quiet or uncontested. Wallace kept real support to the end. Labor organizations, including the CIO and the UAW, campaigned for him at the convention itself, and a Gallup poll taken on the day of the convention showed 65% of delegates still favoring Wallace over Truman. [cite:wiki_1944_dnc] That figure describes a contested, actively fought political battle over the general ideological direction of the party, with the man who lost it still the delegates' preference on the day. That is hard to square with the picture of a quiet substitution arranged to please one constituency.

Why the choice of running mate carried so much weight in 1944 is told in [scene:s07c3|Roosevelt's hidden decline]: the president's doctors knew how ill he was, the voters did not, and the vice-presidential slot was in practice a choice of the next president. The same section sets out the documented reasons Truman was chosen in Wallace's place. What concerns this section is narrower. The sources identify the general pattern historians treat as the main driver of Wallace's removal, and that pattern has no documented connection to Palestine or Zionism. They do not claim an exhaustive account of every reason every delegate or party official opposed him, and a minor factor cannot be ruled out from them. What they do show is that the Palestine explanation has no documentary basis, while the ideological one does.

Wallace did not leave the story in 1944. Four years later, running for president as the candidate of the Progressive Party, he returned to the Palestine question from the side opposite to the one the common assumption gives him. The events belong to the period after this chapter, and only their outline is needed here. His campaign literature included a booklet, Meet Henry Wallace, written by James Waterman Wise, the son of Rabbi Stephen Wise, the Zionist leader whose wartime dealings with Roosevelt run through this chapter. The booklet carried a half-page photograph of Wallace "helping the Jewish settlers in Galilee harvest their fields." At rallies Wallace accused Truman of "playing politics with the lives of the people of Israel," aiming directly at Truman's arms embargo on the newly declared state. That attack was the center of his appeal to Jewish voters. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] It was not the center of his campaign as a whole, which was built mainly on opposition to Cold War policy and support for continued engagement with the Soviet Union. Israel was one real, deliberate element of a broader platform, not its foundation.

The appeal had a measurable effect. New York newspapers reported widespread talk of Jewish voters leaving Truman for Wallace out of dissatisfaction with Truman's Palestine record, and the result was documented as the lowest share of the New York Jewish vote for any Democratic presidential candidate in modern history, except Jimmy Carter's. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist] [cite:algemeiner_wallace_zionist] The sources credit Truman's Palestine record as a contributing factor in that decline, not its only cause. Other parts of Wallace's campaign, and general dissatisfaction with Truman, likely contributed as well.

Put together, the record reverses the assumption twice. In 1944 Wallace was removed for reasons that had nothing documented to do with Palestine, and he was himself a long-standing sympathizer of the Zionist project. In 1948 he became one of Truman's most direct critics from the pro-Israel side, and that criticism cost Truman votes in New York. If the episode points to any electoral incentive, it points the opposite way from the one usually assumed: in the 1948 record it is being seen as insufficiently pro-Israel, not too closely tied to the cause, that carried a cost. That is an inference from one election in one state, and it should be held at that scope. [cite:aish_wallace_zionist]

Several things the record here does not settle. The sources give the New York result only as a ranking, not as a percentage, so the size of the shift cannot be stated from them. They do not separate how much of it came from the Palestine issue and how much from Wallace's wider campaign. And while they find no Palestine dimension to the 1944 decision, they do not record what, if anything, Wallace said in public about Palestine during his vice presidency. What is established is narrower and firmer: the belief that Wallace was pushed aside over Zionism has no documentary support, and the documents that exist point in the other direction.

sections.h: Roosevelt and Ibn Saud at Great Bitter Lake
sections.html:
On 14 February 1945, on his way home from the Yalta Conference, Franklin Roosevelt received King Abdulaziz Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia aboard the USS Quincy in the Great Bitter Lake on the Suez Canal. [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] [cite:wiki_uss_quincy_ca71] The meeting was not a courtesy stop fitted into a crowded itinerary. Roosevelt arranged it himself, two months before his death and visibly declining, immediately after one of the most demanding conferences of his presidency. Ibn Saud, the founding monarch of Saudi Arabia, who reigned from 1932 to 1953, rarely left Arabia and had deep reservations about the journey, yet he travelled by ship specifically for the encounter. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] Both men went to real, documented lengths to sit in the same room, and the principal subject between them was the future of Palestine.

Why an American president would make that effort has a plain answer in the record. By 1945 the Arabian American Oil Company, ARAMCO, had already established the core of the American–Saudi oil relationship. [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] The meeting reflected an existing, high-stakes strategic partnership that the United States government understood clearly, and the Palestine question was becoming entangled with it. The sources establish that the relationship existed and mattered; they do not set out the full scope of ARAMCO's operations or the specific terms of the oil relationship at this date, and nothing here should be read as a claim about them.

The meeting ran for roughly five hours by one account and five and a half by another, longer than most of Roosevelt's wartime sessions with other heads of state. [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] Roosevelt, a habitual chain-smoker, did not smoke throughout it, out of respect for the king's preference. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] Its official record is a memorandum of conversation drafted by William Eddy, the United States Minister to Saudi Arabia, and Yusuf Yassin, the Saudi Deputy Foreign Minister. Both leaders signed it, and the State Department later published it in its own documentary series, Foreign Relations of the United States. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] The memorandum is a summary agreed by both sides, not a transcript. No complete stenographic record of the conversation survives, so specific exchanges quoted from the meeting beyond what the memorandum and the later correspondence document should be treated with caution.

The substance was contested, not ceremonial. Roosevelt argued the case for Jewish settlement in Palestine: one account describes him arguing for a Jewish state, the memorandum-based account for a Jewish national home. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] Ibn Saud pressed back directly and forcefully, describing continued large-scale Jewish immigration as an existential threat to Arab interests in the region. When Roosevelt raised the question of Jewish immigration, the king answered that Jews displaced by Nazi persecution should be given land in Germany, "in the country of their enemies," as he reportedly put it, rather than in Palestine at the expense of its existing Arab population. [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote] In another rendering of the same exchange he proposed that the Jews be given a state in Bavaria. [cite:wiki_abdulaziz_saudi] [cite:brookings_quincy_75years] The exchange is well attested, but it is one moment in a five-hour conversation and does not capture the whole of the king's position.

What Roosevelt gave the king was a specific assurance. The United States government, he said, would make no decision altering the basic situation in Palestine without full, prior consultation with both Arabs and Jews, and would take no action hostile to the Arab people. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] He came away pleased. He later called the meeting "so outstanding a success," and told his daughter Anna that he had "learned more about the whole problem of Palestine and the Middle East by talking with Ibn Saud for five minutes than I could have learned in an exchange of two or three dozen letters." [cite:brookings_quincy_75years]

The king did not leave it at a spoken promise. About three weeks after the meeting he wrote formally to Roosevelt, asking him to oppose continued Jewish settlement in Palestine. [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote] Roosevelt answered on 5 April 1945, one week before his death. In that letter he affirmed that he would "take no action, in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch of this Government, which might prove hostile to the Arab people." [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud] The letter reaffirmed in writing the commitment made aboard the Quincy, which closes any gap between an informal verbal impression and a deliberate written undertaking by the president himself. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] One account describes Roosevelt as taking the king's concerns seriously enough to respond in writing more than once in the weeks after the meeting; the letter of 5 April is the one whose words the sources quote. The wording also limits the promise: it is given in Roosevelt's own capacity as head of the executive branch. Whether such a letter was an isolated gesture or part of a pattern is taken up in [scene:s07c2|Roosevelt's actual position on Zionism], which shows that the State Department, when it confirmed the letter in October 1945, described it as one of several such letters to Arab leaders.

Roosevelt died on 12 April 1945. On 14 May 1948 his successor, Harry Truman, recognized the state of Israel eleven minutes after its declaration, without the prior consultation with Arab leaders that Roosevelt had promised. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] One account traces the recognition decision through Clark Clifford's domestic electoral calculation rather than through consultation with Arab heads of state; that process belongs to the next stage of this history and is told there. The change between the two presidents is documented. What the documents do not show is Truman's own state of mind about Roosevelt's specific commitment: whether he was personally aware of it, considered himself bound by it, or set out to break it. That he knew of it is a reasonable inference from the continuity of the presidency, but it is an inference, not a finding.

The meeting answers two common assumptions. The first is that American support for a Jewish state ran consistently and without a break from Roosevelt to Truman. The record shows a president who, two months before his death, gave the Arab head of state most affected a direct assurance, spoken and then written, that the United States would not act on Palestine without consulting the Arabs, and a successor who acted without that consultation three years later. The second is that Saudi opposition to a Jewish state in Palestine is a modern political position with no deep roots. The king's objection is on the record in February 1945, in a memorandum both leaders signed and in his own letter three weeks later, more than three years before the state existed. [cite:quincy_meeting_1945] [cite:ibn_saud_bavaria_quote]

How to read the gap between promise and outcome is where accounts part. One reading calls it a promise made and not kept: a deliberate commitment by a sitting president, in his own words, to the affected head of state, followed by an action that ignored it. A second, more cautious reading, taken by the account built on the memorandum, records the 1945 letter and the 1948 recognition as standing in direct and unresolved tension, and declines to adjudicate between them. [cite:fdr_letter_ibnsaud] The second reading has the stronger documentary footing on one point: the promise was Roosevelt's, made "in my capacity as Chief of the Executive Branch," and nothing in these sources shows that it bound his successor. The first has the stronger footing on another: the commitment was specific, written and repeated, and the later decision was taken without the consultation it described.

What the record cannot settle is what Roosevelt himself would have done. He died before the partition vote or the recognition decision came before him, and no evidence exists of how he would have weighed his promise to Ibn Saud against the domestic pressures his successor faced. Nor does any complete transcript allow the meeting's exchanges to be reconstructed word for word. This history documents the promise and the later departure from it, and stops there.

sections.h: Labour and Palestine, 1939–1945
sections.html:
In July 1945 Clement Attlee became Prime Minister at the head of a Labour government. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] On Palestine, Labour came to office with a record, going back six years, of opposing the policy it now inherited, and with a conference resolution, adopted seven months earlier, that went much further than anything a British government had proposed. Whether that record would become policy was a question American diplomats were already weighing by the end of the month.

The record began in May 1939. In the House of Commons debate of 22–23 May on the White Paper, whose terms and reception are set out in [scene:rd4_white_paper|the White Paper of 1939], Attlee voted against the policy, and so did Hugh Dalton. Herbert Morrison told the House that the government should not adopt a policy "as to which grave doubt exists as to its consistency with the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] [cite:rs_rd4_lab_jvl_debate] Labour members argued in 1939 that the White Paper's limits on immigration and on land transfers were "contrary to the terms of the Mandate." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] This was a legal argument as well as a political one: the objection was not only that the policy was unwise but that Britain, as the mandatory power, had no right under the Mandate to adopt it. Of the three men named here, one was Prime Minister by July 1945.

In December 1944, with the war not yet over, the party's annual conference adopted a resolution on Palestine. It held that there was no case for a Jewish national home "unless we are prepared to let Jews, if they wish, enter this tiny land in such numbers as to become a majority." It went on: "Let the Arabs be encouraged to move out, as the Jews move in." And it proposed re-examining "the possibility of extending the present Palestinian boundaries." [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] Each clause cut against the White Paper. The White Paper had capped Jewish immigration and made further entry after five years depend on Arab acquiescence; the resolution called for immigration on a scale to produce a Jewish majority. The White Paper had promised an independent Palestine state within ten years; the resolution spoke of moving the existing population and redrawing the frontier.

The phrase about Arabs moving out did not appear from nowhere. Seven years earlier, in July 1937, the Peel Commission's report had recommended an "exchange of population" on the model of the 1923 Greek–Turkish exchange, compulsory in the last resort, the first official British document to put transfer in writing; that proposal and the Zionist movement's response to it are told in [scene:pl_s01|Peel's "exchange of population"]. [cite:wiki_peel_commission] The Labour resolution differed in its language: it spoke of Arabs being "encouraged" to move, not compelled, and it was a party conference's statement, not a royal commission's recommendation to the government. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] But it shows that the idea of moving Palestine's Arab population, first put on paper by a British commission in 1937, was still being written into the programme of a major British party in 1944, now as a call from the side most sympathetic to Zionism.

The sources here record the resolution's words as quoted in an American diplomatic memorandum. They do not include its full text from Labour's own records, the debate that preceded it, who moved it, or how Zionist, Arab or British officials responded to it at the time. What the resolution meant to those who voted for it, and how seriously its authors intended the passage on the Arab population, therefore cannot be settled from this record.

What the new government was likely to do was assessed in Washington by the end of July. A memorandum signed by William Yale of the State Department's Division of Near Eastern Affairs, dated 30 July 1945 and prepared for the Potsdam conference, set out the Labour government's probable Palestine policy. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale] Yale recorded that Labour leaders, Labour members of Parliament and the major trade unions "have consistently given their support to the Balfour Declaration," and he recalled the party's arguments of 1939 that the White Paper's limits were contrary to the Mandate. But he did not expect the conference resolution to become policy. His forecast was that the Labour government would not try to implement it, and would instead "modify or repeal the White Paper policy of 1939," above all on immigration, since the remaining quota would soon be exhausted. He also expected the government to consult the Soviet and American governments before deciding Palestine's future status. [cite:rs_rd4_lab_frus_yale]

The distance between the two columns is the mechanism this section turns on. A party conference could adopt a resolution; only a government could change the policy of the mandatory power, and a government answered to considerations a conference did not have to weigh. Yale's reading was that the Labour government would act on the part of its record that was narrow and legal, its objection to the White Paper's immigration limits, and would leave aside the part that called for moving a population and redrawing borders. He also read the decision as one Britain would no longer take alone: the future status of Palestine, in his forecast, would be settled only after consulting the Soviet and American governments.

The memorandum is a forecast, not an outcome. Whether the Labour government modified the White Paper, how it handled immigration once the quota ran out, and how its relations with Washington over Palestine developed belong to the postwar period and are told in the next stage of this history. What this record establishes is the starting point: a party pledged by its own words in 1939 and 1944 against the White Paper, and an American diplomat predicting in July 1945 that it would keep the first pledge in a modified form and not the second.

Much of the British side of these years is not documented in the sources used here. They do not name the Colonial Secretaries who served during the war, the High Commissioners who governed Palestine on Britain's behalf, or the deliberations of the wartime cabinet on Palestine's future, and they do not cover the appointment of the Labour government's Foreign Secretary. Who governed Palestine for Britain during the war, and how that government's thinking moved between 1939 and 1945, is therefore a question this chapter cannot yet answer.

chapters.label: Stage Five
chapters.title: Execute
chapters.intro:
In the summer of 1945 the war in Europe was over, and the full scale of the Holocaust was becoming documented and public. [cite:sonneborn_toi] Palestine was still a British Mandate, and Britain had a new government: Clement Attlee formed his Labour cabinet on 26 July 1945, with Ernest Bevin as Foreign Secretary. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] In Washington, Harry Truman had been President since 12 April, when Franklin Roosevelt died one week after putting in writing his assurance to Ibn Saud that nothing would be done hostile to the Arabs without consultation. Truman had been Vice President for eighty-two days and arrived with no foreign-policy experience. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The Arab League, founded that March, stood for a "unitary and independent Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The Palestinian Arabs had no functioning leadership body of their own, and the man who would lead them, Hajj Amin al-Husayni, was being held in France. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] In New York, David Ben-Gurion had already reached a judgment of his own: that the Arab states would go to war, and that the Haganah had neither the weapons nor the money to survive it. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

Three years later the Mandate was gone, a Jewish state had been proclaimed and recognized, and most of the Arab population of the territory it came to hold had fled or been driven out. This stage asks how that happened in so short a time: who decided each step, through what instrument, with whose money and whose arms, and who objected. It asks with equal weight what the Palestinian Arab leadership and the Arab states chose to do, and what they were unable to do. The answer is not one decision but a chain of them, taken in London, Washington, Lake Success, Cairo, Amman, Prague and Tel Aviv, and it ends in a war that produced, in the same months, a state for one people and what the other calls the Nakba, the "catastrophe."

The cast is the widest of any stage. In London stood Bevin, Attlee and the Colonial Secretary Arthur Creech Jones. In Washington the President's political advisers, Clark Clifford and David Niles, and his old business partner Eddie Jacobson, faced the Secretary of State George Marshall, the State Department's Loy Henderson and Robert Lovett, the Defense Secretary James Forrestal, the Joint Chiefs and a newly created CIA. The Jewish Agency worked through Ben-Gurion, Chaim Weizmann, Moshe Shertok and Golda Meyerson, and through American supporters such as Rudolf Sonneborn, Henry Montor and Abba Hillel Silver; the Irgun under Menachem Begin, and Lehi, fought on their own account. On the Arab side were the Arab Higher Committee under the Mufti and Jamal Husseini, the commanders Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni and Fawzi al-Qawuqji, the Arab League, and King Abdullah of Transjordan with his British-officered Arab Legion. Andrei Gromyko spoke for Moscow. Dissenters, among them the American Council for Judaism, Judah Magnes and Hannah Arendt, objected throughout and were outweighed.

The sections follow the chain roughly in the order it was forged. They begin with the change of president and the men around him, Truman's own recorded words, and the July 1945 meeting in [scene:s07d|Sonneborn's apartment] that founded an arms network on American soil. Bevin's policy, the Anglo-American Committee and the Jewish armed campaign of 1945–46 lead to Operation Agatha and the King David Hotel. The Jewish Agency's early turn to partition, the White House's inner channels and Britain's decision to hand Palestine to the United Nations set the stage for the Soviet turn, the UN special committee, the written warnings of State, the Pentagon and the CIA, and the dissenters at home. Resolution 181 is followed by the Arab League's control of Palestinian decision-making, the civil war that began on 1 December 1947, the violence against Jews in Arab cities, and the money and arms of early 1948. Plan Dalet, Washington's retreat to trusteeship, Deir Yassin, the fall of the mixed towns and Abdullah's double course lead to independence and the Nakba, recognition, the Arab states' war and [scene:s10b|the actual military balance]. The stage closes with the making of one army and with [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugees], whose return the new government had refused by June 1948.
chapters.outro:
By the end of 1948 the structure that had governed Palestine since 1922 was gone, and what replaced it had been built in three years by different hands, each holding something the others did not.

The legal layer was thinner than it looked. Resolution 181, adopted on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13 with 10 abstaining, recommended two states, an economic union and an international Jerusalem, on a timetable that ran to 1 October 1948; Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen said they regarded it as a recommendation and would not be bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Britain, which had abstained, declined in September 1947 to impose any policy "by force of arms," so the plan's handover had no one to carry it out. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones] The Declaration of 14 May 1948 rested the state on "natural and historic right" and on three international instruments, promised equal rights "irrespective of religion, race or sex," stated no borders, and set a constitution deadline of 1 October 1948 that passed without one. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Recognition came by executive act: American de facto recognition eleven minutes after the proclamation, Soviet de jure recognition on 17 May, American de jure recognition on 31 January 1949, Britain's in January 1949. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] Resolution 194 of December 1948 affirmed a right of return that was never implemented. [cite:morris_1948]

The administrative layer was the most complete, because most of it already existed. The Jewish Agency's institutions became a government's. The order of 26 May 1948 made the Israel Defense Forces the only lawful armed force; the shelling of the Altalena on 22 June and the arrests after Lehi killed Count Bernadotte on 17 September enforced it, and an amnesty in February 1949 released those arrested. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination]

The financial layer was private and transnational. The Sonneborn network bought and smuggled material from 1945, some 800 shipments and about 2,400 tons, while the FBI recommended prosecutions the Justice Department declined. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] [cite:forward_oss] Golda Meyerson's tour was reported to have raised $50 million in about two months, spent largely on weapons. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] The library's funding ledger puts the 1948 United Jewish Appeal at a record $150 million, of which $74.7 million went to the Palestine share. Czechoslovakia sold arms with Soviet consent for almost $14.5 million by its own foreign minister's figure, though estimates run to about $90 million. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] Against this stood an American embargo and a British bill of about £100 million for its forces in 1945–47.

The Palestinian Arab layer was the weakest, and the record shows both choices and constraints. The Arab Higher Committee was re-established in 1946 "by a decision of the Arab League," its chairman the Mufti, who had spent the war allied with the Axis and led from Cairo. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] It boycotted UNSCOP, rejected partition, and promised a "line of fire and blood." [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] In February 1948 the League refused it a government-in-exile and a loan; its Army of the Holy War and the League's Arab Liberation Army did not cooperate. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] By the end of the year two bodies claimed to speak for Palestinians, a government in Gaza and a congress at Jericho, and on the UN's technical estimate about 711,000 had become refugees. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] As early as June 1948 Israel's cabinet had reached a consensus against their return. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

The regional layer was a coalition of states with different ends. The League's cablegram of 15 May spoke of restoring "law and order" and of a "United State of Palestine"; Lebanon chose war deliberately, Saudi Arabia sent a contingent under Egyptian command, and the Arab Legion, on the Office of the Historian's account, entered only areas assigned to the Arab state or Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] [cite:lebanon_1948_war] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The armistices of 1949 left Egypt in Gaza and Jordan on the West Bank, with about 78 per cent of Mandate Palestine under Israeli control. [cite:morris_1948] In Arab cities the vote set off riots against Jews, and the governments of Egypt and Iraq followed with arrests, sequestrations and, in Iraq, a law against Zionism. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951]

The American layer was a government divided against itself. Henderson, the Joint Chiefs, Forrestal and the CIA warned in writing; the President's political advisers prevailed; the delegation retreated to trusteeship on 19 March and was still arguing for it when the President recognized the state. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] [cite:cia_ore55] [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin] [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

What was settled was the existence of the state, its army and the lines its army held. What was contested was nearly everything about how. Zionist leaders could point to a UN plan they accepted, a rejection announced as a "line of fire and blood," and a Declaration that offered Arab citizens equality; Palestinian leaders and their historians to a plan that gave a majority of the land to a community owning under a tenth of it, to a vote taken without them, and, in Khalidi's reading, to a displacement written into Plan Dalet's village clause. Whether that plan was a design for removal or a military plan whose expulsions were decided locally remains argued between Morris and Khalidi. So are Truman's motive, Abdullah's understanding with the Agency, and how far the insurgency drove Britain out. The record also leaves things open: a refugee count that runs from about 520,000 to 957,000 depending on who counted and how, Arab war dead not compiled in these sources, and Deir Yassin's archives still partly closed. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] Above all it leaves the refugees themselves, outside the lines and refused return, the question [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194] inherited.

sections.h: FDR Dies, Truman Chooses
sections.html:
The American decision on Israel was made by a president whom almost no one, three years earlier, had expected to be making it. The story of that decision therefore begins not in 1948, and not even in 1945, but at the Democratic convention in Chicago in 1944.

Henry Wallace had served as Franklin Roosevelt's Vice President since 1941. He was a progressive in the full sense of the word in his time: pro-labor, anti-imperialist and anti-colonial, an early and forceful advocate of civil rights well ahead of the American political mainstream, and a supporter of accommodation rather than confrontation with the Soviet Union. To the Democratic Party's conservative and machine wings he was unacceptable. At the 1944 convention, with an ailing Roosevelt unlikely to survive another term, the party bosses maneuvered Wallace off the ticket and replaced him with a compromise choice, the little-known senator from Missouri, Harry Truman. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman] [cite:trumanlibrary_missouri_compromise] Wallace went on to run for president on the Progressive Party ticket in 1948, lost badly, and died in 1965. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman] The fuller account of his removal, including the reasons behind it and Wallace's own Zionist sympathies, belongs to an earlier part of this book; what matters here is the single substitution and its timing.

Roosevelt himself had one more Middle Eastern act left. In February 1945, aboard the USS Quincy in the Suez Canal, he met King Ibn Saud of Saudi Arabia and gave assurances that no action would be taken hostile to the Arab people without consultation. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] A letter of 5 April, whose words the sources quote, put the assurance in writing. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] One week later, on 12 April 1945, Roosevelt, born in 1882, died at Warm Springs, Georgia, less than three months into his new term and before any of the postwar decisions on Palestine had to be made. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud] That meeting and that letter are told in full in [scene:s07ca|FDR and Ibn Saud]. Their place in this chapter is only their timing: the president who had given the assurance did not live to be tested by it.

What Roosevelt would have done had he lived cannot be known, and this book does not pretend to know it. The record shows the promise and the date of the death, side by side, and nothing more. [cite:arabnews_fdr_ibnsaud]

One interpretive reading, and it is a reading rather than a documented finding, draws a larger lesson from the 1944 convention. On this reading, but for the convention maneuver, Henry Wallace and not Harry Truman would have become president in April 1945, and the 1948 recognition of Israel, along with the opening of the Cold War, might have unfolded very differently. The reading uses Wallace to mark the contingency of the whole story: an American commitment to Israel that is often narrated as destiny turned, at its origin, on a party back-room and a single substitution, so that "FDR dies, Truman chooses" became the operative sequence only because the machine had already chosen Truman over Wallace four years before recognition. The reading's own limit should be stated as plainly as its claim. Wallace's dated removal is documented; what Wallace would have decided about recognition had he been president is not, and no record can supply it. The counterfactual is untestable, and it is offered here as a way of seeing the period, not as a conclusion about it. [cite:wiki_choosing_truman]

Truman, born in 1884, a Missouri Democrat and a former haberdasher turned senator, had been Vice President for eighty-two days when Roosevelt died. He arrived in the presidency with no prior foreign-policy experience and minimal briefing on the major foreign questions then pending. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Over the next three years he would make the single decision on which this chapter's American story turns, and he would make it with a recurring cast around him. That cast is set out here, because its members reappear, in one combination or another, at each American turning point between 1945 and 1948.

The first is Clark Clifford (1906–1998), White House Special Counsel. In November 1947 Clifford sent Truman a memo arguing that the Jewish-American vote was likely decisive in several key swing states, New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, for Truman's uncertain reelection prospects in 1948, and framing early and unambiguous recognition of a Jewish state as electorally advantageous. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] This is not a reconstruction by later historians from indirect evidence. Clifford's own memoir, Counsel to the President, published in 1991, openly describes this domestic-political framework as part of the advice he actually gave Truman, and acknowledges both Marshall's opposition and the argument between the two men. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] It is a rare case of a key adviser putting his own strategic reasoning on the record, after the fact, in his own words, and it is the strongest single document behind the reading that electoral politics drove the timing of recognition. A related document appears in another source: a November 1947 memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews," which analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election. [cite:jvl_truman_index] The sources used here do not say whether that title and Clifford's memo are one document or two.

The second figure is the man who objected to Clifford most strongly. George Marshall, Secretary of State, architect of the strategy that won the war in Europe and of the Marshall Plan, was one of the most prestigious figures in postwar American public life. He told Truman directly: "If you follow Clifford's advice and if I were to vote in the election, I would vote against you." [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] He threatened to resign. Because his standing was so uniquely high, his opposition was politically dangerous to the President. Truman recognized Israel anyway, and Marshall did not resign. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Marshall's decision not to carry out the threat is itself part of the documented record; it does not show that his broader relationship with Truman was permanently damaged.

Behind Marshall stood the third element of the cast, the professional State Department. Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Marshall himself opposed early recognition. Their argument was cold strategic realism: recognizing a Jewish state would damage American relations with the Arab world, jeopardize access to Middle Eastern oil at the opening of the Cold War, and possibly require American troops to enforce partition. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The written warnings they and others filed in the autumn of 1947 belong to a later section of this chapter. The pattern they form is the point here, and it is a pattern this book meets again: the permanent foreign-service establishment judged support for the Zionist program to be against American strategic interest, and the elected political leadership overruled it. Not every career diplomat held an identical view; what is on record is the opposition of these named senior officials.

The fourth figure entered by a door that no organization chart shows. Eddie Jacobson, an American Jew from Kansas City, was Truman's old army comrade and his former partner in a men's clothing store, Truman & Jacobson, which went bankrupt in the early 1920s; Jacobson had been best man at Truman's wedding and remained one of his most trusted friends. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] By March 1948 Truman, worn down by Zionist lobbying, had refused to see Chaim Weizmann through official channels. Jacobson went to the Oval Office and, invoking their friendship and Truman's admiration for the aging Zionist leader, persuaded the President to receive Weizmann privately. That meeting, on 18 March 1948, is documented in multiple biographies and in Truman's own recollections, and historians widely credit it with securing Truman's commitment to recognition. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] Jacobson's documented contribution is that one meeting; the record does not give him a broader coordinating role in the recognition decision.

The meeting with Weizmann had an immediate and awkward sequel. The very next day the American delegation at the United Nations announced a retreat from partition toward a temporary trusteeship, and the collision between what the President had told Weizmann in private and what his diplomats said in public is the subject of [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat in March 1948].

The end of this American arc can be stated briefly here and told in full later. On 14 May 1948, at 6:11 p.m. Washington time, eleven minutes after David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in Tel Aviv, the United States extended de facto recognition. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The speed caught the State Department off guard. It also caught the American delegation at the United Nations, which was at that moment still working the floor for a trusteeship proposal, an alternative to statehood, and learned from the news that its own government had recognized the new state. By the account in the sources used here, Clifford orchestrated the timing, and Marshall's professionals were overruled without being forewarned. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] De jure recognition followed only in January 1949, after Truman's election victory. The Soviet Union, pursuing its own aim of pushing Britain out of the Middle East, extended full de jure recognition first, in May 1948. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The constitutional basis of the President's power to act alone, and the comparison with other governments, are taken up in [scene:rec_s01|who recognizes a nation].

Why did Truman do it? The scene this section draws on gives a pointed answer. On its reading, the recognition was primarily a domestic political calculation for the 1948 election, orchestrated by Clifford: Marshall threatened to resign, the State Department opposed, and the President's personal channel to Zionist leadership ran through his former business partner. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] Eleven minutes, on this reading, is not the interval of a deliberative foreign-policy consensus; it is the interval of a decision executed for maximum effect by a president facing a hard election. Truman's own memoir later presented the recognition as principled, and Clifford's memoir and Marshall's documented opposition tell a different story. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The case is strengthened by Clifford's own admission, which is first-person evidence and not inference.

The familiar account holds the opposite: that Truman recognized Israel out of moral conviction. That account has evidence too, and the strongest form of it rests on Truman's own words. As a senator in 1943, years before any recognition question or any campaign money, he spoke at a mass rally for Europe's Jews, as the next section shows. In February 1947 he publicly called the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading," and said his position had been consistent since 1945. [cite:jvl_truman_feb1947] The same documents that show Clifford's arithmetic also show that Truman was pressed by Zionist lobbying to the point of refusing to see Weizmann, and that it took a friend's personal appeal, not a political operative's, to change his mind about that meeting. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel]

The evidence on both sides does not resolve into a single cause, and the sources this section draws on say as much themselves. Clifford's memo documents one real and significant thread in the decision; it does not show that electoral calculation was the only factor, or that humanitarian and strategic considerations played no part. Multiple motives existing together is the more accurate picture than any single-cause explanation. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] What the record does show, specifically, is a president with little foreign-policy grounding moving faster than his own government's formal machinery, guided partly through a personal relationship outside normal channels, against the explicit, documented objection of his Secretary of State. That was not a uniquely corrupt way for foreign policy to be made; personal relationships and domestic pressure shape presidential decisions in many administrations and on many issues. It was, however, plainly not the product of careful interagency deliberation reaching a clean consensus. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The cast also answers a different and more corrosive question, one the record settles more firmly than the question of motive. Accounts of 1948 as a hidden-hand operation, in which an organized interest secretly controlled American policy, cannot accommodate the documents. A plot that controls a government does not have that government's Secretary of State, its Near Eastern division and its oil-strategic establishment fighting it openly in signed memoranda, as Marshall and Henderson did. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Nor was Jacobson a secret agent; he was the opposite. His role shows the actual texture of the decision: friendship, fatigue, sentiment and access, one old friend reaching a tired president while the professional foreign service advised the other way. To readers inclined to conspiracy he looks like proof of hidden influence; on the record he is proof of something more ordinary, that a haberdasher's personal loyalty could move a president when the State Department could not, and that the channel was a friendship documented in biographies, not a secret. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] What 1948 shows, in this reading of the evidence, is convergence and contingency: a president's political judgment prevailing over his own experts, not coordinated control.

What remains open is the weight of each motive in Truman's own mind. The record establishes the sequence: the 1944 substitution, the April 1945 death, the November 1947 memo, Marshall's threat, the 18 March meeting, the eleven minutes. It establishes who argued what. It does not establish which argument decided the President, and no document yet found does. Nor can it say what Roosevelt, or Wallace, would have done in Truman's place; those questions are counterfactuals, and they stay open by their nature.

sections.h: Truman in His Own Words, 1943–1948
sections.html:
Harry Truman is often remembered as a lifelong and uncomplicated champion of a Jewish state. The record of what he himself said and did between 1943 and May 1948, before any campaign money of the 1948 election entered the story, does not support so simple a picture, and it does not support the opposite picture either. It shows a public conviction, a frank awareness of voters, and a private irritation at the pressure he was under, all in the same man and in the same years. This section sets out those words in order, and identifies each for what it is: a public speech, an official record, a single witness's later account, a private diary.

The first item comes from Truman's years in the Senate. In April 1943, before he was Vice President and long before any decision about Palestine was his to make, Senator Truman spoke at a mass rally in Chicago Stadium urging help for Europe's Jews. According to David McCullough's biography, he said that under "mad Hitler" they were being "herded like animals" into camps. [cite:csm_truman_diary_2003] Whatever weight one gives later political motives, this was said by a senator with no Palestine policy of his own to defend, and it is the earliest documented evidence for the humanitarian side of his outlook.

The second item is the most often quoted and the most carefully to be handled. On 10 November 1945, seven months into his presidency, Truman met his chiefs of mission from the Arab world. The meeting itself is in the State Department's official record. [cite:frus_1945_chiefs_mission] The words most often attributed to him there are not. They come from William Eddy, the American minister to Saudi Arabia, who attended and who wrote, in a pamphlet published in 1954, that Truman had told the diplomats: "I'm sorry, gentlemen, but I have to answer to hundreds of thousands who are anxious for the success of Zionism; I do not have hundreds of thousands of Arabs among my constituents." The historian John Judis has quoted Eddy's account. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_globe] Three cautions apply to it, and all three should be kept in view. It rests on a single witness. It was written down nine years after the meeting. And Eddy was himself a State Department opponent of Zionism, so his account comes from a witness with a settled view of the policy under discussion. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_globe] None of that proves the quotation false; Eddy was in the room. It does mean that the remark, however vivid, cannot carry the weight of an official record, and a careful reader should treat it as one participant's recollection of what was said.

The third item is public and dated. On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the midterm elections, Truman issued a statement urging immediate large-scale immigration to Palestine and saying the United States could support a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine." [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] The statement, the advisers around it and the argument over its timing are the subject of [scene:wh_s01|inside the White House]; here it marks the point at which a president's stated sympathy and an election calendar first visibly coincided.

The fourth item was never meant to be read by anyone else. On 21 July 1947, after Henry Morgenthau telephoned him about the refugees aboard the ship Exodus, Truman wrote in his private diary: "The Jews, I find are very, very selfish." He added that once underdogs gain power, "neither Hitler nor Stalin has anything on them for cruelty." [cite:jvl_truman_diary_1947] [cite:aljazeera_truman_diary] The diary was found at the Truman Library and released by the National Archives in 2003. [cite:cbs_truman_diary] [cite:csm_truman_diary_2003] The entry should be named for what it is. It is a sweeping judgment about Jews as a people, written by a sitting president in anger at a particular telephone call, and it is antisemitic in the plain sense of the word. It is also private, written by the same man who had spoken at the Chicago rally four years earlier and who would recognize Israel ten months later. The entry is evidence of how the pressure felt to him; it is not, by itself, evidence of what his policy would be, and ten months later he recognized the Jewish state.

The fifth group of items brings the record to the decision itself. In November 1947 a memo to Truman titled "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews" analyzed the Jewish vote for the coming election. [cite:jvl_truman_index] In March 1948, after refusing to see Zionist leaders, he met Chaim Weizmann at the urging of his old business partner Eddie Jacobson. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] On 14 May 1948 he granted de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, against the opposition of Secretary of State George Marshall. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] Four days later, on 18 May 1948, he described American Jews as "very emotional." The people around those decisions, Clifford, Marshall and Jacobson among them, are introduced in [scene:s08|the preceding section].

Read together, these items resist every single-motive story. Those who see Truman as a man of principle can point to the 1943 rally, given years before any Palestine decision was his, and to a recognition decision he took against the most respected member of his own cabinet. Those who see electoral calculation can point to Eddy's account, to the Yom Kippur timing and to the November 1947 memo on the Jewish vote. Those who see reluctance can point to the diary, to his refusal to see Zionist leaders until a friend intervened, and to the "very emotional" remark days after recognition. Each reading is built from real documents. None of them accounts for all of the documents.

The fairest summary of the record is that humanitarian conviction, open awareness of voters and private resentment of the pressure all appear in it, in the same man and in the same years, before any 1948 campaign money had changed hands. The record shows that all three were present. It does not show which of them decided the outcome, and this book does not claim to know. The remark attributed to him in November 1945, which would bear most directly on that question, is the one item that rests on a single witness who opposed the policy it describes.

sections.h: The Meeting in Sonneborn's Apartment, July 1945
sections.html:
A common account of Israel's founding war holds that its weapons arrived only after May 1948, once the state existed and could ask the world for help. The documents place the start of the supply effort almost three years earlier, in a private apartment in Manhattan, in the summer that the war in Europe ended.

By July 1945 the fighting in Europe was over, and the full scale of the Holocaust was becoming documented and public.
