David Ben-Gurion, chairman of the Jewish Agency Executive and the de facto head of the Yishuv, the Jewish community of Palestine, had travelled from Palestine to New York with a specific purpose. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] His assessment, made three years before independence and not in response to any declared war, was that the Arab states would go to war against the Jews of Palestine, and that the Haganah, the Yishuv's underground defense force, had neither the weapons nor the money to survive such a war. [cite:sonneborn_toi] He needed a supply and financing pipeline in America, and it was a task he could not ask the Jewish Agency to carry out openly. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

The meeting took place in the Manhattan apartment of Rudolf Sonneborn, a wealthy New York industrialist and scion of an oil-and-chemical business, who had travelled to Palestine himself and formed a friendship with Ben-Gurion. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The sources differ slightly on who called it. One account has Ben-Gurion convening the meeting; another has Sonneborn convening it at Ben-Gurion's request. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two are compatible: the request was Ben-Gurion's, the room and the guest list Sonneborn's. The man who gathered the guests was Henry Montor, who by 1948 was executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal, a connection that would matter again in 1948 when the same Montor arranged Golda Meyerson's appeal to the American federations, told in [scene:us_s07|Golda Meyerson's American tour]. [cite:jta_golda_1948]

The sources also differ on the date and the number present, in small but real ways. One account dates the meeting to 1 July 1945; another says only that it took place on a July afternoon. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] [cite:sonneborn_toi] Accounts describe roughly seventeen prominent Jewish businessmen in the room. [cite:sonneborn_toi] One account gives seventeen American businessmen in one place and seventeen Americans and one Canadian in another. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] Ben-Gurion warned them of the coming war and of the Haganah's poverty, and the men in the room, moved, by later accounts, by the warning together with the recent revelation of the Holocaust's scale, agreed that same afternoon to build what became a Jewish-American arms underground. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

How much weight that last detail can bear needs saying. Firsthand descriptions of the meeting, including Leonard Slater's 1970 book The Pledge, were written decades afterwards, sympathetically, by an author who interviewed participants long after the fact. [cite:sonneborn_toi] The meeting itself, its date, its convener and the organization that came out of it are well documented. Any single participant's stated motives, recorded a quarter-century later, deserve the caution owed to any retrospective account. The record also does not show that every donor or participant fully understood, at the time, that the network would be operating illegally. [cite:sonneborn_toi]

What emerged from the meeting was the Sonneborn Institute, a network that became the financial and logistical backbone of the Haganah's transatlantic supply effort. [cite:sonneborn_jps] [cite:ampalestine_haganah] It was not a fundraising drive in the ordinary sense. It was the operating base of an armed procurement effort that ran for three years outside any registered or public channel, and by one account continuously until 1949. [cite:sonneborn_toi] Ben-Gurion directed its formation; the day-to-day American procurement work was run by Sonneborn and a small operational circle. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] Sonneborn received no formal recognition for his part beyond a private letter of thanks from Ben-Gurion after Israel was founded. [cite:sdjw_winters]

The network worked through a front company, and here the sources disagree on its name. One historical account calls it Materials for Palestine; another calls it Materials for Israel. [cite:sonneborn_jps] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] They also describe its cover somewhat differently. In one account it operated under the guise of an ordinary commercial and charitable enterprise, providing cover for buying and shipping machinery, tools and industrial materials, legally purchasable surplus, destined for Ta'as, the Yishuv's clandestine arms-production effort. [cite:sonneborn_jps] In the other, the network operated under the legal cover of a charity for European Jewish relief, raising funds and moving industrial equipment, machine tools and eventually munitions toward Haganah forces in Palestine. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two descriptions are not contradictory so much as describing different stages: the first stresses the legal machinery bought for production inside Palestine, the second the move toward finished munitions as the war drew closer.

The methods are documented end to end. Donors gave money for which no receipts were issued. The front company bought under its commercial or charitable cover. Shipments moved under falsified manifests and disguised invoices, routed through Panama, Mexico, Czechoslovakia, Canada and France to evade American export controls, and arrived with Haganah forces in Palestine. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] By the time the United States formally tightened arms-export enforcement under the Neutrality Act in December 1947, the network already had two years of working tradecraft in place. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The scale it reached, about 2,400 tons in some 800 consignments by one count, and the routes, aircraft and trials of its working years are told in [scene:s07e|the arms network in operation]. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

The structure was designed around one legal fact. What the network did was, under American law, illegal arms export, and the people who built it arranged matters so that the official Jewish Agency would not be directly exposed. Historians who have documented the network note that it was kept deliberately separate from the Agency, and that this compartmentalization was a choice, not an accident of organization. [cite:sonneborn_jps] They also note that the separation was not total. Abba Hillel Silver, chairman of the Jewish Agency's American section, served as a liaison between the two. [cite:sonneborn_jps] The record therefore shows both things at once: a structure built to insulate the Agency, and a named senior figure connecting it to the Agency anyway. It does not show that the Agency was unaware of what the network did, nor does it give an account of what each Agency official individually knew.

Where the money came from, and how much there was, is less well recorded than how it moved. Donors were issued no receipts. The sources give no total for what the Sonneborn circle raised or spent, and no ledger of individual shipments or transactions. [cite:sonneborn_jps] The panel below places the network in the longer sequence of channels that paid for the Yishuv's defense, from the Jewish Agency's own budget and a community levy of the 1930s to the American appeals of 1948.

That sequence matters because the Sonneborn network sat in the middle of it, and because the same people moved along it. Montor's role in both the 1945 meeting and the 1948 appeal shows that the arms network and the open federation-and-appeal fundraising overlapped directly through named individuals. [cite:jta_golda_1948] Among the network's key financiers was Abraham Feinberg, who met repeatedly with Sonneborn and later founded Americans for Haganah. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] In 1952 the United States government would order him to register as a foreign agent, a later chapter of his story told in [scene:s07f2|Abraham Feinberg]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The procurement network had an intelligence counterpart. The first Jewish intelligence organization in Palestine had been established under the Haganah in 1929, and the Shai (Sherut Yediot, the Information Service) was set up in 1940 as the Haganah's intelligence and counter-espionage arm. [cite:shai_wiki] By 1948, according to the account this book draws on, the Shai had 68 staff, 60 British and Jewish agents and 80 Arab agents, and spent nearly $700,000 a year. Its stated objectives were to promote an independent Israeli state, to infiltrate British Mandate offices, to collect intelligence for propaganda, to penetrate Arab factions, and to secure the Rekhesh arms-smuggling operations. It had American branches, Zionist networks in New York and Detroit that served as procurement and intelligence points, and these were not registered under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. [cite:shai_wiki] [cite:ips_espionage] After 1948 the Shai became the seed from which Israeli military intelligence grew, and its American networks formed the early North American foundation of the Mossad. [cite:shai_wiki]

Rekhesh, Hebrew for "acquisitions," was the Haganah's arms and munitions procurement branch in the United States in the mid-1940s. It built an extensive illegal procurement network despite the arms embargo on the Palestine region. Its operations were funded by American Jewish donors and involved buying surplus military equipment from demobilized United States Army stocks and from black-market dealers, then smuggling it out through covert shipping routes, often with the help of organized crime to get around export controls. [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:medium_zionist] The account this book draws on describes the networks as violating both American export law and the British arms embargo. [cite:forward_oss]

The federal government knew. The FBI documented these operations and repeatedly recommended that key figures be prosecuted or required to register as foreign agents; the Justice Department declined each time. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] One case shows the pattern in detail. The attorney William Bernstein, according to the FBI, trained Mossad agents, incorporated companies that smuggled arms for Zionist groups, and conducted surveillance of Arab delegates at the United Nations; the Bureau linked him to sophisticated technical surveillance of Arab officials and to break-ins at consular offices. The Justice Department declined every FBI recommendation that Bernstein be prosecuted or made to register. [cite:ips_espionage] [cite:medium_zionist] The enforcement record, set side by side, is uneven rather than empty. Federal agencies, the FBI and Customs among them, were aware of the network while it operated. No prosecution of its top organizers, Sonneborn or Feinberg, is documented. At least one participant, Winters, was convicted and sentenced to eighteen months and a $5,000 fine. And the operation was not shut down before the 1948 war ended; it continued through the conflict. [cite:mexico_arms_1948]

A second government agency was watching from a different angle. During the war the Office of Strategic Services, the predecessor of the CIA, ran a Palestinian Desk in its Foreign Nationalities Branch that tracked Zionist activity in the United States. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] A 2016 review of declassified documents by the Forward found that much of its information came from Jewish officials, some highly placed in Jewish organizations, who volunteered it as a wartime patriotic duty and not under coercion. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] Its target list reportedly included Moshe Shertok, later Moshe Sharett, Israel's second prime minister. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk] The desk built a picture of which American Jewish leaders were aligned with which Zionist factions; it took no action against the Rekhesh procurement networks. [cite:forward_oss] The two agencies should not be merged into a single "intelligence community." The OSS's wartime foreign-intelligence interest and the FBI's domestic-security interest had separate rationales and separate reporting chains, and they are documented independently. [cite:forward_oss_palestine_desk]

Why the Justice Department declined is the question on which the sources divide. One account, built on FBI records reported by the Forward and on later analysis, argues that the non-enforcement was deliberate and political: the Truman administration was moving toward support for Jewish statehood, and prosecuting the future state's arms networks, or requiring its American political organizations to register as foreign agents, would have been incompatible with that course. On this reading the decision not to enforce was a foreign-policy decision in the form of prosecutorial discretion, and it set a precedent, never reversed, that later shaped pro-Israel lobbying in the United States; the same account traces it to 1963, when Isaiah Kenen, himself formerly registered as a foreign agent, moved the lobbying function from the American Zionist Council to the newly created AIPAC. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] [cite:ips_espionage] The same sources, in their own accounting, mark the central link as contested. That the FBI recommended prosecution or registration, that the Justice Department declined, and that the procurement operations broke American law are, in their judgment, documented. Whether the Justice Department acted on explicit direction from the Truman White House, or exercised its own discretion, is not established. [cite:forward_oss] The reading of a fixed political will also has to account for the rest of the record of these years: the same administration's State Department opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, as the opening section of this chapter shows, so "the government" did not speak with one voice on Palestine.

The case for the network, as its founders and sympathetic historians put it, also deserves its strongest form. In July 1945 Ben-Gurion expected a war that he believed the Haganah could not survive without weapons it did not have, and a British arms embargo stood between it and the means to get them. On that view the procurement effort was the preparation of a community's defense, organized by American donors who had just learned the full scale of the Holocaust. [cite:sonneborn_toi] [cite:forward_oss] The case against it, as stated in the sources critical of it, is that it was a foreign-directed intelligence and arms operation on American soil that broke American law and was allowed to continue because of whom it served. [cite:forward_oss] [cite:medium_zionist] Both cases rest on the same documented facts: the meeting, the front company, the deliberate separation from the Agency, the false paperwork, and the decisions not to prosecute.

What the record leaves unsettled is substantial. It does not give the total sums raised or spent, or a ledger of shipments. It does not establish what each donor understood about the law when he gave. It records the name of the front company two different ways. It does not show whether the Justice Department's restraint came from the White House or from its own discretion. And by the sources' own account, the full extent of Zionist intelligence operations on American soil in the 1940s is only partly documented, with part of the record still classified. [cite:forward_oss] What it does establish is the starting point: a working, financed, deliberately compartmented supply network on American soil from 1945, three years before the state it was built to arm.

sections.h: Ernest Bevin and the Palestine Question, 1945–1946
sections.html:
A new British government came to office in the summer of 1945. Clement Attlee formed his Labour government on 26 July 1945 and chose Ernest Bevin as Foreign Secretary. Bevin had been born on 9 March 1881; he would die on 14 April 1951. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] Over the next eighteen months his statements set the terms of British policy on Palestine, and his name became attached to it, by the Zionist leaders who fought him, by the Americans who pressed him, and by the historians who have tried to explain him.

His reputation in this story is unusually divided. To many Zionists of the period, and to some of his own colleagues, he was a man who disliked Jews. To his biographer and to Attlee, he was an opponent of a Jewish state, not an enemy of Jews. To a third school, his policy followed from what the Foreign Office took to be Britain's interests in the Middle East, and his personal feelings mattered little. All three readings rest on documents. Before weighing them, it helps to set out what Bevin actually said and did in his first eighteen months.

The general reference works are sparing. Britannica's entry on Bevin offers only one judgement on Palestine: that his plans of 1947–48 "for a federal Jewish-Arab nation or other partition of Palestine collapsed" in the face of the Arab-Israeli conflict. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] The detail lies in his own statements, in American diplomatic reports, and in the scholarship that has tried to explain him.

The statement of 13 November 1945. Bevin's first major act on Palestine came on 13 November 1945. He announced a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship," Until it reported, he said, there would be "no interruption of Jewish immigration at the present monthly rate." The text did not state what that rate was. Looking further ahead, he spoke of a trusteeship agreement that would "supersede the existing mandate." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] The statement also set out the terms in which London saw the problem. Bevin referred to the Palestinian Arabs' "90,000,000 co-religionists in India," and he said that Palestine "does not by itself provide sufficient opportunity" for solving the Jewish problem. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] Read together, the two phrases framed Palestine as one part of an answer for Europe's Jews, not the whole of it, and placed the Arabs of Palestine within a far larger population whose opinion London had to weigh.

The committee itself, its twelve members, its hearings and its report are the subject of [scene:aac_s01|the next section]. What matters here is that the inquiry was Bevin's chosen instrument. It brought Washington into the question, and in the interim it left immigration where it stood.

The same day, Bevin spoke privately to the American ambassador in London, John Winant. Winant's telegram, received in Washington on 14 November 1945, reported that Bevin said he would be willing to "stake his political future on finding solution for Palestine problem," and that he "made a plea against approaching this subject in spirit of racial antagonism." [cite:rs_rd5_frus_winant_1945] The telegram is a primary American record, not Bevin's own text, but it shows how he wished to be understood by the government he most needed to persuade: as a minister who had staked his career on a settlement and who wanted the question kept out of racial politics.

His public words that day did not always match that wish. According to the historian Raphael Langham, Bevin told the House of Commons on 13 November, "We cannot accept the view that the Jews should be driven out of Europe." At a press conference the same day, he warned that if Jews "want to get too much at the head of the queue" there was a danger of an antisemitic reaction. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The first sentence stated a principle: the survivors had a future in Europe and should not be treated as people to be removed from it. The second turned the survivors' claims into the cause of the hostility they might meet. Langham calls the remark "unfortunate." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

"Too many Jews in New York." The pressure Bevin resisted came above all from the United States, where President Truman was pressing for the admission of Jewish refugees to Palestine. At the Labour Party conference in June 1946, Bevin said of that pressure that "They did not want too many Jews in New York." Langham calls it "a gratuitous sneer." It angered Truman and provoked protests in the United States. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The remark was an antisemitic jibe from a sitting Foreign Secretary. It suggested that American support for Jewish immigration to Palestine was a way of keeping Jews out of America, and it was made at a party conference, in public. Whatever conclusion one reaches about Bevin's policy, the sentence itself needs no softening.

The London conference and the American visit. In September 1946 Britain convened a conference at Lancaster House in London. According to Langham, Bevin told the Arab delegation there that no solution could ignore Jewish claims. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] This sits awkwardly beside the remarks above, and that is part of what makes him hard to read: the same minister who sneered at American motives told the Arab states that Jewish claims had to be part of any settlement. Two months later he travelled to the United States, in November and December 1946. During that visit, Langham writes, Bevin reportedly came to the view that Britain would have to give up the Mandate. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The decision itself, taken in February 1947, belongs to [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain's exit], the subject of a later section.

The mechanism. In these months Bevin held the levers that mattered for Palestine: the rate of Jewish immigration, the choice of forum, and the timing of any settlement. The November 1945 statement used each one. It kept immigration at the existing rate rather than opening the gates or closing them, it moved the question into a joint inquiry with the United States, and it pointed toward trusteeship rather than either a Jewish or an Arab state. The parties most affected could not set any of these terms. The Jewish Agency and the Arab representatives could put their cases to the inquiry but could not decide; and Washington, though it pressed hard on immigration, did not govern Palestine. What Bevin could not control was the American response, and his June 1946 remark shows how much that pressure grated.

The dispute over his motives. Why did Bevin oppose a Jewish state? Historians have given three answers, and Langham sets them out side by side. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012]

The first answer is personal hostility. Two contemporaries who dealt with him said so plainly. Christopher Mayhew said that "Ernest detests Jews," and Chaim Weizmann said Bevin was "blinded by his hatred of the Jews." The historian Peter Weiler takes a more careful line: he finds that Bevin "held antisemitic views" but sees "no evidence that they shaped his policy." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is the remarks themselves, which are on the record and were made in public. Its weakness, as Weiler's own wording shows, is the step from a man's prejudices to the reasons for his decisions.

The second answer is that Bevin was an anti-Zionist, not an antisemite. The historian Alan Bullock wrote that he "was not moved by hatred of the Jews." David Ben-Gurion, who had every reason to think the worst of him, said, "I prefer to consider Bevin simply as an anti-Zionist." Attlee defended him in the same terms in the House of Commons in 1949. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] The strength of this case is that it comes in part from Bevin's opponents, Ben-Gurion above all, and that it fits his statement to the Arab delegation in September 1946. Its weakness is that the remarks of November 1945 and June 1946 are hard to describe as political opposition to Zionism alone.

The third answer is strategic interest. A Foreign Office briefing attributed to Harold Beeley stressed Middle East oil, communications and the Suez route as Britain's interests in the region, and Langham cites the historian W. Roger Louis on Britain's Middle East position. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] On this reading, Bevin's policy was the Foreign Office's policy: Britain needed the goodwill of the Arab states and of Muslim opinion, the "90,000,000 co-religionists in India" whom Bevin himself had invoked, and a Jewish state imposed against that opinion would put those interests at risk. The strength of this case is that it explains the policy without needing to explain the man, and that it rests on the Foreign Office's own statement of British interests. Its weakness is that it says little about why the remarks were made.

Langham's own conclusion leans toward the third answer. Bevin, he writes, was probably not motivated by antisemitism when he made policy, and "genuinely thought it was in the best interests of Britain." But his opposition hardened over time into anti-Zionism, and Langham leaves open whether, in that later stage, Bevin crossed into antisemitism. [cite:rs_rd5_langham_2012] That conclusion keeps two things apart that are often run together: what a man said about Jews, which in Bevin's case included antisemitic remarks stated in public, and why his government did what it did, which the documents tie to British strategic interest.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here do not show what "the present monthly rate" of immigration was in November 1945, since Bevin's text gave no figure. They do not show what Bevin said to American officials during his visit in late 1946, only Langham's report that he came to think the Mandate would have to be given up. Nor can any document settle what Bevin felt, as against what he said and did. The remarks are a matter of record; the motive behind the policy remains a matter of judgement, and the historians who have studied him most closely still disagree.

sections.h: The Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, 1945–1946
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that no international body heard the Arab case, or the case for a shared state, before the United Nations voted to partition Palestine in November 1947. The record shows otherwise. More than a year and a half before the vote, a joint British and American committee heard the Jewish Agency, Arab spokesmen, Jewish advocates of a binational state, Christian and Jewish organizations, and the refugees themselves. It then produced a unanimous report that rejected both a Jewish state and an Arab state. What happened next is the more important part of the story. Washington took the one recommendation it wanted and left the rest; London attached a condition to even that one; and the follow-up plan pleased no one.

Twelve members, two governments. The committee was announced in November 1945 by the Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, as a "joint Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry, under a rotating chairmanship" (the announcement and its context are told in [scene:rd5_bevin|the section on Bevin]). [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] It was created as Washington pressed London to admit Jewish displaced persons to Palestine, and it was built to share the question between the two governments. It had six American and six British members. The Americans included Bartley Crum and James McDonald; the British included Richard Crossman. [cite:w_aac]

Hearings on three continents. Between January and March 1946 the committee held hearings in Washington, London, the displaced-persons camps of Europe, Cairo and Jerusalem. [cite:w_aac] It took evidence from governments, the Jewish Agency, Arab states and the Arab Office, Christian and Jewish organizations, and refugees in the camps. It was, in the judgement of the account this book follows, the most complete hearing of competing cases before 1947. [cite:w_aac]

Three of the cases put to it deserve naming. The Jewish Agency's leaders presented the Zionist case. Arab representatives presented theirs, among them the Arab Office, where the historian Albert Hourani gave testimony that the record describes as notable. [cite:w_aac] The sources used here do not give the substance of what Hourani said, so this book does not paraphrase it. The third case came from Jews who opposed a Jewish state. Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, and the Ihud association argued that Arabs and Jews should share one state with political parity. [cite:w_aac] Their testimony shows that a Jewish alternative to partition was argued, in person, before an official body. It was not a position invented afterward by critics of the state that emerged.

The April 1946 report. The committee reported unanimously in April 1946. It recommended four things. First, the immediate issue of 100,000 immigration certificates for Jewish refugees. Second, the repeal of the 1940 land regulations, which restricted land transfers. Third, the continuation of the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship. And fourth, as a principle of the future constitution, that Palestine should be neither a Jewish state nor an Arab state, with neither people dominating the other. [cite:avalon_aac]

The report was a package. The 100,000 certificates answered the plight of the survivors in Europe; the repeal of the 1940 land regulations lifted restrictions on land transfers; trusteeship and the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle expressed the report's principle that neither people should dominate the other. Unanimity mattered: the six Americans and six Britons had agreed on all of it together.

What Washington kept, and what London required. President Truman publicly endorsed the 100,000 and was silent on the rest. [cite:w_aac] The admission of refugees was popular with American voters. The constitutional recommendation against a Jewish state was not something he endorsed. Prime Minister Attlee answered by tying any admissions to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups in Palestine. [cite:w_aac] The British condition was not abstract. At the time, the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi were acting together against British rule, as told in [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]. By making the 100,000 depend on disarmament, London made the one recommendation Washington wanted depend, in part, on the surrender of arms by Jewish groups then in open revolt against British rule.

Morrison–Grady. The two governments tried once more. In July 1946 a follow-up Anglo-American plan, known as Morrison–Grady, proposed provincial autonomy for Palestine. Zionist and Arab leaders both rejected it, and Truman declined to back it. [cite:w_morrisongrady] With that, the joint Anglo-American attempt to settle Palestine was finished. The question went to the United Nations the following year. [cite:w_morrisongrady]

The mechanism. The episode shows how the decision was structured in 1946. The committee could hear anyone and recommend anything, but it could decide nothing. The two governments could decide, but each took from the report what served its own position. Washington, which did not govern Palestine, could press on the one point that cost it nothing at home and had public support. London, which governed Palestine, could attach conditions. The people heard by the committee, whether the Jewish Agency, the Arab Office, Magnes and Ihud, or the refugees in the camps, had a hearing but no hand in what followed. The binational option that Magnes argued, and that the report's "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle partly echoed, had no government willing to carry it.

The two readings. One reading of this record is that the hearing was real and the outcome was a failure of politics: the committee did its work, and the governments that commissioned it then ignored most of it. Another reading, found in the source this book follows, puts it more sharply: what survived into American policy was the part with domestic political value. [cite:w_aac] Both readings start from the same facts. They differ on how much weight to give Truman's own reasons, a question taken up in [scene:wh_s01|the section on the White House]. What neither reading supports is the claim that the Arab and binationalist cases went unheard before 1947. They were heard; they were not adopted.

What the record does not settle. The sources used here name only three of the twelve members, and do not record the committee's internal debates or how it reached unanimity. They do not give the content of Hourani's testimony or of the Jewish Agency's. They do not say what, if anything, London said about the land regulations, trusteeship or the "neither Jewish nor Arab state" principle once the report was published, beyond its disarmament condition on the 100,000. And they do not show whether any of the 100,000 certificates were issued as a result of the report.

sections.h: The Jewish Resistance Movement, 1945–1946
sections.html:
For fourteen months after the Second World War, the three Jewish armed organizations in Palestine fought the British together. The Haganah and the two other organizations, the Irgun and Lehi, whose origins are told in [scene:s07e2|the section on the Irgun and Lehi], had been separate commands. In the autumn of 1945 they joined forces for a time. The arrangement they made has a name, the Jewish Resistance Movement, and a beginning and an end that can be dated. What it cost in lives cannot, at least from the source available here.

That source needs to be named before anything else is said. The account of the movement used in this section comes from the Lehi heritage association, which keeps the memory of one of the three organizations. It is written from Lehi's own perspective, and it gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Every operational detail below is therefore Lehi's account of events, reported as such. British records, Haganah records and independent scholarship on these operations are not part of the material this book has verified for this period.

The agreement. In early September 1945, according to the heritage account, four men agreed to form a united Jewish Resistance Movement: Moshe Sneh and Yisrael Galili for the Haganah, Natan Yellin-Mor for Lehi, and Menachem Begin for the Irgun. The Haganah took part through its Palmah. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The structure matters. Three separate commands kept their own organizations and their own leaders; what they agreed was to act against the British in concert. As the ending of the movement would show, the Haganah's part in it could be switched off by the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress; the Irgun's and Lehi's could not.

The timing also matters. The agreement came in the weeks after a new Labour government took office in London on 26 July 1945. [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin] Its Foreign Secretary, Ernest Bevin, did not set out his policy on Palestine until 13 November 1945, when he announced a joint Anglo-American inquiry and said that Jewish immigration would continue only "at the present monthly rate" in the meantime. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_bevin_1945] The first coordinated operations came almost two weeks before that statement.

The Night of the Trains, 1 November 1945. Operations began on the night of 1 November 1945, remembered as the "Night of the Trains." At the railway station at Lydda, Lehi and Irgun fighters destroyed three engines and damaged a train and a signal box; some police and railway workers were killed or injured. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The heritage account does not give their number or their names. The same night, a Lehi bomb at the Haifa refinery went off early and killed the operation's commander, Moshe Bar-Giora. The heritage account itself calls that operation a failure. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]

The targets of that first night were infrastructure: the railway and the oil refinery. The police and railway workers who were killed or hurt at Lydda were people at work, not combatants, and the source that records their deaths does not count them. That silence is the first of the gaps in this record.

The Night of the Bridges, 17 June 1946. Between the two nights, the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry heard evidence and reported, in April 1946, and the British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, tied the admission of the 100,000 refugees it recommended to the disarmament of the Jewish and Arab armed groups (see [scene:aac_s01|the Anglo-American Committee]). [cite:w_aac] The resistance movement's answer, in the sense that it was the next major operation the heritage account records, came on 17 June 1946, the "Night of the Bridges." The Palmah attacked eleven bridges across Palestine. The heritage account gives no casualty figure. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Where the first night had been carried out by Lehi and the Irgun, this one was the Haganah's own operation, through the Palmah.

Britain's answer and the summer of 1946. Twelve days later, on 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha, a raid by roughly 17,000 troops and police that arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] On 22 July 1946 the Irgun, commanded by Begin, bombed the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, killing 91 people. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Both events are told in the sections that follow, beginning with [scene:s07e3|Operation Agatha].

The halt. In early August 1946 the Jewish Agency's leadership met in Paris, and there, according to the heritage account, the decision was taken to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met. The Congress, meeting in Basel, decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle. After that, in the Lehi account's words, the fight "fell to Lehi and IZL", that is, to Lehi and the Irgun. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]

The mechanism of the ending is the clearest thing in the record. The movement had been an alliance of three commands, but only one of them, the Haganah, answered to the Jewish Agency and the Zionist Congress. When those bodies decided to stop, the fight, in the Lehi account, passed to Lehi and the Irgun; their decisions were not the Congress's to make. The decision in Paris was a political one, taken by the leadership that also had a diplomatic course to pursue that same August (see the Agency's partition proposal, told in its own section). The decision in Basel confirmed it. The united movement thus ended by a political decision on the Jewish side, not by British arms, and the armed campaign against Britain went on without the Haganah.

Two ways of reading it. The movement is remembered in two registers. In the Lehi account, it was a "united armed offensive against the British," and the decisions in Paris and Basel left the fighting to Lehi and the Irgun. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Read from the British side and from the side of those killed or injured at Lydda, the same operations were attacks on railways, a refinery and bridges in which police and workers died. The two readings do not disagree about what happened on the nights the source records. They disagree about what to call it, and the source available here belongs to one side of that disagreement.

What the record does not settle. Much remains open. The heritage account gives no casualty totals for the movement's operations, no number for the police and railway workers killed or injured at Lydda, and no casualty figure for the Night of the Bridges. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] It does not say whether the King David Hotel bombing was carried out under the united movement's coordination or by the Irgun alone, and the material verified here does not settle that question. It does not record the reasons given in Paris for the halt, or whether the bombing of 22 July weighed in that decision; the sequence is plain, with the bombing coming about two weeks before the Paris meeting, but the source draws no causal line, and neither does this book. A full account of the movement would need British military and police records and the Haganah's own papers, set against the Lehi account. Until that work is done, the dates and the targets are as firm as this record gets.

sections.h: Black Sabbath: Operation Agatha, 29 June 1946
sections.html:
Relations between Britain and the Jewish community of Palestine are often described as having worn down slowly after the war, with no single moment at which they broke. The slow wearing-down is real: from September 1945 the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi had acted together against British targets, from the railways at Lydda in November 1945 to eleven bridges on the night of 17 June 1946 (see [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]). [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] But the record also holds a dated break, with a codename, a troop count and an arrest total. Twelve days after the Night of the Bridges, on Saturday 29 June 1946, Britain launched Operation Agatha.

The operation. Roughly 17,000 British troops and police searched Jewish settlements, kibbutzim and offices across Mandate Palestine at the same time. More than 2,700 people were arrested. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The operation was a direct response to the escalating operations of the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi against British installations. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] What set it apart was whom it reached. Those arrested included senior officials of the Jewish Agency. Agatha was not a narrow sweep for known fighters of the two underground groups. It struck the mainstream political leadership's own institutions. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

That choice of target fits what the united resistance had become. The Night of the Bridges had been carried out not by Lehi or the Irgun but by the Haganah, acting through its Palmah. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The campaign Britain was answering was no longer only the work of the two underground groups, and the raid reached past them to the political leadership.

The sources do not give a site-by-site inventory of what was searched, and they do not name the individuals arrested. What they establish is the scale, the simultaneity and the reach of the operation into the Agency's leadership. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

The documents. The arrests were only part of it. British forces also seized a substantial cache of documents from the Jewish Agency's headquarters in Jerusalem. The material was believed to include evidence linking the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] That belief is what gave the seizure its weight. The Jewish movement had kept a deliberate legal and organizational separation between its political leadership and armed resistance. Documents tying the one to the other threatened that separation directly. The sources describe what the documents were believed to contain; they do not set out the actual contents or the full extent of what was taken. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha]

Two names. The operation carries two names, and each records something. "Agatha" was the official British codename. "Black Sabbath" was the name given by the Jewish community whose institutions were raided, because the raid fell on a Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath. [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The second name is itself evidence of how the operation was experienced and remembered by those it targeted. There is no evidence that the British name carried any hidden meaning; codenames of the period were, as a rule, assigned without symbolic intent. The community's own name is the more telling of the two for understanding what the raid meant to those on the receiving end.

Why the King David Hotel. The documents did not stay at the Agency. They were taken to be processed and stored in the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel in Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The building needs describing. Its southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and served as the regional British military headquarters. Hotel business went on in the rest of the building at the same time. It was not a hotel that happened to contain a few government offices; it was, in effect, the centre of British administration in Palestine. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

That double character is what made it a target. In the Irgun's planning, the hotel was at once a symbol of British authority and the physical place where the evidence against the Jewish Agency's leadership was held. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Irgun intelligence assessed that the documents seized in Agatha, including the material believed to implicate the Agency's leadership in coordinating with the Haganah, were being processed and stored in the Secretariat wing specifically. The bombing's documented objective was to destroy that evidence and to strike the administrative apparatus that had just carried out the mass raid and the arrests. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

Twenty-three days. The Irgun's planning for what became the King David Hotel bombing began in direct response to Black Sabbath. Its motive, as documented, was specific, retaliation and the destruction of evidence, rather than a general rise in tension. The bombing took place on 22 July 1946, twenty-three days after the raid. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The line from one event to the other is short and traceable: raid, seizure, intelligence assessment, choice of target, attack.

Two cautions belong beside that line. The first is that it does not establish that retaliation for Black Sabbath was the bombing's only motive; the bombing's planning and its stated objectives are taken up in [scene:s07e4|the next section]. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The second is that tracing a cause is not the same as weighing a deed. The bombing killed 91 people, many of whom had no connection to the administrative work the Irgun meant to strike. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] Setting out the chain from Agatha explains how the hotel came to be chosen. It does not excuse or justify the deaths that followed, and it is not offered here as doing so.

The claim and the record. The familiar account of steadily worsening relations is not wrong so much as incomplete. The armed campaign of 1945–46 and the British response to it built up over months. Within that build-up, Agatha stands out as a single dated operation of a different order, with a troop count, an arrest total, a seizure of the Agency's own papers and a direct line to the deadliest single attack on the British of the whole Mandate period. A gradual decline and a sharp turning point are both in the record.

What the record does not settle. The sources do not name those arrested or say how long they were held. They do not give the contents of the seized documents, so the belief that they tied the Agency's leadership to the Haganah cannot be tested here. They do not record what the British government said, at the time, to justify the decision to arrest the Agency's senior officials. And they do not show how the raid bore on the decisions the Agency's leadership took a few weeks later, in early August 1946, to halt armed action. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] Those questions need the British and Jewish Agency archives, which are not part of the material verified for this book.

sections.h: The King David Hotel Bombing, 22 July 1946
sections.html:
The bombing of the King David Hotel is sometimes passed over as an incident in a British office building, one act of violence among many in the last years of the Mandate. The numbers alone tell against that view. On 22 July 1946 an explosion in the hotel's southern wing in Jerusalem killed 91 people, British, Arab and Jewish. It was the deadliest single attack against the British in the whole Mandate period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] It was carried out by an organization whose commander would later lead the government of Israel, it drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it hardened British opinion toward leaving Palestine. Each of these points is on the record, and each is taken in turn below.

From Agatha to the hotel. The attack came twenty-three days after Operation Agatha. On 29 June 1946 British forces had arrested more than 2,700 people, including senior Jewish Agency officials, and seized documents from the Agency's Jerusalem headquarters; the documents were believed to link the Agency's leadership to Haganah operations, and they were taken to the Secretariat wing of the King David Hotel to be processed and stored (see [scene:s07e3|Operation Agatha]). [cite:wiki_operation_agatha] The hotel's southern wing housed the Mandate Secretariat, the central administrative offices of the Mandate government, and the British military command; hotel business carried on in the rest of the building. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The Irgun, assessing that the seized papers were held there, planned the attack in direct response to the raid, with the documented aims of destroying that evidence and striking the administration that had carried out the arrests. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

The attack. The Irgun was commanded at the time by Menachem Begin. [cite:wiki_menachem_begin] Its fighters placed explosives, reportedly concealed in milk churns, in the basement of the southern wing, beneath the Secretariat and the military command, and detonated them. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The explosion killed 91 people. They were a mix of British, Arab and Jewish civilians and administrative personnel. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The sources give the total and the fact that the dead came from all three communities; they do not itemize who each person was or what work each did. Many had no connection to the administrative functions the Irgun meant to strike. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

The warning calls. Whether those inside were warned is one of the oldest disputes about the attack, and it has not been resolved. The Irgun's own account holds that warning calls were placed about 25 minutes before the detonation to three places: the hotel switchboard, the French consulate and the office of the Palestine Post newspaper, each urging evacuation. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] British investigators, and later historians, have disputed whether any warning actually reached the hotel's management in time to act on it, or whether a call that did arrive was dismissed as a hoax. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

Each side has a case. The Irgun's account is specific: it names the time, the three recipients and the purpose of the calls, and if it is accurate it shows an intention to empty the building rather than to kill those in it. The British case rests on the outcome and on the investigation: 91 people did not leave, and the investigators doubted that any usable warning had reached the people who could have ordered an evacuation. Even on the Irgun's own account, the question of whether a warning of about 25 minutes, sent partly to outside offices, was adequate remains open. The record does not settle which account is right, and this book does not pretend that it does.

The Jewish Agency's condemnation. The Jewish Agency publicly condemned the bombing. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The condemnation carried an edge that is easy to miss. It was the Agency's own documents, seized in Agatha, that the attack was meant to destroy. And the Haganah, whose ties to the Agency's leadership the seized documents were believed to show, had itself been part of the united Jewish Resistance Movement with the Irgun and Lehi since September 1945, carrying out the Night of the Bridges only five weeks earlier through its Palmah. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The condemnation is therefore a real instance, in the open, of the tension between the mainstream political leadership and the paramilitary groups, played out around the most consequential single attack of the period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] The sources record the public condemnation; they do not record the internal debate behind its wording or the private views of individual Agency officials.

Did it end the united resistance? A reader will want to know whether the bombing broke the alliance. The sequence is suggestive. In early August 1946, about two weeks after the bombing, the Jewish Agency's leadership, meeting in Paris, decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met; the Congress, in Basel, decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle, after which, in Lehi's account, the fight "fell to Lehi and IZL", that is, to Lehi and the Irgun. [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance] The only source for those decisions, the Lehi heritage association, does not say that the bombing caused them, and no other source verified for this book does either (see [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement]). The order of events is clear; the link between them is not established.

What it changed in London. The bombing is documented as having significantly hardened British public and parliamentary opinion toward disengaging from Palestine altogether. It contributed directly to Britain's decision, the next year, to hand the whole question to the United Nations. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing] It was one factor among several. The same record that ties the bombing to Britain's change of mind does not claim that the attack alone caused the referral of 1947; other pressures were at work, and how much weight the armed campaign carried in Britain's withdrawal is itself disputed, as the section on [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain's exit] sets out.

Begin, then and later. Menachem Begin personally commanded the Irgun at the time of the bombing. He later served as Israel's sixth Prime Minister, from 1977 to 1983. [cite:wiki_menachem_begin] The line from the command of 1946 to the premiership three decades later is direct and documented. What the sources used here do not provide is Begin's own account: his justification for the attack and what he said about it in later years are not part of this material, and they are not supplied here.

The claim and the record. The view of the bombing as a minor, passing incident does not survive the facts. Ninety-one people from three communities were killed in a single attack, the largest such toll against the British in the Mandate. Its commander went on to lead the government of Israel. It drew a public condemnation from the Jewish Agency, and it moved British opinion toward leaving. On its own documented merits it was among the most consequential single events of the Mandate period. [cite:wiki_king_david_hotel_bombing]

What the record does not settle. Three questions stay open. The first is the warning: whether the calls the Irgun describes were made as it says, whether any reached someone able to order an evacuation, and whether they were treated as a hoax. The second is the full list of the dead, by name, nationality and role, which the sources here do not give. The third is cause and effect after the attack: how far the bombing drove the Jewish Agency's August decision to halt armed action, and how far it, rather than the other pressures on Britain, drove the decision to go to the United Nations. On all three, the documents available here establish the sequence and leave the weighing to further evidence.

sections.h: The Jewish Agency Prepares: Partition as Policy, 1946
sections.html:
The partition plan voted on in November 1947 is usually described as the product of the United Nations' own process: an eleven-member committee that investigated the problem from scratch and reached its recommendation independently. That committee was real, and its conclusions were its own. But one of the parties before it had arrived at partition long before the committee existed. The Jewish Agency had prepared its own partition proposal more than a year before the committee reported, and by then had made partition its declared aim.

Two separate diplomatic tracks lay ahead: recognition by the United States, and a decision at the United Nations. The Agency worked both, and the groundwork for the second was laid early. In August 1946 it submitted its own detailed partition proposal, with boundaries drawn for a Palestinian rump state [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. Those boundaries bear a documented resemblance to the area that became the West Bank after 1948 [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. The resemblance is worth noting and easy to overstate. The source records a likeness between two maps, not a line of descent: it does not show that the United Nations committee, or anyone after it, adopted the Agency's exact lines.

The proposal did not stand alone. Historical accounts of the United Nations process note that by 1946 partition had become the Jewish Agency's avowed, public policy [cite:unscop_testimony]. That is a different thing from a position adopted because an international body demanded one. The Agency did not arrive at partition in reaction to the United Nations. It came to the United Nations with partition already as its stated goal, and with a prepared case for it. The details of what it later presented were not necessarily identical to its 1946 position, and the sources here do not claim they were; what was fixed by 1946 was the commitment itself.

August 1946 was also a turning point in the Agency's other policy, the armed one. According to the heritage association of Lehi, one of the underground groups then allied with the Haganah in the Jewish Resistance Movement, the Agency's meeting in Paris in early August 1946 decided to halt armed action until the Zionist Congress met. The Congress, meeting in Basel, decided on 9 December 1946 to halt the armed struggle, after which, in Lehi's account, the fight "fell to Lehi and IZL", the Irgun [cite:rs_rd5_lehi_resistance]. That account is written from Lehi's own perspective, and it is the only source here for the Paris decision. The sources do not say whether the partition proposal was discussed or adopted at the same Paris meeting, and this book does not join the two. What can be said is that in the same month the record shows the Agency submitting a partition plan, the Lehi account has it standing down from armed struggle until its Congress could meet. The story of that resistance movement is told in [scene:rd5_revolt|the Jewish Resistance Movement].

The timeline makes the central point plain. The Agency's proposal came roughly nine months before the United Nations created its committee, and more than a year before that committee's report. When the committee did hear the Agency in 1947, its head, David Ben-Gurion, told it that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome, and the Agency presented a prepared map and a large body of supporting material [cite:unscop_testimony]. That hearing, and the Arab Higher Committee's decision to boycott it, are the subject of [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair].

None of this makes the committee's recommendation a copy of the Agency's plan, and the evidence here does not support saying so. It does correct the impression that the United Nations faced a blank page. One party came to it with a position fixed and a proposal already drafted, the product of a diplomatic campaign that had begun before the international process did. Whether that preparation shaped the committee's final lines, and by how much, is not something the sources used here can measure. Nor do they say to whom, exactly, the August 1946 proposal was submitted, or set out its boundaries line by line. Those questions remain open; the date and the policy do not.

sections.h: Inside the White House, 1945–1948
sections.html:
American policy on Palestine is often described as a State Department product, made on the merits by career diplomats. In the Truman years that description leaves out the building where the decisions were finally taken. Inside the White House a small number of aides and friends gave the President views and visitors that the State Department did not, and at least one of his most consequential statements was issued at a moment chosen with the electoral calendar in plain view. Who had access, and when the President spoke, are both on the record. Why he spoke as he did is still argued.

The longest-serving of those aides was David K. Niles. He served in the White House from 1942 to 1951, first under Franklin Roosevelt and then under Harry Truman, and he was one of only two Roosevelt aides whom Truman kept on [cite:wiki_david_niles] [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. His brief was minority affairs. Niles was a committed Zionist, and he became an important channel through which American Zionists reached the White House [cite:wiki_david_niles] [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. That is a documented role, not an accusation: he had been entrusted with minority affairs, and his own commitment was to the Zionist cause.

Around Niles stood others. Max Lowenthal advised the President's special counsel, Clark Clifford, on Palestine [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. And outside the staff altogether there was Eddie Jacobson, Truman's personal friend and former business partner, who provided a separate, private channel to the President; his role, including the March 1948 meeting he arranged, is told in [scene:s08|Truman and the men around him]. What they offered was proximity: being in the room, or being able to get someone else into it.

The clearest test of that influence came in the autumn of 1946, after a conference on Palestine in London had adjourned; the conference and Britain's part in it are set out in [scene:rd5_bevin|Bevin and Palestine, 1945–1946]. On 4 October 1946, the eve of Yom Kippur and a month before the congressional midterm elections, Truman issued a statement on Palestine [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] [cite:nuremberg_yomkippur]. He regretted the adjournment of the London conference. He urged immediate, large-scale Jewish immigration into Palestine. And he said that the United States could support a solution along the lines of a viable Jewish state "in an adequate area of Palestine" [cite:avalon_yomkippur_1946] [cite:nuremberg_yomkippur].

The statement landed hard in London. The British Prime Minister, Clement Attlee, was furious, and Truman wrote to him that he "very much" regretted any embarrassment it had caused [cite:frus_truman_attlee_1946]. The apology concerned the embarrassment; the documents cited here do not record any change in the position itself.

The timing invited an explanation, and the New York Times printed one within three days. On 7 October 1946 James Reston wrote in that paper that the President "went against his advisers' foreign policy and chose to follow the promptings of those who were primarily interested in retaining Democratic majorities in Congress" [cite:palestinestudies_christison_truman]. On Reston's reading, the statement was electoral, and its date, a month before the midterms, was part of the evidence.

Truman rejected that reading publicly. In February 1947 he issued a statement calling the impression that partisan and local politics motivated American policy on Palestine "most unfortunate and misleading", and insisting that his position had been consistent since 1945 [cite:jvl_truman_feb1947]. On his own account, the statement of October 1946 restated a view he had held since his first months in office, not a new position adopted for an election.

Each side has real evidence. Reston's case rests on the calendar, which no one disputes, and on his reporting that the statement went against the foreign-policy advice the President had received. Truman's case rests on consistency: the October statement's call for immediate, large-scale immigration was, on his account, the position he had held since 1945, and a statement that restates an existing position is not by itself proof of a new electoral calculation. His own earlier words on the subject are gathered in [scene:tr_s01|Truman in his own words].

The two readings are not mutually exclusive, and the documents do not force a choice between them. Who had the President's ear, and when he chose to speak, are on the record. Whether electoral politics or conviction drove him is argued by named sources on both sides, and the answer can be both: a man may hold a view sincerely and still choose the most politically useful day on which to announce it.

The White House channel was the last link in a longer chain. The map below traces how two American Zionist campaigns of the 1940s, a rival and aggressive one led by the Irgun's delegation in the United States and a disciplined mainstream lobby, moved American opinion through advertising, local committees and Christian supporters into Congress and both parties' platforms. From there the pressure reached the White House, where Niles provided access and the Yom Kippur statement of 1946 put the President on record, and finally the United Nations, where the United States lobbied for the partition vote of November 1947. The map shows how the pieces connected; it does not show that any one of them decided the outcome.

What the record does not settle is the weight of each influence. The sources here document Niles's access but not the content of his advice on any given day, nor whether he drafted or proposed the October statement. They record Lowenthal's role as an adviser to Clifford without detailing what he advised. And no document in this section records Truman saying, in private, that the midterms were or were not on his mind when he spoke on 4 October 1946. The accounts of motive therefore remain what they are: Reston's reporting on one side, the President's own public denial on the other.

sections.h: Britain Lets Go, February–September 1947
sections.html:
In the space of eight months in 1947, Britain went from governing Palestine to announcing that it would leave. The steps were formal and dated: a Cabinet decision in February, a letter to the United Nations in April, and a statement to the General Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee in September. Between them came hangings, kidnappings, riots in British cities and a refugee ship turned back to Europe. The question historians still argue over is how these events related to one another, and in particular how far the Jewish armed campaign drove Britain out.

By the start of 1947 the policy that Ernest Bevin had staked his name on in November 1945 had run out of road; that earlier course, from the Anglo-American Committee to the London conference, is traced in [scene:rd5_bevin|Bevin and Palestine, 1945–1946]. On 14 February 1947 Bevin told the Arab delegates in London that the Cabinet had agreed the question should go to the United Nations without British recommendations, "inasmuch as plan offered by British Delegation had met with no acceptance from either Arabs or Jews". Britain, he said, would present the matter "as impartially as possible" [cite:rs_rd5_frus_gallman_1947]. The words survive in a telegram from the American embassy in London to the Secretary of State.

Four days later, on 18 February 1947, Bevin explained the decision in the House of Commons. In the text reproduced by the Center for Online Judaic Studies, which gives no archival citation, he described "an irreconcilable conflict of principles". For the Jews, the essential principle was a sovereign Jewish state. For the Arabs, it was to resist Jewish sovereignty anywhere in Palestine. He called the Mandate "unworkable in practice", and he put the country's population at about 1,200,000 Arabs and 600,000 Jews [cite:rs_rd5_cojs_bevin_1947]. Because that text could not be checked against Hansard, its wording should be read as reported rather than verified. The historian Raphael Langham adds that in the Commons Bevin blamed the Jews and the United States for the failure [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

The formal handover followed. On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to "place the question of Palestine on the Agenda of the General Assembly at its next regular Annual Session", and to "summon, as soon as possible, a special Session" to constitute a special committee [cite:rs_rd5_un_a286]. The letter was circulated as document A/286, dated 3 April 1947. The mechanism is worth seeing plainly. Britain did not surrender the Mandate in April. It asked the Assembly to take up the question and to set up a committee, while it went on governing. The committee that resulted, UNSCOP, spent the summer in Palestine and the region; its work is told in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP and the empty chair].

Inside Palestine the violence that ran alongside the diplomacy moved in a cycle of death sentences and reprisals. The dates below come from a single encyclopedia entry and are given here as reported, without the casualty and riot figures that the same source carries but which could not be confirmed. On 16 April 1947 Britain executed four members of the Irgun: Dov Gruner, Yehiel Dresner, Mordechai Alkahi and Eliezer Kashani. On 4 May the Irgun broke into Acre prison. Three of the attackers who were captured, Avshalom Haviv, Yaakov Weiss and Meir Nakar, were sentenced to death and hanged on 29 July 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants].

By then the Irgun held two British hostages. On the night of 11 to 12 July 1947 it kidnapped two Intelligence Corps sergeants, Clifford Martin and Mervyn Paice, in Netanya. On 30 July, the day after the Acre men were hanged, it hanged the sergeants, and booby-trapped their bodies [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. The killings provoked a reaction in Britain itself. From 1 August 1947 anti-Jewish rioting broke out, beginning in Liverpool and spreading to other cities [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. It should be named for what it was: antisemitic violence in British cities, aimed at Jews in Britain in response to killings carried out by the Irgun in Palestine.

The same month brought the episode that did most to turn international opinion. In July 1947 a ship formerly called the President Warfield, renamed Exodus 1947, sailed from Sète in France with more than 4,500 Jewish passengers, most of them displaced persons and Holocaust survivors [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus] [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947]. It was one vessel in the clandestine immigration fleet whose wider history is told in [scene:ab_s01|Aliyah Bet]. When the Royal Navy boarded it, three Jews were killed, one crew member and two passengers according to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, and dozens were wounded [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus] [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947].

The two institutions that record the boarding do not agree on its date. Yad Vashem states that the ship was attacked on 17 July in international waters, that three people were killed, and that it reached Haifa on 18 July [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947]. The Holocaust Memorial Museum dates the clash to 18 July 1947 and specifies one crew member and two passengers among the dead [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus]. Neither source explains the difference, and it is left standing here.

What Britain did next made the ship a symbol. The passengers were moved onto three navy transports and taken back to Port-de-Bouc in France. France declined to remove them by force. After a hunger strike of 24 days and about three weeks in the summer heat, they were carried to Hamburg and interned in camps in the British zone of Germany [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus]. Langham records that Bevin insisted the passengers be returned to their port of embarkation, and suggests that prejudice may have played a part [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]. That is Langham's suggestion, and he frames it as a possibility rather than a finding. Yad Vashem states that the voyage was meant to draw the attention of the UNSCOP members then working in the country; the Holocaust Memorial Museum says the "public embarrassment for Britain" helped shift diplomatic sympathy [cite:rs_rd5_yv_july1947] [cite:rs_rd5_ushmm_exodus].

The decision to leave outright, rather than to hand over a question for advice, was announced at the United Nations. On 26 September 1947 Arthur Creech Jones, the Colonial Secretary, told the Ad Hoc Committee that "in the absence of a settlement" Britain had to plan for "an early withdrawal of British forces and of the British administration". Britain, he said, "was not prepared to undertake the task of imposing a policy in Palestine by force of arms" [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_creechjones]. That sentence is the hinge of the whole year. The Assembly could recommend what it liked; Britain would not enforce it. When the Assembly voted on partition on 29 November 1947, Britain abstained [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

There was also a bill. The funding ledger compiled for this library, citing the British government's own end-of-Mandate account, puts the cost of the forces in Palestine in 1945–47 at about £100 million, with some 100,000 troops deployed and about 750 British military and police killed over the period; in today's money the cost is roughly $6.7 billion. The ledger's sources are listed with the panel below, and the full account of Britain's bill appears in the next stage of this book. The panel below sets it beside the other large sums of the pre-state years, for scale rather than as a total. Britain's military bill for 1945–47 is the second-largest item on it, behind only the Jewish capital invested in Palestine between 1921 and 1937, and well above the United Jewish Appeal's wartime giving of 1939–45. The sources used here do not say how much weight the Cabinet gave to that cost when it decided to leave; they show only that the cost was being paid.

How much did the Jewish insurgency, and the sergeants affair in particular, cause the withdrawal? Two positions have serious support. On one view the armed campaign was decisive or close to it. The historian J. Bowyer Bell called the sergeants affair the "straw that broke the Mandate's back", and Creech Jones himself, writing in 1961, listed the sergeants affair as one of four major factors behind the Cabinet's September 1947 decision to evacuate [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_sergeants]. The strength of this case is the testimony of the minister who announced the withdrawal, and the timing: the sergeants were hanged on 30 July, riots broke out in Britain on 1 August, and the withdrawal was announced eight weeks later.

On the other view the insurgency was one factor among several. Britain's own stated reason, in February, was the irreconcilable Arab and Jewish positions and the failure of its own plan; the Cabinet had agreed to hand the question to the United Nations before the executions, the Acre break-in, the kidnapping or the Exodus [cite:rs_rd5_frus_gallman_1947]. Langham points to strategic considerations and Britain's relations with the Arab states [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit]. The strength of this case is the sequence of documents: the decision to give up the problem predates the events of the summer. The two readings are not wholly opposed. February's decision referred the question; September's decision ended the Mandate; the events between may explain why the second followed the first so fast, even if they did not cause the first.

Britain's departure did not end Bevin's part in the story. In May 1948 he told the Commons, "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House", and Britain recognised Israel only in January 1949, with Bevin's acceptance, in Langham's word, "grudging" [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit].

Several things remain unsettled on this record. The Commons text of 18 February 1947 is known here only through a reproduction without archival citation. The Cabinet's own minutes for February and September 1947 are not among the sources used, so the weight the ministers themselves gave to cost, to the insurgency, to American pressure or to Arab opinion cannot be measured from them. Creech Jones's four factors are known from a later account, written in 1961, and only one of the four is named in the source. The exact date of the Exodus boarding differs between two reputable institutions. And whether prejudice shaped Bevin's handling of the Exodus is, in the one historian's account that raises it, a possibility and not a demonstrated fact. What the documents do show is the order of events: Britain referred the question because its plan had failed with both sides, endured a summer of executions, reprisals and a refugee ship that embarrassed it before the world, and then announced that it would not stay to enforce whatever the world decided.

sections.h: Moscow Said Yes First
sections.html:
The popular memory of 1948 has two superpowers in fixed places: the United States as Israel's sponsor, and the Soviet bloc hostile from the start. For the years in which the state was actually made, the record runs the other way on the second point. Between May 1947 and May 1948 the Soviet Union backed a Jewish state earlier, and held to it more steadily, than Washington did. Its satellites voted for partition, it stood firm at the Security Council when the Americans retreated, it was the first government in the world to recognize Israel in law, and arms from a Soviet-bloc country reached the new state while an American embargo was in force. Only at the end of 1948 did the line begin to bend, and only in the 1950s did Moscow turn toward the Arab states.

The first move came at the special session of the General Assembly that Britain had requested. On 14 May 1947, the day before the Assembly created the Special Committee on Palestine [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop], the Soviet representative Andrei Gromyko addressed the session. He said the Soviet Union preferred a single, independent Arab–Jewish state in which both peoples would have equal rights. But if that proved impossible to achieve, he said, partition into two states was a justifiable alternative [cite:israeled_gromyko_speech] [cite:israeled_gromyko_timeline]. Coming from Moscow, that was a reversal. For decades the Soviet state had opposed Zionism [cite:israeled_gromyko_speech]. Gromyko's speech did not endorse partition outright; it ranked it second. But it put the Soviet Union on record, before Washington had committed, as willing to accept a Jewish state.

Why Moscow changed course is not stated in any Soviet document among the sources used here. Analysts at the time and since have read the motive as a wish to remove British influence from the region, [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. It remains an interpretation of Soviet interest, drawn from what Moscow did, rather than a finding from Moscow's own records. What it does explain is why the Soviet Union and the Zionist movement could find themselves on the same side without sharing any larger aim. This was convergence of interest, not alliance.

When the Assembly voted in November 1947, the Soviet Union and its satellites voted for partition [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. The test came four months later. In March 1948 the United States moved to retreat from partition toward a temporary United Nations trusteeship, a shift told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat, March 1948]. The Soviet Union did not follow. At the Security Council it stood behind partition, and Gromyko told the Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce the bloodshed [cite:yated_stalin_israel] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel].

On 14 May 1948 Israel declared its independence, and Truman's recognition followed the same day, but it was de facto recognition. On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, the Soviet Union became the first state to grant Israel full legal, or de jure, recognition [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel]. The Soviet recognition was thus the fuller of the two. The wider story of who recognized Israel, when and on what legal basis, is told in this chapter's section on recognition.

Recognition was not the only support that came from the Soviet side. Arms reached the new state from Czechoslovakia, a Soviet-bloc country, at a time when an American embargo was in force [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel].
