The contracts, the airlift and their price are documented in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline]; the point here is that the first great power to recognize Israel in law and the government behind its Czechoslovak arms both stood on the same side of the Cold War line.

The first sign that the alignment had limits came seven months after independence. In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against United Nations Resolution 194, the resolution on the return of refugees [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli]. The sources used here do not explain the bloc's reasons for that vote, and they should not be supplied by guesswork. The resolution itself, and what followed from it, belong to the next stage of this book and are told in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194]. From the 1950s, Moscow turned toward the Arab states [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli].

That later turn largely erased the earlier record from popular memory. The common account holds that Israel was created by American support while the Soviet bloc was hostile from the start. The documents support only half of it. American support mattered, but it wavered in March 1948. Soviet support came first, held through that wavering, and produced the first full recognition. In 1947 and 1948 both superpowers backed the new state, for different reasons, Moscow earlier and more firmly, apparently to push Britain out.

What the record does not settle is the question of motive. Gromyko's speech, the votes, the Security Council statement and the recognition are all documented acts. The reasoning behind them inside the Soviet leadership is not documented in the sources used here; the "remove Britain" explanation is the reading analysts have drawn from those acts. Nor do these sources show how far Soviet diplomacy and the Czechoslovak arms sales were coordinated as a single policy, rather than running in parallel. The first-to-recognize fact, by contrast, is not in doubt.

sections.h: UNSCOP and the Empty Chair
sections.html:
The plan that the General Assembly voted on in November 1947 began as the report of an eleven-nation committee that spent the summer of 1947 between Lake Success, Jerusalem, Beirut, Amman, Geneva and the displaced-persons camps of Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover. The United Nations Special Committee on Palestine, known as UNSCOP, is usually remembered as a neutral fact-finding body that heard both sides equally and reached its own conclusion. Its own report tells a more specific story. The committee was genuinely international, and it did reach its conclusions by its own votes. But it did not weigh two prepared Palestinian cases against each other. One party, the Jewish Agency, came with a map, witnesses and a proposed itinerary. The other, the Arab Higher Committee, chose to stay away. The Arab case was put to the committee instead by the governments of six Arab states and by Transjordan's king, outside Palestine.

The committee was Britain's doing. On 2 April 1947 Sir Alexander Cadogan, for the United Kingdom, asked the United Nations to put Palestine on the agenda of the next regular Assembly and to summon a special session as soon as possible to constitute a special committee [cite:rs_rd5_un_a286]. (How London reached that point is told in [scene:rd5_britain_exits|Britain hands Palestine to the United Nations].) The special session convened at Flushing Meadow on 28 April 1947. On 15 May it adopted Resolution 106 (S-1), which created the Special Committee on Palestine with "the widest powers to ascertain and record facts" and told it to report by 1 September 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop] [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report].

Who would sit on it was itself contested. Australia proposed eleven members, none of them permanent members of the Security Council. The Assembly adopted that proposal by 13 votes to 11, with 29 abstentions [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The members chosen were Australia, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, India, Iran, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden, Uruguay and Yugoslavia [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:unscop_ecf]. On its face this was a multi-continent body, not a proxy for Washington or London. It held its first meeting at Lake Success on 26 May 1947, and on 2 June elected Justice Emil Sandström of Sweden as chairman and Alberto Ulloa of Peru as vice-chairman [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. Its members arrived in Palestine on 14 and 15 June and first met in Jerusalem on 16 June [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report].

The day before the members landed, the Arab Higher Committee had informed the Secretary-General that it would abstain from cooperating with the committee. On 10 July 1947 its vice-chairman, Jamal Husseini, wrote again to say that it would not reverse that decision [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The boycott was a deliberate political choice with stated reasons. The Arab Higher Committee regarded the whole framework as illegitimate: in its view any United Nations body that set out to decide Palestine's future without first affirming the self-determination rights of the country's existing majority was biased before it began [cite:unscop_ecf]. The Jewish Agency took the opposite course. It engaged fully and supplied detailed logistical help, including its own proposed itinerary for the committee's visits around the country [cite:unscop_ecf].

The consequence inside Palestine was a hearing room in which only one of the two Palestinian communities' organized leaderships made a formal case. For the Jewish Agency the committee heard Moshe Shertok and David Horowitz, and it heard Chaim Weizmann in a personal capacity [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. David Ben-Gurion, testifying as head of the Jewish Agency, told the committee plainly that an independent Jewish state was the only acceptable outcome. The map presented on the Zionist side was substantially the Peel Commission's map of 1937, with the Galilee, the Negev and West Jerusalem added [cite:unscop_testimony]. One historical account describes the Agency's presentation as forthright and exhaustive, overwhelming the committee "with data, logic, and cogent analyses of every central and tangential issue" [cite:unscop_testimony]. That account is a judgment about the presentation's weight, and it is worth reading carefully. The imbalance it describes did not come from the Arab argument being weak. It came from the Arab Higher Committee's argument never being formally put before the committee in Palestine at all. Nor was the Agency improvising. By 1946 partition had already become its avowed policy, and in August 1946 it had drawn up its own partition proposal, more than a year before UNSCOP existed [cite:unscop_testimony] [cite:jewishagency_1946plan]. That earlier preparation is the subject of [scene:s07h|the Jewish Agency's 1946 proposal].

It is here that the familiar charge against UNSCOP, and the committee's own record, have to be read side by side. The charge, as it is often put, is that the committee heard testimony "almost exclusively" from the Zionist side [cite:unscop_ecf]. The committee's report shows something narrower and more exact. No Palestinian Arab body testified, because the Arab Higher Committee boycotted the proceedings [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. But the Arab states did put their case. After an informal visit to Damascus on 21 July 1947, the committee heard the governments of Egypt, Iraq, Lebanon, Saudi Arabia, Syria and Yemen in Beirut on 22 July, with the Lebanese Foreign Minister, Hamid Frangié, among them. Transjordan declined to send a representative outside the country, so on 25 July the chairman and seven members went to Amman to see King Abdullah [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. The committee also travelled through the region and could observe conditions directly; it did not hear literally nothing of Arab objections [cite:unscop_ecf].

Both readings therefore hold, each within its limits. "One side only" is accurate for the Palestinian parties: the Jewish Agency was heard at length and the Arab Higher Committee by its own decision not at all. It is not accurate for the Arab case as a whole, which six governments presented in Beirut and a seventh, Transjordan's king, gave in Amman. What the record establishes is that no prepared Palestinian Arab case, with its own witnesses and its own maps, stood in the committee's record beside the Agency's. That is a more specific claim than "the process was rigged", and a more defensible one.

The committee also looked beyond Palestine. After a vote of six to four, with one abstention, a subcommittee visited displaced-persons camps in Munich, Salzburg, Vienna, Berlin, Hamburg and Hanover between 8 and 14 August 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. The vote on whether to go at all was close, and the record used here does not say which members voted which way or why.

The drafting began in Geneva on 28 July. On 29 August the committee approved eleven recommendations unanimously and a twelfth with two dissents, and it signed its report on 31 August 1947; the report's cover carries the date 3 September 1947 [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]. On the central question, the committee split. A majority of seven, Canada, Czechoslovakia, Guatemala, the Netherlands, Peru, Sweden and Uruguay, recommended partition into a Jewish state and an Arab state joined in an economic union, with an international regime for Jerusalem. A minority of three, India, Iran and Yugoslavia, recommended a single federal state with Jerusalem as its capital. Australia abstained on both votes, which were recorded as 7 to 3 and 3 to 7 [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop] [cite:unscop_wiki].

The precise count matters, because it is sometimes given wrongly. The Center for Israel Education states that eight of the eleven members endorsed partition, and that the Jewish Agency accepted the plan while the Arab Higher Committee rejected it [cite:rs_rd5_cie_unscop]. The committee's own report records seven, with Australia abstaining [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report]. The report is the primary document, and on this point the summary is in error. The split also corrects a second simplification: the recommendation behind the partition vote was not a unanimous international finding but a majority view, with three members preferring a single federal state.

The majority plan became the working text. The Assembly's Ad Hoc Committee revised it in the autumn, and the revised plan went to the General Assembly vote of 29 November 1947 [cite:unscop_wiki]. That vote, its lobbying and its tally are told in [scene:s09|Resolution 181].

Several questions remain open on this record. The documents used here do not say what the Arab governments argued in Beirut, beyond the fact that they were heard, nor what King Abdullah told the members in Amman. They do not record how individual members weighed the Jewish Agency's testimony against the Arab governments' statements, or whether the Arab Higher Committee's absence changed any member's vote; the account of the Agency "overwhelming" the committee is one historian's characterization, not a record of members' private responses. And while the boycott is documented as a choice, with its reasons, whether a Palestinian presence would have altered the outcome is a counterfactual that no document can settle. What the record does show is how the recommendation was built: by a committee chosen in a close vote, that heard one Palestinian party in full, heard the Arab case only through Arab governments, visited the displaced-persons camps after a divided vote, and ended seven to three.

sections.h: The Warnings of 1947: State, the Pentagon and Oil
sections.html:
On 22 September 1947 the State Department's senior official for the Middle East put a blunt judgment on paper: the partition of Palestine was "not workable." Eighteen days later the Joint Chiefs of Staff said much the same in a memorandum of their own, and the Secretary of Defense made the argument in public, before a committee of Congress. The oil company that held America's concession in Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, was lobbying the White House directly. A familiar explanation of American policy holds that the strategic costs of backing partition were not understood until much later, and that the gap was one of limited information or the slow communications of the era. The documents do not support that explanation. Each warning was written down, each was dated, and the most important of them was read aloud to the President. The question the record raises is not whether Washington knew, but why what it knew did not decide the outcome.

The answer is not a hidden hand. It is a government divided against itself: career diplomats, the military command and the Defense Secretary on one side, the President's political advisers on the other, with an oil company pressing from outside and a President who had to choose. This section follows the warnings in the order they were made, then the decision that set them aside.

The State Department's regional expert. Loy Henderson directed the State Department's Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, the office whose job was to understand the practical consequences of American policy in the region. He was not a desk theorist. He had served as American ambassador to Iraq in the mid-1940s and had watched at first hand how Arab governments were reacting as the Palestine question took shape. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994]

On 22 September 1947 Henderson sent Secretary of State George Marshall a memorandum warning that partition was "not workable" and would lead to "untold troubles" in the future. He did not present this as a private opinion. His views, he wrote, were shared by "nearly every member of the Foreign Service or of the department who has worked to any appreciable extent on Near Eastern problems." [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] That sentence turns the memo from one official's dissent into a statement of the settled view of the government's own regional specialists. Later historians have described the memo as one of the most perceptive warnings in the documentary record of the period, and it came from inside the government rather than from a critic outside it.

It was not filed and forgotten. Under Secretary of State Robert Lovett was impressed enough by its substance to read it aloud to President Truman himself. [cite:wrmea_henderson_warning_1994] That is a documented escalation: the warning reached the President in the Under Secretary's own voice. What the record does not show is that every one of Henderson's predictions proved right in every detail. Historians continue to debate how much of the violence that followed was inevitable and how much depended on other factors. What is not in dispute is that the warning existed, in writing, before the vote, and that it came from the department's own experts.

The Joint Chiefs of Staff. The military reached the same conclusion through its own channel. On 10 October 1947 the Joint Chiefs of Staff filed a memorandum titled "The Problem of Palestine." It warned that dividing Palestine into Jewish and Arab states would open the way for the Soviet Union to displace American and British influence in the region, and that it would endanger American access to Middle East oil. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] These were the two concerns, regional alignment and access to resources, that drove American policy in the Middle East generally in these years. The memo did not come from diplomats worried about relationships or from oil executives worried about profits. It came from the country's senior military command, whose task was to assess strategic and resource risk.

The timing is what makes the document stand out. On 11 October 1947, one day after the Joint Chiefs filed it, the United States announced its support for the UN partition plan. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] There are few cases in the period with so narrow a gap between a formal military warning and a policy decision that ran against it. The surviving record documents both the warning and the announcement. It does not contain a stated internal explanation of why this warning, arriving when it did, did not change the timetable. The connection between the two has to be inferred; it is not written down.

The Secretary of Defense, in public. James Forrestal had been Secretary of the Navy and became the first Secretary of Defense, overseeing the consolidation of the armed forces under the new Department of Defense created by the National Security Act of 1947, the same year as his warning. He was the Cabinet official most directly responsible for whether the American military could function. Testifying before a House committee, he said that oil was "the life blood of a war machine," and warned that the Arab world's response to partition would threaten the pipelines carrying oil out of the Persian Gulf, the physical infrastructure on which American forces and the American economy relied. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The sources available here do not give the date of the testimony or the name of the committee.

Forrestal's testimony and the Joint Chiefs' memorandum made the same argument through two different routes, one public and political, the other internal and military. The record does not show that his warning decided any particular administration decision. It shows it as one voice in a chorus of institutional warning, alongside Henderson and the Joint Chiefs, that was set aside together. Forrestal's diary entries decrying the "bullying" that preceded the final vote belong to the story of the vote itself, told in [scene:s09|the partition resolution].

The oil company. The oil industry did not wait on the government. A 1947 memorandum submitted to President Truman was published under the title "Oil and the State Department policy on Palestine: the documentary evidence of how ARAMCO attempts to destroy the partition resolution of the United Nations." [cite:loc_aramco_oil_pamphlet] Its title states its thesis: that it presents documentary evidence of an active lobbying campaign by the Arabian American Oil Company against partition. ARAMCO held the core American oil concession in Saudi Arabia, the same relationship that lay behind Franklin Roosevelt's meeting with King Ibn Saud two years earlier. A Middle East turned against the United States by partition threatened that concession's value and its security.

Here the money and the policy can be seen side by side. ARAMCO's interest was commercial; the Joint Chiefs' was strategic; Henderson's was diplomatic. All three pointed in the same direction at the same time. The sources treat them as separate and independent warnings, not as one coordinated effort, and the convergence is better explained by a shared dependence on Gulf oil than by any common direction. Nor does the published memorandum reproduce ARAMCO's internal communications or give a full account of its methods. What the record establishes is that a documented lobbying campaign existed and that it failed: the company with the most money at stake in Arab goodwill did not move the decision.

The decision. None of this changed the outcome. Truman had heard Henderson's memo directly. According to several historical accounts, he was worried about his prospects in the 1948 election, and his adviser Clark Clifford urged him to endorse partition in order to secure Jewish-American votes in key swing states. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Clifford set out that reasoning in a memorandum to Truman in November 1947, naming New York, Pennsylvania and Illinois, and his later memoirs acknowledged both the political framework and Marshall's opposition to it. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The President's own account of his motives, and the case that conviction rather than calculation moved him, are examined in [scene:s08|Truman's succession and his advisers]; the sources used here present the decision as a political calculation weighed against strategic warnings, not as a failure of information.

The chronology needs one correction. One of the sources says the United States voted for partition at the General Assembly "five days" after Henderson's memo. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The dates in the record do not fit that interval. The memo is dated 22 September; the American announcement of support came on 11 October; the General Assembly vote came on 29 November 1947. [cite:jvp_us_admin_partition_timeline] [cite:unscop_wiki] Whatever the "five days" originally referred to, it cannot be the interval between the memo and the vote, and this book follows the dated documents.

What followed was what the warnings had described. In the months after the vote, Palestine descended into serious violence. By 24 February 1948 George Kennan, the State Department's Director of Policy Planning, was warning that only the introduction of foreign troops could now stop it, an escalation of exactly the "untold troubles" Henderson had forecast five months earlier. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] A month later Washington itself would retreat from partition at the United Nations, a reversal told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|the trusteeship proposal].

The map of the decision. The figure below draws the whole structure at once. Its first node is the Anglo-American Committee, whose unanimous report of April 1946 recommended that Palestine be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state; Washington kept only one of its recommendations, the immediate admission of 100,000 Jewish refugees. [cite:avalon_aac] [cite:w_aac] The next three nodes are the warnings of September and October 1947: Henderson at State, the Joint Chiefs, and Forrestal at Defense. A fifth, the Central Intelligence Agency's estimate ORE-55 of 28 November 1947, came the day before the vote and is the subject of the next section. All five lines run into Truman, and all five are marked as overruled. On the other side of the scale sit Clifford and David Niles, who made the domestic political case, and Eddie Jacobson, Truman's former business partner, whose personal channel brought Chaim Weizmann to the President on 18 March 1948. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The final node is the outcome: American support for Resolution 181 in November 1947, and recognition of Israel in May 1948.

Read as a whole, the map shows a structure rather than a plot. Every warning came through an established institution doing the work it existed to do: the regional desk assessing the region, the military assessing strategic risk, the Defense Secretary speaking for readiness, the oil company protecting its concession. The counterweight came through the White House's own political staff and through a personal friendship. The President stood where those lines met, and he had the authority to decide. Neither the warnings nor the political advice were secret. Both were on paper.

What the record does not settle. Two limits apply. First, the record cannot show that a different decision would have produced a better outcome by every measure; that counterfactual cannot be tested. Second, the surviving documents show the warnings and the decision but do not contain a written internal rationale connecting the two, so the weight Truman gave to the 1948 election, against his own stated convictions, rests on the accounts of his advisers and on historians' readings rather than on a single decisive document. What the record does settle is the question the familiar account gets wrong. This was not a blind spot or a failure of communication. The State Department's regional director, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense reached the same conclusion independently, in writing, within a few weeks of each other, and the President heard it. The decision to back partition was taken in full knowledge of the strategic risk, by a government in which those who warned and those who prevailed both had a documented voice.

sections.h: The New CIA's First Warning: ORE-55
sections.html:
When the State Department and the Joint Chiefs of Staff warned against partition in September and October 1947, the Central Intelligence Agency was only weeks old. Ten weeks after it came into being, it delivered a formal estimate of its own, dated the day before the General Assembly vote. It predicted war if partition passed, and it warned that American backing for partition was already costing the United States prestige and would endanger its interests. A common assumption holds that American intelligence either never assessed partition or supported it. The declassified record shows the opposite: the intelligence service assessed it, in writing, and advised against what the government was about to do.

Who ran American intelligence. Before 1947, American foreign intelligence ran through the wartime Office of Strategic Services, which operated from 1942 and led by William J. Donovan, whom Roosevelt appointed. The OSS was dissolved in October 1945, and its analysts and operatives fed the agencies that followed. In 1946 an interim body, the Central Intelligence Group, carried the work forward. [cite:w_oss] The OSS also had a Palestine desk during the war; that history, and the Zionist intelligence service that operated on American soil in the same years, are told with the July 1945 Sonneborn meeting in [scene:s07d|the network founded in 1945].

The National Security Act of 1947 put the system on a permanent footing. It created the Central Intelligence Agency, the National Security Council, and the structure that became the Department of Defense; the CIA came into existence on 18 September 1947. [cite:w_nsa1947] Its first Director of Central Intelligence was Rear Admiral Roscoe Hillenkoetter, appointed by Truman. [cite:w_hillenkoetter] James Forrestal, the first Secretary of Defense, oversaw the department that grew from the same Act, so his warning on oil and the agency's estimate on partition came from two parts of one newly built national-security structure. The CIA was born four days before Loy Henderson sent his "not workable" memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall.

What ORE-55 said. The agency's Office of Reports and Estimates issued ORE-55, titled "The Consequences of the Partition of Palestine," dated 28 November 1947, one day before the General Assembly voted on partition. The declassified document is held in the CIA's own reading room. [cite:cia_ore55] Its summary makes five points. Armed hostilities between Jews and Arabs would break out if the General Assembly adopted partition. The United Nations would be morally bound to enforce its decision. Jewish forces would at first prevail, because of superior organization and equipment. The United States, by backing partition, had already lost much of its prestige in the Arab world. And imposed partition would place American commercial and strategic interests in serious danger. [cite:cia_ore55]

The first prediction was borne out quickly: sustained fighting began as a two-sided civil war inside Palestine within days of the 29 November vote, five and a half months before the armies of neighbouring Arab states crossed any border. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] The second, early Jewish advantage through organization and equipment, belongs to the long argument over the balance of forces taken up later in this chapter. The estimate's concern for American standing in the Arab world restated, in the language of intelligence, what Henderson had put to Marshall and the Joint Chiefs had put in "The Problem of Palestine." Its summary, as recorded here, does not propose an alternative policy.

A chorus of four. Within ten weeks, four separate parts of the American government warned in writing against American sponsorship of partition: the State Department's Near East office, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense, and the new CIA. Each of the first three is set out in [scene:s07j|the warnings of 1947]. They did not form one coordinated campaign. Each institution reached its conclusion through its own work, and the agreement among them is the finding.

Overruled. The President's domestic political advisers, led by Clark Clifford and David Niles, argued the opposite case, and their view prevailed, first in the partition vote and then in the recognition of Israel eleven minutes after its independence was proclaimed on 14 May 1948. The record shows that the warnings were made and read. It does not show them shaping the outcome. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman]

A later chapter of this library carries the story into 1948 and beyond, and adds claims that should be read with care. It states that declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 warned consistently against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds; that CIA assessments noted Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States and predicted that recognition would at once produce armed conflict with Arab states; that the State Department under Marshall opposed recognition on the same grounds; and that Truman's recognition came at 6:11 p.m. on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after the declaration, the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history, so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared. That account cites no specific document for these points, and they are given here as its claims. It goes on to describe the intelligence relationship with Israel that grew out of 1948, a later story told in [scene:cia_s02|1948: the CIA opposes].

One claim in that account does not match the document examined here. It states that a CIA report predicted that an arms embargo would lead to "peaceful coexistence." No such prediction appears in ORE-55's summary as recorded in this book, which predicts the reverse: armed hostilities if partition passed. If such a report exists, it is a different document, and it has not been identified or fetched for this book.

What the record shows, and what it leaves open. The answer to "didn't they know?" is that they did. American intelligence assessed partition, did so in writing, and predicted war and damage to American interests; the decision was taken anyway. [cite:cia_ore55] What the record does not establish is how much weight the President gave the estimate, which arrived on the eve of a vote whose American position had been announced seven weeks earlier. A document dated 28 November could inform the vote on 29 November only if the decision were still open, and the 11 October announcement suggests it was not. Nor does the summary say what Hillenkoetter or Truman did with it once it was delivered. The estimate stands as a record of what the government's new intelligence service believed, not as evidence of what it changed.

sections.h: Who Objected at the Time
sections.html:
It is sometimes said that no one in the United States questioned the campaign for a Jewish state, or the money raised for it, until much later. The record of the 1940s says otherwise. Objections were raised while the decisions were being made, by an anti-Zionist Jewish organization, by a mainstream Jewish body, by a future intelligence officer and a former college dean, by a foreign parliament, and in 1948 by some of the best-known Jewish intellectuals in the country. They were made in public and published. They were also outweighed. This section sets out who objected, what each said, and how large or small each voice was.

The American Council for Judaism. The most direct objection came from Jews who rejected Zionism on religious grounds. The American Council for Judaism was founded in 1942 and led by Lessing Rosenwald, with Rabbi Elmer Berger. It argued that Judaism was a religion, not a nationality, and it opposed partition. [cite:djn_1948_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman] In 1948 it went further and objected to funds raised by the United Jewish Appeal being used "for political and foreign governmental purposes." [cite:djn_1948_acj] The complaint touched the same charitable campaigns whose 1948 proceeds are traced in this chapter's account of Golda Meyerson's American tour: in the Council's view, charity was being put to political ends abroad.

How representative was it? On this the sources agree more than they differ. The Council's own historian documents it as a small minority that the mainstream Jewish organizations opposed, and Zionist sources describe it as a fringe group. [cite:kolsky_acj] [cite:jvl_acj_truman] Its argument mattered less for its numbers than for its content: it showed that the claim to speak for American Jews as a whole on Palestine was contested from inside the community.

The American Jewish Committee. A larger and more established body took a different path. At the congressional hearings of 1944, the American Jewish Committee, a mainstream organization, proposed an international trusteeship for Palestine instead of a Jewish commonwealth. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] This was not anti-Zionism of the Council's kind. It was an alternative arrangement offered by a leading Jewish organization, and it shows that support for a Jewish state was not yet a settled position among American Jewish institutions in the middle of the war. The same 1944 congressional resolutions drew protest abroad: Iraq's parliament formally objected to them. [cite:djn_1944_marshall]

Judah Magnes, president of the Hebrew University, had argued before the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 for a single binational state shared by Arabs and Jews, an argument told in [scene:aac_s01|the Anglo-American Committee]. He did not stop there. In May 1948, the month of independence, Magnes met Truman to press for a federation under trusteeship. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026]

Kermit Roosevelt and the Gildersleeve committee. In 1948 Kermit Roosevelt Jr. published a 24-page pamphlet, "The Partition of Palestine: A Lesson in Pressure Politics." [cite:ptsem_kr_pamphlet] Its title states its argument: that the partition decision had been produced by political pressure. Roosevelt was later the CIA's field commander in Iran's 1953 coup. [cite:w_kermit_jr] With Virginia Gildersleeve, the former dean of Barnard College, he formed the Committee for Justice and Peace in the Holy Land, which warned that "extreme Zionist pressure" risked disrupting national unity. [cite:mosaic_cia_zionism] [cite:w_kermit_jr] These objections echoed, from outside government, the warnings that the State Department, the Joint Chiefs and the Defense Secretary had made from inside it the year before.

Arendt: "There Is Still Time." The fullest argument came in May 1948. Hannah Arendt's essay "To Save the Jewish Homeland: There Is Still Time" appeared in Commentary that month, on pages 398 to 406. [cite:rs_rd5_arendt_commentary] In the historian Robert Manne's account, Arendt argued that Jewish near-unanimity for a state, reached before any settlement with the Arabs, would bring war, and that even a victorious Jewish state would remain small, surrounded by hostile neighbours and absorbed in its own defence. She proposed instead a gradual binational federation, built on mixed Jewish-Arab local councils under United Nations trusteeship with American and British support, and wrote that "It is still not too late." She condemned the Irgun's attacks, including Deir Yassin. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026]

Arendt worked closely with Magnes, and their proposals ran in parallel: a federation, under trusteeship, in place of partition. In 1952 she called Magnes "the conscience of the Jewish people." Manne also reports that she later estimated the Arab "evacuation" of 1948 at 500,000, a figure that sits among the many estimates of the refugee exodus discussed elsewhere in this chapter. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] Her argument is the strongest form of the dissenting case at the time. As her title said, her aim was to save the Jewish homeland; her case was that a state won by war against its neighbours would leave it small, besieged and absorbed in self-defence.

The Einstein–Arendt letter. The last objection of the year was aimed not at partition, which had happened, but at what one wing of the new state's politics had become. A letter dated 2 December 1948 and published in the New York Times on 4 December, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook, protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States. It described his Tnuat Haherut, the Freedom Party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The Irgun's own path from underground army to political party, after the Altalena and the absorption of the militias into one army, is told in [scene:mil_s01|from three militias to one army].

The letter named Deir Yassin directly. It said that on 9 April "terrorist bands" had attacked a "peaceful village, which was not a military objective," and "killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The figure of 240 is the one in circulation in 1948. Later research has revised the count of the dead at Deir Yassin, and the current state of that evidence is set out in [scene:ma_s01|Deir Yassin, the Hadassah convoy and Tantura]. The letter is evidence of what its signers believed and said in December 1948, not a settled casualty figure.

Raised, published, outweighed. These objections differed in their grounds. The Council for Judaism objected in principle to Jewish nationhood; the American Jewish Committee to the form a solution should take; Roosevelt and Gildersleeve to the political pressure behind the decision; Arendt and Magnes to partition by war rather than federation by agreement; and the signers of December 1948 to a specific party and its record. None of them prevailed. Partition was voted, the state was proclaimed and recognized, and the fundraising the Council objected to continued. Formal action on foreign-agent questions came only much later, with the 1962 order under the Foreign Agents Registration Act and the Fulbright hearings of 1963, told in a later volume.

What the record does not settle is how much support these positions had beyond their authors. The sources measure the Council for Judaism only in words, a small minority in its own historian's account and a fringe in Zionist accounts, and give no membership figures. They say nothing about how many Americans read Roosevelt's pamphlet or Arendt's essay. What they do establish is that the objections existed, in print, in the years the decisions were made, and that several of the most pointed came from Jewish organizations and Jewish writers.

sections.h: Resolution 181: The Vote, the Pause and the Numbers
sections.html:
By the autumn of 1947 the question of Palestine had passed from Britain to the United Nations. A special committee had visited the country and recommended partition (its work is told in [scene:s07i|UNSCOP]). It now fell to the General Assembly, the body that had replaced the League of Nations as the forum of the world's states, to decide what to do with that recommendation. [cite:un_unispal_186560] The Assembly did so in two stages: first in an Ad Hoc Committee on Palestine, where the plan was debated and alternatives were voted down, and then in plenary session, where a two-thirds majority was required. [cite:avalon_res181] [cite:britannica_res181]

The familiar account compresses all of this into one image: the nations of the world, gathered peacefully, created Israel by democratic consensus. The documents do not support that picture, and they do not support its mirror image either. What they show is a recorded international act with real weight, adopted after a contested count, a pause, and pressure applied by one great power to small states, while the other great power voted the same way for reasons of its own, and while the majority population of the country in question had no seat in the room.

The first count came in the Ad Hoc Committee on 25 November 1947. There the partition plan was adopted by 25 votes to 13, with 17 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] On the same occasion the committee rejected the alternative: a draft for a single, unitary state, known as Draft Resolution III, failed by 29 votes to 12, with 14 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] A Pakistani amendment that would have capped land ownership at 10% for each community was also rejected, by 22 votes to 8. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] So by 25 November the Assembly had, in committee, turned down both a unitary state and a limit on land holding, and had approved partition. What it had not yet shown was that partition could clear two-thirds in plenary. The accounts this book draws on describe the initial tally of 25 in favor as short of that threshold, and record that the Assembly's president, Aranha, arranged a three-day postponement before the decisive vote. [cite:un_181_records] [cite:un_181_text] The Yearbook excerpt dates the committee vote to 25 November and the plenary vote to 29 November; the material does not record the exact day on which the postponement was called.

The three days are the hinge of the story. A resolution that lacked the votes and then passed after a pause had a specific window in which something changed. The record of that window is uneven. It does not explain every delegation's reasoning, and it was never meant to; what it does document is several of the forces at work inside it, and the plainest of them was the government of the United States. [cite:un_unispal_186560]

The Truman administration's executive branch pushed for a yes vote. Its own foreign-policy and military establishment pushed the other way: the State Department and the Pentagon opposed the push, citing Arab anger and the Cold War stakes of Middle Eastern oil. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The most senior internal objection on record came from James Forrestal. Forrestal had been a Wall Street financier before entering government, had served as Secretary of the Navy, and had become the first Secretary of Defense. He approached Palestine through strategy and petroleum, and believed that alienating the Arab world would endanger American access to Middle Eastern oil and hand an advantage to the Soviet Union. [cite:un_unispal_186560] His diaries, published after his death as The Forrestal Diaries (1951), record his distaste for what he called the "bullying" and "coercion" of small, dependent states to secure their votes, and his conviction that American policy in the Middle East was being driven by domestic political calculation rather than national interest. [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] [cite:un_unispal_186560]

The weight of that evidence comes from its form. A diary written for oneself, and not for an audience, is a first-person and contemporaneous source, stronger than a later recollection or a historian's characterization. It records a sitting cabinet officer objecting to the pressure campaign his own government was running. Its limits are just as clear. Forrestal's diary records his characterization and his objection; it is not an operational record of which tactics were used on which country by which official. His warnings were overruled. He left office early in 1949 and, weeks later, died in a fall from a high window at Bethesda Naval Hospital, where he was being treated for depression and exhaustion. The death was ruled a suicide; some historians have noted contested details, and it remains one of the unsettled anomalies of the period. [cite:un_unispal_186560] His opposition is documented. Nothing in the record ties the manner of his death to it, and this book builds no theory on the coincidence of timing.

The pressure Forrestal deplored had named targets. Three states moved from a no vote or an abstention to a yes during the postponement: Haiti, Liberia and the Philippines. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] The historian Michael Cohen, in Palestine and the Great Powers (1982), documents the shift and connects it to a broader pattern of pressure on smaller, economically dependent states in exactly this window. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition]

Liberia is the best-documented case, because its dependency was so large and so visible. The Firestone Tire and Rubber Company held a rubber concession in Liberia that the sources put at about 1.1 million acres; the company was the country's dominant employer, its largest source of foreign exchange, and, in effect, its economy. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] One account in this book's research dates the concession from 1926 and describes it as roughly one million acres on a 99-year lease. The research also attributes the Firestone material to two works by Cohen: Palestine and the Great Powers (1982) in most places, and Truman and Israel (University of California Press, 1990) in one. Liberia's own ambassador complained that the American delegation had threatened aid cuts to several countries in the same period. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Firestone had no stake in Palestine. The point of the case is the transmission mechanism: a great power's commercial hold over a small client could be turned into that client's vote on a question a hemisphere away. The economic relationship is well documented; the precise way the leverage was exercised is less fully documented than the relationship itself. The corporate pressure and the diplomatic pressure the ambassador described were two separate channels converging on one small state, not one orchestrated scheme.

The Philippines, a recent American possession bound to Washington by aid and security ties, came under American pressure through those economic ties. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] According to the account this book draws on, the Philippine delegation reversed a speech critical of partition and voted yes after American intervention. General Carlos Romulo, the Philippines' own representative, later wrote of being recalled and overruled by his own president: "This particular chapter in history had been exceedingly unpleasant to me." [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] Haiti changed its position after direct communication from the American executive. [cite:militaryhistory_partition_plan] Reports at the time and since describe private approaches to these delegations in the crucial days by influential Americans inside and outside the government; those reports do not name the individuals in the material available here. The evidence is not equal across the three cases. The Liberian link is documented by a serious historian; the exact mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine shifts is less fully documented, and should be held at that lower confidence.

One delegation said publicly what others did privately. Cuba's delegate announced that Cuba would vote against partition "in spite of the pressure that has been brought to bear upon us." [cite:sagepub_price_resisting_partition] The statement confirms that the same campaign reached states that resisted it as well as those that gave way. Cuba appears in the final list of those voting against. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181]

The other great power needed no persuading. The Soviet Union voted yes, and its motive, as the sources describe it, was not sympathy for Zionism, which Soviet doctrine regarded as bourgeois nationalism. Partition would end British rule in Palestine and weaken Britain's position in the Middle East; many of the Jewish community's leaders were socialists who had grown up in the Russian Empire; and a new state looked, in 1947, like a way to reduce a rival empire and gain influence. [cite:un_unispal_186560] The same logic would bring arms to the new state through Czechoslovakia in 1948. Soviet-Israeli relations cooled within a few years, which fits a vote driven by strategy rather than lasting alignment. (The Soviet record is told in [scene:so_s01|the Soviet layer].) Washington and Moscow, already rivals, pushed the same way for opposite reasons. That is convergence, not consensus.

On 29 November 1947 the Assembly adopted the plan by 33 votes to 13, with 10 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The thirteen against were Afghanistan, Cuba, Egypt, Greece, India, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, Syria, Turkey and Yemen. The ten abstaining were Argentina, Chile, China, Colombia, El Salvador, Ethiopia, Honduras, Mexico, the United Kingdom and Yugoslavia. Those in favour included Australia, Canada, France, Poland, Sweden, the Soviet Union, the United States and Uruguay. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] One name in the list carries its own story. Britain, the Mandatory power that would have to hand over the country, abstained.

The resolution was more than a line on a map. It set a timetable. The Mandate was to end "as soon as possible but in any case not later than 1 August 1948." An area with a seaport in the Jewish state was to be evacuated "not later than 1 February 1948." Provisional councils of government were to be in place by 1 April 1948, and the two states were to come into existence two months after the evacuation and "not later than 1 October 1948." A Palestine Commission of five states, Bolivia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Panama and the Philippines, was to carry it out. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The plan, in short, depended on an orderly handover by a power that had abstained, carried out by a commission of five states, against fixed dates.

The two cases presented to the Assembly deserve to be heard in their strongest form. The Jewish Agency's argument, as the UN Yearbook records it, set the plan against the map of the region. The Arab states held about 17,000,000 Arabs in roughly 1,290,000 square miles. Palestine, after the separation of Transjordan, was about 10,000 square miles. On that reckoning the plan gave the Jewish National Home less than one-eighth of the territory originally set aside for it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The Agency accepted the plan, though it disliked the borders and the separation of Jerusalem. The Jewish Virtual Library, a pro-Israel reference source, states that the Jews of Palestine were dissatisfied on both counts but "welcomed the compromise." It also reports, citing the writers Avneri and Horowitz, that Arab League Secretary-General Azzam Pasha told David Horowitz and Abba Eban on 16 September 1947: "The Arab world is not in a compromising mood." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] That exchange is reported second-hand and should be read as such.

The Arab delegations argued on law as well as justice. Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen denounced the plan as contrary to the Charter, illegal and immoral, said they regarded it as a recommendation, and declared that they would not feel bound by it. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] The Palestinian historian Muhsin Yusuf, of Birzeit University, sets out the reasons for rejection as he reads them: fear of later expulsion and of land confiscation; the injustice of granting statehood to a largely immigrant minority while the majority was denied self-determination; and a view of Zionism as a European imperial project. He recalls that the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee in 1946 had promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002]

Behind both arguments lay the same contested facts: how many people lived where, and who owned the land. The Arab majority of Mandate Palestine had no vote in the General Assembly and no direct representation in the decision that partitioned the territory. [cite:britannica_res181] Arab member states voted against; the people most affected were an object of the resolution, not a participant in it. The 1947 British Mandatory census, as summarized in this book's research, counted about 1.3 million Arabs and 630,000 Jews in Palestine, which is the reason the familiar claim that the land was largely empty before 1948 does not survive contact with the record. On the overall shares, the sources agree in outline: Jews were roughly a third of the population (one account gives about 30%), Arabs roughly two-thirds (about 70%). [cite:britannica_res181]

The sources do not agree on the precise allocation, and the disagreement matters, because each figure is used to argue a different case. One account in this book's research gives the Jewish state 55% of the territory and the Arab state 45%, with Jerusalem as an international zone. [cite:britannica_res181] Another, and Yusuf, give the Jewish state 56%; Yusuf gives the Arab state 43%, the other account 44%. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] On population inside the proposed Jewish state, the gap is wider. Yusuf counts about 498,000 Jews and about 494,000 Arabs, a near-even split; the Arab state about 725,000 Arabs and 11,000 Jews; and the Jerusalem district about 105,000 Arabs and 100,000 Jews. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The Jewish Virtual Library, citing the historian Howard Sachar, gives the Jewish state about 5,500 square miles with 538,000 Jews and 397,000 Arabs, and the Arab state 4,500 square miles with 804,000 Arabs and 10,000 Jews; citing Aharon Cohen, it adds that about 60% of the Jewish state was Negev desert. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_myths_partition] Yusuf's figure supports the argument that the Jewish state would have had barely a Jewish majority; Sachar's supports the argument that it would have had a clear one, on land much of which was desert.

Ownership is a separate question from allocation. One account in this book's research says the Jewish population legally owned under a tenth of the land. [cite:britannica_res181] The summary of the pre-1948 record puts Jewish ownership at approximately 7% of the country's land in 1947. Yusuf gives about 6% of Palestine overall, and about 10% of the land inside the proposed Jewish state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] These figures are close enough to agree on the essential point: the plan assigned a majority of the territory to a community that owned a small fraction of it. They differ enough that any single number should be quoted with its source.

The dashboard panel above sets the two ratios side by side: about 7% of the land in Jewish ownership in 1947, and 56% of the territory allotted to the Jewish state by the plan. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002] The overview panel below places the same two figures among the other numbers of the pre-state build-out; its land figures are the ones discussed here, and its other figures are taken up where they belong in this library.

The map that follows shows where the vote sits in the larger structure. Resolution 181 stands at the point where two lines meet, the special committee's recommendation of partition and the American campaign for votes, and from it runs the line marked "legal basis claimed" to the state proclaimed in May 1948. This section has documented the American line as it appears in the record of the three days: an executive pressing for votes, over the objection of its own professionals.

What, then, did the vote decide? It recorded a two-thirds majority for partition, and it created a timetable and a commission. It also left decisive questions open. Those voting against, and several of those abstaining, regarded the resolution as a recommendation; Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Iraq, Syria and Yemen said so in terms. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Within days the country was at war with itself, and the question of who accepted the plan and who fought over it became a separate story, told in [scene:s09b|the two escalations]. The territorial and demographic shares would soon be overtaken: the war of 1948 produced roughly 700,000 Palestinian Arab refugees, a figure documented by Israeli, Palestinian and international historians, including Israeli scholars working in declassified military archives from the 1980s, and Israel's lines in 1949 lay far beyond those of the plan.

Several things remain unsettled. The record establishes the three-day window, the three changed votes and the leverage on Liberia; it does not establish the full mechanism behind the Haitian and Philippine changes, or which American officials made which approaches. The population of the proposed Jewish state is given differently by serious sources, from a near-even split to a clear Jewish majority, and the land shares vary by a point or two depending on the account. And Forrestal's death, ruled a suicide, remains questioned at the margins without any documented link to his politics. What the record does settle is the shape of the decision: not a serene consensus and not a secret plot, but a contested vote, carried over the line by great-power pressure on small states during a three-day scramble, about a people who were not in the room.

sections.h: Who Spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, 1945–1948
sections.html:
In the years when the Jewish Agency was building a diplomatic case, an arms network and a government in waiting, the Arab side of Palestine's politics was being reorganized from outside the country. The central fact of the period is institutional. The decisions that shaped the Palestinian Arab response to partition were taken, for the most part, not in Jerusalem or Jaffa but in the council chambers of the Arab League, in Cairo, Bludan, Aley and Alexandria. The Palestinian leadership had a voice in those rooms, and a record of its own choices. It did not control the instruments that mattered most: money, arms and the recognition of other states.

The League's line was set early and held for more than two years. From its founding in March 1945 until Britain's decision to withdraw in the autumn of 1947, the Arab League consistently supported, in the historian Avi Shlaim's words, a "unitary and independent Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] It was the position the Arab case to the Anglo-American Committee had set out in 1946, when it promised that Jews "will be full citizens" of a Palestinian state. [cite:rs_rd5_yusuf_2002]

The League also rebuilt the Palestinians' own leadership body. The Arab Higher Committee had first been formed in 1936, by the Palestinian parties themselves. After a nine-year hiatus it was re-established in 1946, and this time, Shlaim notes, not by the Palestinian parties but "by a decision of the Arab League." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The difference in origin would define the committee's position for the rest of the period: it spoke for the Palestinian Arabs, but it held its mandate from the League.

Its chairman was Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti of Jerusalem. Al-Husayni had spent the Second World War allied with the Axis powers, a record told in [scene:s07a5|the Arab Revolt and Berlin]. After the war he was refused asylum in Switzerland and held by France, which declined a British proposal to deport him to the Seychelles. In May 1946 he escaped from his residence near Paris to Cairo, where King Faruq of Egypt gave him asylum, and the Arab League made him chairman of the new Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The man who led the Palestinian Arabs through 1947 and 1948 therefore did so from exile in Egypt, under the protection of an Arab king, at the head of a body the League had created.

The League's own decisions on Palestine can be followed session by session. The list compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library from League records, a pro-Israel reference source drawing on the League's documents, gives the following. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] In December 1945 the Council set up a committee to enforce a boycott of Zionist goods (Resolution 16) and provided for up to three Palestinian representatives to sit on the Council (Resolution 17). In March 1946 it approved a company with £E1 million to buy Arab land in Palestine. In June 1946, at Bludan, it made the boycott part of the "creed of the Arab nations," called for land sales to Zionists to be made a crime (Resolution 72), and created a Higher Arab Executive for Palestine (Resolutions 80 and 82). In December 1946 it rejected partition (Resolution 142). In October 1947, at Aley, it adopted a resolution titled "Defending Palestine" (the League's own Resolution 181, not to be confused with the UN resolution of the same number a month later), calling for military preparations along the Arab borders. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague]

The money in these decisions tells its own story. The League's chosen instruments in 1945 and 1946 were economic: a boycott of Zionist goods, a land fund of £E1 million to keep Arab land from being sold, and a call to criminalize sales to Zionists. They were aimed at the mechanism by which the Jewish community had been acquiring land, and they were controlled by the League's member governments rather than by the Palestinian leadership. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] When, in February 1948, the Arab Higher Committee asked the League for a loan to meet its administrative costs, the League refused. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990]

The year 1947 brought the decisive tests. The Arab Higher Committee chose to boycott the United Nations special committee that visited Palestine that summer, a decision told in [scene:s07i|the UNSCOP section]. The UN partition vote of 29 November then moved the question from argument to war. Two League sessions in the months that followed show how far the League was prepared to go, and how far it was not. For the Cairo session of December 1947, the list records no public announcement, and a decision against formal military intervention unless the United States and Britain intervened militarily. In February 1948 the Council approved political, military and economic measures, including the withholding of petroleum concessions and sanctions on states aiding the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_arableague] The League would arm volunteers and threaten oil concessions; it would not, as of December 1947, commit its member states' armies.

The Mufti wanted something the League would not give. At the Council sessions in Aley in October 1947 and Cairo in December 1947, Shlaim writes, al-Husayni "pleaded passionately for the establishment of a shadow government" under the Arab Higher Committee. In February 1948 the League rejected his demand for a government-in-exile, and refused the loan for the committee's administrative costs. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] In the months when the Jewish Agency was preparing the institutions of a state, the Palestinian leadership was refused both a government and the money to run its own committee.

The fighting forces reflected the same division. The Arab Liberation Army was created by the Arab League and led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji; its forces were volunteers. The Army of the Holy War was made up of Palestinian volunteers and was subordinate to the Husayni family. The two acted without cooperating. [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] And one League member had plans of its own. The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict describes the League as divided: King Abdullah of Transjordan "opposed every move toward Palestinian independence" and refused to deal with al-Husayni. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] Abdullah's separate course, and his contacts with the Jewish Agency, are told in [scene:rd5_abdullah|Abdullah between the Agency, Britain and the League].

The League changed course only after the state of Israel had been proclaimed and the Arab armies had entered the war. The story runs past this chapter's end, but its first steps belong here. On 8 July 1948 the League's Political Committee agreed on a "temporary civil administration" for Palestine, responsible to the League. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] On 20 September 1948, at Alexandria, the Political Committee announced an All-Palestine Government with its seat in Gaza, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi. On 22 September the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed Palestine independent, and on 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the Mufti's chairmanship. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] Egypt recognized the new government first, in mid-October 1948, followed by Iraq, and then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia. Britain refused. Abdullah opposed it and said it would not operate in the areas held by his Arab Legion. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990]

Abdullah answered with an assembly of his own. On 1 December 1948, according to Shlaim, a congress of about 3,000 delegates at Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] Abdullah afterwards stripped al-Husayni of the title of Mufti of Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] By the end of 1948, then, two rival claims to speak for the Palestinian Arabs existed: a government in Gaza recognized by five Arab states and chaired in council by the Mufti, and a congress at Jericho that had placed the Arab parts of Palestine under the Transjordanian crown.

Historians weigh this record differently, and the difference is a question about Palestinian agency itself. Shlaim reads it as a story of control: the League reconstituted the Arab Higher Committee, refused it a government-in-exile until September 1948, and armed the Arab Liberation Army under its own command. On this reading the Palestinian leadership's instruments were in other hands, and decisions about Palestine were made by states with their own interests. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] The Dictionary of the Israeli-Palestinian Conflict gives more weight to Palestinian choices, and is harder on them. The Mufti and the Arab Higher Committee pursued their own line, boycotting the UN special committee, pressing for a shadow government and forming the Army of the Holy War; but the 1946 committee was ineffective, its paramilitary forces were uncoordinated, and the League around it was divided. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The two readings are not exclusive. One explains what the Palestinian leadership could not do; the other records what it chose to do, and how weakly it was able to do it.

The record leaves several questions open. The League's session list comes from a compilation of League records rather than from the full minutes, and for the Cairo session of December 1947 it records a decision without any public announcement; what was said in that room is not in the material here. The date and attendance of the Jericho Congress rest on Shlaim's account alone. And the counterfactual that hangs over the period, whether a Palestinian government formed in early 1948, when the Mufti asked for one, would have changed the course of the war, is one the documents cannot answer. What they do establish is the sequence: a League committed to a single Palestinian state, a Palestinian leadership created and financed on the League's terms, a refusal of government in February 1948, and a government granted in September 1948, four months after the Mandate had ended.

sections.h: Acceptance, Rejection and the Two Escalations
sections.html:
One sentence has long served as the summary of what followed the partition vote: Israel accepted, the Arabs rejected and started the war. In its fuller form the familiar account holds that the Arab side rejected a peaceful UN compromise and at once launched a war against a state that had only accepted it. That sentence joins two separate questions. The first is who accepted and who rejected Resolution 181. The second is how the fighting began, and between whom. The record gives each its own answer, and the answers are not the same shape.

On the first question the familiar account is accurate, and it should be said plainly before anything else. The Jewish Agency accepted Resolution 181, reluctantly, with real misgivings about the plan's narrow borders. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab League rejected the plan in its entirety. Jamal Husseini, speaking for the Arab Higher Committee, told the United Nations that the partition line would be "nothing but a line of fire and blood." [cite:wiki_un_partition_plan] [cite:palquest_un_partition_1947] On the narrow matter of who said yes and who said no, the documented record is one-sided. The arguments each side made, and the contested figures behind them, are set out in [scene:s09|the section on the vote].

The second question is where the single sentence starts to mislead. Violence escalated sharply from 1 December 1947, immediately after the vote. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] What followed for the next five and a half months was not yet a war between states. It was a civil war inside Mandate Palestine, between the Jewish and Arab communities and their paramilitary forces, fought while Britain still formally governed the country. The neighbouring Arab states' armies did not cross a border until 15 May 1948.

The forces on the Arab side were of two kinds, and they did not work together. The Arab Liberation Army was created by the Arab League and led by Fawzi al-Qawuqji. Its forces were volunteers, in the historian Magdalena Pogońska-Pol's description "few in number, and poorly armed." [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] The Army of the Holy War (Jaysh al-Jihad al-Muqaddas) was made up of Palestinian volunteers and was subordinate to the Husayni family. The two acted without cooperating, and, Pogońska-Pol concludes, neither stopped the Jewish forces. [cite:rs_rd5_lodz_2019] The Army of the Holy War's commander was Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni. He re-entered Palestine across the Egyptian border in December 1947 and, after the Arab Higher Committee proclaimed a jihad, re-formed and commanded the force. His explosives unit blew up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem; the source does not give the date. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader]

The American government's own historians describe the fighting of these months in terms that favour the familiar account. The State Department's Office of the Historian describes irregular Palestinian Arab bands, attached to Arab Liberation Army units, attacking Jewish cities, settlements and forces, with the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi fighting back. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war] That is the strongest documentary support for the reading that the Arab side began the fighting and the Jewish side responded.

Other documented attacks run the other way. In early January 1948 a car bomb at the former Ottoman government house in Jaffa killed 26 people; the material available here gives the toll but does not name who planted the bomb. On 15 February 1948 Haganah and Palmach forces attacked the village of Qisarya near Haifa. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] [cite:aljazeera_remix_partition_transcript] The sources this book draws on place Qisarya within a documented pattern of Jewish paramilitary attacks on Palestinian towns and villages in the war's first months, well before the massacre at Deir Yassin, which is told in [scene:ma_s01|Deir Yassin, the Hadassah convoy and Tantura]. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] That is the strongest documentary support for the reading that a two-sided war began at once.

The decisive struggle of the spring was over the road to Jerusalem. At the end of March 1948 Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni went to Damascus to seek arms from the Arab League's Military Committee. While he was away, Jewish forces took al-Qastal, the village overlooking the Jerusalem–Jaffa road. He was killed on 8 April 1948 leading the counter-attack. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader] The episode compresses the Palestinian predicament of these months: a local commander who had to travel to the League's Military Committee in Damascus to ask for weapons, and who died on the road he was trying to hold.

Before the Mandate ended, a state army had already entered the fighting in one place. The Arab Legion of Transjordan attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some were massacred. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] The source, the historian Avi Shlaim's seminar notes, does not give the date or the number killed, and this book does not supply them.

The second escalation came on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel's declaration of independence, when the armies of neighbouring Arab states invaded. The war they entered ended in 1949 with Israel's territory extending far beyond the lines of the UN plan. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] The invasion is real, documented and significant; its course, the Arab League's own stated reasons for it and the forces on each side are told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the Arab states' war]. Its place in the sequence is the point here. It followed five and a half months of civil war already under way. It did not start the fighting.

Set against the record, both popular stories lose something. The reading that "the Arabs rejected and attacked" is supported on the vote, which was a clean Arab rejection backed by a public threat of "fire and blood," and it has support on the fighting: the Office of the Historian describes Arab bands attacking and Jewish forces fighting back, Abd al-Qadir's men bombed the Jewish Agency building, and the Arab Legion attacked Gush Etzion before the Mandate ended. What it cannot carry is the claim that the war began on 15 May with an unprovoked attack on a purely defensive new state. By then the country had been at war for five and a half months, with documented Jewish paramilitary attacks on Arab villages and towns among the events of those months.

The reading that "a two-sided war began at once" is supported by the dates: violence from 1 December, attacks documented in both directions, Qisarya in February, the Jerusalem road in April. What it cannot carry is any suggestion that the rejection was incidental, or that Arab forces were merely reactive. The Arab Higher Committee had promised resistance in advance, and the Army of the Holy War and the Arab Liberation Army were organized to fight. Treating the sequence as a single, uninterrupted chain from the vote to the invasion, in either direction, skips over the civil-war phase that the record documents: a one-sided vote, then a two-sided civil war, then a state-level invasion.

Some things this record does not settle. It does not establish who fired first in the opening days of December, and the sources here do not attempt to. It does not give a count of the dead in the civil-war months, on either side. It leaves the perpetrator of the Jaffa car bomb unnamed in the material available, and leaves the date of the Jewish Agency bombing and the date and toll of Gush Etzion unstated. Nor does it deliver a verdict on responsibility: it does not argue that the Arab League's rejection was justified, or that the later invasion was unprovoked. It establishes the shape of the sequence, and leaves the moral weighing of each side's decisions within it to the reader.

sections.h: After the Vote: Jews of the Arab World, 1947–1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 is usually told as a war inside Palestine, and its refugees as one people's loss. The record of the same months shows a second set of events running in parallel, outside Palestine. From the day after the partition vote, Jewish communities in Syria, Egypt, Lebanon, Aden, Bahrain, Iraq, Libya and Yemen came under attack from mobs, under arrest and sequestration by governments, and in Iraq under a law that made Zionism a crime. These were not acts of "the Arabs" in general. Each was carried out by a named government, a mob in a named city, or a named organization, and this section ties each one to its author. Together they began the decline of these communities, a story that runs well past 1948 and is set beside the Palestinian displacement in [scene:s00e3|two displacements].

The riots of 30 November to 5 December 1947. On 30 November 1947, the day after the General Assembly voted for partition, anti-Jewish riots broke out in Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo, Beirut and Aden, according to the Center for Israel Education. In Cairo, the same account reports, leaders of al-Azhar declared a holy war against the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] The worst damage that the sources record in Syria was in Aleppo. A mob broke into the Great Synagogue, destroyed Torah scrolls and damaged the Aleppo Codex; most of the Codex was saved and smuggled to Jerusalem in 1958. Across the city, according to the same account, 150 Jewish homes, 50 shops, five schools and 18 synagogues were destroyed. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] On 5 December 1947, in Bahrain, Jewish homes and shops were looted, the synagogue was destroyed and one Jewish woman was killed. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities]

The deadliest of these riots took place in Aden, then a British colony. The Center for Israel Education lists Aden among the cities where violence broke out after the vote; the accounts of Aden itself date the riots there from 2 December 1947. The toll is disputed. The Center for Israel Education gives 82 Jews killed and 76 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_arabcities] The Jewish Virtual Library, which credits Wikipedia for its entry, gives between 76 and 82 Jews killed, and also 38 others killed: 33 Arabs, four Indian Muslims and one Somali. It records that 106 of the 170 Jewish-owned shops in Crater were looted. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_aden] A study of 1951 gives 76 killed and 78 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The sources agree on the order of magnitude, between 76 and 82 Jewish dead, and differ on the exact count. The sources here do not say how the 38 others died.

What the 1951 study is. Much of what is known about the official measures of 1948 comes from one document, and the reader should know what it is. It is "The Situation of Jews in Moslem Countries," by H. Dewey Anderson, chapter XIV of The Arab Refugee Problem, a set of proposals submitted to the United Nations General Assembly in December 1951. It is available today through the Center for Israel Education, which presents it as a UN report. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] It is a contemporary compilation by a named author, written three years after the events and placed inside a work about the Arab refugees. It is not a resolution or a finding of the General Assembly. Its dates and figures are specific, and they are used below as Anderson's, attributed to him, because the sources gathered for this book do not test them against the governments' own records.

Egypt: arrests, sequestration and bombings. When the Arab armies entered Palestine in May 1948, the Egyptian government turned against the Jews of its own cities. According to Anderson, more than 1,000 Jews were arrested in Cairo on 15 May 1948. Proclamation No. 26, issued on 29 May, sequestered the property of internees; of the 68 sequestration orders issued up to 30 September, 67 involved Jews. Proclamation No. 30, of 6 June, allowed Jews to be searched without a warrant. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] These were acts of state, published as proclamations, and the ratio of 67 to 68 shows on whom they fell.

Violence followed in Cairo's Jewish quarters. On 20 June 1948 a bombing struck the Karaite quarter. Anderson records 12 houses destroyed and 20 people killed; Wikipedia, citing the historian Beinin, gives 22 killed and 41 wounded. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] The Cicurel department store was bombed on 19 July, and a bombing on 22 September killed 19 people. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] In November 1948 the government arrested 32 leaders of the Muslim Brotherhood and banned the organization, and in a trial in 1950 members of the Brotherhood were charged with the bombings of June to November. [cite:rs_rd5_wiki_cairo1948] The sources gathered here record the charge; they do not record the verdict.

Iraq: a law, a hanging and an armistice never signed. Iraq took part in the war from the start.
