It joined the invasion on 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, and when the fighting ended it was the only Arab state that had fought which refused to sign an armistice with Israel, leaving a formal state of war that, in the Israeli government's account, has never ended. [cite:govil_aliyah] The invasion itself is told in the section on the Arab states' war. At home, according to accounts of the Iraqi Jewish community, the measures escalated after the partition vote from mob violence to the confiscation of property and prosecutions those accounts call trumped-up. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia]

The central instrument was a law of July 1948, and the sources describe its penalty differently. Anderson writes that it made Zionist activity punishable by death or by at least seven years' imprisonment. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] An account in Yated Ne'eman dates the law to 19 July 1948 and gives the penalty as up to seven years in prison. It adds that every Jew was presumed to be a Zionist under the law, so that it worked as a blanket criminalization of the community, and that the testimony of two Muslim witnesses was enough to convict, with little means of appeal. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] The two accounts agree on the month and on the law's target; they disagree on the maximum and minimum sentence, and this book cannot settle which is right from the sources it holds.

Further orders followed. On 28 August 1948 Jews were barred from banking and from dealing in foreign currency, and on 19 October they were ordered discharged from government departments, according to Anderson. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] Between those two dates came the case that the community's own accounts treat as the turning point. On 23 September 1948 Shafiq Ades, a prominent and well-connected Jewish businessman, was publicly hanged in Basra on charges of selling weapons to Israel and to the Iraqi Communist Party. His body was left hanging for hours. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The case is widely cited as the event that convinced much of the community that no one, however powerful, was safe. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] That is a judgement about how Iraqi Jews read the hanging, recorded by those who wrote their history; the charges themselves were never tested in any proceeding the sources describe.

Syria, Libya and Yemen. Anderson records that on 15 May 1948, the same day as the Cairo arrests, 250 Jews were imprisoned in Aleppo; that a "second wave of violence" struck the Jews of Tripoli, in Libya, on 14 June 1948; and that in December 1948 the ruler of Yemen permitted the country's Jews to leave. In what became known as "Magic Carpet," 45,009 were evacuated. [cite:rs_rd5_anderson_1951] The airlift itself belongs to the years after this chapter and is told in [scene:ye_s01|the Yemeni airlift].

What 1948 began. The events of 1947–48 were a beginning, not the whole of the story. Over the following decades the large Jewish communities of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt, Syria and North Africa shrank dramatically. Estimates of the total who left the Arab countries and Iran between 1948 and the 1970s commonly fall between 800,000 and 900,000 people, and the causes varied by country: emigration, pressure, expulsion and state persecution in different proportions. [cite:w_jewish_exodus_arab] Morocco shows the variety. Its Jewish community, rooted there for some two thousand years, numbered in the hundreds of thousands in the 1940s and largely emigrated after 1948, mostly to Israel; between 1961 and 1964 about 97,000 left in Operation Yachin, with payments to the Moroccan government that historians record. [cite:w_yachin] The later exodus from Iraq is told in [scene:irq_e05|the Iraqi exodus].

How to read this record. The war of 1948 is often described simply as a war between Israel and its neighbours, and Iraq's part in it as one army among several. The record of these months adds two things that description leaves out. Iraq's war had a domestic side, a law and a public hanging aimed at its own Jewish citizens, and it ended without the armistice every other Arab combatant signed. [cite:govil_aliyah] [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] And the same pattern, in different degrees, appears in Egypt, Syria, Aden, Bahrain and Libya: riots on the day after the vote, the destruction of synagogues, killings, and proclamations and laws aimed at Jews by the governments of Egypt and Iraq. That was antisemitic violence and discrimination, and it should be called so. The record does not support treating it as the conduct of an entire people or faith. It names mobs in particular cities, particular governments issuing particular orders, the leaders of a particular institution, al-Azhar, declaring holy war, and, in Cairo, a particular organization whose members were charged in court.

What the record does not settle. The exact death tolls in Aden and in the Cairo bombings remain in dispute, as the figures above show. The penalty in Iraq's July 1948 law is given differently by the two sources. Much of the official record of 1948 reaches this book through a single compilation, Anderson's, made in 1951 for a debate about refugees, and the governments' own archives are not among the sources used here. The outcome of the 1950 trial in Cairo is not recorded in them. Nor do they give the number of Jews who left the Arab countries in 1948 itself, as distinct from the totals for the decades that followed. What is established is the pattern of the first thirteen months: violence by mobs, arrests and sequestration by governments, and a law in Iraq that put a whole community under suspicion.

sections.h: Golda Meyerson's Tour: The Money of Early 1948
sections.html:
A common account holds that the new state was built and defended chiefly on its own resources. The man who led it said otherwise. When David Ben-Gurion looked back on the winter of 1948, he credited a single fundraising campaign in the United States, and the woman who ran it, with making the state possible. The campaign lasted about two months. It was run by Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, and it depended on an American fundraising network that had been built over a quarter of a century and that, through one man, reached directly into the arms network of the same years.

A failed trip, and a substitute. After the partition vote of November 1947, the Jewish Agency needed money quickly. Its treasurer, Eliezer Kaplan, travelled to the United States to raise $7 million and failed. Ben-Gurion proposed going himself; the Agency's executive sent Meyerson instead. [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:reformjudaism_golda] She was then acting head of the Jewish Agency's political department, and she left for America in January 1948. [cite:jta_golda_1948]

The organizer. Her opening came through Henry Montor, executive vice-chairman of the United Jewish Appeal. Montor pressed the Council of Jewish Federations to give her a speaking slot at its assembly in Chicago, and it did. [cite:jta_golda_1948] He was not a newcomer to the cause's covert side. Three years earlier, in 1945, Montor had gathered seventeen wealthy businessmen to meet Ben-Gurion at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment, the meeting that founded the arms-buying network described in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting]. [cite:jta_golda_1948] The same organizer thus stood behind both the network that bought weapons and the public appeal that paid for them.

The money. The figures come from later reporting, and they are given here as reported. The early response, according to reports, came to about $25 million in the first month. Chicago's Jewish federation took out a $5 million loan and handed the proceeds to her. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jewishpress_golda_25m] She went on to some twenty cities, and when she returned on 19 March 1948 she was reported to have raised $50 million. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m] By one comparison, that was several times Saudi Arabia's oil revenue for 1947. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] The money went largely to weapons, including the arms bought from Czechoslovakia. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m]

Ben-Gurion's response is on record in his own words. He wrote in his diary that her success was "the only ray of light," and he said that history would record that "there was a Jewish woman who got the money which made the state possible." [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:yu_golda_archives] Her return date gives the diary entry its context. She came home on 19 March 1948, the same day the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out by peaceful means, a retreat told in [scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat]. The American government was stepping back from partition in the week that private American money arrived to pay for its defence.

The machinery behind the speech. The tour was a personal campaign, but it ran on structure. Ben-Gurion's tribute, in the record's own summary, credits American donors' money raised through a federation-and-appeal network that had been built since the 1920s and that, through Montor, overlapped directly with the arms network. [cite:jta_golda_1948] [cite:yu_golda_archives] Meyerson did not have to build an audience. The federations already existed in the cities she visited, and the Chicago assembly brought their leaders into one room. Kaplan had failed to raise $7 million; Meyerson, speaking through that apparatus, was reported to have raised about seven times as much in about two months.

The library's funding ledgers set the tour inside the larger flow of American money that year. The first chart below ranks the dollar sums in the record. The reported $50 million is the second-largest sum shown, behind only the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949, and well ahead of the $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms in 1948.

The tour also overlapped with the United Jewish Appeal's regular campaign, so its sum cannot simply be added to the appeal's. The ledger, compiled from the JTA archive's year-end report on the 1948 campaign, records a record $150 million for the United Jewish Appeal that year, about $2.0 billion in today's dollars. Of that, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, the share for Palestine and then Israel; $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe; and $10.4 million to resettlement in the United States. The Palestine share was just under half. The ledger notes that Keren Hayesod's own history lists defence among the things its money financed before statehood, and that in 1948 Meyerson's campaign money went largely to weapons.

In constant dollars the 1948 campaign stands at the top of a steep rise. The ledger converts the appeal's totals to 2025 dollars: about $0.32 billion in its first year, 1939; an average of about $0.35 billion a year during the war; then about $1.65 billion in 1946, about $1.59 billion in 1947 and about $2.0 billion in 1948. The peak year was the year of the war.

What the record supports, and what it does not. The documents support three things firmly. Kaplan's attempt failed; Meyerson's succeeded on a scale far beyond his target; and the money paid largely for arms, including the Czechoslovak arms told in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline]. They also support the point Ben-Gurion made himself: the claim that the state was built chiefly on its own resources does not survive his own account of where its money came from in the months before independence. What they do not support is any reading of the money as American government money. It came from private donors through private institutions, and in the same weeks the American government was retreating from partition and keeping its arms embargo in place.

The gaps are real. The $25 million and $50 million figures are reported totals, not audited accounts, and the sources do not say how much of the $50 million was new money and how much came through the United Jewish Appeal's own campaign. They do not break down what the money bought item by item, or how much of it reached Czechoslovakia. The comparison with Saudi oil revenue is given without its underlying figure. Ben-Gurion's verdict is a judgement, by the person best placed to make it, and not a measurement; other parts of this chapter show that weapons, diplomacy and the state's own forces each have a claim on the outcome of 1948.

sections.h: The Arms Network in Operation, 1945–1948
sections.html:
The network founded at Rudolf Sonneborn's apartment in 1945, described in [scene:s07d|the Sonneborn meeting], was not a fund or a statement of intent. For three years it bought real weapons, aircraft and machinery in the United States and moved them, through a set of named front operations and transit countries, to the Haganah in Palestine. Two claims about it are common, and the record contradicts both. One is that American law enforcement knew nothing of an organized effort to arm the Haganah before 1948. The other is that the new state's founding war was armed only by its own government. The documents show federal agencies watching parts of the operation while it ran, and a large share of the material reaching Palestine from private American buyers through third countries.

The routes. The network's first problem was the law. Both the United States and Britain maintained embargoes on arms for Palestine, and the network's purchases were designed to defeat them. Academic research on the operation documents purchases of trucks, radios, aircraft parts and weapons components, funnelled through countries that were neutral in the conflict: Czechoslovakia, Panama, Mexico, Canada and France. [cite:mexico_arms] Mexico was one of the named and documented transit points, not an incidental stop. [cite:mexico_arms] The method was simple to describe and hard to police. Goods left the United States for a country that was not at war, and were re-shipped from there to Haganah operatives. The research documents the strategy and the countries; it does not give a shipment-by-shipment ledger of what went by which route. [cite:mexico_arms]

The scale. By late January 1948 the operation had already moved thousands of tons of disguised military material. Over its whole life it sent some 800 disguised shipments, roughly 2,400 tons, and most of them reached their destination before the war ended. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The volume matters for the second common claim. The weapons that the new state carried into 1948 were bought in part by American citizens, with American donations, and moved through other countries' ports; the Czechoslovak supply that began in January 1948 is the other half of that story, told in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak pipeline].

Al Schwimmer's airline. The most elaborate single operation was in the air. Al Schwimmer, a veteran of the US Army's Air Transport Command, bought roughly 30 surplus American warplanes and moved them toward Palestine via Panama, Brazil and Casablanca, evading the FBI and the State Department for months. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] The two accounts of his operation name its cover differently. One describes a fictitious Panamanian airline, Lineas Aereas de Panama, created to carry the aircraft. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] The other describes a near-bankrupt charter airline, Service Airways Inc., used as commercial cover to fly aircraft and parts out of the United States. [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] The accounts do not say whether both companies were used at different stages, and this book does not resolve the point.

The crate on the New Jersey dock. By the end of January 1948, a crate marked "used industrial machinery" broke apart while it was being loaded onto a freighter in New Jersey, spilling explosives onto the dock. It was one of 76 identical crates bound for Palestine. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] The two accounts weigh the incident differently. In one, the accidental spill, not investigative work, gave US authorities their first concrete evidence that the network existed. [cite:schwimmer_sdjw] In the other, the FBI, the Customs Service and other federal authorities had already been uncovering parts of the network while it operated, and the spill accelerated their work into open prosecution. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The two can be read together: the first account itself claims only that the crate supplied the first concrete evidence, not that the authorities had no suspicion before it.

What the government knew. The fuller record supports the second account. Later scholarship and reporting from the era of declassification confirm that the FBI, the Customs Service and the intelligence units descended from the wartime OSS each uncovered parts of the smuggling operation while it was running, not after the fact. A National Security Council memorandum of the period referred to the operation directly. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] Enforcement was real but partial. Some participants were charged and most were not, and the network's core organizers were never prosecuted. [cite:ampalestine_haganah] Most of the material, as noted, arrived. [cite:mexico_arms_1948] The pattern is not one of a government blind to the network. It is one of agencies that saw parts of it and a government that prosecuted a few of the people at its edges.

A separate investigation. One thing the FBI was doing in the same months is easily confused with this case, and the record keeps them apart. Records obtained decades later under the Freedom of Information Act by the Cato Institute show that the FBI maintained an investigative focus on the Zionist Organization of America, founded in 1897, in 1947–48. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] Its reason was not the arms network. The Bureau believed, incorrectly on the evidence of what it overheard, that the organization had been infiltrated or influenced by Communists. The activity it monitored was constitutionally protected and showed no violation of federal law by the organization. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] Between September 1947 and May 1948 the FBI also wiretapped Sol Rotenberg, a Jewish political activist tied to the International Workers Order, on the theory that the Order was a Communist Party front. [cite:cato_fbi_wiretap] These were two distinct concerns running at the same time: a Neutrality Act investigation of the arms network, and a counter-subversion inquiry into suspected Communist influence. Reading the wiretaps as part of the arms case, or the arms case as an outgrowth of the wiretaps, merges two files the record keeps separate.

The trial and the pardons. Nine men involved in the network were tried in a federal courthouse in Los Angeles in 1950. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] Schwimmer was convicted under the Neutrality Act and lost his American citizenship. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] One account adds that he was fined $10,000. [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] He later moved to Israel and led its aircraft industry; one account says he founded Israel Aerospace Industries, the other that he became head of Israel Aircraft Industries. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] Charlie Winters was charged with conspiracy to export military aircraft in violation of the Neutrality Act, pleaded guilty and served 18 months in prison. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_winters] One account describes him as the only participant in the network with a documented felony conviction for this activity. [cite:sdjw_winters]

The sources disagree on several details of the legal record, and the disagreements are set out below rather than resolved. Each account is internally specific; neither is obviously the stronger, and the primary court and pardon records are not among the sources used here.

On every version, both men were eventually pardoned by an American president, decades after the trial. [cite:schwimmer_wiki] [cite:sdjw_schwimmer] [cite:sdjw_winters] A man convicted of breaking the Neutrality Act went on to lead the new state's aircraft industry, and the United States later formally forgave both him and Winters. The arc runs from a federal prohibition, through a selective prosecution, to official absolution.

What the record does not settle. The documents establish the routes, the scale of some 800 shipments and roughly 2,400 tons, the Los Angeles trial and the pardons. They do not provide a full ledger of what moved by which route, or a total cost; the library's funding ledger records Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft without a price. They name only two of the nine men tried in 1950 and do not give the charges and sentences of the other seven. They do not explain why the network's core organizers were never prosecuted while the agencies knew of its activity, and they disagree on the details shown above. The question of who decided to prosecute so few, and why, remains open.

sections.h: "Czechoslovak Arms Saved the State": The Pipeline of 1948
sections.html:
A familiar belief holds that the United States armed Israel from its founding. In 1948 it did the opposite. Washington kept its arms embargo in place, and the government that sold the Jewish side the fighters and rifles it used in the war was communist Czechoslovakia, acting with Soviet consent. Some of the money that paid for them was raised in the United States, but the weapons came from the East. The American military relationship with Israel that later defined its arms supply did not exist in 1948. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel]

The first contract. The pipeline opened before the state did. On 14 January 1948 the Jewish Agency signed its first arms contract with Czechoslovakia, coordinated through "Secretariat D" of the state engineering-works holding. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:wiki_operation_balak] Two dates frame it. It came four months before independence, at a time when the purchaser was not a state but the Agency that represented the Jewish community of Palestine. And it came three months before the United Nations Security Council imposed its own arms embargo on 17 April 1948, in Resolution 46. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:wiki_operation_balak] A third date sits awkwardly between them. Czechoslovakia became communist in the coup of February 1948, a month after the first contract, and from then on sold with Stalin's consent. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] The sources record Soviet consent for the sales; they do not explain how Moscow's position related to a contract signed before the coup.

Operation Balak. The most striking deliveries came by air. From May to August 1948 a secret airlift, Operation Balak, ran from the Žatec airfield west of Prague, code-named "Zebra," to Ekron. It carried arms, ammunition and personnel, and it carried fighters: the Avia S-199, a Czech-built derivative of the German Messerschmitt Bf 109, dismantled and crated inside C-46 and C-54 transport aircraft. About 25 were delivered, and they formed 101 Squadron. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:machal_avia_s199] The airlift did not stay secret for long. A defector exposed the Zebra base, the United States pressed the United Nations to have it closed, and operations moved to Nikšić in Yugoslavia. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:machal_avia_s199] The episode shows Washington's posture plainly: it did not supply arms, and it acted to shut down the supply that was reaching the new state.

The rifles. More came by sea. The deliveries included some 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles and heavy weapons, many of them originally produced for the Wehrmacht. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] The rifles of the new state's first war were, in large part, German-pattern army rifles sold by a Soviet-bloc government.

The other side's suppliers. Czechoslovakia was not the only outside power arming a party to the war. Britain, according to the same sources, supplied aircraft and training to the Arab air forces, while the United States maintained its embargo. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] And the Soviet bloc's choice was not lasting. Within months, the record notes, it began shipping the same kind of weapons toward the Arab side. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] The Soviet diplomacy behind the bloc's position in 1947–48 is told in [scene:so_s01|the Soviet layer]; what the arms record shows is a convergence of interest for a period, not an alliance.

The price. In a 1952 report, the Czechoslovak Foreign Minister, Viliam Široký, put the receipts from the sales at almost $14.5 million. [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] That is the seller's own figure, given four years later, and it is the one the record can cite to a named official. The library's funding ledger shows how uncertain the true cost is. It gives a range for the Czechoslovak arms from $14.5 million to about $90 million, about $0.19 billion to $1.2 billion in today's dollars, and notes that estimates vary up to six-fold. It sets this beside the reported $50 million from Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent mostly on arms, $3 million in letters of credit from Nicaragua's Somoza for arms buying, and Al Schwimmer's roughly 30 aircraft, whose cost the record does not total. Its conclusion is that no audited grand total for the war's arms has been published.

The two ends of the Czechoslovak range each have a case. The low figure has a documentary source in the seller's foreign minister, and it measures receipts. The higher estimates in the ledger are not attributed in the sources used here to a named document, and this book cannot say what they include that Široký's figure leaves out. What is clear is the link between the two halves of the year's money. The reported $50 million that Golda Meyerson brought back from the United States financed weapons purchases, including those from Czechoslovakia, as told in [scene:us_s07|Golda Meyerson's tour]. [cite:reformjudaism_golda] [cite:jwa_golda_50m] American private money paid, in part, for Soviet-bloc arms.

The library's summary of the money behind the state sets these sums side by side: the reported $50 million from the 1948 tour; about $14.5 million paid for Czechoslovak arms, with Stalin's approval; and a $100 million US Export-Import Bank loan earmarked for Israel after recognition. Only the last came from the American government, and it was a loan for building the state, not weapons.

When American arms came. The aid ledger's timeline fixes the American side. From 1948 to 1961 US aid to Israel consisted of economic aid and loans only; Washington avoided selling arms for fear of alienating the Arab oil states. The first American military aid came in 1962, and then as loans. The larger military relationship that followed, from the first congressional earmark in 1971 to the airlift of 1973 and beyond, belongs to later volumes of this library.

Ben-Gurion's verdict. Ben-Gurion left no doubt about how he weighed the shipments. In 1968 he said: "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely." [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] It is the judgement of the man who led the war, given twenty years later. It sits beside his tribute to Meyerson's fundraising as "the money which made the state possible," and the two are not in conflict: the first, in part, paid for the second.

What the record does not settle. The sources establish the first contract's date, the airlift's route and months, the number of fighters and rifles, and Široký's figure. They do not settle the true price, which ranges six-fold in the estimates, or itemize what was bought for it. They do not show how the January contract, signed before the communist coup, related to the Soviet consent recorded afterwards. They name the defector who exposed the Zebra base only as a defector. And Ben-Gurion's verdict, however weighty, is an assessment rather than a measurement of how much the Czechoslovak weapons, as against other factors, decided the war; the balance of forces is examined separately in this chapter.

sections.h: Plan Dalet: The Document and the Argument
sections.html:
On 10 March 1948 the general staff of the Haganah, the largest Jewish armed force in Palestine, issued the operational plan that would govern its conduct in the weeks before and after the British withdrawal. In Hebrew it was Tochnit Dalet; in English it is usually called Plan D or Plan Dalet. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] A long-standing popular account holds that Palestinians left their homes in 1948 of their own accord, at the urging of Arab leaders, before Jewish forces did anything to them. That account has to reckon with this document. Its text is a primary source and is not in dispute. What historians dispute, working from the same archives, is what the plan was for.

The plan did not come from nowhere. It was the fourth in a series. Walid Khalidi, the Palestinian historian who first set out the argument that it was a master plan, dates the earlier Plan B to September 1945 and Plan C, or Gimmel, to May 1946. Plan C, he writes, was put into practice from 1 December 1947, the first day of the fighting that followed the United Nations vote. Plan D was, in his words, "finalized on 10 March 1948," and its operational objectives were put into practice from 1 April 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The dates matter. Plan D was issued nine days before the United States told the Security Council that partition could not be carried out peacefully ([scene:rd5_trusteeship|Washington's retreat]), and its operations began three weeks later.

Khalidi first made his case in a 1961 essay titled "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine." When the Journal of Palestine Studies republished it in its Autumn 1988 issue (volume 18, number 1), it printed the text of Plan D, dated 10 March 1948, as an appendix. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The quotations below are from that translation.

The plan opens with its purpose: "The objective of this plan is to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders." Its scope reached past those borders, to "areas of Jewish settlement and concentration which are located outside the borders." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The plan's provisions on villages are the passage at the center of the argument. They applied to villages inside and near the territory to be held. Brigades were to encircle and search them, and to garrison or demolish them according to their strategic position. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] Section 4(b) sets out the alternative to holding a village:

Destruction of villages (setting fire to, blowing up, and planting mines in the debris)

Where resistance was met, the same section provides, "the population must be expelled outside the borders of the state." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] In practical terms, the text gave brigade commanders two courses for a village in or near their area: hold it if it submitted, or, if it resisted, destroy it and expel its people. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

The mechanism is worth stating plainly. The plan was issued from the top, by the general staff. It was carried out by brigades. And it left the judgment at the point of contact, whether a village had resisted, to the commanders on the spot. That last feature is the hinge on which the scholarly argument turns. A reader who sees the text as a design for removing a population reads the discretion as a formality. A reader who sees it as a military plan reads the same discretion as the reason outcomes differed from place to place.

Khalidi also listed the operations that, in his account, carried the plan out between 1 April and 14 May 1948. The names, dates and objectives below are as he gives them. They are his translations and his characterizations, not an Israeli official list. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988]

The list covers the weeks in which the mixed towns fell: Haifa, Jaffa, Safed and others, with the depopulation of several hundred villages. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] What happened in Tiberias and Haifa, and the separate argument over why Haifa's Arab population left, are told in [scene:rd5_cities|the fall of the mixed towns]. One discrepancy belongs here. In this list Khalidi assigns Haifa to Misparayim and the Jaffa villages to Chametz. In his separate study of Haifa he writes that the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The two accounts by the same historian do not line up, and the material gathered for this book does not resolve which name the Haifa operation finally carried.

Khalidi's own text contains a correction that is easy to miss. He wrote that "Up to 1 March not one single Arab village had been vacated by its inhabitants." A footnote amends the sentence: at least ten villages had been captured by 1 March 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The correction cuts in a specific direction. It weakens the cleanest form of his chronology, in which nothing happened to villages before Plan D. It does not support the older account of a voluntary departure, since the villages in question were captured, not abandoned on instructions.

On what the plan meant, three positions stand side by side.

The first treats Plan Dalet as a master plan. Khalidi's 1961 essay and Ilan Pappé's 2006 book The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine read it as the blueprint for deliberately removing the Arab population from the territory of the Jewish state. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] In his 1988 restatement Khalidi argued that Plan D created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product. He called the claim that Arab leaders had ordered an evacuation "a piece of mythmaking," citing the radio monitoring records of the BBC and of FBIS. And he faulted Benny Morris for treating the exodus in "an historical vacuum." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Pappé went further on the question of terms, arguing that the plan meets the United Nations definition of ethnic cleansing. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] The strongest form of this case rests on the document's own words: destruction and expulsion were written into an order issued before the Arab states invaded, and the operations Khalidi lists began within three weeks of it.

The second reading is Benny Morris's. His archival work documented the expulsions of 1948 in detail. He reads Plan Dalet as a military plan to secure territory and lines of communication before the Arab states' invasion. Its village provisions, in his account, gave local commanders discretion, which they exercised in some places and not others. Expulsions were decided at brigade level rather than ordered from the center, and the outcome was produced by war and by those local decisions, not by a single master plan. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] The strongest form of this case rests on the same text read differently: the plan states a military objective, makes expulsion conditional on resistance, and, in Morris's reading, the record of 1948 shows villages treated in different ways under the same orders.

Between these stand other historians, and a third position that this book takes as its own working rule. The text of Plan Dalet is settled, and so is the depopulation that followed. Whether the text caused the depopulation by design, or supplied the frame within which local commanders brought it about, is a genuine dispute among serious historians working from the same archives. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet]

The disagreement is narrower than it first appears, and it does not run where the popular account would place it. None of the three positions supports the claim that Palestinians left before any Jewish forces acted. Khalidi's own footnote records villages captured before March. Morris, whose reading is the less sweeping, is also the historian whose research documented the expulsions. What remains in dispute is design and cause, not whether expulsions took place. How large a part Arab leaders' orders played is a separate question, and the estimate most often cited, from an Israeli army intelligence report of June 1948, is taken up in [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugee section]. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

Several things the record gathered here does not settle. It does not show what written instructions reached each brigade, or how each commander read the village clauses on the day. The operation list rests on Khalidi's translations and characterizations, and his two accounts of the Haifa operation's name do not agree. And the central question, whether the plan was written to produce the exodus or produced it through the choices of men in the field, remains open among historians who have read the same files. This book records the document and the readings, and leaves the reader to set them against the events that follow.

sections.h: Washington Retreats: The Trusteeship Proposal of March 1948
sections.html:
On 18 March 1948 Harry Truman received Chaim Weizmann at the White House. He had refused to see the Zionist leader through official State Department channels, and the meeting happened only because Eddie Jacobson, his former partner in a Kansas City clothing store, asked him to. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] The meeting is widely credited with securing Truman's commitment to the Jewish state. [scene:s08|The president and his advisers] tells how it came about. The next day, 19 March, the American ambassador to the United Nations stood up in the Security Council and announced that the United States was stepping back from partition.

Warren Austin told the Council that the partition plan "cannot now be implemented by peaceful means." In its place, he said, "a temporary trusteeship for Palestine should be established under the Trusteeship Council." He asked the Council to request a special session of the General Assembly, under Article 20 of the Charter, and to instruct the United Nations Palestine Commission to "suspend its efforts to implement the proposed partition plan." [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin]

A common shorthand holds that the United States backed the Jewish state steadily from the partition vote to recognition. The record of these four months shows something else: a government that voted for partition in November, proposed to suspend it in March, and recognized the new state in May, with its own delegation at the United Nations still arguing for trusteeship when the recognition was announced. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The scale of the retreat is clearest set against what the United States had voted for. On 29 November 1947 it was among the 33 states, with 13 against and 10 abstaining, that adopted the partition resolution. That resolution set a timetable. The Mandate was to end "as soon as possible but in any case not later than 1 August 1948." Provisional councils of government were to be in place by 1 April 1948. The two states were to come into existence two months after the British evacuation and "not later than 1 October 1948." A five-member Palestine Commission, made up of Bolivia, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, Panama and the Philippines, was to carry it out. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] Austin's statement asked that body to stop, less than two weeks before the date the resolution had set for the provisional councils.

Trusteeship was not a new idea, and it had not belonged to one side. In 1944 the American Jewish Committee had proposed an international trusteeship instead of a Jewish commonwealth. [cite:djn_1944_hearings] In April 1946 the Anglo-American Committee of Inquiry recommended continuing the Mandate toward a United Nations trusteeship, and declared that Palestine should be neither a Jewish nor an Arab state. [cite:avalon_aac] In May 1948 Hannah Arendt would argue in print for a binational federation under United Nations trusteeship, and Judah Magnes would meet Truman to press the same case. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] What was new in March 1948 was that the government that had led the vote for partition now offered trusteeship as its replacement.

The reasons the State Department gave for caution were on record well before Austin spoke. Loy Henderson, director of Near Eastern Affairs, Under Secretary Robert Lovett and Secretary of State George Marshall opposed early recognition of a Jewish state, arguing that it would damage American relations with the Arab world and endanger the oil supply. [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] Austin's own stated ground was narrower and practical: partition could not be carried out without force. [cite:rs_rd5_avalon_austin] By then fighting between Palestine's Jewish and Arab communities had gone on since 1 December 1947 [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition], and nine days before Austin spoke the Haganah had issued Plan Dalet, its plan for the period of the British withdrawal ([scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]).

The two events of 18 and 19 March collided because they came from two different parts of one government. The meeting with Weizmann ran through a personal channel, an old friend reaching a tired president, while the professional foreign service was strongly advising the other way. [cite:forward_state_dept_truman_israel] [cite:forward_state_dept_told_truman] The statement at the Security Council came from the diplomatic machinery that Henderson, Lovett and Marshall directed. The material gathered for this book does not show whether Truman knew that Austin would speak on 19 March, what he had told Weizmann in detail, or who drafted the statement and cleared its timing. Those questions are left open here rather than answered by inference.

The reactions were immediate. The Secretary-General, Trygve Lie, saw the new American position as "a rebuff to the United Nations." According to his memoir, as footnoted in the State Department's documentary history, he suggested that he and Austin should both resign; Austin declined. [cite:rs_rd5_frus_austin_1948] An American memorandum recorded that the Arab representatives "were pleased with this latest turn of events, but they did not gloat." [cite:rs_rd5_frus_austin_1948]

For the Jewish Agency, Abba Hillel Silver answered in the Council the same day. He called the proposal "a shocking reversal" of the American position and warned that it was likely "to lead to increased violence in Palestine." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] On 20 March David Ben-Gurion went further, and his answer amounted to a refusal:

We shall not agree to any kind of trusteeship, whether permanent or temporary, even for the shortest time

He called the reversal "a surrender to the terrorism of the Arab gangs" and said it would not "prevent the establishment of the Jewish State." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_trusteeship] The two characterizations of what had moved Washington could hardly be further apart. Austin spoke of the impossibility of a peaceful partition. Ben-Gurion spoke of surrender to force. Each was stating his own government's or movement's case, and neither statement settles the motives of the officials who drafted the policy.

The Soviet Union took the opposite course from Washington. When the United States moved toward trusteeship, Andrei Gromyko told the Security Council that the rapid creation of two states was the only way to reduce bloodshed, and Moscow stood behind partition. [cite:yated_stalin_israel] [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] The Soviet calculation is taken up in [scene:so_s01|the Soviet section]; here it matters that in March 1948 the two powers that had voted together in November were on opposite sides of the question.

Austin's proposal did not stop the Jewish Agency from preparing for statehood, as Ben-Gurion had said it would not. On the same day Austin spoke, Golda Meyerson returned from her American fundraising tour with a reported $50 million, spent largely on weapons. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] Plan Dalet's operations began on 1 April. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Eight weeks later the United States extended de facto recognition to Israel eleven minutes after its proclamation, while the American delegation at the United Nations was still working for trusteeship. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition]

The record assembled here leaves gaps. It holds Austin's statement and the first reactions to it, but not the proceedings of the special session he requested or what became of the trusteeship draft there. It does not document the internal deliberations that produced the statement, and it cannot say how far Truman's private meeting with Weizmann and his ambassador's public retreat were known to each other at the time. What it does establish is that in the spring of 1948 the United States held two positions at once, and that both were visible to everyone watching.

sections.h: Deir Yassin, the Hadassah Convoy and Tantura: The Massacres of 1948 and How the Record Changed
sections.html:
Two opposite claims about 1948 circulate widely. One holds that no massacres took place. The other holds that only one side suffered them. The record supports neither. In the spring of 1948 Jewish forces killed Arab villagers, and Arab forces killed Jews, sometimes within days of each other and sometimes in answer to each other. What has changed over the decades is not whether these events happened but how much is known about them, and much of that knowledge came from Israeli archives, an Israeli student and Israeli veterans.

Deir Yassin was a village west of Jerusalem. On 9 April 1948 it was attacked by the Irgun and Lehi, two right-wing Zionist militias, supported by the Haganah and the Palmach. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75] The attack came on the day after Abd al-Qadir al-Husayni, commander of the Palestinian Army of the Holy War, was killed leading the counter-attack at nearby al-Qastal, which overlooks the road from Jerusalem to Jaffa. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader] For decades the number killed at Deir Yassin was given as 254. Current scholarship puts it at about 110, generally within a range of 107 to 120, many of them women, children and elderly people. A Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies in a cave. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin]

The higher figure entered the record at the time. In December 1948 a letter to the New York Times, dated 2 December and published on 4 December and signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook, protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States. It said that on 9 April "terrorist bands" had attacked Deir Yassin, a "peaceful village, which was not a military objective," and "killed most of its inhabitants (240 men, women, and children)." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] Arendt had already condemned the Irgun's attacks, Deir Yassin among them, in the essay she published in May 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_manne_2026] The letter's figure of 240 is the one current in 1948; it is not the figure scholars now give. The letter's argument against Begin's new party is told in [scene:rf_s01|the section on dissent].

The killings had effects well beyond the village. Benny Morris wrote that Deir Yassin was followed by mass Arab flight. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] Another strand of the research gathered for this book, drawn from Israeli historians, adds two details: that the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages, which the official Haganah history by Yehuda Slutsky records, and that Ben-Gurion later noted in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight. That account gives the toll as about 107 civilians, at the low end of the current range. [cite:morris_1948] Material on Deir Yassin in Israeli military archives remains classified. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75]

Four days later the violence ran the other way. On 13 April 1948 Arab forces attacked a convoy travelling to Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses. The attack was a reprisal for Deir Yassin. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The victims were medical staff on their way to a hospital, and their deaths belong in the same record, with the same weight, as the villagers killed four days before.

The Hadassah convoy was not the only such killing of Jews in these weeks. Before the Mandate ended, the Arab Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered, and some of them were massacred, according to Avi Shlaim's account. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] Earlier, the Army of the Holy War's explosives unit had blown up the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem; the source does not give the date or the toll. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_abdelqader] These belong to the civil war that had begun on 1 December 1947, in which attacks ran in both directions. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition]

Tantura shows most clearly how the record has grown. It was a coastal village captured by the Alexandroni Brigade on 22–23 May 1948, a week after the state was proclaimed. A master's thesis by Theodore Katz later recorded testimony that villagers had been killed after the village surrendered. Veterans of the brigade sued him for libel, and he retracted. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura]

The question did not end with the retraction. In the 2022 Israeli documentary Tantura, veterans then in their nineties described on camera killings and a mass grave near what is now Dor Beach, a popular resort. A document shown in the film acknowledges that soldiers dug a mass grave. Other veterans deny that any massacre took place, and the number killed cannot be established. [cite:npr_tantura] [cite:jewishindependent_tantura]

The Deir Yassin numbers show how a toll can move in both directions. The figure of 254 was repeated for decades; contemporaries in December 1948 wrote 240; scholarship now gives about 110. The Red Cross representative's 150 bodies is a count of what one witness saw in one place, not a total. None of these figures is a final count, and each should be read with its source.

The way these events entered the record is itself part of the history. Much of what is known came from Israelis: historians working in Israeli archives, a student who gathered veterans' testimony, and veterans who decided late in life to speak. [cite:npr_tantura] Atrocities against Jews in the same weeks, at the Hadassah convoy and at Gush Etzion, are equally part of the record. The later expulsions at Lydda and Ramla in July 1948, with their own disputed tolls, are told with the Arab states' war in [scene:rd5_invasion|the invasion and the war].

Much remains unsettled. Israeli military archives on Deir Yassin are still partly closed, so the exact toll and the full chain of command cannot yet be documented. The number killed at Tantura cannot be established, and the veterans who were there disagree about what happened. The research gathered here gives no date for Katz's thesis or for the libel case, and no toll for the bombing of the Jewish Agency building. For Gush Etzion it says that some defenders were massacred but gives no number. What the record does establish is that killings of civilians and prisoners took place on both sides in these weeks, and that the documentary record of them is still growing.

sections.h: The Fall of the Mixed Towns, April–May 1948
sections.html:
For four months after the partition vote, the fighting in Palestine was a civil war, with attacks in both directions. [cite:explaininghistory_un_partition] In April 1948 it changed character. The Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi writes that the Zionist forces "did not begin to seize and hold on to Arab territory" until the offensive that began on 1 April 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] That offensive opened under Plan Dalet, issued three weeks earlier ([scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]). Within six weeks the towns in which Arabs and Jews had lived side by side, and the Arab towns near them, had changed hands one after another.

Khalidi's phrasing is precise, and it should be read beside his own correction elsewhere: a footnote in his study of Plan Dalet records that at least ten Arab villages had been captured by 1 March 1948. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The two statements can stand together. Villages were taken before April; the systematic seizing and holding of Arab territory, in his account, began with the April offensive.

Tiberias was the first town to fall, on 18 April 1948. Its Arab population, about 4,500 to 5,000 people and swollen by refugees from nearby villages, was evacuated. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

Haifa followed within the week, and its fall is the best documented and the most argued over. Early on 21 April 1948 the Haganah's Carmeli Brigade, under Moshe Carmel, attacked as British forces withdrew from their dividing positions in the city. That same day Major-General Hugh Stockwell, the British commander, had told Arab representatives that his forces would redeploy. The city fell on 22 April. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

The cost is known from British figures, which Khalidi cites: about 100 Arabs killed and 200 wounded, and about 20 Jews killed and 40 wounded. On 22 April about 50,000 Arabs were crowded into the Old Town. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

On 22 April the Arab delegates met Stockwell at the Town Hall over the terms of a truce; Haifa's Jewish mayor was there too, according to one account. What was said there, and what it meant, is the heart of the dispute over why Haifa's Arabs left. Khalidi's account, which draws on an account by Koussa, runs as follows. Stockwell warned the Arab delegates that if they did not sign the truce he would not be responsible if "three or four hundred more" were killed. The delegates had asked Damascus for instructions and had no reply. Their request for transport out of the city, according to Koussa's account, was made "on the spur of the moment," not under orders from the Arab states. Khalidi concludes: "Within a week, some 50,000 Arab inhabitants had been expelled." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa]

Khalidi goes further on the British role. He argues that the Haganah had advance knowledge of the British redeployment, and he calls Stockwell "an accomplice in the fall of Haifa." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The strongest form of his case is that the timing of the attack, the redeployment and the ultimatum at the Town Hall fit together too closely to be chance, and that the evacuation request was the improvised act of men without instructions under military pressure, not a plan from outside.

A sharply different account appears in an opinion article in the Jewish Chronicle by Florit Shoihet, published on 12 August 2026. According to that article, Haifa's Jewish mayor, Shabtai Levy, pleaded with the Arab delegates at the same meeting: "Stay in the city and be equal citizens." Stockwell, it reports, told the delegates, "You have made a foolish decision." The Haganah, it says, broadcast assurances of safety and civil rights, and about 60,000 Arabs left. [cite:rs_rd5_jc_haifa] The strongest form of this case is that Haifa's Arabs were offered terms of equal citizenship by the Jewish mayor and urged to stay by the British commander, and that their own delegation chose to leave. The article is an opinion piece and cites no specific archive for these details, and it should be weighed as such.

The third position is the historian Benny Morris's, as Khalidi reports it, and it has shifted. Morris first acknowledged, in 1987, that there were no Arab evacuation orders. He later argued that such orders were issued after the fighting. Khalidi disputes the later position. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] The broader question of evacuation orders, and the June 1948 Israeli intelligence estimate that attributed no more than 5 per cent of departures to them, is set out in [scene:rd5_refugees|the refugee section]. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref]

The two departure figures, 50,000 and about 60,000, come from opposite sides of the argument and are not far apart. The dispute is less about how many left than about why.

There is also an unresolved question about the operation's name. Khalidi writes in his Haifa study that the operation planned as Misparayim was renamed Chametz. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_haifa] In his list of Plan D operations, however, he dates Misparayim to 21 April and assigns it to Haifa, and dates Chametz to 27 April and assigns it to the villages around Jaffa. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The research gathered here does not reconcile the two.

After Haifa the other towns followed in the last three weeks of the Mandate. Khalidi's operation list gives the frame: Chametz against the villages around Jaffa from 27 April; Yiftach in eastern Galilee from 28 April; Matateh in the Tiberias area from 3 May; Gideon at Beisan from 11 May; and Ben Ami at Acre on 14 May, the day the state was proclaimed. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Jaffa and Safed fell in these weeks. [cite:wiki_plan_dalet] During the war an estimated 100,000 to 110,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were displaced into Lebanon, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

The record gathered for this book is uneven across these towns. Tiberias and Haifa are documented in detail; Jaffa, Safed, Beisan and Acre appear here only through Khalidi's list of operations, and the exact dates on which Jaffa, Safed and Acre fell were not established in this research. For Haifa, the British casualty figures and the timing of the redeployment are documented. Whether the Haganah knew of the redeployment in advance rests on Khalidi's argument. What was said at the Town Hall rests on two accounts that cannot both be complete: Khalidi's, from the Arab side, and an opinion article that cites no archive. And Morris's own changing view shows that the question of evacuation orders in Haifa has not been settled even by a historian whose archival work documented the expulsions in detail.

sections.h: Abdullah Between the Jewish Agency, Britain and the Arab League, 1947–1948
sections.html:
Of the Arab rulers who sent armies into Palestine in May 1948, one had been talking to the Jewish Agency for months beforehand. King Abdullah of Transjordan commanded the Arab Legion, a force trained and commanded by British officers, and he had territorial aims of his own. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] A familiar account holds that Jordan went to war in 1948 solely to destroy the new Jewish state alongside its allies, with no separate interest of its own. The record of his meetings, and of what his army actually did, tells a more complicated story. Whether it amounts to "collusion" is one of the longest-running arguments in the history of the war.

Abdullah's separate position was visible before the partition vote. When the United Nations Special Committee on Palestine toured the region in the summer of 1947, Transjordan declined to send a representative to testify outside the country. Instead the committee's chairman and seven of its members visited the king in Amman on 25 July 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_unscop]

In early November 1947, at Naharayim on the Jordan, Abdullah met Golda Meyerson, later Golda Meir, of the Jewish Agency. According to the Center for Israel Education's account, he told her that he intended to annex the Arab areas of Palestine, and she replied that the Zionist leaders would not oppose this if there were no clashes between Jewish and Transjordanian forces. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] The historian Avi Shlaim calls the understanding reached that November a "tacit agreement." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] Nothing was signed. What existed, on this account, was a shared expectation: the king would take the Arab part of Palestine, and the Jewish state would not fight him for it.

The British side of the triangle came into view in February 1948. That month Britain's Foreign Secretary, an office Ernest Bevin had held since July 1945 [cite:rs_rd5_britannica_bevin], met the prime minister of Transjordan and John Glubb, the British officer who commanded the Arab Legion. After that meeting, according to Graham Jevon's study of Glubb and the Legion (Cambridge University Press, 2017), Glubb "actively sought to thwart the efforts of the Arab irregular forces" in Palestine and sought a military accord with the Zionists. Jevon writes that his findings corroborate Shlaim's disputed claim that Britain gave Abdullah a "green light" to occupy the areas allotted to the Arab state. He also concludes that Glubb was not the architect of this Greater Transjordan scheme but the man who carried it out. [cite:rs_rd5_jevon_2017] The abstract of Jevon's chapter, which is what this book has drawn on, does not give the date of the meeting or record what was said.

Shlaim states the British policy plainly. Britain, he writes, "was resigned to the emergence of a Jewish state but supported her client, King Abdullah," and in doing so "helped to abort the birth of a Palestinian state." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ab]

The Arab League pulled Abdullah the other way. The League's anti-Hashemite members suspected him of collaborating with the Zionists. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] He, for his part, opposed every move toward Palestinian independence and refused to deal with Hajj Amin al-Husayni, the Mufti, who led the Arab Higher Committee. [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni] The quarrel over who would speak for the Palestinians is told in [scene:rd5_arab_leadership|the section on Arab leadership]. On 30 April 1948 the League's Political Committee decided that "all the Arab states must prepare their armies for the invasion of Palestine on 15 May." Under pressure from Transjordan and Iraq, Abdullah was named commander-in-chief. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] The man suspected of a private arrangement with the Jewish Agency was now the nominal head of the Arab war against it.

On 10 May 1948, four days before the end of the Mandate, Meyerson crossed into Transjordan again, this time to Amman, with Ezra Danin. The two travelled disguised as an Arab couple. According to the Center for Israel Education, Abdullah told her that he was now "one of five" and asked: "why don't you wait a few years? Drop your demands for free immigration." [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] Meyerson's own report at the time, as summarized in Shlaim's notes, records that the king did not deny their earlier understanding, said he had no choice but to join the invasion, and that they did not part as enemies. On 13 May Yaacov Shimoni of the Jewish Agency weighed it up: the king "has not entirely betrayed the agreement, nor is he entirely loyal to it." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab]

On 15 May, as the armies moved, Syria's president, Shukri al-Quwwatli, urged a halt to the advance. Abdullah refused. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab]

What the Arab Legion then did is consistent with the limits Abdullah had set out. Even before the Mandate ended, the Legion attacked the Gush Etzion bloc of Jewish settlements; its defenders surrendered and some were massacred, according to Shlaim's notes. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_cw] Once the war between states began, the State Department's Office of the Historian records, Transjordanian forces intervened only in areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the separate Jerusalem zone of the partition plan. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Within those limits the Legion fought hard. In the first round, according to Shlaim's notes, the Jewish Quarter of Jerusalem surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and 9 June, were repelled by the Arab Legion. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] After the second truce began on 18 July, the Legion continued shelling West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the Latrun pumping station, which the United Nations held, according to an Israeli army account. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce2] The Legion's commander was also the source of many of the most-quoted figures on the balance of forces, which historians treat with caution because he commanded one of the sides. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

By the end of the war the Legion held East Jerusalem's Old City and the West Bank. It was Jordan's most consequential military action of the war, and the territory remained under its administration for the next nineteen years. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Under the armistice agreements of 1949, Jordan kept the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The Arab League's All-Palestine Government, proclaimed in Gaza in September 1948, was opposed by Abdullah, who said it would not operate in areas held by the Arab Legion. On 1 December 1948 a congress of about 3,000 delegates at Jericho proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged him as king; the figures come from Shlaim alone. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_jps_1990] [cite:rs_rd5_dipc_husayni]

The formal annexation came later and is told in full in [scene:ijr_src_s05|Jordan's war, armistice and annexation]. In brief: on 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament annexed the West Bank, declaring support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State." [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Only Britain, Iraq and Pakistan recognized it, and Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem. The strongest opposition came from Jordan's fellow Arab League states, whose Political Committee ruled in Cairo that the annexation violated the League's earlier resolution and considered expelling Jordan. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] During the nineteen years of Jordanian rule that followed, Jewish access to the Western Wall and other religious sites in the Old City was denied, contrary to the 1949 armistice terms, and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed. One reading notes that the 1950 resolution's "two banks" language mirrors the Revisionist Zionist claim, associated with Jabotinsky, that both banks of the Jordan belong together, used here in the opposite direction; it is a structural parallel, and the record does not show that either side was answering the other.

Was there collusion across the Jordan? The case that there was, in substance, is Shlaim's, and on the British side Jevon's study says its findings corroborate it. On this view there was a tacit understanding between Abdullah and the Jewish Agency to divide the territory the United Nations had allotted to an Arab state, Britain gave the king a green light to take his share, and Glubb restrained the Arab irregulars and sought an accord with the Zionists. The Legion's conduct fits: it stayed out of the territory allotted to the Jewish state, and the Palestinian state that the partition plan foresaw was never born. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ab] [cite:rs_rd5_jevon_2017] [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b]

The case that the arrangement was partial at best rests on the same meetings. In Amman on 10 May Abdullah called himself "one of five," asked the Jews to defer statehood and drop their demand for free immigration, and joined the invasion. The Jewish Agency's own Shimoni judged him neither loyal to the understanding nor in full breach of it. And the Legion fought Israeli forces hard where their aims met, in Jerusalem and at Latrun. [cite:rs_rd5_cie_golda] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_ab] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war]

The two cases are not as far apart as the word "collusion" suggests. Both accept that Abdullah and the Jewish Agency talked, that he wanted the Arab part of Palestine, and that he went to war as part of the Arab coalition. They differ on how firm the understanding was and how much it shaped the fighting. Several things remain unsettled by the record gathered here. The Naharayim and Amman exchanges come largely through an Israeli educational account and Meyerson's own report, not through a Jordanian record. The February 1948 meeting is known from the abstract of Jevon's study, without its date or the words spoken. And the Legion's restraint toward the Jewish state's territory can be read as the keeping of an understanding or as the pursuit of the king's own aims, which happened to coincide with it.

sections.h: Independence and the Nakba, 1948
sections.html:
On Friday 14 May 1948, at four in the afternoon, David Ben-Gurion stood in a hall of the Tel Aviv Museum and read out the Declaration of the Establishment of the State of Israel. The British Mandate was due to expire at midnight, a few hours later. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] [cite:morasha_czech_arms] The document itself notes the hour: it was signed "on this Sabbath eve." Its dating is not quite consistent. The signing line reads "5th day of Iyar, 5708 – 14th May 1948," while the body of the text, referring to the end of the Mandate, gives "6th Iyar, 5708 (15th May, 1948)." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The discrepancy stands in the text as it is reproduced.

Ben-Gurion, born in 1886 and dead in 1973, was a Polish-born organizer of the labour Zionist movement. He became the new state's first Prime Minister and the most consequential single figure in its creation. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] Palestinians call what followed the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe." [cite:morris_1948] The founding of the state and the displacement of much of the Arab population from the territory it came to hold took place in the same months, and this section follows both. Along the way it tests two claims that have long been taught about 1948. The first is that the Palestinians left of their own accord, on instructions broadcast by Arab radio. The second is that America created and armed Israel. Both claims rest on something real, and the record contradicts both.

The Declaration began with its grounds. It based the state on "our natural and historic right," on the Balfour Declaration of 2 November 1917, on the Mandate of the League of Nations, and on the General Assembly resolution of 29 November 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The order matters. The first ground was a claim of right that did not depend on any outside power. The other three were international instruments: a British pledge, a League mandate and a United Nations vote. Taken together, the text claimed the state both as an inheritance and as an act of international law.

The document also made promises. It pledged equality of social and political rights to all inhabitants "irrespective of religion, race or sex." It appealed to the Arab inhabitants of the state "to preserve peace" and to take part in building it on the basis of "full and equal citizenship." To the neighbouring states it extended "an offer of peace and good neighbourliness." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] These clauses are the strongest written form of the founders' case. They promised a state for the Jewish people in which its Arab citizens would be full citizens, and they offered peace to its neighbours. Whether and how the first promise was kept is a question for the later volumes of this library, because the record of the Arabs who stayed inside Israel begins after 1948. The answer to the second came within hours: armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded, and Transjordanian forces entered the areas designated for the Arab state and Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] That war is the subject of a later section of this chapter.

Two further features of the text are often missed. The Declaration stated no borders. It referred to Eretz-Israel, the Land of Israel, and it pledged steps toward "the economic union of the whole of Eretz-Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] Economic union between the two states was what the UNSCOP majority had recommended in 1947. [cite:rs_rd5_unscop_report] And it set a deadline for its own replacement. The People's Council became the Provisional Council of State, and a constitution was to be adopted by an elected Constituent Assembly "not later than the 1st October 1948." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration]

That deadline passed. When the First Knesset met, it deadlocked over what a constitution should contain, above all over the place of religion in public life. Instead it resolved to enact Basic Laws one at a time. [cite:gov_legalclarity] The first came in 1958. There are now fourteen, covering the Knesset, the government, the military, the judiciary and civil rights, and the Supreme Court treats them as having constitutional weight, though a simple Knesset majority can amend them. [cite:basiclaw_britannica] The constitution promised in May 1948 has never been adopted. The consequences of that gap belong to a later period and are traced in [scene:ilgov_s01|No Constitution, Only Basic Laws].

The structures of the new state appeared quickly, because most of them already existed. The institutions the Jewish Agency had built under the Mandate became, almost overnight, the institutions of a sovereign government. The Haganah, the pre-state militia, became the Israel Defense Forces; a state intelligence service, the Mossad, was established in 1949. The United States extended de facto recognition within eleven minutes, a timing arranged by Clark Clifford over the State Department's objection. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Recognition is examined in the next section. What matters here is a distinction the familiar account often blurs. Recognition was a political act. Weapons were another matter.

The United States imposed an arms embargo on all parties to the 1948 war. The Truman administration recognized Israel within minutes, but it did not lift the embargo. [cite:morasha_czech_arms] The weapons that reached the new army in the decisive months came instead from communist Czechoslovakia. By this account they were former German arms: Mauser rifles, Messerschmitt Bf 109G fighters and ZK 383 submachine guns, flown in by C-54 transports from Žatec airfield in an airlift code-named Operation Balak. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] [cite:wiki_czech_arms_shipments] Israeli military historians have documented the operation, and so has Zeev Sternhell in his work on the founding. Ben-Gurion's verdict, quoted from his memoir, was that "Czech arms saved the State of Israel." [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal]

The detailed record of the pipeline, set out in [scene:cz_s01|the Czechoslovak arms section], adds some precision. It describes the fighters as Avia S-199s, a Czech-built derivative of the Messerschmitt Bf 109, of which about 25 were delivered. It dates the first contract to 14 January 1948, before the Security Council's arms embargo of 17 April (Resolution 46). It records about 35,000 German-pattern Karabiner 98k rifles sent by sea, and a 1952 report by the Czechoslovak Foreign Minister, Viliam Široký, that put receipts at almost $14.5 million. [cite:wiki_czech_arms_israel] [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] It gives Ben-Gurion's words in their 1968 form: "Czechoslovak arms saved the State of Israel, really and absolutely." [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] It also records that Britain supplied aircraft and training to the Arab air forces. That sits awkwardly with the shorter statement that the United States, Britain and the United Nations all embargoed. Both versions are given here. Nor was Czechoslovakia the only source. The clandestine American procurement network, and the money Golda Meyerson raised in the United States early in 1948, are described in earlier sections of this chapter.

Czechoslovakia did not act alone. It lay inside the Soviet sphere, and the sales went ahead with Moscow's permission. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] The motive usually given is the same one read into the Soviet vote for partition in November 1947: anything that hastened the end of the British Mandate weakened Britain's position in the eastern Mediterranean. [cite:wiki_operation_balak] On that reading, Soviet interest and the new state's survival ran in the same direction for a few years and then parted. Two conclusions are sometimes drawn from this episode, and both go too far. The first is that the state later regarded as America's closest ally was armed at birth by the Soviet bloc while Washington held back. That is accurate for 1948, but it was a dated episode, and Soviet-Israeli relations changed markedly in the years that followed. The second is that Israel was a Western implant. The arms record is the strongest evidence against that view: at the decisive moment, the Western power most often credited with Israel's birth was withholding weapons from it.

The same months produced the Nakba. The figures most often given are between 700,000 and 750,000 Palestinians displaced, with about 500 villages depopulated or destroyed. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] Benny Morris estimates 700,000. Walid Khalidi gives 750,000, and Rashid Khalidi accepts the higher figure. Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) documents the villages one by one. [cite:walid_khalidi_all_that_remains] Much of the sustained documentation comes from Israeli historians writing from inside the country's own archives: Morris's 1948: A History of the First Arab-Israeli War, Ilan Pappé's The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine, Tom Segev's 1949: The First Israelis and Avi Shlaim's The Iron Wall. [cite:morris_1948] [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing]

One account in this library calls the 750,000 figure undisputed by any credible historian. The wider record does not bear that out. The UN Conciliation Commission's technical estimate of 1949 was about 711,000. Other figures run from a past Israeli government estimate of 520,000 up to 850,000 from Palestinian researchers. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] Counts of depopulated villages also vary with method, from 369 in Morris's 1987 count to 418 in Khalidi's and 531 localities in the Palestine Land Society's list, which includes towns and tribal lands. [cite:rs_rd5_plands_villages] There is no dispute that the displacement happened, or about its rough scale. The exact numbers are disputed, and [scene:rd5_refugees|the section on the refugees] sets out each estimate and its method.

The territorial figures show what the war decided. By 1948, land in Jewish ownership, bought parcel by parcel over decades, amounted to roughly seven percent of Mandate Palestine. [cite:morris_1948] The same account elsewhere puts legally purchased land at 9.8 percent, so the sources disagree on the exact figure, but both are under a tenth. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Resolution 181 had allotted about 55 percent of the country to the Jewish state (56 percent in other sources used in this chapter). By the 1949 armistice, about 78 percent of Mandate Palestine was under Israeli control. [cite:morris_1948] Purchase accounts for the first figure. The difference between it and the last was made by the war and by the departure of most of the Arab population. The familiar phrase about making the desert bloom on land that was bought and settled describes the first figure. The rest has a different history.

How the departure happened is the core of the dispute. Plan Dalet, or Plan D, is the central document in it. The Haganah finalized it on 10 March 1948; according to the account in this book's research it was later released from the Israeli archives in the 1980s. Walid Khalidi published its text as an appendix to his article "Plan Dalet: Master Plan for the Conquest of Palestine," republished in the Journal of Palestine Studies in 1988. [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] The plan states its purpose plainly: "The objective of this plan is to gain control of the areas of the Hebrew state and defend its borders." That aim included "areas of Jewish settlement and concentration which are located outside the borders." Section 4(b) provides for "Destruction of villages (setting fire to, blowing up, and planting mines in the debris)" and states that, where resistance is met, "the population must be expelled outside the borders of the state." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] One account in this book's sources summarizes the plan as authorizing three things.
