The first was securing the areas assigned to the Jewish state by expelling villages that resisted. The second was taking Arab-majority cities in those areas. The third was the use of a stated vocabulary of destruction (haricha) and expulsion (gerush). [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] The plan, its predecessors and the operations carried out under it are set out in detail in the section on Plan Dalet.

What the plan meant is where historians divide. Walid Khalidi argues that it created "the military fait accompli upon which the state of Israel was to be based," and that the exodus was its product. He faults Morris for treating the exodus in "an historical vacuum." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] Pappé argues in The Ethnic Cleansing of Palestine (2006) that Plan Dalet meets the UN definition of ethnic cleansing. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] Morris, who stands politically to Pappé's right and does not use that term, documents many of the same operations. In Zachary Lockman's summary, however, Morris concludes that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel. He finds that the flight up to June 1948 came mainly from direct military action, and that deliberate expulsions from June onward produced about 300,000 further refugees. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] Shlaim writes that Morris rejected both the "Arab order" and the "Jewish robber-state" explanations and treated the refugee problem as "a by-product of the war." Shlaim himself holds that the evidence "suggests a far higher degree of Israeli responsibility." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ref]

One summary in this book's sources holds that "the debate is over the term, not the facts," and that the Haganah carried out a plan to secure and expel which produced the outcome of 750,000 displaced. [cite:pappe_ethnic_cleansing] That is one reading. The fuller record shows the disagreement reaching further, into the facts of intent. Was there a central decision to remove the Arab population, or a military plan whose village clause left expulsion to local commanders and the course of battle? The documents cited on each side are real. The disagreement is over what they show.

The record names particular episodes. On 9 April 1948, Irgun and Lehi forces, the two right-wing militias later folded into the Israel Defense Forces, attacked the village of Deir Yassin west of Jerusalem. [cite:morris_1948] This book's research gives the toll as about 107 civilians. The section on the massacres of 1948 gives the fuller picture. For decades the toll was given as 254. Current scholarship puts it at about 110, generally between 107 and 120. A Red Cross representative reported seeing some 150 bodies. Haganah and Palmach forces supported the attack, and Israeli military archives on it remain partly classified. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] [cite:aljazeera_deir_yassin_75] According to Yehuda Slutsky's official history of the Haganah, the attackers announced the killings by radio to nearby villages in order to spread panic, and in the following weeks many families in those villages fled. Ben-Gurion later wrote in his diary that Deir Yassin "had a decisive effect" on Arab flight. [cite:morris_1948] The account in this book's sources argues that the panic was the purpose, not a by-product: terror used as an instrument of removal. That is an inference from Slutsky's record and from the flight that followed, and it is presented here as such. Four days after Deir Yassin, on 13 April, Arab forces attacked a convoy to the Hadassah Hospital on Mount Scopus and killed 78 Jews, most of them doctors and nurses, in reprisal. [cite:wiki_deir_yassin] The two killings belong in the same account.

The same account argues that the mechanism did not depend on any one militia, and points to Lydda and Ramla in July 1948. There, it says, about 50,000 civilians were expelled on written orders signed by Yitzhak Rabin, with no Irgun or Lehi involvement. [cite:morris_1948] It calls the force that carried this out the Haganah. By July, however, the Haganah had been merged into the Israel Defense Forces under the provisional government's order of 26 May. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] The research on the war gives a wider range of numbers. Lockman puts the two towns' combined population at 50,000 to 70,000, about 15,000 of them refugees already, and Palquest estimates about 70,000 driven out on 13 July. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Citing Morris, both sources report that on 12 July Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them," and that Rabin then signed the expulsion order. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] The operation and its competing death tolls are part of the section on the Arab states' war.

Ben-Gurion appears on both sides of this record. He led a community that included Holocaust survivors and refugees from the Middle East to statehood against invading armies. He also held executive authority over a founding that included the documented expulsions. The account in this book's sources calls him the architect of the new state's territorial and demographic policy, and his own diaries and directives are part of the evidence for the expulsions. [cite:hasbara_czech_arms_deal] That account also admits that it does not trace every decision he made about them. Whether his authority amounted to a general policy of expulsion is the point on which Morris and his critics differ. Neither the heroic version of his career nor the purely damning one can be kept without leaving out half of what the record shows.

The first of the two taught claims was put to a direct test in 1961. For years after the war, it was widely said that Arab governments had broadcast instructions telling Palestinians to leave their homes for a short time, with the promise that they could return once the Arab armies had won. If true, the claim placed the cause of the refugee problem with Arab leaders, not with events on the ground. The Irish journalist Erskine Childers went to the monitoring records. The BBC Monitoring Service had recorded and transcribed Middle Eastern radio throughout the period for British intelligence, and American monitors had done the same. These records were made at the time, independently of any later political narrative. Childers searched them for the evacuation orders and published his findings in The Spectator: [cite:spectator_childers_1961]

There was not a single order, or appeal, or suggestion about evacuation from Palestine from any Arab radio station, inside or outside Palestine, in 1948. There is a repeated monitored record of Arab appeals, even flat orders, to the civilians of Palestine to stay put.

He challenged anyone to produce the broadcasts, and no one did. [cite:decolonizepalestine_childers] Walid Khalidi, citing the BBC monitoring and its American counterpart, the FBIS, called the evacuation-order claim "a piece of mythmaking." [cite:rs_rd5_khalidi_1988] One summary in this book's sources says that Morris, working in the archives in the 1980s, found no evidence of the broadcasts in Israeli, Arab or British records either. [cite:decolonizepalestine_childers]

The Israeli archival record Morris used adds one detail. In Lockman's summary, an IDF intelligence report of June 1948 estimated that about 240,000 Arabs had fled the areas of the Jewish state and about 150,000 other areas by 1 June. It attributed about 70 percent of that flight to direct Jewish military operations, 2 percent to psychological warfare and 2 percent to expulsion orders, which Morris considers an underestimate. It attributed no more than 5 percent to evacuation orders from Arab leaders. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] So some local evacuation orders were given; the Israeli army's own estimate at the time counted them as a small cause, and they were not the blanket radio campaign of the later story. Lockman also writes that Yosef Weitz's report of October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] Childers's finding is narrow, and its narrowness is its strength. It does not explain every departure, village by village; the record shows many different circumstances of flight and expulsion. What it settles is that a single blanket explanation, repeated for years, was not in the broadcast record when someone checked.

The account of 1948 in this book's sources closes with a moral argument, stated here as its authors' own. Jewish need for safety after the Holocaust was real. The Zionist claim that Europe's Jews needed a place of refuge after 1945 was not false. That need was met in a land whose Arab inhabitants bore no responsibility for the crimes committed in Europe, and the cost of meeting it fell on them. On this view, the founding was at once the rescue of one people and the dispossession of another. Neither half cancels the other, and an account that drops either one is incomplete.

The same sources set a second contrast beside this one, again as an interpretation, not a finding. Jewish communities had lived among Arab populations across the Muslim world for more than a millennium: in Andalusia's Golden Age, under the Ottoman millet system, in Baghdad, with a community of 140,000, and in Damascus, Cairo, Sana'a and Fez. That life was not a utopia, and pogroms occurred. [cite:morris_righteous_victims] The claim that this coexistence was "substantial" and of a kind "Europe never matched" is a reading of a long and varied history, and is offered as one. The exodus of roughly 850,000 Jews from Arab lands between 1948 and 1972 had several documented causes, including active recruitment by Israeli and Jewish Agency operations. [cite:morris_righteous_victims] The violence against Jews in Arab cities after the partition vote, which was among those causes, is set out in its own section of this chapter.

A smaller decision closed the founding year. On 28 October 1948 the Provisional Council adopted the state flag. It chose the design of the First Zionist Congress at Basel in 1897, a Magen David between blue stripes, and placed the ancient Menorah on the state seal. [cite:wiki_flag_of_israel] [cite:wjc_flag_unveiled_1948] The date and the choice are documented. One symbolic reading holds that the choice shows which lineage the new state saw itself as continuing: the political project of 1897 rather than the ancient Temple. That is an interpretation, not a finding. Placing the Menorah on the seal did not mean it was disregarded. It shows only the order of precedence the Council set between two available symbols.

The refugee question did not end in 1948. On 11 December 1948 the General Assembly's Resolution 194 affirmed a right of return for the refugees. It has never been implemented. Israel has refused it on the ground that a return would end the Jewish majority in the state. [cite:morris_1948] The Palestinians registered with UNRWA as descendants of the displaced now number some 6 million, most of them stateless. Resolution 194 and the negotiations that followed it belong to the next stage of this volume.

The account of the Nakba in this book's sources goes further, and its argument should be stated in full and labelled for what it is. It holds that the Nakba was not a single event but a structure that has continued for 78 years. It lists, as of 2026, what it treats as later expressions of that structure. Among them are the occupation of the West Bank since 1967 and the blockade of Gaza since 2007, with some 2 million people in 365 square kilometres. West Bank settlers numbered 110,000 in 1993 and more than 500,000 in 2025, plus 250,000 in East Jerusalem, according to Peace Now and Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics. The list includes the war in Gaza since October 2023, South Africa's genocide case at the International Court of Justice, filed on 29 December 2023, and the International Criminal Court's arrest warrants for Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, issued on 21 November 2024. It also cites the conclusions of Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch and B'Tselem that the two legal systems in the West Bank meet the international-law definition of apartheid, and Israel's unilateral annexation of East Jerusalem in 1980 under Basic Law: Jerusalem. Those conclusions are the organizations' own legal judgements and are attributed to them here. The account then traces the effects across the region. In Jordan, more than 2 million Palestinians hold citizenship, about 40 percent of the population. Lebanon hosts about 500,000 refugees in 12 UNRWA camps, barred from most professions and from owning property. Syria hosts about 500,000, many displaced again since 2011. Egypt administered Gaza from 1948 to 1967. In Egypt's 1979 treaty, Jordan's of 1994 and the Abraham Accords of 2020 with the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco and Sudan, Arab states normalized relations with Israel without resolving the Palestinian question. The book's sources do not attach citations to these present-day figures. They are reported here as that account gives them, with the date, and they are examined in the volumes that cover those years. The opposite reading treats each of these episodes as a separate event with its own causes. This volume does not settle between the two. It records that the refugee problem created in 1948 was not resolved in 1948, and that every later chapter of this history inherits it.

The year-by-year ledger for this stage sets 1948 beside the two years before it. In 1946 and 1947 the entries are the Anglo-American Committee, the King David Hotel bombing, UNSCOP, the CIA's estimate ORE-55 and Resolution 181, a sequence of pressure, inquiry and warnings overruled. The entry for 1948 lists Deir Yassin, Plan Dalet, independence, the eleven-minute recognition, the Czech arms and the Nakba under a single heading: execution. Its money column holds two sums. The first is about $50 million reported raised on Golda Meyerson's American tour, spent largely on weapons. The second is almost $14.5 million in Czechoslovak arms receipts. [cite:jwa_golda_50m] [cite:jpost_czech_arms_saved_israel] The objectors' column for the year names the letter of December 1948, signed by 28 people including Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt, which protested Menachem Begin's visit to the United States and described his new party, which had grown out of the Irgun, as bearing "the unmistakable stamp of a Fascist party." [cite:rs_rd5_einstein_nyt] The two sums show the connection the ledger draws. Money raised in America paid for weapons sold by the Soviet bloc, under an American embargo.

Much remains unsettled. The number of refugees is known only within a range, and the count of villages depends on what is counted. Whether the expulsions followed a central decision or accumulated from local orders under a plan that allowed them is still the main point of disagreement between Morris and his critics, and the documents do not close it. The death toll at Deir Yassin is now put at about 110, but part of the Israeli military record remains classified. The tolls at Lydda and Ramla vary by source. This book has not yet compiled the Arab military and civilian dead of the war. The radio claim is settled in its broad form and not in every local detail: the Israeli army's own estimate allowed a small share for Arab evacuation orders. On the arms, the scale of Czechoslovak supply is clear, but the sources differ on the aircraft, on Britain's role and on whether any other supplier mattered. What is not in doubt is the pairing at the centre of this section: in the same months, one people gained a state and another lost most of its towns and villages. Both facts are documented, and much of the documentation is Israeli.

sections.h: Who Recognizes a Nation?
sections.html:
The United States recognized Israel on the day it was declared. The decision is sometimes remembered as an act of Congress, as if the House and Senate had voted the new state into American favour. They did not. Recognition came in a short press release from the White House, issued on the authority of one office, and Congress had no vote on it. How that power came to rest with one office, how Truman used it, and how other governments answered the same question in 1948 and 1949 together show what recognition did and did not decide.

The constitutional basis is a single clause. Article II, Section 3 provides that the President "shall receive Ambassadors and other public Ministers." [cite:const_art2s3] In Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015) the Supreme Court held that the clause gives the President the exclusive power to recognize foreign sovereigns. [cite:scotus_zivotofsky] The ruling came sixty-seven years after 1948, so it does not describe a rule that anyone cited at the time. It states the law as it now stands, and it confirms that the power Truman used was his alone.

He used it on 14 May 1948. Eleven minutes after Israel's proclamation, he announced de facto recognition in a short press release. [cite:truman_recognition] De facto recognition accepted the new government as the authority actually in control. Full legal recognition, de jure, followed on 31 January 1949. [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] In one account in this library, the second step came only after Truman's election victory. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] Two accounts in this library give the time of the first announcement as 6:11 p.m. Washington time. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The Declaration had been read in Tel Aviv at four in the afternoon, and the Mandate expired at midnight. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_declaration] The sources do not say whether the eleven minutes are counted from the reading or from the moment the state came into being at the Mandate's end. The figure is exact; its starting point is not stated.

The speed was arranged. Clark Clifford, the President's counsel, managed the timing against the objection of the State Department, which was not told in advance. The American delegation at the United Nations was caught out too: at that moment it was still pressing the trusteeship proposal that Washington had put forward in March as an alternative to partition. [cite:trumanlibrary_recognition] The decision came after Eddie Jacobson, Truman's old business partner, had brought Chaim Weizmann to see him, and after a November 1947 memorandum had analysed "The Politics of 1948 and the Jews." [cite:jvl_dejure_1949] [cite:jvl_truman_index] Recognition went against the written advice of the Secretary of State, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the CIA. The CIA's estimate ORE-55, dated 28 November 1947, the day before the partition vote, had predicted armed hostilities if partition passed and warned that American commercial and strategic interests would be put in danger. [cite:cia_ore55] One account in this library goes further. It describes declassified CIA assessments predicting that recognition would immediately produce war with the Arab states, and calls the eleven minutes the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history. Those claims are that account's own and are not repeated in ORE-55's summary. The warnings and the advisers who overrode them are traced in [scene:ore_s01|the CIA's estimate].

Why Truman acted as he did is argued in the opening sections of this chapter. One reading stresses the domestic calculation that Clifford's memorandum set out. Another stresses Truman's own repeated statements of humanitarian conviction. The record holds evidence for both. The constitutional point holds whatever his motive. Because the power to recognize was the President's alone, the months of argument over partition, trusteeship, oil and strategy ended in one decision by one man. The State Department, the Pentagon and the new intelligence agency could advise. Advocates could press. Only the President could decide.

Congress's part was real but indirect. It could pass resolutions of support, it controlled appropriations, and the Senate confirmed ambassadors, including the first American ambassador to Israel. None of these powers decided whether the United States would recognize Israel. They shaped what recognition would mean in practice afterwards.

Other governments answered the question differently, and on different grounds. The Soviet Union went further than Washington, and almost as fast. On 17 May 1948, three days after independence, it became the first state to recognize Israel de jure, while the American recognition was still de facto. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] It was the same course Moscow had followed since Andrei Gromyko's speech at the United Nations in May 1947, and analysts at the time and since have read its motive as removing British influence from the region. That is their reading, not a stated Soviet aim. [cite:washinst_who_saved_israel] The convergence had limits. In December 1948 the Soviet bloc voted against Resolution 194 on the return of refugees. [cite:wiki_soviet_arab_israeli] The fuller Soviet story is told in [scene:so_s01|Moscow said yes first].

Britain, the outgoing Mandatory power, came slowly. It had abstained in the partition vote of 29 November 1947. In May 1948 Ernest Bevin told the House of Commons that "there are, after all, no Arabs in the House." Britain recognized Israel in January 1949; the historian Raphael Langham describes Bevin's acceptance as "grudging." [cite:rs_rd5_langham_exit] The government that had issued the Balfour Declaration and held the Mandate accepted the state that emerged from it only after eight months.

Some governments declined altogether. In 1947, according to later reports, Ben-Gurion sent a secret telegram or telephone message to Muhammad Ali Jinnah, the founder of Pakistan, proposing that Pakistan recognize the Jewish state when it was established. Jinnah's reply was reportedly negative. [cite:timesofisrael_blog_secret_diplomacy] [cite:infogalactic_israel_pakistan_relations] The account rests on secondary reporting, not on a surviving primary document, and should be read with that limit. Pakistan has never recognized Israel and has no diplomatic relations with it. The later record of unacknowledged contacts between the two belongs to a later volume.

The Holy See withheld recognition for longer than almost any other major power. Its documented reasons were three: Catholic doctrine on the place of the Jewish people in salvation history, the unresolved status of the holy sites of Jerusalem, and concern for the Christian and Muslim communities of Palestine under the new state. [cite:jcpa_vatican_israel_recognition] Its opposition was active. In 1949 the Vatican pressed at the United Nations to make Israel's admission conditional on two commitments: a return of Palestinian refugees and formal guarantees for the Christian and Muslim holy sites, above all in Jerusalem. Ben-Gurion is recorded as saying that year: "There is a major religion in the world, which has to settle with us a historical reckoning." The campaign failed. Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949 without the guarantees the Vatican had sought. The Holy See did not establish diplomatic relations until the Fundamental Agreement of 30 December 1993, forty-five years after independence. [cite:wiki_fundamental_agreement] How that change came about is told in [scene:vat_s01|the Vatican's long refusal].

Set side by side, these answers show what recognition was in 1948. It was a decision each government took alone, through whatever office its own constitution named, and for its own reasons. In Washington that office was the presidency, and the reasons were contested inside the government itself. In Moscow, on the analysts' reading, the reason was Britain. In London it was reluctant acceptance of a settled fact, and in Rome theology and the holy places. None of these decisions created the state, which existed by its own proclamation. What recognition decided was who would deal with it, and on what terms.

Some questions remain open. The press release and the date of de jure recognition are documented. The exact moment from which the eleven minutes are counted is not stated in the sources used here. The approach to Jinnah is known only from later secondary accounts. The details of the Vatican's 1949 campaign at the United Nations, beyond its two demands and its failure, are not documented in this book's sources. How much any single adviser or argument weighed with Truman remains, as the earlier sections show, a matter of interpretation.

sections.h: The Arab States' War, May 1948 – 1949
sections.html:
The British Mandate ended at midnight on 14 May 1948. Within hours the fighting already under way inside Palestine became a war between the new State of Israel and the armies of its neighbours. The fighting that followed lasted, with two long truces, into the winter. It ended not in peace treaties but in a set of separate armistice agreements signed in 1949, whose lines became the borders of the next two decades.

The familiar account of this war has two versions, and each tells only part of the story. In one, five Arab armies set out to destroy a newborn state on the day of its birth. In the other, the Arab states sent their armies to protect the Palestinian Arabs from a Jewish force already on the offensive. The documents show that both sides had grounds for their account. They also show that the armies did not come as one, did not come in the strength their own planners had called for, and did not all come for the same purpose.

The League's own words. On 15 May 1948 the Secretary-General of the Arab League sent a cablegram to the Secretary-General of the United Nations, registered as document S/745. It is the Arab states' own statement of why they were going to war, and it deserves to be read as such. The Mandate, it said, had ended "leaving no legally constituted authority behind," and the Arab states were therefore intervening "to restore law and order and to prevent disturbances prevailing in Palestine from spreading" into their own territories. [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] The cablegram made two further claims. It stated that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes," and it declared support for "the creation of United State of Palestine based upon the democratic principles." [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] The first was a statement about the displacement already under way before a single Arab army had crossed the frontier; the second was a political aim, a single state in place of the partition the General Assembly had voted for six months earlier. The document thus carries both readings of the war within it. It framed the intervention as an act of order and pointed to a displacement already under way; it also set out, in its own words, to replace the partition plan with a single state.

Who came, and how. The US State Department's Office of the Historian records that the war began with an Arab air attack on Tel Aviv on the eve of 14 May. Armies from Lebanon, Syria, Iraq and Egypt invaded; a Saudi formation fought under Egyptian command; and Transjordanian forces intervened only in the areas designated for the Arab state or for the Jerusalem corpus separatum, the international zone the partition plan had drawn around the city. Through all of it the United States kept an arms embargo on all belligerents. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Other accounts in this library describe the entry differently. The record on Lebanon says that on 15 May Lebanon "joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan, and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state," and the record on Egypt likewise counts Jordan among the invaders. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] The difference matters. Whether Transjordan's Arab Legion invaded Israel or entered the parts of Palestine the United Nations had assigned to the Arabs is the heart of a long argument about King Abdullah's intentions, told in the section on his dealings with the Jewish Agency.

Each state made its own decision. Lebanon's is often passed over. It fielded the smallest of the five Arab armies, and its choice to fight was its own. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] According to Makram Rabah, a history lecturer at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led Lebanon to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states while holding one. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] Lebanon's posture was thus a deliberated political choice, not simply a reaction imposed from outside. Egypt joined the invasion in May 1948 after the end of the Mandate. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] Saudi Arabia did not launch an invasion of its own. Its part was a small contingent of troops placed under Egyptian command. [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] Accounts of the kingdom's role explain the modest scale by its greater distance from Palestine. Its larger weapon was economic. The Arab League's boycott of Israel, formalized in 1948, barred member states from any direct economic relationship with the new state; a secondary boycott added in 1950 extended the bar to foreign companies doing business with Israel, and a tertiary boycott later reached companies dealing with those on the secondary list. Saudi Arabia was among its most consistent enforcers and kept it in some form for over seven decades. It never established diplomatic relations with Israel.

How many men. The size of the armies is itself disputed. Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops, and argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] His seminar notes add that the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League," and that the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] A US assessment of July 1948, discussed in [scene:s10b|the next section], counted about 90,000 Israeli forces by then. The two figures describe different dates and should not be merged. The fuller argument over the balance, and over whose numbers the "outnumbered" story rests on, belongs to that section.

The first round, 15 May to 11 June. Shlaim's notes give the outline of the first four weeks. The Egyptian advance stalled at Ramat Rahel on 24 May and at Ashdod on 29 May. The Syrians were stopped at Degania but held Mishmar Hayarden. The Iraqis held the triangle of Jenin, Nablus and Tulkarem. In Jerusalem the Jewish Quarter surrendered on 28 May, and three frontal Israeli attacks on the Arab Legion's position at Latrun, on 25 and 30 May and on 9 June, were repelled. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] Syria's army fought on the northern front and ended the war holding small areas west of the international border. [cite:tf_zaim] Lebanon's invasion was repelled, and Israeli forces for a time occupied part of southern Lebanon. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The first round thus ended with the Egyptian and Syrian advances stopped, the Iraqis holding their triangle, the Jewish Quarter lost and Latrun still in the Legion's hands. Shlaim calls the truce that followed "a turning-point." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war]

The first truce, 11 June to 9 July. The United Nations mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, had been appointed on 21 May. The truce he supervised ran 28 days, from 11 June to 9 July 1948, with observers from Belgium, France, Sweden and the United States. According to the Israel Defense Forces' own account, published by the Jewish Virtual Library, materiel reached the Israeli army during the truce from Europe, "particularly Czechoslovakia." [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] Bernadotte used the pause to propose a settlement: the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs, and Jerusalem under the United Nations. Both sides rejected it. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] The arms that crossed during those four weeks are the subject of the section on the Czechoslovak pipeline; Bernadotte's own fate, at the hands of Lehi in September, is told in the section on the founding of the army.

Lydda and Ramla, July 1948. Fighting resumed on 9 July. Operation Dani was launched from Ben Shemen on the night of 9–10 July. The assault on Lydda began on 11 July, and by 12 July the town was under full Israeli control, without a formal surrender. According to Sana Hammoudi's account in the Interactive Encyclopedia of the Palestine Question, between 80 and 176 people were killed at the Dahmash mosque and more than 400 in the town. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Both that account and Zachary Lockman, each citing the Israeli historian Benny Morris, report that on 12 July David Ben-Gurion answered a question about the inhabitants with the words "Expel them." Yitzhak Rabin then signed an order to expel Lydda's inhabitants quickly. Israeli censors later made Rabin remove the episode from his memoir. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war]

The numbers are disputed, and the two sources should be read side by side. Lockman, summarizing Morris, puts the combined population of Lydda and Ramla at 50,000–70,000, about 15,000 of them refugees, with 250–400 Palestinian civilians and four Israeli soldiers killed. The Palestinian encyclopedia estimates that about 70,000 people were forced out on 13 July and that close to 1,000 died in the towns and on the march that followed. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war] [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] Neither figure is a count; both are estimates, and the higher one includes deaths on the march.

The second truce and Jerusalem. The second truce began at 19:00 on 18 July 1948. It did not bring quiet to Jerusalem. According to the IDF account, the Arab Legion continued to shell West Jerusalem through October and on 12 August demolished the pumping station at Latrun, then held by the United Nations. A "sincere cease-fire" in the city was agreed only on 30 November. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce2]

The armistices of 1949. The war ended in separate armistice agreements between Israel and Egypt, Lebanon, Transjordan and Syria; Egypt kept the Gaza Strip and Jordan the West Bank. The Office of the Historian dates them, collectively, to "February 1949." [cite:rs_rd5_oh_war_b] The individual agreements in the record carry later dates for two of them. The agreements with Egypt were negotiated on the Greek island of Rhodes; they set a ceasefire line, not a peace, which served as the de facto border along the edge of the Gaza Strip for the next two decades. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] From 1948 to 1967 Egypt governed Gaza directly as a military protectorate, and its officials maintained throughout that it had not annexed the territory. Why Cairo avoided annexation is not settled by the record: some accounts stress an Arab League consensus against it, others Egyptian strategic caution. Lebanon's armistice, signed on 23 March 1949, restored the internationally recognized border. [cite:lebanon_1948_war]

Syria's took longer, and the delay holds one of the war's least-known episodes. After Husni al-Za'im seized power in Damascus in March 1949, armistice talks opened on 5 April; Za'im offered a peace treaty and military cooperation, proposed meeting Ben-Gurion or Moshe Sharett, and offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 Palestinian refugees in Syria, with the border drawn through the middle of Lake Hula and the Sea of Galilee. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] Ben-Gurion would not stake policy on him, partly from distrust of his ties to Washington. [cite:majalla_zaim] The armistice signed on 20 July 1949 turned the areas Syria evacuated into demilitarized zones, which became the fault line of the frontier; in August Za'im was deposed and executed in Syria's second coup of the year, and the offer died with him ([scene:sy_s01|Syria and Za'im's offer]). [cite:ecf_zaim]

The cost. More than 6,000 Israelis were killed in the war, about 1% of the roughly 650,000 Jews then in the country, according to a Reuters figure published by Ynet in 2005. [cite:rs_rd5_ynet_dead] The war's other costs fell on the Palestinian Arabs: the quarter of a million already displaced by 15 May on the League's own count, and many more after it, as told in [scene:rd5_refugees|the section on the refugees]. In Lebanon alone an estimated 100,000–110,000 arrived from northern Palestine. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

What the record does not settle. Several things remain open on the sources gathered for this book. The number of Arab soldiers and civilians killed in the war has not been established here, and no figure is offered. The fighting of the autumn and winter of 1948–49, between the second truce and the armistices, is not covered by the research behind this section beyond the Jerusalem front. The sources disagree on whether Transjordan invaded Israel or entered only the areas assigned to the Arab state, and on the date of the armistices. The tolls at Lydda and Ramla rest on estimates that differ by a factor of two or more. And the deepest question, whether the armies came to save the Palestinian Arabs, to prevent a Jewish state, or to take territory for themselves, has no single answer: the League's cablegram, Lebanon's deliberated choice, Saudi Arabia's distant contingent, the Legion's entry, on the Office of the Historian's account, only into the areas assigned to the Arab state or the international zone, and Egypt's nineteen-year administration of Gaza without annexation point in different directions, because the states that went to war in May 1948 were pursuing different ends.

sections.h: The Military Balance of 1948
sections.html:
Two stories about the military balance of 1948 have outlived the war. In the first, Israel was a tiny nation, vastly outnumbered, that defeated overwhelming Arab armies through will and endurance, a story often told as a near-miracle. In the second, Israel won not through real capability but because international sympathy, born of the Holocaust, tipped the scales. Each is repeated as if it described the whole war. The documents describe something neither story accounts for: a balance that changed, in stages, between the invasion of May 1948 and January 1949.

A report written during the war. The most valuable single document is a US government assessment dated 1 July 1948, written while the outcome was still unknown. It put Israeli forces at roughly 90,000 in total, with about 35,000 of them used in active operations. It also found that the Arab armies were, at that moment, stronger than Israel in artillery and tanks, while carrying a wide variety of small arms. [cite:frus1948_military_situation] Its value lies in its timing. Nobody writing it could shape the numbers around how the war ended, because nobody yet knew. Its limit lies in the same place: it is a snapshot of one moment, not an account of the war's course.

The sources for this section disagree on what kind of report it was. The account on which this section draws calls it, in one place, a contemporaneous CIA assessment and, in another, a US State Department report. [cite:frus1948_military_situation] This book has not resolved which office produced it, and refers to it here simply as the July 1948 US assessment.

Two phases, not one picture. Historians describe the war as two distinct military phases. From the invasion of 15 May until the first truce in June 1948, accounts describe the Israeli forces as initially inferior in both numbers and armament. After the truce, new enlistments and arms deliveries, among them the Czechoslovak shipments traced in [scene:cz_s01|the section on the Czech arms], allowed Israel to seize the initiative. One historical anthology states that for most of the war, excluding that first period, "the Jews were superior in personnel, equipment, logistics and organization." [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] The early disadvantage was real; so was the reversal that followed it.

On one point within that first phase, the sources do not agree. Avi Shlaim gives the forces on 15 May 1948 as 35,000 Israeli troops against 20,000–25,000 Arab troops. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] His seminar notes put it more precisely: the Israeli army had more men but weaker firepower, and the forces the Arab states actually sent were "well below the level demanded by the Military Committee of the Arab League." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] On Shlaim's figures, then, Israel was not outnumbered even in May; it was outgunned. The anthology's "inferior in both numbers and armament" and Shlaim's "more men but weaker firepower" cannot both be right about numbers, though they agree about weapons. The reader should also keep the dates apart. Shlaim's 35,000 describes 15 May. The US assessment's 90,000 describes 1 July, and its own figure of about 35,000 refers to the troops in active operations at that later date, not to the army's size at the invasion. The coincidence of the two 35,000s is not a confirmation of either.

Shlaim calls the June truce "a turning-point," and he argues that "illicit arms-imports decisively tipped the military balance in favour of Israel." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_seminar_war] [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_war] That judgment places the turn where the anthology places it: in the weeks of the first truce, when arms reached the Israeli army and the Arab states did not match them. The course of that fighting, from the first round to the armistices, is told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the section on the Arab states' war].

Whose numbers. Much of the popular "tiny, outnumbered Israel" arithmetic traces back to estimates by John Glubb, commander of Jordan's Arab Legion during the war. Historians who have worked on the order of battle note that, as the commander of one of the fighting armies, Glubb had a direct and plausible incentive to exaggerate Israeli numbers and play down Arab ones. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] This is ordinary source criticism, and it cuts only so far. It does not show that Glubb falsified anything; it shows that a widely repeated figure comes from an interested party, a fact rarely mentioned when his numbers are cited as neutral.

The ending the story leaves out. By the later stages of the war, accounts state that Israel's army outnumbered the combined Arab armies by roughly two to one. The Arab states reinforced their forces over the course of the war, but they never matched the pace of Israeli growth in men and arms. [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance] A story about beating impossible odds usually implies that the odds stayed impossible until the end. On this record they did not: the advantage had passed decisively to Israel well before the fighting stopped. That does not make the outcome inevitable or easy in hindsight. The difficulty of the first weeks, when the Arab armies held real advantages in heavy weapons, stands in the record beside the reversal.

Why neither story survives. The underdog story holds, at most, for the opening weeks, and even there it leans on one commander's disputed figures and on a count of men that Shlaim's figures contradict; what the record does support is an Arab advantage in firepower, in artillery and tanks, which the US assessment still found on 1 July. The sympathy story fares no better. To hold, it must pass over a dated military reversal, the arms that arrived during and after the first truce, and a final numerical advantage of about two to one that owed nothing to international goodwill and a great deal to logistics, organization and weapons that arrived and were used. [cite:jvl_israel_studies_1948] [cite:decolonizepalestine_military_balance]

What remains open. The record gathered here does not settle the size of the Israeli force on 15 May: one account says it was inferior in numbers, Shlaim says it was larger. It does not say which office of the US government wrote the July 1948 assessment. It gives the final two-to-one ratio as an approximation without a precise date or count of either side. And it offers no independent figures for the Arab armies' strength after May against which Glubb's estimates could be checked. What it does establish is the shape of the war's balance: a real early disadvantage in firepower, a turn at the first truce, and a decisive Israeli superiority by the end.

sections.h: From Three Militias to One Army, May 1948 – February 1949
sections.html:
It is often assumed that Israel's army was a single national force from the day of independence. It was not. On 14 May 1948 three armed bodies claimed to fight for the new state: the Haganah; the Irgun, commanded by Menachem Begin; and Lehi, led by three men. Each had its own command and its own arms. Making them one army took four months, an order, a confrontation on a Tel Aviv beach in which Jews killed Jews, and an assassination that the new government itself called terrorism.

The order of 26 May 1948. Twelve days after the declaration of independence, the provisional government headed by David Ben-Gurion issued an order establishing the Israel Defense Forces. It outlawed any other armed force and required the Haganah, the Irgun and Lehi to merge into the new army. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] The order was the instrument; the question was whether the undergrounds would obey it. The war with the Arab states, told in [scene:rd5_invasion|the section on the Arab states' war], was then in its second week, and the new army was being formed while it fought.

The Altalena, June 1948. The test came within a month. In June 1948 the Irgun brought an arms ship, the Altalena, to the coast, carrying weapons that it intended partly for its own units. Ben-Gurion refused to let the cargo bypass the army. The two positions could not both stand: an Irgun that kept its own weapons was an army beside the army, which the order of 26 May had outlawed. On 22 June IDF units under the command of Yitzhak Rabin shelled the ship off the Tel Aviv beach. Sixteen Irgun members and three IDF soldiers were killed, nineteen dead in all. The Irgun's separate units were then disbanded. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair]

The episode fell during the first truce of the war, which ran from 11 June to 9 July, when arms were reaching the Israeli army from Europe. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] The dispute over the Altalena was therefore not about whether weapons should come in, but about who would hold them once they arrived. The same commander, Rabin, would sign the order to expel the inhabitants of Lydda three weeks later. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda]

The killing of Bernadotte, September 1948. The second test came from Lehi. Count Folke Bernadotte had been appointed United Nations mediator on 21 May 1948; he had supervised the first truce and proposed a settlement giving the Galilee to Israel, the Negev to the Arabs and Jerusalem to the United Nations, which both sides rejected. [cite:rs_rd5_jvl_truce1] On 17 September 1948 members of Lehi assassinated him in Jerusalem. The government's response was the strongest it had: it declared Lehi a terrorist organization and arrested its members. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The word matters: the government of the new state applied it, in its own name, to a Jewish underground.

The arrests did not last. In February 1949 the Lehi members were released under a general amnesty. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The record gathered here does not say why the amnesty was granted, how many were held, or whether anyone was tried for the killing.

Absorbed, then promoted. The pattern that emerges is not one of suppression alone. Within four months of its founding the state had established a monopoly of armed force, by order, by shelling and by dissolution. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] Within thirty-five years it had placed the leaders of both absorbed undergrounds in the prime minister's office. Menachem Begin, whose ship the army had shelled, became prime minister in 1977. [cite:wiki_altalena_affair] Yitzhak Shamir, one of Lehi's three leaders, became prime minister in 1983. [cite:wiki_bernadotte_assassination] The line of armed undergrounds that runs through the years before 1948 ends not in their disappearance but in succession to the state's highest office. Begin's new party drew a public protest in a letter signed by Albert Einstein and Hannah Arendt in December 1948, discussed in [scene:rf_s01|the section on the dissenters].

Two readings of this sequence are possible, and the record supports parts of each. One stresses the state's resolve: a provisional government, at war, fired on its own citizens rather than tolerate a private army, and named a Jewish underground's assassination of a UN mediator for what it was. The other stresses how quickly the line was redrawn: the arrests ended in an amnesty within five months of the killing, and the men who had led the Irgun and Lehi later became prime ministers. Both are true of the same events.

What the record does not settle. The sources gathered for this book give the dead of the Altalena but not the fate of its cargo. They name Lehi's members as the assassins of Bernadotte but not the individuals who planned or carried out the killing, and they record the amnesty without its terms or its reasons. They do not say how the Haganah's own structure was carried into the new army. These gaps are real, and this section does not fill them.

sections.h: The Refugees of 1948
sections.html:
The war of 1948 produced two outcomes that have shaped everything since: a Jewish state, and a Palestinian Arab population largely displaced from the territory that state came to hold. Palestinians call the second the Nakba, Arabic for "catastrophe." [cite:npr_hamashistory] Three questions about it have been argued over ever since, and they are best kept apart. How many people became refugees? Why did they leave? And why did they not return? The record answers the first within a range, the second only in part, and the third more clearly than is often supposed.

How many. The displacement began before the Arab armies entered. In its cablegram of 15 May 1948 the Arab League told the United Nations that "approximately over a quarter of a million of the Arab population have been compelled to leave their homes." [cite:rs_rd5_un_s745] That was the League's figure, given on the day of the invasion; an IDF intelligence estimate of June, discussed below, gave a higher one for 1 June.

The figure most often cited for the whole war comes from the United Nations itself. In a report dated at Lausanne on 19 August 1949 (document A/AC.25/Com.Tech/9), the Technical Committee of the UN Conciliation Commission for Palestine adopted an estimate made by P. J. Loftus of the UN Statistical Office: about 711,000 refugees from the territory under Israeli control, a figure the committee described as "as accurate as circumstances permit." [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] The same report explained why the number of people drawing relief was larger than the number of refugees: duplicate ration cards, people displaced from other areas, and destitute people who were not refugees at all. [cite:rs_rd5_unccp_1949] The warning matters, because UNRWA's later figure drew on relief rolls.

Rex Brynen's Palestinian Refugee ResearchNet at McGill University set out the range in 1996. It gives the Conciliation Commission's figure as 726,000; UNRWA's 1950 figure as 957,000; the Israeli government's past figure as "as low as 520,000"; and Palestinian researchers' upper estimate as 850,000. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] The two figures attributed to the Conciliation Commission, 711,000 in its own technical report and 726,000 in Brynen's summary, do not match, and this book gives both. A widely used round figure is approximately 700,000. [cite:npr_hamashistory]

The panel above sets that figure, about 700,000 with the UN estimate of about 711,000, beside the land and immigration numbers of the Mandate years. The range around it is wide, and each figure carries its method.

Where they went. According to Brynen, about a third of the refugees went to the West Bank, a third to Gaza, and the rest to Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and beyond. [cite:rs_rd5_prrn_1996] Gaza was then under Egyptian administration and the West Bank under Jordanian. [cite:npr_hamashistory] Lebanon received an estimated 100,000–110,000, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, in a country of about 1.3 million people. The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that resulted. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy] The receiving states treated them differently. Jordan later gave citizenship to most Palestinians who had come after 1948, under its 1954 nationality law; Lebanon restricted their work and, much later, their right to own property; and the Arab League instructed its members not to grant citizenship, in its words "to avoid dissolution of their identity and protect their right of return." That divergence, and the arguments on both sides of it, are told in [scene:sq_s20|the section on the host countries]. [cite:jns_arab_citizenship] [cite:fmr_lebanon] The displacement became, in the words of one account, the foundational political fact around which every later Palestinian political movement organized. [cite:npr_hamashistory]

Why they left. This is the most disputed of the three questions, and the evidence has to be read with care for who produced it. The most cited single document is an intelligence report of the Israel Defense Forces from June 1948, known through the work of the Israeli historian Benny Morris and summarized by Zachary Lockman. It estimated that by 1 June 1948 about 240,000 Arabs had fled the areas of the Jewish state and about 150,000 had fled other areas. It attributed about 70% of the flight to direct Jewish military operations, 2% to psychological warfare and 2% to expulsion orders, a figure Morris considers an underestimate, and no more than 5% to evacuation orders from Arab leaders. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] Those numbers were compiled by the army that was doing the fighting, and its own share of responsibility is the largest it records.

The claim that Palestinians left on the orders of their own leaders, broadcast by Arab radio, corresponds to that last category, and the IDF's own estimate put it at 5% or less. The investigation of the radio claim itself is told in the section on independence and the Nakba.

From June 1948 the pattern changed. Morris concludes, according to Lockman, that deliberate expulsions helped create about 300,000 further refugees, but that there was no explicit, general Israeli decision to expel. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] The expulsion from Lydda and Ramla in July, after Ben-Gurion's reported words "Expel them" and Yitzhak Rabin's signed order, is the best-known case; its tolls are disputed and are set out in the section on the Arab states' war. [cite:rs_rd5_palquest_lydda] [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_war]

Historians divide on what this evidence adds up to. Morris, as Avi Shlaim summarizes him, "rejected both the 'Arab order' and the 'Jewish robber-state' explanations" and treated the refugee problem as "a by-product of the war." Shlaim holds that the evidence "suggests a far higher degree of Israeli responsibility." [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ref] Walid Khalidi's reading goes further: that the flight was produced by design, under Plan Dalet, the plan discussed earlier in this chapter. [cite:rs_rd5_shlaim_hnn_ref] The strongest form of Morris's case is that the flight came in waves with different causes, that most of it followed fighting rather than orders, and that no general order to expel has been found. The strongest form of the opposing case is that the army's own estimate assigns the great majority of the flight to its operations, that deliberate expulsions grew from June, and that a policy need not be written as a general order to be carried out.

Why they did not return. On this point the record is plainer. "As early as June 1948," Lockman writes, "the cabinet had reached a consensus against allowing the refugees to return to their homes." [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] The decision came while the war was still being fought, and before the expulsions from Lydda and Ramla in July. Lockman also writes that a report by Yosef Weitz in October 1948 falsely blamed Arab leaders for organizing the flight. [cite:rs_rd5_lockman_ref] That is Lockman's judgment of Weitz's report; the point it carries is that the "Arab leaders' orders" explanation was being put forward inside Israel's own administration within months. One offer to settle part of the question came from an Arab government: in 1949 Syria's new military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, offered to resettle 250,000–300,000 refugees in Syria as part of a peace treaty, an offer Ben-Gurion declined and which ended with Za'im's overthrow and execution that August. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] [cite:ecf_zaim] The United Nations' response, and the negotiations that followed, belong to the next stage: see [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194] and [scene:lau_s01|Lausanne].

The villages. How many Arab villages were emptied depends on what is counted. Morris, in 1987, counted 369. Walid Khalidi's All That Remains (1992) counted 418, excluding towns and 151 places found on other lists. Aref al-Aref counted 399; Nijm and Muammer 443; Saleh 472; and the Palestine Land Society 531 localities, counting tribal lands and towns. [cite:rs_rd5_plands_villages] The source attributes the spread to method: what counts as a village, whether towns and tribal lands are included, and which lists are merged.

What the record does not settle. No single count of the refugees commands agreement; the sources range from 520,000 to 957,000, and even the Conciliation Commission's figure is reported two ways. The share of the flight caused by deliberate expulsion, as against fighting, fear and the collapse of Palestinian society, is estimated from an army report that its own principal interpreter considers incomplete on expulsions. Whether the flight was the product of a plan or of the war is the central argument among historians, and it is not resolved here. The number of Arabs who remained inside Israel in 1948–49 has not been established in the sources gathered for this book. What is not in dispute is the outcome: by the summer of 1949 several hundred thousand Palestinian Arabs were outside the territory Israel held, and its government had decided, a year earlier, that they would not come back.

chapters.label: Stage Six
chapters.title: Consolidate and Account
chapters.intro:
On 20 May 1948, six days after Israel declared its independence, the United Nations appointed Count Folke Bernadotte, head of the Swedish Red Cross, as its mediator in Palestine. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The war he was sent to stop was still being fought. Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq had invaded on the Mandate's last day, and Jordan's Arab Legion held the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] The new state had been recognized by the United States eleven minutes after its declaration, but only de facto, over the written objections of the State Department and the CIA; full legal recognition would wait until January 1949. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] Inside the lines Israel held, its statisticians would count 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews at the end of the year. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] Beyond them, by December, some 700,000 Palestinians were refugees, a number disputed from the first day it was given. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix]

This stage asks what became of all that once the shooting stopped. The war had produced facts: positions held, villages emptied, houses occupied, a state with an army and no borders. In the years that followed, each fact was either written into law and treaty or left in suspense, and the choice was rarely made by one party alone. The stage follows both processes, consolidation and accounting. It asks who fixed the lines, who took title to the land, who was admitted as a citizen and who was not, who paid, and what the new international order did, and could not do, for the people the war had displaced. It also closes the account on the years before the state: who funded the build, through which channels, and what the record can and cannot show about money and American politicians.

The cast is the widest in the volume. Israel's government under David Ben-Gurion and Moshe Sharett, and its first parliament, made most of the decisions that turned wartime facts into statute. The United Nations acted through Bernadotte, through Ralph Bunche, who negotiated the armistices after Bernadotte's murder, and through a Conciliation Commission of France, Turkey and the United States. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] In Washington Harry Truman moved between his Secretary of State, George Marshall, his political aide Clark Clifford and the donors of an election year. Among the Arab states, King Abdullah of Jordan, Egypt's government and a Syrian officer, Husni al-Za'im, each pursued a different settlement. Palestinian leaders acted on both sides of an inter-Arab rivalry, in a government proclaimed in Gaza under Ahmad Hilmi and Hajj Amin al-Husayni, and in a congress at Jericho that asked to be joined to Abdullah's crown. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The Jews of Iraq, Yemen, Libya, Egypt and Morocco, West Germany's Konrad Adenauer, the Holy See and an American lobby in the course of renaming itself complete it.

The sections begin with the mediator's two plans and with Truman's decisions from the summer of 1948 to May 1950, including the one decision that a historian ties to a campaign contribution. They then follow how return was barred and the border hardened, who came to govern Arab Palestine, and the regime imposed on the Arabs who stayed inside Israel, before tracing the laws that turned flight into state ownership of land. One week in December 1948 produced the Universal Declaration and Resolution 194; the armistices of 1949 drew lines that, by their own text, were not borders; Lausanne failed over which should come first, peace or return. Israel's constitution was deferred, Syria's offer of peace was declined, and Israel entered the United Nations while the question of Jerusalem stayed open. The refugees' host states, the exodus of the Jews of the Arab world, the mass immigration and the Yemenite children, and the laws defining who belonged follow. The stage then closes the books: the organization that became AIPAC, how the state was paid for, how the flight was explained, how the case was put to Americans, who paid for the pre-state build, and the whole sequence from a bank to a state.
chapters.outro:
This volume began with a loan. In 1694, 1,268 subscribers lent the English Crown £1.2 million through a newly chartered company that became the Bank of England, and a state at war learned to borrow from private lenders on a regular footing. [cite:rs_rd0_boe_museum] It ends two and a half centuries later with a state drawing on outside money in its own name: a loan from the Export-Import Bank of the United States, bonds sold to buyers abroad, and reparations from West Germany. Between the two lie the structures this volume has traced, laid by many hands over many decades and never by one design. By the early 1950s they stood in six layers, and each held something the others did not.

The legal layer was the longest in the making. The Ottoman Land Code of 1858 required titles to be registered, turning land into something that could be bought and sold. [cite:wiki_ottoman_land_code_1858] Balfour's letter of 1917 had no legal force until the Mandate of 1922 wrote it into an instrument of the League of Nations, recognized a "Jewish agency" in Article 4, and bound Britain in Article 2 to the national home, to self-governing institutions and to the rights of all inhabitants, with no rule for choosing among them. [cite:rs_md_avalon] The General Assembly's partition resolution passed on 29 November 1947 by 33 votes to 13. [cite:rs_rd5_un_yearbook_181] After 1948 the new state supplied its own law: the Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950, the Law of Return of 5 July 1950, the Nationality Law in force from 14 July 1952, and the Land Acquisition Law of 1953. [cite:un_absentees_property_law_text] [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn] [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality] [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] Its sovereignty and membership of the United Nations, granted by Resolution 273 on 11 May 1949, were settled. [cite:rs_rd6_unga273_text] Its borders were not. Each armistice of 1949 reserved the final settlement, and the Egyptian text said the line was "not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary." [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Nor did the state give itself a constitution: the Harari Resolution of 13 June 1950 promised one in chapters, with no deadline. [cite:rs_rd6_dickerman_2007] What was contested was the force of the older texts. Israel held that the Arab invasion had nullified partition and that Resolution 194 tied return to peace; the Arab states at Lausanne demanded the 1947 lines and return first. [cite:un_ccp_fourth_report] [cite:unispal_194_survey]

The administrative layer showed the most continuity. The Mandate's High Commissioner had governed from 1923 with no elected chamber beside him. [cite:rs_lc_albright] The Defence (Emergency) Regulations that Britain issued in 1945 passed into Israeli law in 1948, and under them a military government ruled most Arab citizens of Israel until 1 December 1966. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The strongest case for it, made at the time and endorsed by the Rattner Commission in 1956, was that a state with armistices but no peace needed such controls; the strongest case against, made by the historian Alina Korn, is that its purpose was to control movement and keep Arabs from confiscated land, and it rests on conviction figures: about 95 percent of Arab citizens' convictions under the regulations were for administrative offences, such as lacking a permit. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The record documents both purposes and does not weigh them.

The institutional and financial layer was built first by the movement and then by the state. The Jewish Colonial Trust of 1899, the Jewish National Fund of 1901 and Keren Hayesod, which raised $20.1 million worldwide in 1921–29, made fundraising permanent; by 1948 the United Jewish Appeal raised $150 million from more than a million American contributors, of which $74.7 million went to Palestine and $64.9 million to relief in Europe. [cite:jta_kh_decade] [cite:jta_uja_1948] After 1948 a Custodian, a Development Authority and the Fund itself received the land of those classed as absentees; BADIL puts the transfers at nearly 2.4 million dunams, a figure the scholarly sources here do not confirm. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] The money became a state's money: $100.0 million of American aid in 1949, all of it economic, more than $52 million in Israel Bonds in their first year, and German reparations that made up 12–14 percent of Israel's imports for a decade. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The Knesset voted to negotiate with Germany by 61 to 50, while opponents led by Menachem Begin called the payments "blood money." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] What the record leaves open is a total: no audited sum exists for the pre-state build or the Haganah's budget.

The Palestinian Arab layer was a national movement that never acquired a state's instruments. Its congresses and the Arab Executive under Musa Kazim al-Husseini were never recognized by Britain, and its boycott of 1923 defeated the Legislative Council but won no recognition. [cite:palquest_musa_kazim] [cite:rs_lc_cojs_boycott] In 1948 Palestinian leaders proclaimed a government in Gaza that Avi Shlaim calls "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states," while notables at Jericho asked to be joined to Abdullah's crown. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The refugees were counted from 520,000 to a million, depending on who counted. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] They were given relief through UNRWA, left outside the 1951 Refugee Convention by its Article 1D, and promised in paragraph 11 of Resolution 194 that those wishing to return "should be permitted to do so." [cite:unrwa_who] [cite:w_refconv] [cite:unispal_194_survey] Their strongest case is that return is a right, reaffirmed by the Assembly every year since 1949; Israel's is that the resolution made return conditional on peace, and that the Arab states first rejected it. [cite:wiki_res_194] [cite:unwatch_194] The 156,000 non-Jews counted inside Israel at the end of 1948 voted from the first election, most of them while living under military rule. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] [cite:rs_rd6_idi_nazareth] [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Whether the expulsions of 1948 were planned remains disputed; the claim that the refugees left on a general Arab order is no longer defended by mainstream scholarship. [cite:w_morris_birth]

The regional layer was redrawn twice. Britain made conflicting wartime promises in 1915–16, to Sharif Hussein and to France, and at Cairo in 1921 gave Iraq to his son Faisal and Transjordan to his son Abdullah. [cite:w_mcmahon] [cite:w_sykes_picot] [cite:w_cairo1921] In 1948–50 one of them, Abdullah, annexed the West Bank, and the Arab League condemned him for it. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Iraq and Saudi Arabia signed no armistice, and the League's boycott carried the conflict into trade. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Syria's military ruler, Husni al-Za'im, offered a peace treaty and the resettlement of 250,000–300,000 refugees, and Ben-Gurion declined. [cite:tf_zaim] [cite:majalla_zaim] The war also ended Jewish life in much of the Arab world: Iraq made Zionism a crime in July 1948, and by the end of 1952 Israel had received 377,251 immigrants from Muslim countries. [cite:yated_ezra_nechemia] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_immigrants_4852] Philip Mendes explains that exodus by push and pull together, against the partisan accounts on either side. [cite:rs_rd6_mendes_2010]

The American layer had the deepest roots and the newest weight. A Christian restorationist lobby pressed for a Jewish return in 1839. [cite:wiki_christian_zionism] Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration in 1922, both party platforms adopted the movement's aims in 1944, and the American Zionist Emergency Council worked Congress district by district. [cite:wiki_lodge_fish] [cite:aja_azec_appraisal_1944] [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Truman recognized the state against his strategists' advice. In the election summer he stopped pressing Israel on territory and refugees, in part, by John Judis's account, because his campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann; then he threatened a "revision" of policy in May 1949 that he never enforced. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] The claim that donors bought policy has that one documented case and no other; the claim that money played no role is contradicted by it. Whether money reached members of Congress before 1948 cannot be known, because the law did not require the records until 1971. [cite:wiki_fcpa_1925]

What, then, did the road from 1694 settle? It settled that a Jewish state existed, with an army, a parliament, a land regime and a law of immigration, and that it rested on institutions built over half a century before it was declared. It did not settle where the state ended, what was owed to the people displaced in its founding, or who would govern the rest of the land. The Holocaust gave the build its urgency; it did not create the apparatus. And the war of 1948, not any plan, decided where the lines ran. Those lines were, by their own text, still not borders. Every volume that follows begins from that fact.

sections.h: The Mediator: Count Bernadotte's Two Plans, May–September 1948
sections.html:
In the first weeks of the war of 1948 the United Nations named a mediator. For four months, from late May to mid-September 1948, one man carried the organization's attempt to stop the fighting and to sketch a settlement. He produced two sets of proposals, very different from each other. Neither was accepted. He was killed the day after he signed the second. Yet his last report outlived him, and several of its ideas passed almost directly into the resolutions and institutions that framed the refugee question for the rest of the century.

The man and the appointment. Folke Bernadotte came to the post with a reputation made in the last months of the Second World War. As head of the Swedish Red Cross he is credited with saving some 20,000 inmates of German concentration camps. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] He was appointed United Nations mediator in Palestine on 20 May 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio]

The sources differ, in a small way, on who appointed him. The UN's own press release of 17 September 1948 records that he was chosen by the five permanent members of the Security Council, sitting as a committee of the General Assembly under a General Assembly resolution of 14 May 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] Encyclopaedia Britannica says more simply that the Security Council named him. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] The difference is not trivial for a reader trying to understand where his authority came from. On the UN's account his mandate flowed from the General Assembly, the body that had voted for partition the previous November, with the great powers acting as its committee. On the shorter account it came from the Council. The UN's own contemporary record is the more detailed of the two, but this book records both.

The two truces. His first task was to stop the shooting. The first truce he negotiated took effect on 11 June 1948 and lasted until 9 July. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] Fighting resumed when it lapsed. On 15 July the Security Council ordered a second truce, which was to last "until a peaceful adjustment of the future situation of Palestine is reached." [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The difference in wording mattered. The first truce was a pause with an end date, negotiated with the parties. The second was ordered by the Council and had no end date at all: it was meant to hold until there was a settlement. It was inside that open-ended truce that Bernadotte wrote his final report.

The Rhodes suggestions of 28 June 1948. During the first truce, on 28 June 1948, Bernadotte presented the parties with a set of written suggestions at Rhodes. The American government's published diplomatic record preserves their text. [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] They did not start from the partition plan. They proposed that Palestine, including Transjordan, might form a union of "one Arab and one Jewish" member. Within that union, the Negev, in whole or in part, would go to Arab territory, and Western Galilee, in whole or in part, to Jewish territory. The City of Jerusalem would be included in Arab territory, with municipal autonomy for its Jewish community. Each member would control immigration within its own borders. [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june]

Two shared facilities would serve the whole union: a free port at Haifa, including the refineries and terminals, and a free airport at Lydda. And the suggestions proposed recognition of the right of people displaced by the conflict "to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property." [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] That phrase is the first appearance in this chapter of the language of return. It was unconditional. It set no date, required no prior peace, and offered no alternative of compensation.

According to the mediator's own later report, both parties "flatly rejected" the June suggestions. [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The sources gathered for this book record the rejection but not the parties' own statements of their reasons, and the prose should not supply them. What the text itself shows is what each side was being asked to accept. The Jewish side was asked to accept a union rather than an independent state with its own frontiers, and to see Jerusalem, with its Jewish community, placed in Arab territory with only municipal autonomy. The Arab side was asked to accept a Jewish member of a joint union, with its own control of immigration. Whatever reasons each gave, the mediator's second plan started from different premises.

The Progress Report of 16 September 1948. The report Bernadotte completed in September, dated 16 September 1948, began from a premise the June suggestions had avoided: "A Jewish State called Israel exists in Palestine." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The union with Transjordan was gone. In its place the report drew a territorial settlement between a recognized Jewish state and the Arab territory around it.

On territory it reversed part of the June scheme and kept part. The Negev should be Arab territory and Galilee should be Jewish territory. Ramleh and Lydda should be in Arab territory. The precise frontiers would be set by a UN technical boundaries commission. Jerusalem would no longer be placed in Arab territory; it would be under "effective United Nations control." Haifa would be a free port and Lydda a free airport, as in June. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress]

On the refugees, the report urged that Arab refugees be allowed to return to Jewish-controlled areas "at the earliest possible date," with adequate compensation for those choosing not to return. It proposed a Palestine conciliation commission to carry the settlement forward. And on the Arab territory, it saw "compelling reasons for merging the Arab territory of Palestine with the territory of Transjordan." [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_palquest_progress] The idea of joining Arab Palestine to Transjordan survived from June, but now as a merger of the Arab part alone, not a union that took in the Jewish state as well.

Set side by side, the two plans show how far the mediator moved in eleven weeks. The June suggestions treated Palestine and Transjordan as one framework to be divided into two members. The September report accepted Israel as a state, gave it Galilee, took the Negev, Ramleh and Lydda from it, removed Jerusalem from either side's control, and turned the right of return "without restriction" into return "at the earliest possible date," paired for the first time with compensation as the alternative.

The assassination. Bernadotte was killed in Jerusalem on 17 September 1948, the day after the report was dated, by members of the Stern Gang (Lehi). A French air force colonel serving as a UN observer, André-Pierre Sérot, was killed with him. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The UN noted that the completed report reached Paris almost simultaneously with the news of his death. [cite:rs_rd6_un_bernadotte_bio] The government's response to the killing, including the dissolution of Lehi and the amnesty that followed, belongs to [scene:mil_s01|the absorption of the undergrounds into one army].

What the report left behind. A plan that both parties rejected in June and that its author did not live to defend in September might have died with him. It did not, for two reasons. The first was Washington.
