Four days after the killing, on 21 September 1948, Secretary of State George Marshall endorsed the plan, including its award of the Negev to the Arab side, and the endorsement became an issue in an American presidential campaign; how President Truman then backed away from it is told in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after the election money]. The second was the General Assembly. Two of the report's central proposals, a conciliation commission and the return of refugees with compensation for those who chose not to return, reappeared in the Assembly's Resolution 194 of December 1948, whose full text and competing readings are set out in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194]. Britannica also credits Bernadotte's work with laying the groundwork for the UN Truce Supervision Organization and for UNRWA, the relief agency for Palestinian refugees. [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte]

What the record does not settle. The documents here establish what Bernadotte proposed, when, and that both sides rejected his first plan. They do not record, in the parties' own words, why each rejected it, nor how either side responded formally to the September report before events overtook it. Nor do they settle the narrower question of which UN body appointed him; the UN's contemporary account and Britannica's summary differ, and both are recorded above. What is beyond doubt is the direction of travel between June and September. A mediator who had begun by trying to fold the new state into a union with Transjordan ended by taking its existence as the starting point, and by writing the refugees' return, with compensation as its alternative, into the framework that the United Nations then adopted.

sections.h: Truman After Recognition: A Retreat, a Pledge, and a Threat Not Kept, 1948–1950
sections.html:
American recognition of Israel in May 1948 did not settle Washington's policy toward the new state. It opened a two-year sequence in which Harry Truman's decisions moved sometimes toward Israel's position and sometimes against it. Two accounts of that sequence circulate, and they are mirror images. One holds that once the donors had paid, Truman did whatever Israel wanted. The other holds that money had nothing to do with it, and that his policy followed from conviction and from the interests of the United States. Each has a strong form. The first can point to a named donor, a named sum and a historian's account of a decision that changed. The second can point to a president who signed legislation he called discriminatory against Jewish refugees and later threatened Israel in writing. The way to weigh them is to put the decisions in the order they were made, with their dates.

The decision that came first. Recognition itself had been made against the advice of the government's own specialists. Declassified CIA and State Department documents from 1947 and 1948 record consistent warnings against recognizing Israel on strategic grounds. The CIA's assessments noted the Zionist arms-procurement networks operating across Europe and the United States, predicted that recognition would immediately produce armed conflict with the Arab states, and warned of damage to American access to oil. One CIA report held that an arms embargo would lead to peaceful coexistence, the opposite of what followed. The State Department under George Marshall opposed recognition on strategic grounds as well. Truman overruled both. He recognized Israel at 6:11 pm on 14 May 1948, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, a recognition so fast that his own State Department was caught unprepared. It has been called the fastest diplomatic recognition in American history.

The familiar explanation is that Truman acted from moral conviction about Jewish statehood after the Holocaust, and that the CIA's concerns were one input among many. The documents support a narrower statement: the strategic advice was clear and was set aside, and the decision was political rather than strategic. One reading, made with the advantage of hindsight, holds that this set a pattern in which political decisions overrode intelligence assessments, and that the intelligence relationship which followed began on terms Israel could shape. That is an interpretation of later history, not a finding about 1948, and the later relationship, from James Jesus Angleton's tenure as the CIA's counterintelligence chief from 1954 to the Khrushchev speech of 1956, is told in [scene:cia_s02|the CIA and Israel after 1948].

25 June 1948: the Displaced Persons Act. The first decision of the summer concerned Jewish refugees in Europe rather than the new state itself. On 25 June 1948 Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act "with very great reluctance," saying that it "discriminates in callous fashion against displaced persons of the Jewish faith." [cite:truman_institute_dpact] He did not leave the matter there. He pressed Congress for two years, until the act was amended in 1950. [cite:wjc_dpact] [cite:truman_institute_dpact] The episode does not fit a president acting on donors' instructions, nor one indifferent to Jewish refugees: he signed a law he condemned and then spent two years trying to change it.

Summer 1948: what Truman wanted and did not press. Through the summer, Truman privately wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the partition lines, and he was disturbed by its refugee policy. He backed away from pressing either point. The historian John Judis documents that his nearly broke whistle-stop campaign needed $100,000 from two donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann, at that moment, and that this need was part of the reason he stopped pushing. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The donors, the sum and the way Judis frames it are the subject of [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. The point for this sequence is its date: the retreat came in the summer and autumn of an election year, when the campaign was short of money.

21–28 September 1948: the Bernadotte plan. On 16 September the UN mediator, Count Folke Bernadotte, completed a report that would have given the Negev to the Arab side; the next day he was murdered in Jerusalem. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_progress_report] [cite:rs_rd6_britannica_bernadotte] On 21 September 1948 Secretary of State Marshall endorsed the plan. On 28 September the White House aide Clark Clifford was upset that Marshall had approved it without the President's endorsement, and the camp of Truman's opponent, Thomas Dewey, sought to exploit the episode. [cite:jvl_clifford_bernadotte] [cite:djn_marshall_bernadotte_1948] Truman backed away from the plan. The episode shows that the American government was not of one mind. The Secretary of State and his department pressed a settlement that cut Israel's territory; the President's political staff, alert to the campaign, objected; and the President sided with his staff.

24 October 1948: the pledge. Ten days before the election, and two days after a statement by Dewey, Truman went further. He quoted the Democratic platform, which pledged full recognition of Israel and revision of the arms embargo "to accord to the State of Israel the right of self-defense," and he directed government agencies to expedite Israel's applications for loans. [cite:ucsb_truman_oct24_1948] The timing tells its own story. The statement answered an opponent's statement within forty-eight hours and came in the campaign's last fortnight.

29 November 1948: the Negev. After winning, on 29 November, Truman reassured Weizmann that Israel would keep the Negev. Two months earlier his Secretary of State had endorsed a plan that would have taken it away.

January 1949: recognition and a loan. The October pledges were then kept. An Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, and on 31 January 1949 the United States granted de jure recognition, full legal recognition of the state. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:docsteach_dejure_1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note]

The loan's size is best seen against the other dollar sums in this story. The library's money dashboard sets every documented American dollar flow of the pre-state and founding years side by side, in nominal dollars of the year reported. The $100 million loan is the largest bar on it. The $100,000 that Feinberg and Kaufmann raised for the campaign train is the smallest, one-thousandth of the loan. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman]

The contrast cuts both ways. Those who argue that donors bought policy point to the sequence: the campaign took the smaller sum in 1948, and the state received a government loan a thousand times larger in 1949. Those who argue that money played no role point to the scale: a government loan of $100 million was a decision of the United States made through the Export-Import Bank after an election had been won, not a return on a campaign contribution. The documents do not show a link between the two sums. What they show is that the $100,000 was raised at the moment a policy was in play, and that the loan followed a public pledge made in the campaign's last days.

28 May 1949: the threat. Then the pressure returned. On 28 May 1949, while the Lausanne talks were under way, Truman had a secret note delivered to David Ben-Gurion. It said the United States was "seriously disturbed" by Israel's position on territory and refugees. It said Israel should offer territorial compensation for the land it held beyond the partition lines. And it warned that if Israel continued to reject the UN resolution of December 1948, "a revision of its attitude toward Israel has become unavoidable." [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] The note took up exactly the two questions, territory and refugees, on which Truman had stopped pressing in the summer of 1948. With the election behind him, he raised them again, in writing.

June 1949: rejection, and no revision. Israel rejected the demands in June. The threatened revision was not carried through. [cite:jvl_truman_note_may1949] [cite:djn_1977_truman_note] The documents gathered here do not explain why Washington did not follow its warning with action. What came at Lausanne after the note is told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

May 1950: the Tripartite Declaration. In May 1950 the United States joined Britain and France in the Tripartite Declaration on the region. Its text has not been researched for this book, and its terms are not described here.

What the dated record supports. Laid out in order, the decisions have a clear shape. The two moves most favourable to Israel in 1948, the retreat from the Bernadotte plan and the October pledges, came when money and votes were most needed. After the election Truman both delivered and pushed back: he kept his pledges on recognition and the loan, and then, six months later, threatened a revision of policy over the very issues he had set aside. He did not enforce the threat. That record fits neither simple account. It is not the record of a president who did whatever Israel's supporters asked, since in May 1949 he sent a note threatening a revision of policy over territory and refugees. Nor is it the record of a president untouched by his campaign's finances, since a historian names financial need as part of the reason he stopped pressing a point he cared about, at the moment he stopped. Put in a sentence: the shift clustered around the election; then the pressure returned, and faded.

Several things remain unsettled. The documents establish timing, not motive: they show when Truman moved, not how much weight he gave to money, votes, conviction or advice at each step. Judis's account attributes the summer retreat to financial need "in part," and no source here measures that part. No document here links the campaign contribution to the 1949 loan. And the record gathered for this book does not say why the threatened revision of May 1949 was never carried out, which is perhaps the most consequential question of the sequence, since it was the moment at which Washington had stated its terms and then let them go.

sections.h: Abraham Feinberg: One Donor, One Decision, 1945–1958
sections.html:
Abraham Feinberg's name is absent from most popular accounts of 1948. It belongs in them, for a specific reason. He is the person through whom the documented record comes closest to showing a campaign contribution changing a particular decision of the American president. That claim needs to be stated at exactly its documented size, no larger and no smaller, and the rest of his career helps show why.

The man. Abraham "Abe" Feinberg was born in 1908 and died in 1998. He was born and raised in the Bronx and built his fortune in the hosiery business. From 1945 he played a significant role behind the scenes in the relationship between the United States and Israel, a role that lasted until 1968. Across those years he served as a confidant and a key financier to three presidents: Truman, Kennedy and Johnson. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis] [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb] He was also one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute, the arms-procurement network founded in 1945, whose place in the wider American structure is mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up]. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis]

That second fact matters for what follows. Feinberg was not a donor who appears once in the record and then disappears. He links two structures that are often told separately: the private arms-procurement network that operated on American soil from 1945, and the presidential campaign of 1948.

The $100,000. In mid-1948 Truman's campaign was broke, and Thomas Dewey was widely expected to make him a one-term president. Truman needed $100,000, a large sum in 1948, to pay for a whistle-stop tour by train through the Midwest. Feinberg and the jewelry magnate Ed Kaufmann led the fundraising that produced that amount, at that moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:prnewswire_feinberg_fbi]

Feinberg later described his own method plainly. "My path to power," he said, "was cooperation in terms of what they needed — campaign money." [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:prnewswire_feinberg_fbi] The words are his, on the record, not an outside reading of his motives. They describe an exchange in general terms: he supplied what politicians needed, and he gained access in return. They do not, by themselves, say what any president gave him.

The decision. The link between the money and a decision comes from the historian John Judis. In mid-1948, by Judis's account, Truman wanted Israel to stop seizing territory by military force beyond the UN partition lines, and he was personally "disgusted" by Israel's refugee policy. He is reported to have said that Jews had turned their own narrative on its head by denying Palestinians the right of return. Judis documents that Truman folded on these impulses in part because he needed the $100,000 from Feinberg and Kaufmann for the whistle-stop tour at that moment. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] The dated sequence of what Truman did and did not do on territory and refugees, from the Bernadotte plan to the threat he sent Ben-Gurion in May 1949, is set out in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after recognition].

The familiar account holds that Truman's support for Israel was a matter of personal conviction and of a broad political calculation about Jewish voters, with no instance in which financial dependence changed a specific decision. Judis's account is such an instance. It names a donor, a sum, a moment in a campaign, and an objection the President stopped pressing. That is a different and more precise kind of claim than the general statement that money influenced politics.

It is also a limited one, and the limits are in Judis's own words. He says Truman folded "in part" because of the financial need. Money was one cause among others, not the only one. The account is one historian's reading of one decision. It does not show that Feinberg's money bought American policy toward Israel in general, and it does not show what Truman thought he was giving in return. When Truman later threatened Israel over the same two questions, territory and refugees, the money of 1948 did not prevent him. Some accounts go further and place the recognition of Israel, eleven minutes after its declaration of independence, inside the same financial relationship. The sources gathered here document no such link for recognition itself; they tie the $100,000 to the summer retreat and to nothing else.

Why the smallest sum matters most. Set beside the other dollar flows of the founding years, the $100,000 is tiny. On the library's money dashboard it is the smallest bar, one-thousandth of the $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] Yet it is the only sum in that record that a historian ties to a specific policy decision. Most of the other money built institutions. This sum, by Judis's account, was raised at the moment a decision was being made. Its importance comes from its timing, not its size.

The FARA order of 1952. The federal government did eventually reach Feinberg, not for arms but for publishing. In 1952 he was formally ordered to register as an agent of a foreign principal under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The order concerned Israel Speaks, a bimonthly publication he ran on behalf of Israeli interests, the successor to an earlier publication aligned with the Haganah. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] [cite:israellobby_feinberg_fbi] Feinberg briefly considered selling the publication to the Jerusalem Post. Instead he shut it down entirely rather than register. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] The outcome was compliance by closure: there was no prosecution and no fight in court.

The order corrects a claim sometimes made about the Sonneborn network, that none of its figures was ever required to register as a foreign agent and that the network enjoyed complete legal immunity. At least one was ordered to register. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] It was the first documented order of its kind against a figure from that network, seven years after the network's founding.

The same FBI file, released decades later, shows more. It documents Feinberg's continuing meetings with Sonneborn, and it shows that the Israeli government tasked him with intervening in the criminal prosecutions of members of the arms-smuggling network who had been caught. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file] It is the clearest documented link in the whole chronology between the smuggling network of 1945–48 and a named figure to whom the foreign-agent law was applied.

"Call Abe," 1958. Feinberg's role did not end with the 1948 campaign. According to the historian Avner Cohen's history Israel and the Bomb, David Ben-Gurion secretly named Feinberg his chief coordinator for raising private American funds for Israel's clandestine nuclear weapons program, beginning in 1958. Ben-Gurion is said to have told his staff simply to "call Abe." [cite:nationalinterest_feinberg_bomb] [cite:israellobby_feinberg_fbi] On that account, the man who helped fund a desperate whistle-stop tour in 1948 became a decade later the secret point person for funding one of the most sensitive programs Israel ever undertook, a documented escalation of his role. The account is Cohen's. It establishes Feinberg's role and the instruction; it does not give the program's finances or the sums he raised, and that story belongs to a later volume.

What the record shows, and what it does not. Feinberg's career runs from the arms network of 1945 through a presidential campaign, a foreign-agent order and, by 1958, a nuclear fundraising role. Over those years he is documented as a channel: for money into a campaign, for a publication on Israel's behalf, for Israel's government into an American prosecution, and for private funds into a secret program. The one point at which the record ties his money to a specific American decision is the summer of 1948, and it does so through one historian's account, qualified by the words "in part." The record does not show how much weight Truman gave that need against votes, conviction or advice. It does not show any later president changing a decision because of Feinberg's money. And it does not document the size of his later fundraising. Those limits are part of the finding. The case is real, named and specific, and it is one case.

sections.h: Barring Return and Hardening the Line, 1948–1956
sections.html:
The question most often asked about the Palestinian refugees of 1948 is why they did not go home when the fighting stopped. The answer has two parts, and both were in place before the armistices of 1949 were signed. The first was a decision taken by Israel's government in the middle of the war, and the facts that grew up around it. The second was a frontier regime that, in the years after the war, treated those who tried to cross back as intruders. This section follows both, from June 1948 to the eve of the 1956 war.

The decision of 16 June 1948. The decision is known through the research of the historian Benny Morris. As Arthur Hertzberg summarized Morris's research in 1988, Israel's cabinet decided on 16 June 1948 that "there could be no return during the war," leaving the question to be reconsidered later. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] The decision was framed as temporary. It barred return for the duration of the fighting and deferred a final answer.

The date matters. It fell during the first truce, twelve days before the UN mediator, Count Bernadotte, proposed at Rhodes that displaced people be allowed "to return to their homes without restriction and to regain possession of their property." [cite:rs_rd6_frus_bernadotte_june] Israel's government had decided against return before the international proposal for it was put on the table.

The facts on the ground. A deferred decision did not leave the question open in practice. Hertzberg, summarizing Morris, wrote that from the summer of 1948 abandoned houses and property were quickly occupied by Jews, and that by the time of the 1949 armistices Israel was both unwilling and unable to allow substantial return. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] "Unable" is the important word. Once houses and property had been taken over, a return would have meant undoing that occupation. The legal machinery that converted this occupation into state ownership, from the Custodian of Abandoned Property to the Absentees' Property Law of 1950, is set out in [scene:ap_s01|the section on absentee property].

Who decided the flight itself. Morris's research also bore on the older and more charged question of how the refugees came to leave. According to Hertzberg's account, Morris found no formal decision to expel taken by the highest leaders, while the authority of commanders in the field shaped what happened. [cite:rs_rd6_nyrb_hertzberg_1988] Both halves of that finding are used in argument, often one without the other. Those who reject the charge of a planned expulsion cite the absence of a top-level order. Those who see the outcome as intended point to what commanders did with the authority they held. Morris's own finding contains both: no order from the top, and a war in which those on the ground had wide latitude. The barring of return in June 1948 then fixed the result in place, whatever had caused it.

The "infiltration" years. Once the armistice lines of 1949 were drawn, people crossed them. Israel called them infiltrators. Who they were and why they came is the central dispute of this period, and the word itself carries one answer to it.

The most detailed study is Morris's Israel's Border Wars. As Avi Shlaim reported in his review of it in 1994, Morris estimated that "90 per cent or more" of the infiltrations of 1949–56 were driven by economic and social concerns rather than political aims: people returning to their homes, their fields, their property or their relatives. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Morris estimated that between 2,700 and 5,000 infiltrators were killed in 1949–56, "the great majority of them unarmed." [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] Israel's army, border guard and police adopted a policy of shooting suspects on sight. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The figures need to be read as what they are. The range of 2,700 to 5,000 is an estimate, and a wide one. The 90 per cent is Morris's judgement of motive across thousands of crossings, not a count. Both come to this book through Shlaim's review, not from Morris's text directly. And the word "infiltration" covered very different acts: a farmer going back for a harvest, a family visiting relatives across the line, and, increasingly in the mid-1950s, an armed raid. Seen from one side of the line, these were refugees going home to what was theirs. Seen from the other, they were illegal entries into a sovereign state that had just fought a war for its existence.

Retaliation and Qibya. Israel's answer to cross-border attacks was retaliation across the line. Its most notorious instance came in October 1953 at Qibya. Unit 101, under Ariel Sharon, blew up 45 houses and killed 69 Jordanian villagers, "the majority of them women and children." The raid provoked international protest. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

Israel's leadership was divided over this policy. Morris divided them into "activists," led by David Ben-Gurion and including Dayan and Lavon, and "moderates," led by Moshe Sharett. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994] The division ran through the same government. Shlaim, reviewing the book, faulted Morris for underplaying Sharett's secret contacts with Nasser. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The fedayeen. The Israeli case rests above all on what the border became by 1955. The Jewish Virtual Library, presenting the Israeli account, records that on 31 August 1955 Nasser announced that Egypt would dispatch "her heroes" to Israel's borders. It describes the fedayeen as fighters trained and equipped by Egyptian intelligence to carry out attacks inside Israel, in breach of the armistice agreements' ban on paramilitary hostilities. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_fedayeen] On this account, whatever most crossings had been in 1949, by 1955 a hostile state was organizing armed attacks across the line, and Israel was entitled to defend itself against them. The armistice agreements whose terms the fedayeen breached are described in [scene:rd6_armistices|the section on the 1949 armistices].

Two readings of the same border. The dispute over what infiltration was is not a dispute about whether people crossed. Both readings accept that they did, in large numbers, and that many died. It is a dispute about proportion and about cause.

The first reading, built on Morris's archival work, holds that the crossings were overwhelmingly the movement of refugees toward homes, crops and families they had lost months before; that most of those killed were unarmed; and that a policy of shooting on sight, followed by reprisal raids such as Qibya, turned a refugee problem into a cycle of violence. Its strongest evidence is the 90 per cent estimate and the death toll, both from a historian working in Israel's own archives. [cite:rs_rd6_lrb_shlaim_1994]

The second reading, presented by the Jewish Virtual Library, holds that the border was a security threat that, by 1955, included fedayeen organized by a hostile government's intelligence service, and that retaliation was Israel's answer to attacks on its citizens. Its strongest evidence is Nasser's own public announcement and the fact that the attacks breached signed agreements. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_fedayeen]

The two readings describe different parts of the same record and, to a large degree, different years. Morris's estimate covers the whole period of 1949–56; the fedayeen belong chiefly to its last two years. Neither cancels the other. A border can be crossed mostly by unarmed people seeking their property and also be the route of organized armed attacks, and a state can face real attacks and also kill thousands of people who posed no armed threat.

What came next, and what the record leaves open. The years of the border wars ended in a larger war. On 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai war, a Border Police unit enforcing a curfew killed 49 Arab citizens of Israel returning home to Kafr Qasim, a village about a kilometre from the Green Line. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] That killing, and the trial that followed it, are told in [scene:mg_s01|Kafr Qasim, 1956].

Several things this section cannot settle. The cabinet decision of 16 June 1948 is known here through Hertzberg's summary of Morris, not from the cabinet record itself, and it is described as deferring the question, not closing it; the sources here do not say when, or whether, the government formally reconsidered it. The number of infiltrators killed is an estimate with a range of nearly two to one. And the number of Israelis, civilian and military, killed in cross-border attacks between 1949 and 1956 is not established in the sources gathered for this book. Without that figure the human cost of the border can be counted on one side only, and the reader should know that the count is incomplete, not that the other side's losses were small.

sections.h: Who Would Govern Arab Palestine, 1948–1951
sections.html:
By the late summer of 1948 the question of who would govern the parts of Palestine that Israel did not hold had become a contest among Arab governments as much as a matter for Palestinians themselves. Three answers were offered within a few months of one another: an Arab League administration, a Palestinian government proclaimed in Gaza, and union with the Hashemite kingdom across the Jordan. By April 1950 the third had prevailed on the West Bank, Egypt held the Gaza Strip under military administration, and the Gaza government had become, in one historian's word, a phantom. This section follows that contest from September 1948 to the assassination of King Abdullah in July 1951.

A common account holds that the Arab states went to war in 1948 for one purpose only, to destroy the new Jewish state, with no territorial aims of their own. The record of these three years does not bear that out. Jordan's army took and kept territory, and its parliament annexed it. Egypt took and governed another strip of land for nineteen years. Their rivalry over what would become of Arab Palestine was itself one of the forces that shaped the outcome.

The armies came first. Egypt joined Jordan, Syria, Lebanon and Iraq in invading the newly declared State of Israel in May 1948, after the end of the British Mandate. [cite:wikipedia_1948_war] Jordan's Arab Legion, trained and commanded by British officers, took the Old City of Jerusalem and the West Bank. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] It was Jordan's most consequential and successful action of the war, and the territory it held afterward would stay under Jordanian administration for the next nineteen years. Egypt's forces ended the war holding the Gaza Strip. Where the armies stood when the fighting stopped decided, in practice, which Arab government would have the power to act in each part of the country.

The Arab League tried to set the terms first. On 8 July 1948 it created a temporary civil administration for Palestine, and in September it agreed to an Arab government seated in Gaza, announced on 20 September. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] Two days later, on 22 September, a communiqué of the Arab Higher Committee declared Palestine independent under the All-Palestine Government, headed by Ahmad Hilmi Abdul Baqi. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] On 30 September a Palestinian National Council met in Gaza under the presidency of Hajj Amin al-Husayni. It adopted a provisional constitution and declared independence over the whole of Palestine. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

These were acts of Palestinian political leaders, taken in their own name, and they claimed the whole country, not a partition share of it. Five Arab states recognized it. Egypt recognized the new government first, then Iraq, then Syria, Lebanon and Saudi Arabia in the middle of October. King Abdullah of Transjordan refused. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

His refusal was not a passing objection. On the same day the National Council met in Gaza, 30 September 1948, a rival congress in Amman pledged loyalty to Abdullah. On 1 December 1948 the Jericho Congress went further: it proclaimed the union of Palestine and Transjordan and acknowledged Abdullah as king. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] Palestinians were thus present on both sides of the contest. One set of notables proclaimed independence in Gaza; another, in Amman and Jericho, asked to be joined to the Hashemite crown.

Why did the Arab states back a government in Gaza at all? The historian Avi Shlaim, in a study of the All-Palestine Government published in 1990, argues that Egypt sponsored it as a "focal point of opposition to Abdullah," to frustrate the king's plan to join Arab Palestine to Transjordan. His verdict is severe: the government was "a phantom deliberately created by the Arab states, with Egypt at their head." [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990] The events bear out how little ground it had to stand on. After Israel's October 1948 offensive its ministers were moved to Cairo, and it governed nothing from there. Gamal Abdel Nasser closed its offices in 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_shlaim_apg_1990]

Shlaim's judgment and the Palestinian initiative are both part of the record, and they do not cancel each other. The declaration of 22 September and the Council of 30 September were real political acts by Palestinian leaders who claimed a state in the whole of their country. What they lacked was the means to make that claim good: an army, a territory under their own control, and patrons whose interest lay in their success rather than in blocking a rival. The government in Gaza depended on Egypt's sponsorship, and its fate followed Egypt's purposes.

Egypt's own position in Gaza took a form that set it apart from Jordan's. From 1948 to 1967 Egypt administered the Gaza Strip as a military protectorate. It governed the territory directly but never annexed it as Egyptian territory, and Egyptian officials kept to that distinction throughout. The record shows the fact of non-annexation more clearly than the reasons for it. Some accounts stress the Arab League's consensus against any formal annexation of Arab Palestine; others stress Egyptian strategic caution. The sources used here do not settle which weighed more. After the revolution of 1952, Nasser's rise made Egypt the leading voice of pan-Arabism through the 1950s, and in 1956 his nationalization of the Suez Canal brought an invasion by Israel, Britain and France that was reversed under American and Soviet pressure. [cite:wikipedia_suez_crisis] That war belongs to a later volume. The common belief that Egypt never had any administrative role in Gaza is mistaken: for nineteen years it was the governing power there, a history that still shapes Egypt's relationship with the territory's border.

On the West Bank, Abdullah moved step by step. He took the title of king in December 1948, and in April 1949 he ordered the country renamed the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] The scale of what he was absorbing was large. About 500,000 Palestinian Arabs had taken refuge in Transjordan or the West Bank. The West Bank itself had about 500,000 indigenous residents. Transjordan's prewar population had been about 340,000. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] By these estimates the Palestinians brought under the crown, residents and refugees together, outnumbered the kingdom's original subjects by roughly three to one. Elections were held on both banks in April 1950, and after them Abdullah formally annexed the West Bank. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] The ceasefire lines on which this rested were fixed in the Jordanian–Israeli armistice of April 1949, which is told in [scene:rd6_armistices|the Rhodes armistice agreements].

On 24 April 1950 Jordan's parliament passed the resolution of union. The sources render its central phrase in two slightly different translations. One gives it as support for "complete unity between the two sides of the Jordan and their union into one State," grounded in what the resolution called the "national, physical and geographical unity" of both banks. [cite:wiki_jordan_annexation] Martin Kramer, writing in 2020, quotes it as "complete unity between the two banks of the Jordan, the eastern and western, and their union in one single state." [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] The meaning is the same in both.

The language is worth reading slowly. The idea that the two banks of the Jordan belong together as one political unit had appeared earlier in this history in Ze'ev Jabotinsky's Revisionist Zionist program, which claimed both banks for a Jewish state. In 1950 the Hashemite Kingdom used the same territorial reasoning in the opposite direction, to bring the West Bank under the crown in Amman. The parallel is one of structure. The sources do not show that either movement borrowed the idea from the other or was answering it.

The next day, 25 April 1950, the British cabinet agreed to recognize the union of Arab Palestine and Jordan together with the State of Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_cab128] The decision paired two recognitions: Britain accepted Jordan's annexation and Israel in the same act.

How many other states recognized the annexation is disputed, and the sources consulted for this book do not settle it. The Library of Congress country study of Jordan says it was recognized only by Britain and Pakistan. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Kramer notes that Israelis customarily say either that only Britain recognized it or that Britain and Pakistan did. [cite:rs_rd6_kramer_annexation] Another account, used elsewhere in this library, names three states, Britain, Iraq and Pakistan, and adds that even Britain's recognition excluded Jerusalem. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] All agree that the list was very short and that Britain was on it.

The strongest opposition to the annexation came not from Israel or the Western powers but from Jordan's partners in the Arab League. The Library of Congress study records that the annexation was condemned within the League as advancing Hashemite dynastic ambitions. [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] Weeks after the vote, the League's Political Committee met in Cairo, with Jordan absent, and ruled that the annexation violated the League's own earlier resolution, which had declared that annexation of Arab Palestine by any single Arab state would be treated as a breach of the Charter and subject to sanctions. The committee went so far as to consider expelling Jordan from the League. [cite:sixdaywar_jerusalem] Later scholarship links this rejection partly to competing Arab state ambitions over Palestine's future, a thread the sources here do not fully unpack. The same rivalry that produced the Gaza government in September 1948 shaped the reaction to Jordan's union in 1950.

Jordan's rule over the Old City had another side, which the record documents plainly. During the nineteen years of Jordanian administration, Jewish access to the Western Wall and the other Jewish religious sites of the Old City was denied, contrary to the terms of the 1949 armistice agreement, and dozens of historic synagogues were damaged or destroyed. These facts are corroborated across independent historical accounts.

The contest ended in violence. On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was assassinated as he entered al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem for Friday prayers, with his grandson Hussein at his side. The assassin was a Palestinian, reportedly hired by relatives of Hajj Amin al-Husayni, [cite:rs_rd6_loc_jordan] the man who had presided over the National Council in Gaza less than three years before. The account of who hired him is reported, not established in the sources used here.

By the summer of 1951 the shape that would last until 1967 was in place. Jordan held and had annexed the West Bank and East Jerusalem. Egypt administered Gaza without annexing it. The All-Palestine Government survived only as offices in Cairo. The refugees who had crossed into both territories, and how the host governments treated them, are the subject of [scene:dsp_s01|where the refugees went].

Several questions remain open in the record used here. It does not establish how much support each side commanded among Palestinians in 1948–1950, whether the Gaza government or the Jericho union. The April 1950 elections are recorded, but the sources give no figures on how they were conducted. The reasons Egypt chose administration over annexation in Gaza are disputed. The list of states that recognized Jordan's annexation is given three ways, and the assassin's sponsors are named only on the strength of report. What the record does settle is that no independent Arab government came to rule any part of Palestine in these years, and that the rivalry between Egypt and Jordan, as well as the war with Israel, had much to do with it.

sections.h: The Arabs Who Stayed, and the Military Government
sections.html:
Not every Palestinian Arab inside the lines Israel held in 1949 had left. According to Israel's Central Bureau of Statistics, as compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, the state's population at the end of 1948 was 716,700 Jews and 156,000 non-Jews. By 1950 it was 1,203,000 Jews and 167,100 non-Jews. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_population] Those Arabs who remained became citizens of the new state, and for the next eighteen years most of them lived under a regime that applied to them and not to the Jewish majority.

It is often said that the Arab citizens of Israel have enjoyed equal civil rights since 1948. Part of that is true. They voted from the first election. Yet from the war's last months until December 1966, most of them needed a permit from a military officer to leave their own town or village, lived under curfews, and could be barred from whole districts by a commander's order. Both facts belong in the account.

The vote came first in the public record. In the first Knesset election, in 1949, the Democratic List of Nazareth, an Arab party described as a satellite list of Mapai, won 7,387 votes, 1.7 percent of the total, and 2 seats. [cite:rs_rd6_idi_nazareth] Arab citizens could vote and stand for parliament. The terms on which former Palestinian citizens became Israeli nationals, including the residence test of the 1952 Nationality Law, are told in [scene:rd6_law_of_return|the Law of Return and the Nationality Law].

The military government had begun before that election. The sources date its start differently. The account of the period followed elsewhere in this library dates it from 1949. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The historian Alina Korn dates its official establishment to October 1948, with five military governors, and notes that when the fighting ended the regime was "neither cancelled nor was it legally regularized." [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The difference is between the formal creation of the governorates in wartime and the regime's settled form after the armistices. Either way, it outlived the war by seventeen years.

Its legal tools were mostly British. The Defence (Emergency) Regulations of 1945, issued by the Mandate government, were absorbed into Israeli law by Article 11 of the Law and Administration Ordinance of 1948. The most important of them was Regulation 125, which allowed the military commander to declare "any area or location a closed area." To these were added the Emergency Regulations (Security Zones) of 1949. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The mechanism was simple. A commander closed an area. No one could enter or leave it without his written permit. Anyone found outside without one had committed an offence and could be tried for it.

The power to act sat with the commander. The Arab citizen could apply for a permit but could not compel one. According to Korn, the travel-permit requirement had no legal foundation at all for its first 18 months, until January 1950. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Permits were not easily come by. In 1958, Korn reports, only one in three Arabs in the areas under military government held a travel permit. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah]

The courts carried the regime's weight. Korn reports that between 1948 and 1967 about a third of all convictions of Arab citizens were for violations of the Defence Regulations, and that about 95 percent of these were administrative offences, such as lacking a permit. In 1955, 2,714 of the 2,888 people convicted under the regulations were Arab. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] The regulations were written in general terms and could in law be applied to anyone. In practice, more than nine in ten of those convicted under them that year were Arab citizens.

What was the regime for? The government justified it on grounds of security. Israel had signed armistices with its neighbours, not peace treaties. The Rattner Commission, which reviewed the regime in February 1956, concluded that it should not end until "true peace" existed. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] That is the strongest form of the case made at the time: a population with ties across an armistice line, in a state still formally at war, required controls that would be unnecessary in peace.

Korn argues that the regime's main purposes were different: to control the movement of Arab residents and to prevent their access to land that had been confiscated. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Her evidence is the pattern of its use: on her figures, the great majority of convictions were for administrative offences such as lacking a permit, not for acts of violence. The two instruments worked together. Military rule restricted the movement of internally displaced citizens and, combined with the absentee property law, kept them from returning to reclaim their homes. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] That law is told in [scene:ap_s01|the Absentees' Property Law]. Both readings rest on documented material: the security rationale on the government's own statements and the Rattner Commission's finding, the control reading on the conviction figures and the regime's link to the land. The sources used here do not show which consideration weighed more with those who kept the regime in force year after year.

The regime's worst single event came on 29 October 1956, the eve of the Sinai War. Brigadier Issachar Shadmi moved up a dusk curfew on villages near the Jordanian border, without adequate notice to the villagers. When Major Shmuel Malinki asked how to treat villagers returning from work who did not know of it, Shadmi's reply, according to the court record, was that anyone who left his house would be shot. Two of the three units given the order disregarded it. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The Border Police unit at Kafr Qasim, about a kilometre from the Green Line, did not. It killed 49 villagers returning home after a curfew they had not been told of: 19 men, 6 women and 23 children, the count including an unborn child. [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60]

The aftermath documented both accountability and its limits. Eight officers and men were convicted in 1958, and all were released within a few years. Shadmi, tried separately, was fined one-hundredth of an Israeli lira, a sum Palestinian citizens remember as "Shadmi's penny." The same trial established the doctrine that a soldier must refuse a "manifestly illegal" order, one over which "a black flag flies," a standard the Israeli army still teaches. [cite:conversation_kafr_qasim_60] [cite:wiki_kafr_qasim_massacre] The Sinai War that began that week, and Egypt's part in it, belong to a later volume.

The regime ended slowly. The Knesset eased it in 1962 and rejected bills to abolish it in 1963. It voted on 8 November 1966 to end the military government, which was abolished on 1 December 1966. [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah] Six months later, on 4 April 1967, the Prime Minister's adviser on Arab affairs, Shmuel Toledano, wrote to Levi Eshkol that "in practice, hardly any restrictions have been loosened," since closed areas and travel passes remained. [cite:rs_rd6_akevot_toledano] An official close to the policy thus recorded that the formal end of the regime had changed less than its abolition suggested.

Some accounts draw a further conclusion: that before Israel governed a single Palestinian in the West Bank or Gaza, it had already run an eighteen-year separate administration for Palestinian citizens inside its own borders, and that the occupation after 1967 inherited a model rather than inventing one. That is an argument about continuity, and it rests on the resemblance of the instruments: permits, closed areas and military courts. The later regime is the subject of a later volume.

The record leaves several things unsettled. The sources used here give conviction figures but not the number of permit applications refused, or how permits were allocated among villages and individuals. They date the regime's start two ways. They do not give a source-backed count of Israeli casualties from cross-border attacks in these years, a figure that would bear directly on the weight of the security case. And they do not settle the central dispute, whether security or control of movement and land was the regime's main purpose. What they do establish is the structure: a population with the vote, held for eighteen years under British emergency law, through a permit system that for its first eighteen months had no legal basis at all.

sections.h: The Absentees' Property Law: From Flight to State Title, 1948–1953
sections.html:
The war of 1948 left hundreds of Palestinian localities empty of their inhabitants. [cite:rs_rd6_plands_villages] Flight alone did not decide who would own the land and houses left behind. That was settled afterward, on paper, by a sequence of regulations and statutes passed between July 1948 and 1953. Together they moved the property of the refugees first into the custody of the state, then into its ownership and that of the Jewish National Fund, and finally beyond legal challenge. The same chain reached people who had never left the country at all.

It is widely believed that the Palestinian Arabs who stayed inside Israel in 1948 kept their homes and land as full citizens. Many did. But tens of thousands who had moved from one village to another inside the lines Israel held were classed in law as "absentees," and their property was taken on the same terms as that of refugees across the border. They were registered as citizens and could vote, and still could not reclaim what they had owned.

The first link came during the fighting. A Custodian of Abandoned Property was appointed on 15 July 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The occupation of empty houses that followed, and the cabinet decision of June 1948 against return during the war, are told in [scene:rd6_return_barred|how return was barred]. In December 1948 the government issued Emergency Regulations on absentees' property, which transferred control to a new Custodian of Absentee Property. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] Even the date of this step is uncertain. The historian Michael Fischbach, working from Israeli sources, gives 2 December 1948; an American document he cites refers to an "Israeli ordinance of December 12, 1948." [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The sources consulted here do not resolve which is correct.

The regulations were temporary in form. The international body charged with a settlement objected to them while they were still temporary. In April 1949 the United Nations Conciliation Commission for Palestine proposed, as a preliminary measure, "suspension of the application of the Absentee law until the final peace settlement." Arab delegations argued that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens. Israel did not suspend it. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The talks in which that request was made are told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

Instead the regime was made permanent. On 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law, an expanded version of the 1948 regulations, and it remained the main law governing refugee property for decades. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The law, numbered 5710-1950, is plain in its terms. All absentees' property is vested in the Custodian. Every right an absentee had passes automatically to the Custodian. Anyone holding absentee property must hand it over. And the fact that an absentee's identity is unknown does not prevent property from being vested. [cite:un_absentees_property_law_text] [cite:wiki_present_absentee] Anyone found occupying such property, including its original owner, was in breach of the law.

Everything turned on the definition of an "absentee." The law reached anyone who, during the war, had left his usual place of residence for areas outside Israeli control, or for anywhere else. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] The second clause was the decisive one. It captured not only the refugees beyond the armistice lines but also Arabs who had moved between villages inside Israel and had then been registered as citizens, issued identity numbers, and allowed to vote and to stand for the Knesset. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] In law they were absent. In fact they were citizens living a few miles from their homes. They came to be called "present absentees."

Their numbers were large and remained so. By 2001 the present absentees were estimated at about 200,000 people, nearly 17 percent of Israel's Arab citizens, and half the populations of the two largest Arab towns in Israel are internally displaced. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day] [cite:cornell_bilsky_absentee_law] The law did not act alone on them. Military rule over Arab citizens restricted their movement and, combined with the absentee laws, prevented the internally displaced from physically returning to reclaim their homes. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day] That regime is described in [scene:rd6_military_government|the military government].

One interpretive reading, used elsewhere in this library, borrows a term from programming for what the law did: the word "absentee" kept its everyday meaning in public while its working definition was quietly widened to include people who were present. It is a reading of the mechanism, not a finding about anyone's intent.

Custody was not yet ownership. The next steps moved the land on. Fischbach records that in early 1949 Ben-Gurion wanted to sell a significant amount of refugee land to the Jewish National Fund, and that the Fund wanted legal title transferred to it. His book tabulates a sale in January 1949 and a further purchase in 1950 known as the "second million" dunams. [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003] The exact acreage and prices of these transactions are not reproduced here, because they could not be confirmed from the material consulted.

In 1950 a Development Authority was established. A 2016 study in the Journal of Israeli History describes it as both a major allocator of land and the body that set "the rules of the game." The same study finds that the ban on selling "national lands" was strictly kept in rural areas but not in urban ones. [cite:rs_rd6_jih_devauthority] According to an analysis published by the organization BADIL, the 1950 law allowed the Custodian to transfer absentee land to the Development Authority, which could in turn pass it to the Jewish National Fund. BADIL states that nearly 2.4 million dunams were transferred in this way, "more than trebling the JNF's holdings as of 1941," and that by 1951 the government, together with the Fund, held 92 percent of the land within the state. [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime]

The last link closed the chain. The Land Acquisition (Validation of Acts and Compensation) Law of 1953 retroactively validated land seizures made during and after the war on grounds of security and development. The Finance Minister said its purpose was to "instill legality in some acts undertaken during and following the war." [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] The minister's own words concede that some of the earlier seizures had needed legality supplied after the fact. Adalah, in its database of laws it classes as discriminatory, states that 1.2 to 1.3 million dunams were expropriated from Arab owners under the 1953 law, from 349 towns and villages, and that Arab ownership has fallen to 3 to 3.5 percent of the land, compared with 48 percent in 1948. [cite:rs_rd6_adalah_landacq] These are Adalah's figures. Over a longer span, Salman Abu-Sitta estimates that more than 1,000 square kilometres were expropriated from Arab citizens between 1948 and 2003. [cite:wiki_present_absentee] [cite:wiki_land_day]

Who gained and who bore the cost follows from the chain. The property of the refugees and the present absentees passed first to a state custodian, then to a development body, and from there to the state's own land holdings and to the Jewish National Fund. The owners, inside and outside the country, lost title. The law offered them no route back to it: occupying one's own former house was itself a breach.

The two sides of the argument were set out at the time. The Israeli government's stated grounds, written into the 1953 law, were security and development, and in its own account it was regularizing acts taken in war. Israel declined the Conciliation Commission's request to suspend the regime pending a peace settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime] [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The Arab delegations' objection, made in 1949, was that the law treated nationals of Palestine as enemy aliens, and the Commission's own proposal implied that permanent measures should wait for a final settlement. [cite:un_ccp_absentee_1949] The present absentees are the hardest case for any reading of the law as a wartime measure against the enemy's side, because they never left the state's territory and became its citizens.

According to the sources used here, the Absentees' Property Law remains in force and has been applied in East Jerusalem. [cite:wiki_present_absentee]

The record does not settle the totals. The 2.4 million dunams and the 92 percent figure come from BADIL, and the 1.2 to 1.3 million dunams, the 349 localities and the fall from 48 percent to 3 to 3.5 percent come from Adalah. Both are advocacy organizations, and the scholarly sources consulted here, Fischbach and the 2016 study, describe the same legal chain without confirming those totals in the material available. The acreage of the Jewish National Fund's purchases of 1949 and 1950 is unconfirmed, and so is the exact date of the December 1948 regulations. What the record establishes beyond dispute is the mechanism: the text of the 1950 law, the Conciliation Commission's request to suspend it, the definition that turned residents into absentees, and the 1953 law that validated what had been taken.

sections.h: One Week in December 1948: The Rights Order and the Refugees
sections.html:
In the second week of December 1948 the United Nations General Assembly adopted, on three successive days, the founding texts of the modern human-rights order and its first resolution on the return of the Palestinian refugees. In those same days the refugees themselves were being counted. It is sometimes assumed that the new international system examined the Palestinian displacement and passed judgment on it in 1948. The chronology tells a different story. The machinery that might have judged what happened did not yet exist, and the machinery that was built in the following three years set the Palestinian refugees apart from every other refugee population.

Before 1948 there was no worldwide system of human-rights treaties. The League of Nations' Permanent Mandates Commission reviewed Britain's administration of Palestine, but there was no treaty of individual rights and no court to which an individual could turn. The International Committee of the Red Cross worked under the laws of war, the Geneva Conventions of 1929. Its delegate Jacques de Reynier entered Deir Yassin on 11 April 1948 and reported what he found. That was a record of events, made under the laws of war. It was not a judgment, and no body existed to turn it into one.

Then, in a single week, the General Assembly adopted three instruments. On 9 December it adopted the Genocide Convention. [cite:w_genocideconv] On 10 December it adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, by 48 votes to 0 with 8 abstentions. Article 13(2) of the Declaration reads:

Everyone has the right to leave any country, including his own, and to return to his country. [cite:un_udhr]

On 11 December came Resolution 194, on the return of refugees and compensation for those choosing not to return. Its text, its vote and the two readings of it are set out in [scene:rr_s01|Resolution 194 read as a whole]. The modern rights order was thus written in the same days that the Palestinian refugee population was being counted. [cite:w_genocideconv] [cite:un_udhr]

How many people that count covered was itself disputed from the start. Some 700,000 Palestinians were already refugees by that week, and the UN Conciliation Commission later estimated about 711,000. Israel's official figure was lower and Arab officials' figures higher, as [scene:rr_s01|the next section] shows. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The dashboard panel below gives the round figure of about 700,000 displaced, with the Commission's estimate beside it.

The two figures are close, and both are estimates: the roughly 700,000 is a round number, the 711,000 the Commission's own. Neither is a registration count. UNRWA's registration, which counted 726,000, produced a different total again. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix]

Article 13(2) and Resolution 194 became the two texts most often cited together. Palestinians cite the Declaration's article alongside the resolution as grounds for a right of return. Israel has argued that neither creates a binding right of return for descendants. The text of Article 13(2) itself is not disputed. [cite:un_udhr] What is disputed is its reach: whether a declaration of general rights binds a state with respect to a mass displacement in wartime, and whether a right "to return to his country" passes to children and grandchildren born elsewhere. The sources used here record the positions; they do not settle the legal question.

The institution that was actually built for the refugees was an agency of relief, not of rights. The General Assembly created the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees, UNRWA, in December 1949, and it began work in May 1950. It provides schools, health care and relief to registered Palestine refugees. Its mandate is relief and works. It is not charged with resettlement, with legal protection, or with securing return. [cite:unrwa_who] Where the refugees lived and how host governments treated them in these years is told in [scene:dsp_s01|where the refugees went].

The decisive step came in 1951. The Refugee Convention adopted that year defined who was a refugee and what protection states owed. Its Article 1D excluded people already receiving protection or assistance from another United Nations agency. Because the Palestinian refugees had UNRWA, the clause left them outside the protection system that covers every other refugee population, and outside the durable-solutions mandate of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees. [cite:w_refconv]

In practice, this meant that through the 1950s the Palestinian refugees had an agency that gave them relief, schooling and health care, but no international body whose task was to protect their legal status or to find them a permanent solution, whether return, settlement where they were, or settlement elsewhere. The one body with a political mandate, the Conciliation Commission created by Resolution 194, was a commission of three member states, not a protection agency. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Relief and protection, which the 1951 system joined for other refugees, were split for the Palestinians.

There was also no court. No international criminal court existed to examine the events of 1948. The Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court was adopted in 1998 and entered into force in July 2002, without retroactive reach. Palestine acceded in 2015, which is why the Court's jurisdiction in Palestinian matters begins in that era. [cite:w_romestatute] The displacement of 1948 was counted, relieved and debated, but it was never adjudicated by any international tribunal.

The common claim that the international human-rights system examined the Palestinian displacement and judged it in 1948 therefore runs ahead of the record. In 1948 the system consisted of declarations and a convention on genocide, with no enforcement body for individual rights. What followed was relief through UNRWA and a refugee convention that, by its own text, did not apply to the Palestinians.

The record leaves open why the drafters of the 1951 Convention wrote Article 1D as they did, and the sources used here do not give the debates. Nor do they settle the legal weight of Article 13(2) for the 1948 refugees and their descendants, which remains the subject of the opposing positions set out above. What is not in dispute is the sequence: rights declared in December 1948, relief organized in 1949 and 1950, protection withheld by the 1951 text, and no court until 2002.

sections.h: Resolution 194: What It Says, How Each Side Reads It, and How Many Refugees There Were
sections.html:
Resolution 194 is usually remembered for one paragraph, the eleventh, on the return of the refugees. It is a longer document than that, and it was adopted as a plan for ending the war as a whole: a commission to conduct the peace, an international regime for Jerusalem, protection for the Holy Places, and a settlement of the refugee question. Each side has since read it selectively. Two popular versions dominate: that international law guarantees every refugee's descendant a return, or that the resolution means nothing. Neither matches the text, which is short enough to read as a whole.

The General Assembly adopted Resolution 194 (III) at its 186th plenary meeting on 11 December 1948, by 35 votes to 15, with 8 abstentions. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_194] It followed the September 1948 report of the UN Mediator, told in [scene:rd6_bernadotte|Bernadotte's mission].

Paragraph 2 established a Conciliation Commission of three UN member states. France, Turkey and the United States were named to it. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] [cite:rs_rd6_ecf_194] Paragraph 5 urged the governments concerned to negotiate "the final settlement of all questions outstanding between them." Paragraph 7 called for the protection of, and free access to, the Holy Places, including Nazareth, under "effective United Nations supervision." [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Paragraph 8 called for the Jerusalem area to be treated separately and placed under "effective United Nations control," asked the Security Council to ensure its demilitarization, and instructed the Commission to propose a permanent international regime for it. Paragraph 9 called for the "freest possible access to Jerusalem by road, rail or air." [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] What became of the Jerusalem paragraphs in 1949, when the Assembly returned to the city and Israel moved its parliament there, is told in [scene:rd6_un_admission|Israel's admission and the Jerusalem question].

Then came paragraph 11. It resolved:

that the refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so at the earliest practicable date

and that compensation should be paid for the property of those choosing not to return. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194] The paragraph did not stop at return. It instructed the Conciliation Commission to facilitate the "repatriation, resettlement and economic and social rehabilitation" of the refugees and the payment of compensation, working with the Director of United Nations Relief for Palestine Refugees. [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_194] Resettlement thus sat in the same sentence as repatriation. The resolution offered the Commission both tools and did not say how the choice between them was to be made, beyond the refugees' own wish to return.

The General Assembly has reaffirmed the resolution every year since 1949. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:wiki_res_194] At the time of its adoption, however, the Arab states and Palestinian representatives rejected it, because it implied acceptance of Israel. Only later did Palestinians come to cite it as the foundation of the right of return. [cite:wiki_res_194]

Israel's reading was stated by Ben-Gurion to the UN conciliators. The words "live at peace with their neighbours," he argued, made return contingent on peace with the Arab states. [cite:unispal_194_survey] [cite:unwatch_194] Critics of the Palestinian reading add three further points. General Assembly resolutions are recommendations, not binding law. The text says refugees "should be permitted" to return, not that they have a right to. And the return of several million descendants would end Israel's Jewish majority. [cite:unwatch_194] In its strongest form, the Israeli case is that the resolution itself made return part of a peace, and that no peace was made.

The Palestinian reading treats return as a right, not a concession. Its supporters argue that the right is grounded in broader international law, not in this resolution alone, and they cite Article 13(2) of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted the day before. They also point to the Assembly's annual reaffirmation, and to the terms on which Israel was admitted to the United Nations in May 1949, which they say came with a pledge to honor the resolution. [cite:wiki_res_194] The exact assurances given on Israel's behalf at that time are not confirmed in the UN records consulted for this book, and they are not relied on here. In its strongest form, the Palestinian case is that the right does not depend on this resolution's wording at all, and that the Assembly's repetition of it every year since 1949 shows how the international community has understood it.

The two readings met at the conference the Conciliation Commission convened at Lausanne in 1949, and the talks broke down on this question; it remained unresolved at Camp David in 2000. [cite:wiki_res_194] The sequence of offers at Lausanne is told in [scene:lau_s01|the Lausanne conference].

Behind the dispute over the text lay a dispute over numbers, which began at once and has never been closed. Benny Morris's survey of the estimates gives the range. Israeli spokesmen publicly said "about 520,000," and Israel officially held to a figure of 520,000 to 530,000. Arab officials, from 1949, spoke of 900,000 or one million. The British estimated 810,000 in February 1949: 210,000 in Gaza, 320,000 in the West Bank, and 280,000 in Lebanon, Syria and the East Bank of the Jordan. The UN Economic Survey Mission and UNRWA counted 726,000. [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The UN Conciliation Commission's own estimate, given in the previous section, was about 711,000.

One private Israeli judgment stands out. According to Morris, in late 1950 Walter Eytan, director-general of Israel's Foreign Ministry, privately called UNRWA's registration of 726,000 "meticulous," but said that "the real number was close to 800,000." [cite:rs_rd6_morris_appendix] The official public figure and the Foreign Ministry's private view thus differed by more than a quarter of a million people.

The question of compensation also produced a number. The Conciliation Commission's progress report of November 1951 put the value of abandoned Arab immovable property at about P£100 million, P£100,383,000 exactly, on 16,324 square kilometres of land, of which 4,574 were cultivable. For its calculations the Commission took the refugee population as approximately 900,000. [cite:rs_rd6_unccp_1951] That figure was a working approximation for the property estimate, not a count. How the property itself passed to the state is told in the section on the Absentees' Property Law.

The count of places emptied in the war differs as much as the count of people, and here the difference lies mostly in definitions. Benny Morris, in 1987, identified 369 villages. Walid Khalidi, in 1992, counted 418, excluding towns and sites without permanent structures. Earlier lists gave 399 (al-Arif), 443 (Nijm and Muammer) and 472 (Saleh). The Palestine Land Society, counting towns, tribal lands and police stations as well, gives 531 localities. [cite:rs_rd6_plands_villages] The lower figures count villages in a narrow sense. The highest counts every kind of inhabited place. Each total is accurate on its own terms, and none can be compared with another without its definition.

Much here remains unsettled. The record does not establish a single agreed number of refugees: every estimate between 520,000 and one million had an official source behind it, and the private Israeli view, close to 800,000, lay nearer the UN and British figures than to Israel's public one. Whether paragraph 11 created a right or a recommendation is a question of law and interpretation, not of record, and both readings are documented. What the text itself settles is narrower and clearer: it tied return to the refugees' wish and to living at peace, it set compensation beside return, it named resettlement and rehabilitation as tasks for the Commission, and it placed Jerusalem under international control. Most of that program was never carried out.

sections.h: The Rhodes Armistices, 1949: Lines That Were Not Borders
sections.html:
The war of 1948 did not end with a peace. It ended with four separate agreements, signed between February and July 1949, each of which declared in its own text that it settled nothing political. The lines they drew lasted until 1967 and became known as the Green Line. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map] Because the lines lasted so long, they are often remembered as the borders the war produced. The documents themselves say the opposite, and they say it repeatedly.

The man who brought the parties to the table was Ralph Bunche, who had succeeded the assassinated UN mediator, Count Bernadotte. In January 1949 he brought Israeli and Egyptian delegations to negotiate on the island of Rhodes. [cite:rs_rd6_nobel_bunche] The mediation he inherited had already cost lives: in July 1949 he reported to the Security Council that ten members of the UN mission, the Mediator among them, had died over fourteen months, and that about twice as many had been wounded. [cite:rs_rd6_bunche_letter_1949] The plans Bernadotte had put forward, and the killing that ended his mission, are told in [scene:rd6_bernadotte|the mediator's mission]. Bunche's task was narrower than Bernadotte's had been. He was not drawing a settlement. He was stopping a war.

The first agreement, between Egypt and Israel, was signed at Rhodes on 24 February 1949. Mahmed Seif El Dine and M. K. El Raliniany signed for Egypt; Walter Eytan, Yigael Yadin and Elias Sasson signed for Israel. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Its operative terms dealt with three places. Egyptian forces encircled in the Al Faluja pocket were to withdraw beyond the Egypt–Palestine frontier under UN supervision, a movement that Annex I set to begin at 0500 GMT on 26 February 1949. The village of El Auja and its surroundings were demilitarized under Article VIII. In the Gaza–Rafah area, Article VI froze Egyptian forces at the positions they held. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] The Gaza Strip, which Egypt held under the armistice, became the territory whose administration is described in the section on Arab Palestine after the war. [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map]

The Egyptian text is also the clearest statement of what an armistice was meant to be. Article IV(3) says that its provisions are "dictated exclusively by military considerations" and are valid only for the period of the armistice. Article V says that the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary," and that it is drawn without prejudice to the rights of either party in the ultimate settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text] Supervision was given to a seven-member Mixed Armistice Commission: three members appointed by each party, with the Chief of Staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in the chair, and its headquarters at El Auja. The agreement was to remain in force "until a peaceful settlement between the Parties is achieved" (Article XII). [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text]

The structure explains who could act and who could not. Neither side could change the line by itself without breaking a signed agreement; neither side gave up its claims by signing; and the body set up to supervise the agreement was a commission on which the two parties had equal numbers and a UN officer held the chair. The agreement froze the military facts. It left every political question exactly where the war had left it.

Lebanon had entered the war by its own government's decision. On 15 May 1948, the day after Israel declared independence, Lebanon joined Egypt, Syria, Jordan and Iraq in declaring war and invading the new state, fielding the smallest of the five Arab armies. Israeli forces repelled the invasion and temporarily occupied part of southern Lebanon. The armistice signed on 23 March 1949 restored the internationally recognized border between the two states. [cite:lebanon_1948_war] The decision to fight was not simply imposed on Lebanon from outside. According to Makram Rabah, a historian at the American University of Beirut, the country's founding leaders, chiefly Riad al-Solh and Bechara el-Khoury, who had led it to independence from France in 1943, had debated and rejected an alliance with the Zionist movement before 1948, concluding that they could not keep relations with the neighbouring Arab states if they made one. [cite:lebanon_1948_war]

The armistice returned the frontier to where it had been. It did not return the people who had crossed it. During the war an estimated 100,000–110,000 Palestinian Arabs, the large majority from northern Palestine, including the Acre area, fled or were displaced into Lebanon, a country of about 1.3 million people at the time. The International Committee of the Red Cross, and from 1950 UNRWA, ran the camps that received them. [cite:lebanon_refugee_policy]

The agreement with the Hashemite Jordan Kingdom was signed at Rhodes on 3 April 1949. Colonel Ahmed Sudki El-Jundi and Lieutenant-Colonel Mohamed Maayte signed for Jordan; Reuven Shiloah and Lieutenant-Colonel Moshe Dayan signed for Israel. Article II(2) repeats the reservation of the Egyptian text: no provision shall prejudice the rights, claims and positions of either party in the final settlement. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text]

Two features set this agreement apart. The first was Jerusalem. Article VIII set up a Special Committee whose agreed agenda included free access to the Holy Places and cultural institutions, use of the cemetery on the Mount of Olives, the resumption of the institutions on Mount Scopus, and free movement on the Bethlehem road and the Latrun–Jerusalem road. [cite:rs_rd6_arm_jordan_text] That agenda was written into the text. Whether it was carried out is another matter: according to Germany's Federal Agency for Civic Education, Jews were denied access to their holy sites in the eastern part of the city that Jordan held after the war. [cite:rs_rd6_bpb_jerusalem] The fate of the city at the United Nations is taken up in the section on Israel's admission and Jerusalem.
