One account dates AIPAC's emergence to 1963, when the Council's lobbying functions were spun off into it after the foreign-agent order. [cite:aipac_wiki] The other dates its founding to 1953–54, when Kenen created the American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, and its present name to 1959. [cite:cjh_kenen_papers] [cite:britannica_aipac] Read closely, the two accounts refer to different things. The earlier date marks the creation of a distinct committee and the later name change; the 1963 date marks the moment the American Zionist Council's own lobbying work was moved into that committee and the committee was restructured to rest on American donations alone. Both are true of their own subject. What neither account in the material supplies is a full picture of how the Council and Kenen's committee related to each other between 1954 and 1963: who directed which lobbying, and how money moved between them, if it did.

Either way, the claim that AIPAC had no earlier institutional history does not survive the record. Its lineage runs through Kenen's 1953–54 committee and, from 1963, through the lobbying work of the Council that descended from the wartime AZEC. The 1953 founding date also coincides with the Anglo-American coup in Iran; the two are paired in [scene:s11|another chapter], which states plainly that no operational link between them is documented.

The gaps should be stated as plainly as the findings. The material does not say why the Justice Department withdrew its 1962 demand, or exactly when. It does not establish whether the $5 million allegation was ever tested, and it does not assess whether the 1963 restructuring fully answered the questions the order had raised; it documents what changed and the reason given for the change, not a legal judgment of its adequacy. Nor does it trace AZEC's place in the wider American network beyond these institutional steps; that network, including the 1962 finding as it concerned the Council rather than AZEC, is mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up].

sections.h: Paying for the New State, 1949–1953
sections.html:
The state that emerged from the war of 1948 had to house and feed a mass immigration, a story told in [scene:rd6_ingathering|the mass immigration of 1948–1952]. The money for that effort came from three outside channels that opened in quick succession: loans and grants from the United States government, bonds sold to buyers abroad, and reparations from West Germany. Each worked differently, each was paid for by different people, and one of them divided Israel's own public more sharply than any question of foreign policy in these years. A common assumption is that American military support flowed to Israel from the beginning. The documents of the period show something else: American help in these years was economic, modest and uneven, and the largest single agreement of the early 1950s was made with West Germany.

The first channel was the American government. After Truman's re-election an Export-Import Bank loan of $100 million was earmarked for Israel, a decision placed in its political sequence in [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after the election]. The Congressional Research Service's table of US aid to Israel, compiled by the Jewish Virtual Library, records the year-by-year sums in millions of dollars: 100.0 in 1949, from the Export-Import Bank and other sources; nothing in 1950; 35.1 in 1951; 86.4 in 1952; 73.6 in 1953; 74.7 in 1954; 52.7 in 1955; 50.8 in 1956; 40.9 in 1957; 85.4 in 1958; and 53.3 in 1959, the last including a first military loan of 0.4. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] Added together, the table's eleven years come to $652.9 million, an average of under $60 million a year, with the largest single figure in the first year.

The character of that aid mattered as much as its size. From Israel's founding through the early 1960s, US assistance was economic aid and loans only. According to one study of the aid relationship, Washington avoided direct arms sales because it did not want to alienate the Arab oil-producing states. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990]

Set beside the other American-dollar flows in the record from 1921 to 1949, the $100 million loan of 1949 is the largest single sum, double the $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 American tour and a thousand times the $100,000 that Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann provided for Truman's whistle-stop campaign. The comparison is a reminder that the largest flows are not always the most politically consequential: the smallest figure on that chart is the one the historian John Judis ties to a specific decision, a case examined in the section on Feinberg. The loan, by contrast, was a government credit, open to view and recorded in the official tables.

When American military aid began is a point on which the sources differ, and both versions should be stated. The CRS table shows a military loan of $0.4 million in 1959. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table] The study of the aid relationship cited above dates the first US military aid, itself in the form of loans rather than grants, to 1962. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The sources do not explain the difference; a reader can say only that a very small military loan appears in the official table three years before the date usually given for the start of military aid.

The later shape of the relationship belongs to later chapters and can be summarized in a few dates. Congress first designated a dedicated earmark for Israel in 1971. [cite:everycrsreport_israel_foreign_assistance] The 1973 war was the turning point: President Nixon ordered an emergency military airlift and requested $2.2 billion in emergency aid, a rise of roughly 800 percent over prior annual levels. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] [cite:legalclarity_when_did_us_start_funding] Economic aid became all grants in 1981, and military aid in 1985, the year of a separate $1.5 billion supplemental economic package, the largest aid package for a single country since the Vietnam War era. [cite:legalclarity_when_did_us_start_funding] [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990] The often-quoted cumulative total of $300 billion is the Council on Foreign Relations' inflation-adjusted estimate; the Congressional Research Service, using the same appropriations data without adjusting for inflation, places cumulative bilateral assistance and missile defense funding at about $174 billion. [cite:cfr_aid_four_charts] [cite:legalclarity_how_much_money_given] Those totals were built almost entirely after the period of this chapter, as told in [scene:iaa_s01|how the aid relationship grew].

The second channel was private, but organized by the state. According to the Jewish Virtual Library's history of the program, David Ben-Gurion conceived an overseas bond issue in 1950, amid economic crisis and mass immigration. In September 1950 he convened American Jewish leaders at the King David Hotel in Jerusalem, and sales were launched in the United States the following spring with a rally at Madison Square Garden. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] The 1951 Independence Issue paid 3.5 percent, and first-year sales topped $52 million. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds] Within six years, the same source reports, bond sales accounted for 35% of Israel's special development budget, financing the National Water Carrier, the Dead Sea Works, power plants, ports and immigrant towns. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds]

The mechanism differed from the charitable campaigns of the pre-state years. The 1951 issue paid its buyers interest rather than asking for a gift, it was sold in the United States, and its proceeds went to the state's special development budget and the projects named above. The record cited here does not give the month of the first sales, saying only that they began the following spring.

The third channel was the most contested. On 12 March 1951 Moshe Sharett presented a claim of $1.5 billion against Germany. It was calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 victims of the Nazis at $3,000 each. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] The method framed the claim as compensation for a concrete burden on the new state: the cost of resettling survivors. On 9 January 1952 the Knesset voted 61–50 to negotiate directly with West Germany, while thousands demonstrated outside and police used tear gas. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]

The opposition was led by Menachem Begin, who spoke at mass demonstrations in the spring of 1952. Opponents called the payments "blood money" from the "land of the murderers." [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The dispute was not between Israel and its adversaries but within Israel. The case for the agreement, in the government's own terms, was that the new state was bearing the cost of absorbing hundreds of thousands of the Nazis' victims and that Germany should meet it. The case against, in the opponents' own words, was that money from the "land of the murderers" was "blood money" and should not be taken. The narrow vote, 61 to 50, shows how evenly the Knesset was divided.

The agreement was signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952 by Sharett, Nahum Goldmann and Konrad Adenauer, and took effect on 21 March 1953. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] Payments ran in annual instalments from 1 April 1953 to 31 March 1966. They came not as cash transfers but in kind: 30% for crude oil bought in Britain and 70% for German goods. Over the decade they made up 12–14% of Israel's annual imports. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]

How much the agreement was worth is itself disputed between the two sources. The Jewish Virtual Library, citing Israeli Foreign Ministry documents of 1953 and the Encyclopaedia Judaica, gives a total of $845 million, of which $100 million went to the Claims Conference, paid over 14 years from 1953 to 1966. [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations] The National Library of Israel gives goods and services valued at 3.5 billion marks over 12 years, plus 450 million marks more. [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations] The two figures are expressed in different currencies and over periods described differently; the sources do not reconcile them, and this book does not either.

Taken together, the three channels answer the question of who paid for the new state in its first years only in part. The American government lent and granted modest sums, without arms, for reasons tied to its relations with Arab oil producers. Private buyers abroad lent money through bonds that built the state's water, power and ports. West Germany paid in oil and goods, over the objections of a large part of Israel's own public. What the record cited here does not settle is the whole: it gives no single account of the state's budget in these years, no measure of how much of the cost of absorption fell on Israel's own taxpayers and on the immigrants themselves, and no agreed figure for the largest of the three transfers. The month the first bonds were sold, and the reason the two sources date the first American military loan three years apart, also remain open.

sections.h: How the Flight Was Explained, 1948–1988
sections.html:
Once the war ended, the question of why so many Palestinian Arabs had left their homes became a political argument as much as a historical one, because the answer seemed to settle who was responsible for the refugees. For more than a decade the account that prevailed in the West was that they had left voluntarily, on the orders of Arab leaders, and that this had been established at the time. The record shows a slower and more complicated history: some of the war's events were reported within days, the explanation for the mass flight that took hold was not the one the documents supported, and the correction came in stages, the last and weightiest of them from Israel's own archives forty years later.

Parts of what happened were known almost at once. The killings at Deir Yassin in April 1948 were reported in Western newspapers within days, and they were documented by the delegate of the Red Cross who entered the village. [cite:w_morris_birth] News of the massacre spread through Arab Palestine. The Israeli historian Benny Morris, writing four decades later, records it as a major accelerant of flight. [cite:w_morris_birth] The Red Cross's place in that moment, before any international human-rights treaty existed, is part of [scene:ud_s01|the week of December 1948].

Objection in the West was public, and some of the most pointed came from prominent Jews. On 4 December 1948 a group that included Albert Einstein, Hannah Arendt and Sidney Hook published a letter in The New York Times warning against Menachem Begin's new Herut party. The letter described Deir Yassin and called the party fascist in its methods. [cite:w_arendt_letter] It is a documented Jewish objection, made at the time and printed in America's paper of record. It also shows that the facts of Deir Yassin were not hidden in 1948; what remained in contest was the larger question of why the flight as a whole had happened.

On that larger question an explanation took hold that ran the other way. Arab leaders, it held, had broadcast orders by radio telling civilians to leave. In the 1950s this became the standard explanation in Western and Israeli official accounts. Its political effect was clear: it placed responsibility for the refugee problem on the Arab states. The strongest form of the account rested on a real point that later research would confirm in part, that some evacuations were ordered by Arab commanders. Its weakness was that the general claim, a broadcast order to an entire population, was a claim about a record that existed and could be checked.

The broadcasts had been monitored. In 1959 the Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argued from Arab sources that no such general order had been given. [cite:w_childers] In May 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers published "The Other Exodus" in The Spectator. He reported that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of Arab broadcasts in 1948, described in another summary as the BBC's and American records, and had found no evacuation orders; what he found were appeals to stay. [cite:w_childers] The article set off a long published dispute, with claims and counterclaims running for weeks in the magazine's letters pages. [cite:w_childers] The exchange did not settle the matter in public opinion. Childers's test was of one kind of evidence, the broadcasts; it could not by itself show what had driven people from particular towns and villages.

That evidence lay in Israeli military and state files. In 1988 Benny Morris published The Birth of the Palestinian Refugee Problem, drawn from those newly opened archives. He concluded that the main causes of flight were military attack, expulsion and fear. In some places local Arab commanders had ordered the evacuation of women and children, but there was no general Arab order to leave. [cite:w_morris_birth] Later editions of the book found more expulsion orders. [cite:w_morris_birth]

The three tests did not cover the same ground, and the order in which they came matters. Khalidi and Childers answered the specific claim about broadcasts. Morris answered the larger question of causes, and he did so from the files of the Israeli state. The documents that corrected the early account were therefore not an adversary's claims but Israel's own.

Where this leaves each side's case can be stated fairly. The account that the refugees left on orders is no longer defended by mainstream scholarship in its general form. [cite:w_morris_birth] What survives of it is real but limited: Morris's own research found local evacuation orders by Arab commanders in some places, and he named fear, alongside attack and expulsion, among the main causes. The Palestinian account, that people were driven out by attack and expulsion, found strong support in the Israeli archives, and later editions of Morris's work added to the record of expulsion orders. [cite:w_morris_birth]

What the record does not settle is intent. Historians still disagree about intent and planning, an argument that turns on the military plan discussed in [scene:pd_s01|Plan Dalet]. The material here establishes the causes of flight that the archives show; it does not resolve the question of design. It also does not explain, beyond the sequence of dates, why the early account held for so long. What it does show is the length of the gap: the explanation that took hold in the 1950s was checked against the broadcasts only in 1959 and 1961, and against Israel's own archives only in 1988.

sections.h: How the Case Was Made to Americans: Refuge, Bible and Democracy
sections.html:
A familiar explanation for American support of Israel runs backward from the present. Because the two countries later became close strategic partners, it is assumed that Americans backed the new state in 1948 for the same reason: that Israel was already a proven ally whose value to Washington was plain. The record of 1948 does not bear this out. The case put to the American public in the founding years rested on three different arguments, none of them strategic, and the men responsible for American strategy in that period made the opposite case in writing.

The first and central argument of 1945–48 was refuge. In Europe after the war some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons were still waiting in camps, and the destruction of European Jewry in the Holocaust was recent and fully known. The argument was humanitarian before it was political: the survivors needed somewhere to go. America's own door was part of the same argument. When Truman signed the Displaced Persons Act on 25 June 1948 he did so "with very great reluctance," saying that it "discriminates in callous fashion against displaced persons of the Jewish faith," and he pressed Congress for two years until it was amended in 1950; that story belongs to [scene:tr_s02|Truman's decisions after 1948]. [cite:truman_institute_dpact]

The second argument was religious. Christian restorationist belief, the conviction that the Jews would be restored to the land of the Bible, had an organized American following that went back to 1839, long before political Zionism existed. For Christian supporters the new state could be read as a biblical fulfillment. The third argument was political in the plainest sense: the new state was presented to Americans as a democracy.

Against all three stood the American national-security establishment. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Secretary of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency each warned that American backing for a Jewish state would harm American interests. The warnings were consistent and on paper. Declassified CIA documents from 1948 predicted that recognition would produce armed conflict and damage American access to oil. Far from calling the future state a strategic asset, the government's own strategists treated it as a strategic liability. Truman overruled them. He recognized Israel eleven minutes after its declaration of independence on 14 May 1948, so quickly that his own State Department was caught unaware. The White House aides who argued the domestic political case, Clark Clifford and David Niles among them, and the personal channel that reached him through his friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the day. [cite:wiki_david_niles]

The map above lays out that contest as the documents record it: each formal warning against partition and recognition from 1946 to 1948, set against the political advice and the personal channel that prevailed. Its point for this section is simple. Whatever moved American policy in 1948, it was not a consensus inside the government that Israel served American strategy. The government's strategic voices said the reverse and lost.

The publicity of the period also had a hostile side, aimed at the Arab opponents of partition. Here the record requires care in both directions. Pro-Zionist publicity drew heavily on the wartime collaboration of the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem with Hitler. That collaboration was real and is documented; it was not invented for propaganda. What the publicity did with it was another matter. A single leader's alliance with the Axis was used as a broad brush to color Arab opposition as a whole, which the documented episode does not support. The episode should be stated plainly, as fact, and the generalization drawn from it should be named for what it was.

It is tempting to read later developments back into this period, and two of them in particular. The first is the organized anti-Islam network in the United States. The organized, well-funded anti-Islam network is documented mainly from the 2000s, building on currents that formed after 1967 and after 1979. [cite:cap_fear_inc] It was not part of the 1948 argument. The anti-Arab framing of 1948 leaned on a specific wartime episode, not on an industry.

The second is the argument most often assumed to have been there from the beginning. The claim that Israel was a strategic asset to the United States grew after Israel's victory in 1967, a generation after the founding, and was formalized under President Reagan, who called Israel a strategic asset and signed a strategic-cooperation agreement with it in 1981. Until then American aid was cautious: from 1948 into the early 1960s it consisted of economic aid and loans, with Washington avoiding direct arms sales for fear of alienating Arab oil-producing states, a pattern taken up in [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for]. [cite:merip_us_aid_israel_1990]

Set side by side, the sequence corrects the familiar account. In 1948 Americans were asked to support Israel as a refuge for survivors, as the fulfillment of a promise that some Christians read in scripture, and as a new democracy. The strategic argument was then being made by the other side of the debate, inside the American government, and it pointed against support. The alliance framing came later and was built on later events.

What the record does not settle is how much each argument weighed with the public at the time. The documents establish which arguments were made and which officials opposed the policy; they do not measure how many Americans were moved by the survivors, how many by scripture and how many by the language of democracy, or how far the hostile portrait of Arab opposition shaped opinion. No survey or source in this chapter's research answers that, and this book does not guess at it. Nor does the record here trace the precise path by which the 1967 argument became the 1981 doctrine; that belongs to a later volume.

sections.h: Did Money Buy the Politicians? What the Record Can Show, and Where It Goes Dark
sections.html:
The question of what money did to American policy on Palestine before and during 1948 is usually answered in one of two ways. In one version, Zionist money bought Congress and the White House. In the other, money played no role at all. Both answers share a flaw: they treat a bundle of separate claims as a single claim, and so they deliver one verdict where the evidence supports several different ones. Pulled apart, the question becomes four claims. They stand on very different footing, and one of them cannot be settled in either direction with the records that exist.

The first claim is that there was organized political pressure. This is documented in detail, much of it in the movement's own files. The American Zionist Emergency Council, the movement's national lobbying body in the 1940s, built local committees across the country and ran letter and telegram campaigns aimed at members of Congress. It compiled legislators' statements of support into a book, America and Palestine, and used it to press for more. The same files document the campaign around both parties' 1944 platforms and the Wagner–Taft resolution in Congress. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Nothing about this was hidden. It was lobbying, organized openly and on a national scale, and the way it worked is traced tie by tie in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up].

The second claim is that money changed a specific decision. This is documented once. The historian John Judis records that in mid-1948 Truman wanted Israel to stop taking territory beyond the United Nations partition lines and was disturbed by its refugee policy, but backed away from pressing either objection, in part because his nearly broke campaign needed $100,000 from Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann for a whistle-stop tour. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] That account, and the man behind it, are set out in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. It is one historian's account of one decision. It is specific, dated and sourced, and it is also the only instance of its kind in the record.

The panel above makes the point by contrast. Among the dollar flows the record documents between 1921 and 1949, the Feinberg–Kaufmann money is the smallest, about a tenth of a million dollars beside a $100 million Export-Import Bank loan of 1949 and tens of millions raised for arms. [cite:jvl_truman_marshall_dejure] [cite:israelaffairs_italy] Yet it is the only sum tied in the historical literature to a particular policy decision. Most of the other money built institutions over decades; this sum arrived at the moment a decision was being made. The size of a payment and its documented effect are different measures, and here they point in opposite directions.

The third claim is that members of Congress were paid, systematically, before 1948. This cannot be established either way, and the reason is legal rather than historical. Until the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971, the governing law was the Federal Corrupt Practices Act of 1925. It required disclosure mainly from party committees operating in more than one state rather than from candidates. It carried few penalties. It left enforcement to Congress itself, and it was rarely enforced. It was riddled with loopholes, and the donors to individual candidates were largely undisclosed until 1971. [cite:wiki_fcpa_1925] [cite:sage_fec_history] [cite:crs_campaign_finance] The records that would answer the question were never required to exist. In the absence of disclosure, any claim that particular legislators were paid is unsupported. So is any claim that they were not. Silence of this kind is not evidence of innocence and not evidence of guilt; it is a gap produced by the law of the time, and it should be reported as a gap.

The fourth claim is the one most often left out by those who argue that money explains the outcome: other documented forces pushed in the same direction without money. The moral urgency of the Holocaust years was real and widely felt. Jewish voters were concentrated in electorally important states such as New York. Christian restorationist conviction, the belief that the Jews would be restored to their ancient land, was sincere and had an organized American history going back to 1839. Henry Wallace held Zionist views of his own. And the 1922 Lodge–Fish resolution, by which Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration, is credited to lobbying with no payment documented. Each of these points the same way as the money, and none of them needs it.

The opposing record belongs in the same account. The State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, and they were overruled. The documented forces that beat them were political: organization, votes, conviction and access. A financial force is documented only in the single case above.

Set out this way, the two familiar answers both fail. "Money bought Congress and the White House" stretches one documented episode, involving one decision and one campaign, into a general claim about legislators for whom no payment record exists. "Money played no role at all" contradicts the one case that is documented. The defensible position sits between them and is narrower than either: an organized, well-funded political movement with direct access to decision-makers, plus one documented case in which money shifted a decision.

The note above, from the dashboard that follows the money of these years, states the same limit in its own terms. The record documents private, organized finance and one specific episode of money bearing on policy in 1948. It does not show that any government secretly funded the movement, and it does not show that money decided every outcome. The money itself, how much there was and where it went, is the subject of [scene:gf_s01|the next section].

What remains open is exactly what the law of the time left open. Whether any member of Congress received money in connection with a vote on Palestine before 1948 cannot be known from the records that exist, and this book does not supply an answer the documents cannot. Nor does the Judis account, by itself, measure how much weight the campaign's need carried against the other pressures on Truman in the summer of 1948; it records the need as one reason among others, and that is how it is reported here.

sections.h: Who Paid for It All? The Ledger, 1899–1949
sections.html:
Two explanations of how the pre-state movement was financed have long circulated, and they point in opposite directions. One holds that it ran on a handful of wealthy patrons, the Rothschilds or a few Jewish bankers. The other holds that it ran on secret government money. The documented record supports neither. What it shows is organized private giving on a mass scale, conducted openly through permanent institutions, raised from donors in many countries and, by the 1940s, overwhelmingly from the United States. It was not cheap, and it was not secret. The slogan version of the patron myth is taken apart, alongside the founding slogans, in [scene:pn_s01|the closing account of the founding narratives]; this section sets out the ledger itself.

The panel above carries the headline sums, each shown as it was then and in today's dollars. The largest single figure is the United Jewish Appeal's campaign of 1948: $150 million, about $2.0 billion today, raised from more than a million contributors in 4,950 American communities. [cite:jta_uja_1948] [cite:bls_cpi] At the time it was described as the largest non-government humanitarian campaign in American history. [cite:cambridge_solidarity] Behind it lay the wartime appeals of 1939–45, more than $124 million, and before those the worldwide giving of the 1920s. [cite:raphael_uja] The panel also lists the transfer of German Jewish capital in the 1930s, whose terms and sums are told in their own place earlier in this volume.

The story begins with a permanent fund. Keren Hayesod, created as the Zionist movement's standing fundraising arm, raised $20.1 million worldwide between April 1921 and December 1929, roughly $370 million in today's money. More than half of it, $11.0 million, came from the United States. The rest came in descending order from South Africa ($1.5 million), Germany ($0.98 million), Romania ($0.88 million), Britain ($0.88 million), Poland ($0.82 million) and Canada ($0.74 million). [cite:jta_kh_decade] Measured over the fund's first twelve years in sterling, the United States gave about half of the £4.82 million raised. [cite:jta_kh_12yr] Before 1948 the fund's mandate covered immigration, settlement, defense, water development and public works. [cite:jvl_kh] Defense appears on that list from the start; it was not a later addition.

The country breakdown shows how early the balance had shifted. In the 1920s the American share was already larger than every other country's combined. The gap only widened. In the late 1930s American Jewish organizations set up their own joint campaign, the United Jewish Appeal, formed in 1939. It raised more than $124 million during the war years of 1939–45 and $100 million in 1946. [cite:raphael_uja] In 1947 it raised about $110 million. [cite:cambridge_solidarity] In 1948 it reached the record $150 million. [cite:jta_uja_1948] Over those last three years alone, 1946 to 1948, the campaigns raised some $360 million, about $5.2 billion in today's dollars. A single American year in 1948 brought in more than seven times what the entire world had given Keren Hayesod in its first decade.

The scale makes one distinction essential, and it is the one most often lost. The United Jewish Appeal did not raise money for Palestine alone. It split its proceeds three ways. Of the $150 million raised in 1948, $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, the Palestine and Israel arm; $64.9 million went to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe; and $10.4 million went to the United Service for New Americans, which resettled refugees in the United States. [cite:jta_uja_1948] Roughly half of the dollar went to Palestine, some 43 percent to Europe and about 7 percent to resettlement at home.

Much of the 1948 total, in other words, fed and housed Holocaust survivors in Europe. Counting all of it as "funding Israel" would roughly double the true Palestine figure. The Palestine share alone, $74.7 million, comes to about $1.0 billion in today's dollars. [cite:bls_cpi] That share paid for what Keren Hayesod's own history lists as its prewar purposes: immigration and absorption, settlement, defense, water and public works. [cite:jvl_kh]

The chain of giving can be followed from donor to purpose. Contributors gave through local federations; the federations passed their campaign totals to the national appeal; the appeal divided them among its three beneficiary agencies; and each agency spent on its own mandate.

War money is harder to count. Arms for the 1948 war were bought through front companies, and the record yields ranges rather than a total. Estimates of what was paid for Czechoslovak arms run from about $14.5 million to roughly six times that figure. Golda Meyerson's American fundraising tour in early 1948 raised about $50 million, which went largely to weapons. The government of Somoza's Nicaragua extended $3 million in letters of credit for arms buying. [cite:israelaffairs_italy]

The arms table shows why no single number can be given. Its Czechoslovak line spans a six-fold range, and Golda Meyerson's money flowed in part through the same community federations as the United Jewish Appeal, so that adding her $50 million to the appeal's $150 million would count some dollars twice. For that reason the ledger keeps every stream separate and never adds them into one sum.

Every "today's dollars" figure in this section follows one method, the method of the United States government's own inflation calculator: the amount is multiplied by the ratio of the consumer price index for 2025, which stands at 321.943, to the index for the year in question. Sums in pounds are first converted to dollars at the exchange rate of the period, and values from before 1913 are approximate. [cite:bls_cpi] The conversions are a guide to scale, not a claim that a 1948 dollar bought exactly what its modern equivalent buys.

The answer to the question this section asks is therefore plain in outline and incomplete in detail. The money came overwhelmingly from organized private giving: decades of worldwide contributions through a permanent fund, then American federated campaigns on a scale without precedent, joined in 1948 by arms purchases financed partly by the same donors and, in one documented case, by a foreign government's credit. What the record does not provide is a grand total. No audited sum for the whole pre-state operation has been published, the arms figures are ranges, and several streams overlap. The honest ledger is a set of documented streams side by side, not a single figure, and that is how it is given here. What the money for the army looked like inside these budgets, and what Britain spent on the other side of the ledger, is the subject of [scene:gf_s02|the operating budgets and Britain's bill].

sections.h: Charity for an Army: The Operating Budgets and Britain's Bill
sections.html:
Two assumptions often sit beneath accounts of the Mandate's last decades. The first is that the Jewish community's underground army was paid for secretly, by means no one can now trace. The second is that Britain held Palestine cheaply. Neither survives the documents. The defense money moved through budgets, a community levy and, by 1948, an openly advertised charity channel, all of which left a paper trail. Britain's own accounts, meanwhile, record a bill that by the end ran to about £100 million in three years. What the record does not contain is a single audited total for the army itself, and that gap is stated at the end of this section.

The clearest early view of the operating budget comes from an American diplomat. After the Zionist Congress of 1939, the United States consul in Jerusalem reported that the Jewish Agency's budget had been set at £720,000, about $74 million in today's money. Of that, £100,000 was earmarked for refugee settlement and £80,000 for what the budget itself called "the Jewish security service (defense)." [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget] The line is small, about one-ninth of the whole, but it is explicit: defense sat inside the Agency's published budget, under its own heading, nine years before the state.

The budgets grew quickly during and after the Second World War, and American money carried most of the growth. In 1944 the Jewish National Fund spent $10.8 million and the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod together $14.9 million of money raised in the United States, some $25.7 million in all. The United Palestine Appeal's budget for 1945 was $35.3 million. [cite:djn_1945_upa] In 1946 the Agency reported that it had received $12 million from the United States the previous year and asked for a budget of $56 million, about $0.93 billion in today's dollars. [cite:djn_1946_budget] In seven years the ask had moved from hundreds of thousands of pounds to tens of millions of dollars.

The table above sets these budgets beside Britain's spending, each in the money of its year and in today's dollars. It also shows the private capital that immigrants themselves brought into the country, which was mostly not donated money and belongs to a different account from the campaigns; the rows are placed side by side for scale and are not meant to be added together.

Inside Palestine, the community taxed itself for defense. In 1938 the Jewish National Council created Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund central security and expand the Haganah. [cite:w_kofer] It was run by the community's own council, not by the Mandate government, and it gave the Haganah a revenue stream raised inside the country alongside the money that came from abroad.

By 1948 the line between charity abroad and defense at home had all but disappeared. In June 1948 a community campaign in Detroit ran an advertisement telling donors that "the United Jewish Appeal is the official American agency for aid to Haganah," and that the only channel for aid to the Haganah was the local Allied Jewish Campaign. The advertisement warned that collecting money for the dissident militias was fraud. [cite:djn_1948_haganah] The same campaign that fed survivors in Europe and resettled refugees in America was, in its own words, the official channel for the Haganah. Charity and defense ran through the same pipe, and the advertisement said so in print.

The warning about dissident militias matters as well. It shows the mainstream campaign separating the Haganah from the armed groups outside it in what it told American donors, and naming one channel as the only legitimate one.

The flow above follows the defense money from the £80,000 budget line of 1939 through the 1938 levy to the American arms network of 1945–48, Golda Meyerson's tour of 1948, which raised about $50 million largely for weapons, and the advertisement naming the United Jewish Appeal as the channel for Haganah aid. [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget] [cite:w_kofer] [cite:israelaffairs_italy] [cite:djn_1948_haganah] Each step is documented separately. None of them was secret in the sense the familiar account implies; the levy was public, the budget line was reported to a foreign consul, and the charity channel was advertised.

The other side of the ledger is Britain's. The cost of governing Palestine rose steadily under the Mandate. Civil government spending grew from £P1.9 million in 1922–23 to £P3.2 million in 1934–35, a rise of about two-thirds in twelve years; the Palestine pound was then at par with sterling. [cite:horowitz_1937] The garrison was a separate charge, paid by Britain: £1.5 million in 1923–24. [cite:league_report_garrison] In today's dollars those figures are roughly $161 million and $388 million for the civil budget and $129 million for the garrison.

The bill rose sharply at the end. By the British government's own account in its statement on the termination of the Mandate, the military forces in Palestine cost the British taxpayer about £100 million in 1945–47, roughly $6.7 billion today. [cite:hmg_termination_1948] Parliament debated keeping 80,000 to 100,000 soldiers in the country, and some 100,000 troops were deployed. [cite:hansard_1947_08] The human cost was about 750 British military and police killed over the period. [cite:nam_palestine] Measured in today's dollars, Britain's three-year military bill was larger than any single year of American giving, and larger than the whole of the wartime appeals of 1939–45.

Put together, the two sides of this ledger correct both assumptions. The Jewish community's defense was financed through documented channels: a budget line, a community levy, an arms network funded by American donors and, at the end, a national charity that called itself the Haganah's official American agency. The figures are partial, but the mechanism is on paper. Britain, for its part, did not hold Palestine cheaply. Its civil and garrison costs grew through the interwar years, and its last three years cost it about £100 million and some 750 lives.

The gap is the army's own total. No audited figure for the Haganah's budget is publicly available, and the documents gathered here do not allow one to be reconstructed: they show individual streams, not the sum of them, and some of those streams overlap with the campaigns described in [scene:gf_s01|the ledger of who paid]. The Jewish National Fund's full annual income series is likewise not available as an audited total.

The note above records the same limit. The Agency budgets of 1939 and 1944–46, the Mandate's civil spending, Britain's military cost and the defense channels are all documented. The Haganah's own budget is not, and this book gives no figure for it.

sections.h: The Network of the American Build-Up, 1897–1948
sections.html:
A common picture of American support for Zionism before 1948 is of a loose and scattered sympathy: individuals of goodwill, a few friendly senators, some generous donors, acting each on their own. The documented record shows something more organized than that. Its pieces were connected, and the connections can be named: who founded which body, who chaired which committee, who sponsored which resolution, who raised which money and who carried which message to the President. Laid out by distance from the center, they form a network with a clear structure and two loops that fed themselves.

A word first on what such a map shows. Every tie below is a documented relationship of a specific kind: an organizational founding, a chairmanship, a sponsorship, an appointment, a transaction. None is inferred from shared identity, religion or background. A senator appears because he chaired a named committee or sponsored a named resolution; a donor appears because he raised a named sum. Where the record does not establish a tie, the map does not draw one.

At the apex stood the Jewish Agency and the World Zionist Organization, led in these years by Weizmann and Ben-Gurion. They set the movement's program and goals. [cite:aja_azec_local_1945] One later document defines the financial side of the relationship more sharply than anything from the 1940s. In November 1962 the Justice Department ordered the American Zionist Council to register as a foreign agent, alleging that it had received more than $5 million from the Jewish Agency over the preceding eight years. [cite:azc_fara_doj] The precision matters. The 1962 finding concerned the American Zionist Council, the body into which the wartime emergency council was renamed in 1949, and the years it covered; it was not a finding about the emergency council of the 1940s, and the record here does not document Agency funding of that earlier body. The later case is traced in [scene:s07g|the organization after statehood].

At the first degree, bound to the apex by direct organizational ties, stood three American bodies. The American Zionist Emergency Council, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, ran the national political campaign of the 1940s. The Zionist Organization of America was the mass-membership body; it had reached 147,000 members by 1918. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] Hadassah completed the first ring.

At the second degree were bodies created or coordinated by those first-degree organizations. The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine presented themselves as independent voices of American and Christian opinion. Both were organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has described them as "hardly autonomous." [cite:hnn_clark_truman] The United Jewish Appeal, under its executive Henry Montor, was the fundraising engine described in [scene:gf_s01|the ledger of who paid]. The Sonneborn Institute and its front company, Materials for Palestine, were set up at Ben-Gurion's 1945 meeting with American donors, to buy arms. Abraham Feinberg, who appears again at the third degree, was one of the original seventeen members of the Sonneborn Institute. [cite:emory_feinberg_thesis]

At the third degree were the political and financial endpoints, the people through whom the network reached decisions. In Congress, Senator Robert Wagner chaired the American Palestine Committee, and Senator Robert Taft co-sponsored the 1944 Palestine resolution. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III gave their names to the 1922 resolution endorsing the Balfour Declaration. Sol Bloom, chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, was a target of the telegram campaigns. [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation] In the White House, the aides David Niles, Clark Clifford and Max Lowenthal, and Truman's friend Eddie Jacobson, carried the Zionist case to the President. [cite:wiki_david_niles] Among donors, Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann raised the $100,000 that Truman's 1948 campaign needed, and Golda Meyerson's tour of 1948 raised about $50 million through Montor's network, largely for arms. [cite:mondoweiss_judis_truman] [cite:israelaffairs_italy]

The diagram simplifies in one respect. The White House channel, Niles, Clifford, Lowenthal and Jacobson, sat at the third degree but did not hang beneath any one second-degree body; it connected to the legislators on one side and, through the 1948 campaign money, to the donors on the other. It is left out of the tree for legibility and shown in the network drawn with this section.

Two parts of the structure were circular, and these loops are the most telling finding in the map. The first was a commitment loop. The emergency council collected statements of support from legislators; printed them in its book America and Palestine; mailed the book to every member of Congress; used it to press for votes and platform planks; and so gathered new statements, which went into the next round. Each public commitment became leverage for the next one.

The second was the Montor loop, and it ran through one fundraiser. Henry Montor gathered the donors for the 1945 Sonneborn meeting; that meeting produced the arms network; Montor then secured Golda Meyerson's platform before American audiences in 1948; and her tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms, which returned the money to the purpose the 1945 meeting had set. [cite:israelaffairs_italy] One man's network ran from the founding of the arms channel to its largest single injection of money. Feinberg's place inside it continued after 1948: the FBI file released decades later documents his ongoing meetings with Sonneborn, and in 1952 he was ordered to register as a foreign agent over a publication he ran, a story told in [scene:s07f2|the section on Abraham Feinberg]. [cite:feinberg_fbi_file]

The headline figures above give the scale of what this network sat on top of. Two of them belong to it directly: the Zionist Organization of America's 147,000 members by 1918, the mass base of the first degree, and the roughly $50 million of Golda Meyerson's 1948 tour, the largest single return of the Montor loop. [cite:aja_azec_local_1944] [cite:israelaffairs_italy] The land and population figures in the same panel, the share of land in Jewish ownership in 1947 and the share the 1947 partition plan allotted, are taken up in the chapter's closing account of the founding narratives.

The money panel sets four documented sums side by side: Golda Meyerson's tour at about $50 million, the transfer of German Jewish capital in the 1930s, about $14.5 million for Czechoslovak arms in 1948, and the $5 million raised by the American delegation of 1921–22 that met President Harding. [cite:israelaffairs_italy] They are separate events in different years and currencies, shown together for scale. Two of them, the tour and the Czechoslovak purchases, are the financial output of the second-degree arms and fundraising network in its final year.

What the map establishes is structure, not control in the conspiratorial sense. It shows a movement that built its own institutions, created allied committees that presented themselves as independent, organized the money and the arms channel through a small number of named people, and reached Congress and the White House through named legislators, aides and a friend of the President. Each tie is a public or documented relationship. Against it stood the State Department, the Joint Chiefs and the Defense Secretary, who opposed the policy in writing; the network's success was political, and it was contested inside the government it sought to move.

What the map does not establish is how much each tie weighed. It records that Niles and Clifford carried the case to Truman, not how far they changed his mind; that legislators made statements, not what moved each of them to make one; and that the Agency funded the American Zionist Council in the decade before 1962, not whether or how it funded the wartime council before 1949. Those questions are left where the documents leave them.

sections.h: Seven Founding Narratives, Checked Against the Record
sections.html:
By the early 1950s the founding of Israel had acquired a story, and much of that story was taught in American schools and repeated in the press as settled history. Volume II has followed the record stage by stage. This section gathers seven founding narratives that many people learned as fact and sets each beside what the documents show. Six of them belong to the familiar founding account. The seventh comes from the opposite direction: the claim that the Rothschilds, or a few Jewish bankers, paid for it all. It is included on purpose. A standard of evidence that corrects only one side's stories is not a standard, and the same documents that complicate the founding slogans also dispose of the conspiracy myth about who paid.

The narratives do not fail in the same way. Some are contradicted outright. Others contain something true and become misleading only in the telling. In each case below, the strongest version of the familiar claim is given first, then the documented figure that tests it.

"A land without a people for a people without a land." The slogan described a country waiting, empty, for settlers. Britain's own census, taken in 1922, two years into the Mandate, counted 757,182 people, about 11 percent of them Jewish. The slogan did not describe the country it named. The figures that followed show how quickly the balance then changed: Britain recorded 376,415 Jewish immigrants between 1920 and 1946, and the UN Special Committee on Palestine put the population at about 1.85 million in late 1946, by which time the Jewish share was about a third. The country was neither empty in 1922 nor static afterwards. Its population was counted, and the count was British.

"They left because Arab leaders told them to." This was the standard Western and Israeli official explanation of the refugee exodus through the 1950s, and it placed responsibility on the Arab states. Its strongest form rests on something real: some local Arab commanders did order evacuations of women and children in particular places. But in 1959 the Palestinian historian Walid Khalidi argued from Arab sources that no general order had been given, and in May 1961 the Irish writer Erskine Childers reported in The Spectator that he had examined the British and American monitoring records of Arab broadcasts in 1948 and found no evacuation orders, but rather appeals to stay [cite:w_childers]. In 1988 the Israeli historian Benny Morris, working from Israeli military and state archives, concluded that the main causes of flight were military attack, expulsion and fear, with local evacuation orders in some places and no general Arab order [cite:w_morris_birth]. The account is no longer defended by mainstream scholarship; how it was built and then dismantled is told in [scene:np_s01|how the flight was explained]. What remains disputed is not whether there was a general order but how far the expulsions were intended and planned.

"A miracle against impossible odds." The war of 1948 was fought and won; that part of the story stands. The picture of a few against many does not. A contemporary CIA assessment from 1948, and research since, describe a war in two phases that Israel ended with roughly a two-to-one advantage in manpower. The victory was real. The odds at the end of the war were not those of the familiar image.

"Israel was born of the Holocaust." The genocide in Europe transformed the urgency of the Zionist case, the politics around it and the moral argument for a state, and in 1945–48 the plight of some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe was the central argument made to the American public. But as a statement about origins the claim inverts the sequence. The program, the British pledge and the Mandate all predate Hitler, by between 11 and 37 years; the record dates them to 1896, 1917, 1920 and 1922. The Holocaust accelerated support. It did not create the program, and the institutions that carried it, as the next section shows step by step, were already built.

"Israel accepted partition; the Arabs rejected it and started the war." The first half holds. The vote on partition split as the familiar account says, with acceptance on one side and rejection on the other. The second half compresses two different escalations into one. The fighting began as a two-sided civil war inside Palestine months before the Arab armies entered in May 1948. The claim that the war simply began with the Arab invasion leaves out the months of fighting that came before it.

"The land was bought fair and square." This claim is true in its narrow legal sense and misleading as a description of how the land came to be held. Purchases were made legally, from absentee owners. But in 1947 only about 7 percent of Mandate Palestine's land was in Jewish ownership, roughly 2 million of some 26 million dunams, while the UN plan of that year allotted 56 percent of the territory to the Jewish state. Purchases from absentee landlords under Ottoman land law displaced the tenant farmers who worked the land, and those evictions are documented. After 1948 the larger transfer was not by purchase at all. The Absentees' Property Law of 14 March 1950, building on regulations of 1948, vested the property of those who had left in a state Custodian [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003], and the chain by which that property passed to the Development Authority and the Jewish National Fund is set out in [scene:ap_s01|the absentee property law]. Inside the 1949 armistice lines, which Israel's Foreign Ministry describes as enclosing about 78 percent of the Mandate area, the land that had been bought was a small part of the land that was held [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map].

The opposite myth: "the Rothschilds paid for it all." This story borrows from real names in the record. Edmond de Rothschild in Paris did fund early colonies, and the Balfour Declaration of 1917 was addressed to Lord Rothschild. But the Paris Rothschild who funded colonies opposed Herzl, and the documented money came overwhelmingly from mass giving. Keren Hayesod raised $20.1 million worldwide between April 1921 and December 1929, $11.0 million of it from the United States [cite:jta_kh_decade]. In 1948 alone the United Jewish Appeal raised a record $150 million from more than a million contributors in 4,950 American communities [cite:jta_uja_1948]. Even that figure cannot simply be counted as "funding Israel": $74.7 million went to the United Palestine Appeal, $64.9 million to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe, and $10.4 million to resettling refugees in the United States [cite:jta_uja_1948]. A founding paid for by a few financiers is not in the ledger. A founding paid for by very large numbers of ordinary donors, much of whose money fed survivors in Europe, is. The full accounting is in [scene:gf_s01|who paid for it all].

Set side by side, the seven checks look like this.

Two things follow from the table. The first is that "contradicted" and "complicated" are different findings, and the difference matters. A reader who learns that the land was not bought fair and square may conclude that no land was bought; it was, legally, in a small fraction of the country. A reader who learns that the war was not a miracle may conclude it was never in doubt; the record does not say that either. The second is that the corrections run in every direction. The census that undoes the empty-land slogan, the archives that undo the orders-to-flee story and the campaign ledgers that undo the Rothschild myth are the same kind of evidence, read the same way. That is the only ground on which any of them can be trusted.

The record also leaves some questions open. Historians still disagree about intent and planning in the expulsions of 1948, and nothing here settles them. No audited grand total of the money raised before 1948 exists, so the scale of mass giving can be shown but not summed to a single figure. And the 2-to-1 manpower ratio describes the end of the war, not every front at every moment in it. What the record does settle is narrower and firmer: none of the seven narratives, in its familiar form, survives the documents intact.

sections.h: Fifty-One Years From a Bank to a State: The Whole Sequence, Step by Step
sections.html:
A familiar account treats Israel's creation as a sudden event: a response to the Holocaust, ratified by a postwar decision at the United Nations and completed in a single war. Each part of that account touches something real. The genocide in Europe did change the politics of the question; the General Assembly did vote in November 1947; the war of 1948 did decide where the lines would run. What the account leaves out is everything that had to exist before any of those moments could produce a state. Laid end to end, the documents of Volume II show a sequence built over five decades and across two continents, each step resting on the one before. The movement did not start cold and turn hot in 1947. This section closes the volume by setting that sequence out in order, and then by showing what the years from 1948 to 1953 added on top of it.

1897–1920: a bank, a land fund, a machine, a promise. In 1897 the Basel Congress set the goal. Two years later, in 1899, the movement founded the Jewish Colonial Trust, a bank chartered in London and capitalized by small shareholders. In 1901 the Jewish National Fund began buying land on a principle that defined it for the next half-century: land it bought was held permanently and never resold. In 1902 came the Anglo-Palestine Bank. These were the movement's first financial and land-holding instruments, and every later step drew on them. Between 1912 and 1918 an American organization took shape around them: Hadassah; Justice Brandeis with access to President Wilson; and the Zionist Organization of America, which reached 147,000 members by 1918 [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]. In 1917 Britain issued the Balfour Declaration, addressed to Lord Rothschild. In 1920 the movement created Keren Hayesod, its permanent fund, whose mandate before 1948 covered immigration, settlement, defense, water and public works [cite:jvl_kh].

1921–1933: tours, Congress, a currency and a wider money base. In 1921 Weizmann and Einstein toured the United States, and a $5 million delegation tour of 1921–22 met President Harding. Keren Hayesod's worldwide receipts from April 1921 to December 1929 came to $20.1 million, of which $11.0 million came from the United States, followed by South Africa, Germany, Romania, Britain, Poland and Canada [cite:jta_kh_decade]. In 1922 Congress endorsed the Balfour Declaration through the resolution sponsored by Senator Henry Cabot Lodge and Representative Hamilton Fish III [cite:aja_azec_silver_resignation]. In 1927 came a Palestine pound managed from London. In 1929 non-Zionist American money joined an enlarged Jewish Agency, widening the base beyond the movement's own members. Christian committees were organized from the Zionist political office in 1932, when the American Palestine Committee was formed, and again in 1941–42. The American Palestine Committee and the Christian Council on Palestine were both organized by the Zionist executive Emanuel Neumann, and one historian has described them as "hardly autonomous" [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. In 1933 came the Haavara transfer agreement, valued at 105 million Reichsmarks, about $40 million at the time, over 1933–39.

1938–1948: a levy, a budget, a demand, a lobby, an arms network. In 1938 the Jewish National Council in Palestine created Kofer HaYishuv, a levy on cigarettes, restaurant bills and luxuries, to fund the Haganah [cite:w_kofer]. In 1939 the Jewish Agency's budget was set at £720,000, of which £80,000 was for "the Jewish security service (defense)," as the American consulate reported [cite:frus_1939_ja_budget]. In 1942 the Biltmore program committed the movement to a Jewish commonwealth. In 1943 the American Zionist Emergency Council, co-chaired by Abba Hillel Silver and Stephen Wise, built a national lobbying machine of local committees, letter and telegram campaigns and a published record of legislators' statements [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]. In 1944 both American party platforms adopted the movement's aims, and US-raised spending that year reached $10.8 million through the Jewish National Fund and $14.9 million through the Jewish Agency and Keren Hayesod [cite:djn_1945_upa]. In 1945 a secret meeting convened by Ben-Gurion, with donors gathered by the United Jewish Appeal's Henry Montor, set up the Sonneborn Institute and its front company, Materials for Palestine, which linked American fundraising to arms [cite:hnn_clark_truman]. In 1946 the Agency sought a $56 million budget [cite:djn_1946_budget]. In 1948 the United Jewish Appeal raised a record $150 million from more than a million contributors [cite:jta_uja_1948]; a June 1948 campaign advertisement called it "the official American agency for aid to Haganah" [cite:djn_1948_haganah]; Golda Meyerson's American tour raised about $50 million, largely for arms; arms were bought in Czechoslovakia; and banknotes for the new state were printed in New York. In the same year Abraham Feinberg and Ed Kaufmann raised the $100,000 that, in one historian's account, weighed on a single presidential decision.

Beneath all of this lay older foundations: the Ottoman and British layers of administration, a Christian restorationist lobby dating from 1839, and the Rothschild colonies in Palestine dating from 1882. The documented ties that bound the American part of the sequence together, organization to organization and person to person, are mapped in [scene:nw_s02|the network of the American build-up].

Two maps draw the same sequence from different angles. The first follows the institutions and the votes, from the Basel Congress through the bank and the land fund, the Balfour Declaration and the Mandate, the Jewish Agency and the American political machine, to the UN Special Committee, Resolution 181 and the state. The second follows the money, from the blue-box coins of small donors through the Colonial Trust, the land fund and Keren Hayesod to the Haavara transfer, the Sonneborn network, Golda's tour and the Czech arms.

What the Holocaust changed, and what it did not. The strongest form of the familiar account deserves to be stated plainly, because part of it is right. The Holocaust changed the urgency of the question, the politics around it and the moral case for a state. In 1945–48 the argument made to Americans rested first on refuge for some 250,000 Jewish displaced persons in Europe. The money changed in scale: the United Jewish Appeal, formed in 1939, raised more than $124 million across all of 1939–45, then $100 million in 1946 alone [cite:raphael_uja], about $110 million in 1947 [cite:cambridge_solidarity] and $150 million in 1948. Much of that money was for the survivors themselves: $64.9 million of the 1948 campaign went to the Joint Distribution Committee for relief in Europe [cite:jta_uja_1948]. What the record does not support is the step from "the Holocaust changed everything" to "the Holocaust created the state." The bank, the land fund, the recognized agency, the American fundraising and lobbying machinery, the congressional endorsement and the defense levy all existed before 1939. The arms channels were assembled in 1945 by people and networks that were already in place. The catastrophe gave the apparatus its urgency; it did not build the apparatus.

Nor does the record support the opposite overstatement, that the sequence was a single plan executed on schedule. Each step was contingent, and each met opposition. Edmond de Rothschild, who funded the early colonies, opposed Herzl. In Washington the State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed the policy in writing, the CIA warned that American backing would harm American interests, and all were overruled. Britain spent about £100 million on its forces in Palestine in 1945–47 alone, with some 100,000 troops deployed, before giving up the Mandate [cite:hmg_termination_1948][cite:hansard_1947_08]. What the documents show is accumulation, not inevitability: institutions built early, and kept running, so that when the political moment came the instruments to use it already existed.

What 1948–1953 added. The state that was declared on 14 May 1948 inherited this apparatus and, within five years, built a second layer on top of it. This chapter has told each part in its place; seen together, they complete the architecture.

The first addition was territorial. The four armistice agreements of 1949 fixed the lines the war had produced. They were not borders by their own terms: Article V of the Egyptian agreement says the demarcation line "is not to be construed in any sense as a political or territorial boundary" [cite:rs_rd6_arm_egypt_text]. But they enclosed what Israel's Foreign Ministry describes as about 78 percent of the Mandate area [cite:rs_rd6_mfa_armistice_map], against the 56 percent the 1947 plan had allotted. How those lines were drawn and supervised is told in [scene:rd6_armistices|the armistice agreements].

The second addition was legal title to land, and here the pre-state instrument and the new state's law met directly. A Custodian of Abandoned Property was appointed on 15 July 1948; emergency regulations in December 1948 transferred control to a Custodian of Absentee Property; and on 14 March 1950 the Knesset passed the Absentees' Property Law [cite:rs_rd6_fischbach_2003][cite:un_absentees_property_law_text]. A Development Authority established in 1950 became, in the words of a 2016 study, both a major land allocator and the body that set "the rules of the game" [cite:rs_rd6_jih_devauthority]. According to an analysis published by BADIL, the 1950 law let the Custodian pass absentee land to the Development Authority and on to the Jewish National Fund; nearly 2.4 million dunams were transferred, "more than trebling the JNF's holdings as of 1941," and by 1951 the government and the Fund together held 92 percent of the land within the state [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime]. Those are BADIL's figures, and the scholarly sources in this chapter do not give a settled total of their own. The Land Acquisition Law of 1953 then retroactively validated seizures made during and after the war [cite:rs_rd6_badil_landregime]. The land fund founded in 1901 to buy land and never sell it had held about 936,000 dunams by 1947. After 1948 it also became a receiver, by sale and transfer from the state, of land that its owners had never sold.

The third addition defined who belonged. Section 1 of the Law of Return, dated 5 July 1950, states that "Every Jew has the right to come to this country as an oleh" [cite:rs_rd6_mjl_lawofreturn]. Presenting it, Ben-Gurion said the right "preceded the State of Israel," and the Encyclopaedia Judaica links the law to the Basel Program of 1897, Article 6 of the Mandate of 1922 and the Declaration of Independence [cite:rs_rd6_ej_lawofreturn]. The reference work itself draws the line from the state's immigration statute back to the first step of the sequence above. The Nationality Law, in force from 14 July 1952, made every immigrant under the Law of Return a national "by return," while former Palestinian citizens could become nationals "by residence" only if they met a registration test tied to 1 March 1952 [cite:rs_rd6_refworld_nationality]. In the same years, Arab citizens lived under a military government established in October 1948 and administered through the British Defence (Emergency) Regulations of 1945 [cite:rs_rd6_korn_adalah].

The fourth addition was money, and its sources shifted. Private American giving remained, but now beside it came a state's own instruments. The United States government gave $100.0 million in 1949, through the Export-Import Bank and other channels, then nothing in 1950, $35.1 million in 1951 and $86.4 million in 1952, all of it economic [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_usaid_table]. Israel Bonds, launched in the United States in 1951, sold more than $52 million in their first year and within six years were financing 35 percent of the state's special development budget [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_bonds]. And the reparations agreement with West Germany, signed in Luxembourg on 10 September 1952, paid in oil and German goods that made up 12 to 14 percent of Israel's annual imports over the following decade [cite:rs_rd6_nli_reparations][cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]. Here the Holocaust entered the architecture directly: Sharett's claim of $1.5 billion was calculated as the cost of absorbing 500,000 Nazi victims at $3,000 each [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]. The agreement's total value is given differently in two sources, and the Knesset vote to negotiate, 61 to 50 on 9 January 1952 with protesters outside, shows how divided the new state's own public was [cite:rs_rd6_jvl_reparations]. These are told in full in [scene:rd6_financing|how the new state was paid for]. On the American side, the lobbying council of 1943 was renamed the American Zionist Council in 1949 [cite:azec_powerbase], and in 1953–54 Isaiah Kenen founded a separate American Zionist Committee for Public Affairs, renamed AIPAC in 1959 by one account, while another dates AIPAC's emergence to a restructuring in 1963 [cite:cjh_kenen_papers][cite:aipac_wiki].

The architecture as it stood in 1953 can be drawn in one figure. Its center was a sovereign state with a parliament and a government. Around it were the four instruments the state had built in its first five years, and beyond it the three outside channels that paid for it. Two of the four inside instruments, the land regime and the Law of Return, connected directly back to institutions or principles laid down before 1948, and the diaspora channel ran partly through an organization that had existed since 1943.

The finding of this volume, stated at its documented size, is this. Israel was not improvised in two years. The bank, the land fund, the recognized agency, the American fundraising and lobbying machinery, the congressional endorsement and the arms channels were assembled over five decades, and the state's first laws on land and immigration were built on them. The Holocaust changed the urgency, the politics and the moral case; it did not create the apparatus. None of the steps listed here is an inference. Each is sourced where it is told. What a synthesis adds is the order, and the order is the argument.

Some things the order cannot show. It does not show that any single person or body designed the whole, and the documents point the other way: different founders, different decades, different organizations. It does not give an audited total of the money raised before 1948, because none exists, and the Haganah's full budget is not documented. It cannot establish whether money reached individual members of Congress before 1948, because the disclosure records that would show it in either direction were never required. And it does not settle what the armistice lines would become; in 1953 they were, by their own text, still not borders. One interpretive way of reading the sequence as a whole follows in the next section, labeled as what it is.

sections.h: The Mechanism, in Plain Terms: A State Set Running Before It Was Declared
sections.html:
What follows is a reading, not a finding. It offers a way of picturing the sequence set out in the previous section, borrowed from computer programming. It adds no fact to that sequence, and where the comparison and the record part ways, the record governs.

The familiar statement is that Israel was created in 1948. As a statement about the declaration of 14 May 1948, it is accurate. As a statement about when the state's working parts came into being, it misleads, and the comparison is one way of seeing why 1948 can look like a beginning when the documents show it as the end of a long build.

The comparison comes from Objective-C, a programming language in which a program can contain a routine named +load. The language's runtime calls that routine on its own, at the moment a piece of the program is loaded into memory, before the program's main sequence, the part a user sees, ever begins. No one has to invoke it. In the illustrative version, four setup steps run inside that early routine, in order: capitalize a bank, buy land and hold it permanently, have an agency legally recognized, and build a lobby. By the time the main sequence starts, all four have finished. The main sequence then prints a single line, "State declared." It is the only line a casual reader of the program's output ever sees.

The same point can be made in a street version, with no code vocabulary at all. Picture a restaurant on the night of its grand opening. The opening is real, and for most people it is the first moment the place exists. But the kitchen was built in 1899. The land was bought in 1901. The permit was granted in 1922. The marketing team had been working the neighborhood since the 1940s. Everything that made the opening possible happened before the sign went up, and most of it happened out of public view.

Each part of the picture stands for a documented institution, every one of them in place before May 1948. The kitchen is the financial base: the Jewish Colonial Trust and the Anglo-Palestine Bank, founded between 1899 and 1902. The land is the permanent holdings of the Jewish National Fund, which began buying in 1901 and did not resell. The permit is Article 4 of the Mandate of 1922, which recognized a "Jewish agency" and so gave the movement's agency legal standing. The marketing team is the American political machine of the 1940s, the American Zionist Emergency Council, whose local committees and letter campaigns worked Congress district by district [cite:aja_azec_local_1944]. The declaration, in this reading, was the first line of the main program. It was not the first line of the program.

The reading has limits, and they matter as much as the picture. A program has a programmer who writes every line in advance; the build traced in this volume had no single author. Its institutions were founded by different people in different decades, in London, Palestine and the United States. A routine that runs automatically also meets no resistance, and this one met it at every step. Edmond de Rothschild, who funded the early colonies, opposed Herzl. In Washington the State Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff and the Secretary of Defense opposed American support in writing, the CIA warned against it, and all were overruled. Britain spent about £100 million on its forces in Palestine in 1945–47 before it gave up the Mandate [cite:hmg_termination_1948]. And the outcome on the ground, the lines that the state actually held, was decided not by anything loaded in advance but by the war of 1948 and the armistices that followed it.

The reading's own summary is a single line: the state was initialized long before it was declared. So the comparison is useful for one thing only: it explains why an observer who looked first in 1948 would see a sudden beginning, when the institutions that made the beginning possible had been running for close to fifty years. It does not show that the outcome was planned from the start, or that it was inevitable. The record shows accumulation and contingency together, and the comparison should be read as a picture of the first, never as proof against the second.
